## OF GOD.

Though God has given us no innate ideas <note>This refers to the philosophical concept that the mind is born as a blank slate and that knowledge of God must be reached through reason and experience rather than being hard-wired from birth.</note> of Himself, He has furnished us with the faculties our minds are endowed with. Therefore, He has not left Himself without a witness, since we have sense, perception, and reason. We cannot lack a clear proof of Him as long as we carry any thought of ourselves within us. To show, therefore, that we are capable of knowing—that is, being certain—that there is a God, and how we may arrive at this certainty, I think we need look no further than ourselves and the undoubted knowledge we have of our own existence. 

I think it is beyond question that man has a clear perception of his own being: he knows certainly that he exists, and that he is something. In the next place, man knows by an intuitive certainty that absolute nothingness can no more produce a real being than it can be equal to two right angles <note>A geometric analogy: just as it is mathematically impossible for "nothing" to equal 180 degrees, it is logically impossible for "nothing" to create "something."</note>. If, therefore, we know there is some real being, it is an evident proof <note>original: "demonstration"</note> that from eternity there has been something. This is because whatever was not from eternity had a beginning, and whatever had a beginning must be produced by something else. 

Next, it is evident that whatever has its being from another must also have everything that belongs to its being from that source as well. All the powers it possesses must be owed to, and received from, the same source. This eternal source of all being must also be the source and origin of all power; and so, this eternal being must also be the most powerful.

# AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES.

...existing from eternity. If it is said that there was a time when that eternal Being had no knowledge, I reply that it would then have been impossible for there ever to have been any knowledge at all. It is as impossible for things that are completely devoid of knowledge—operating blindly and without any perception—to produce a conscious <note>original: "knowing"</note> being, as it is impossible for a triangle to make its own three angles larger than two right angles. Thus, by considering ourselves and what we unmistakably find in our own makeup, our reason leads us to the knowledge of this certain and evident truth: that there is an eternal, most powerful, and intelligent Being. Whether anyone chooses to call this Being "God" does not matter. The fact is evident; and from this idea, when properly considered, we can easily deduce all those other attributes we ought to assign to this eternal Being.

From what has been said, it is plain that we have a more certain knowledge of the existence of a God than of anything that our senses have not immediately revealed to us. In fact, I presume I may say that we know more certainly that there is a God than that there is anything else outside of us <note>original: "without us," meaning external to our own minds</note>. When I say "we know," I mean that such knowledge is within our reach; we cannot miss it if we will only apply our minds to it as we do to other inquiries.

Since it is unavoidable for all rational creatures to conclude that something has existed from eternity, let us next see what kind of thing that must be. There are only two types of beings in the world that man knows or can imagine: those that are purely material, without sense or perception; and conscious, perceiving beings, such as we find ourselves to be. For our present purpose, we shall call these two types thinking <note>original: "cogitative"</note> and non-thinking <note>original: "incogitative"</note> beings; these terms are more useful here than "material" and "immaterial."

If, then, there must be something eternal, it is very obvious to reason that it must necessarily be a thinking being. This is because it is as impossible to conceive that bare, non-thinking matter should ever produce a thinking, intelligent being, as it is that "nothing" should produce matter on its own. Let us suppose any portion of matter to be eternal; we shall find it unable to produce anything by itself. Let us suppose its parts are firmly at rest together; if there were no other being in the world, must it not remain so forever—a dead, inactive lump? Is it possible to imagine that it can add motion to itself or produce anything? Matter, then, by its own strength, cannot produce even motion in itself. Any motion it has must also be from eternity, or else be added to matter by some other being more powerful than matter. But even if we suppose motion is eternal too, non-thinking matter and motion could never produce thought. Knowledge would still be just as impossible for "nothing" to produce. Divide matter into as many minute parts as you like, and vary its shape and motion as much as you please, but it will still only affect other bodies...

# A KEY TO MEDICINE, <note>original: "Physic"</note>

...of proportional size <note>original: "proportionable bulk"</note> than it did before this division. The smallest particles of matter collide with, repel, and resist one another just as larger ones do, and that is all they are capable of doing. Therefore, if we assume that nothing is eternal, then matter could never have begun to exist. If we assume that raw matter without motion is eternal, then motion could never have begun. If we assume only matter and motion are eternal, then thought could never have begun. It is impossible to imagine that matter—whether moving or still—could originally possess sense, perception, and knowledge within itself. This is evident because if it did, then sense, perception, and knowledge would have to be an eternal property inseparable from every single particle of matter.

Therefore, since whatever is the first eternal being must necessarily be a thinking being <note>original: "cogitative"</note>, and since the source of all things must contain within itself—and actually possess—at least all the perfections that can ever exist afterward, it necessarily follows that the first eternal being cannot be mere matter. If it is clear that something must necessarily have existed from eternity, it is equally clear that that something must be a conscious, thinking being. It is just as impossible for unthinking <note>original: "incogitative"</note> matter to produce a thinking being as it is for nothingness—the total absence of all being—to produce actual matter.

This discovery of the necessary existence of an eternal mind leads us directly to the knowledge of God. From this, it follows that all other conscious beings who have a beginning must depend on Him; they have no power or knowledge except what He gives them. Therefore, if He created those beings, He also created the less magnificent parts of this universe, including all inanimate bodies. Through this, His all-knowing nature <note>original: "omniscience"</note>, power, and divine guidance <note>original: "providence"</note> are established, and all His other attributes follow logically from that.

In this way, the presence of the Deity is visible in all His works. There is not the smallest part of the vast space our eyes see or our imaginations conceive that is not filled with His presence. The worlds that revolve with such order, beauty, and harmony through the immensity of space—the sun, moon, stars, and planets—are upheld by His favor <note>original: "the light of his countenance"</note>. Without it, they would fall from their orbits and, plunged into a vast abyss, would return to their original state of chaos.

We owe all the blessings of this life to the mercy of God as a reward for good and virtuous actions. To His anger, we rightly attribute all violent natural disasters <note>original: "concussions of the elements"</note>, famine, plague, and pestilence, and so on, brought upon a wicked and abandoned people—much like the storm of fire and brimstone sent upon Sodom and Gomorrah. The vengeance of God cannot be more powerfully described than by King David in his Psalms; these should serve as a timely warning to atheists, unbelievers, and to those wicked, idolatrous, and corrupt countries whose detestable crimes have so often brought about these terrible punishments <note>original: "scourges"</note>. To what has been stated above, I would earnestly recommend a careful reading <note>original: "attentive Perusal"</note> of what I have written in the first volume of my *Complete Illustration of the Occult Sciences*, from page 71 to 80. # CONCERNING NATURE.

No word used by authors or spoken by people is more inconsistently applied or less understood than the word "Nature." When we speak of the "nature" of a thing, we usually mean its essence—that is, the qualities or causes that make it what it is, whether that thing is physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> or not (for example, when we try to define the nature of a fluid or a triangle). We also often confuse what a person has by "nature" with what they inherit by birth, such as when we say a person is "noble by nature." Sometimes we use "nature" to mean an internal principle of movement, such as saying a stone falls to the ground by nature. At other times, we understand "nature" to be the established order and course of things. Occasionally, we use it to describe the sum of powers belonging to a single body, especially a living one; in this sense, doctors <note>original: "physicians"</note> say that nature is "strong," "weak," or "exhausted," or that in certain diseases, "nature," if left to itself, will provide the cure. Finally, we sometimes use the term "nature" to mean the entire universe, or the whole system of God’s physical works, as when it is said of a

# A KEY TO MEDICINE <note>original: PHYSIC</note>

...phoenix, or any imaginary being, saying that there is no such thing in nature. Sometimes, too, and not infrequently, we use the word "nature" to describe a kind of semi-deity or supernatural spirit presiding over all things.

This general misuse of the word "nature" is by no means unique to the English people or language; it prevails more or less in all countries and among all sects, and seems to have been copied from the legendary ideas of the ancients. Aristotle wrote an entire chapter specifically to list the various meanings of the Greek word *physis* <note>original: $\varphi\acute{\upsilon}\sigma\iota\varsigma$</note>, which is translated into English as *nature*. Among Latin writers, there are no fewer than fifteen or sixteen different meanings of the same word, with countless advocates for each interpretation. Most of them insist that the word "nature" fundamentally means the system of the world, the machine of the universe, or the collection of all created beings. In this sense, they speak of the "Author of nature" and call the sun the *eye of nature* because it illuminates the universe, and the *father of nature* because it warms the earth and makes it fruitful. Others, understanding the word in a more restricted sense, apply it to each of the various types of beings, both created and uncreated, spiritual and physical. Thus, they say *divine nature*, *angelic nature*, and *human nature*, meaning all people collectively who possess the same spiritual, rational soul. In this sense, the scholars and theologians use the terms *nature naturing* <note>original: *natura naturans*</note> and *nature natured* <note>original: *natura naturata*</note>. They speak of God as "nature naturing" because He gives being and "nature" to all others, as opposed to created beings, who are "nature natured" because they receive their nature from the hands of another.

Nature, in an even more limited sense, is used for the essence of a thing. For example, the *Cartesians* <note>Cartesians: followers of the philosopher René Descartes</note> say it is the *nature* of the soul to think, and that the nature of matter consists of extension <note>extension: the property of taking up physical space</note>. Others more accurately use the word "nature" for the established order and course of material things, the series of secondary causes, or the laws that God has imposed on every part of creation. In this sense, people say, "*nature makes the night follow the day*" or "*nature has made breathing necessary for life*," and so on. In line with this, St. Thomas Aquinas speaks of nature as a kind of divine art shared with created beings, which directs and carries them toward the purposes for which they were intended. In this sense, nature is nothing more or less than a chain of causes and effects, or the order and management <note>original: œconomy</note> that God has established in all parts of His creation. Still others consider nature more strictly as the action of Providence and the fundamental principle of all things. They see it as that spiritual power or being which is spread throughout creation, moving and acting in all bodies, giving them unique properties and producing unique effects. In this sense, our modern philosopher Mr. Boyle <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691), a famous scientist and pioneer of modern chemistry</note> considers nature to be nothing other than God, acting...

This corresponds closely with the opinion of a sect of ancient philosophers who made Nature the god of the universe, *The All* <note>original Greek: To Παν</note>, whom they believed presided over and governed all things. However, they acknowledged this to be only an imaginary being, and that "nature" meant nothing more than the qualities or virtues that God implanted in His creatures, which their poets and orators had figuratively personified as a god. Consequently, Father Malebranche <note>Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715), a French Oratorian priest and rationalist philosopher.</note> was provoked to say,

> "that the 'nature' so often discussed in the academic schools is only fit to lead us back to pagan idolatry; since it teaches us to understand something which, without being God, acts continually throughout the universe,"

according to which, he supposes nature would be adored as an idol—conceived to possess an actual principle which, in cooperation with God, was the next and immediate cause of all the changes that happen to matter.

Aristotle, with the goal of concentrating these ideas of nature into a single point best suited to the works of an infinitely perfect and all-powerful Being, defines nature as: *the principle and cause of motion and of that in which it is fundamentally in itself, and not by accident* <note>original Latin: "principium et causa motus et ejus in quo est primo per se, et non per accidens"</note>. This definition being misunderstood by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> and the Stoics, they concluded that the principle of nature was a certain spirit or virtue diffused throughout the universe. They believed this spirit gave everything its motion by the invariable order of an inevitable necessity, without any freedom or knowledge. This led to the idea of a **plastic nature** <note>In this context, "plastic" means "formative" or "shaping"—a force that molds matter into living forms.</note>, which several learned modern writers have described as a non-physical created substance. They argued it was endowed with a "vegetative life" (capable of growth) but not with sensation or thought. This substance was thought to penetrate the entire created universe, extending alongside it, and, under God’s direction, moving matter to produce phenomena that cannot be explained by the laws of mechanics. It was seen as active toward ends unknown to itself, not being conscious of its own actions, and yet having an obscure idea of the action it was about to perform.

In support of this **plastic nature**, Dr. Cudworth <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), a leading figure among the Cambridge Platonists.</note> argues as follows:

> "Since things are not produced by pure chance, nor by the unguided mechanism of matter, and since it is unreasonable to think that God Himself does everything immediately and miraculously, it may well be concluded that there is a *plastic* or *formative nature* under Him. As an inferior and subordinate instrument, it executes that part of His providence which consists in the regular motion of matter. Yet, beyond this, a higher providence must be acknowledged which, presiding over it, often supplies its defects and sometimes overrules it, because this plastic nature cannot act by choice or with its own discretion."

This doctrine, he believes, had the support <note>original: "suffrage"</note> of the best philosophers of all ages: Aristotle, Plato, Empedocles, Heraclitus, Hippocrates, Zeno, and the Stoics, as well as the later Platonists and Peripatetics, the chemists, the followers of Paracelsus <note>Paracelsians: doctors and alchemists following the theories of Paracelsus, who emphasized chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>, and several modern writers.

# A KEY TO PHYSIC,

...say that a cause is nothing more than that which gives existence to another thing, which is the effect of it, in whatever way it occurs, according to the various types of causes.

The *First Cause*, which acts by itself and by its own supreme power and will, is God. This is a truth so evident and so obvious that it cannot be denied. The existence of a First Cause may be deduced from the certainty of our own existence; for the fact that we exist in the world is a self-evident truth, but that we came into it on our own, or by accident <note>original: "casualty"</note>, necessity, or chance, is absolutely impossible. The source of our existence must therefore be derived from some being who, as the author, must also be the free principle of that essence or life we possess. To say that we ourselves were the cause of our own being would be ridiculous, because it would follow from that logic that we existed before we had an existence; that we gave ourselves that which we did not already possess; and that the cause and the effect were one and the same thing—which is also impossible. It is no less an error to claim that we are in the world by necessity; for if that were the case, our existence would never have had a beginning, and we would have been unchanging, independent, and infinite in every kind of perfection. But, as these qualities are only applicable to a first cause, it follows that such a cause must be Almighty.

Those who are convinced of the existence of a first cause must necessarily attribute to it all the perfections which are or can be in the world. It is not only most perfect and most noble, but also, all the effects which it has produced, or is capable of producing, are contained within itself in the utmost perfection; and every one of them is infinite in the unity of its being. It is necessary that it should possess the perfections of those beings it has produced or can produce; otherwise, it would be said to provide what it neither has nor can have. The first cause would not be absolutely perfect if it were not eternal; for then it would have had a beginning and might have an end, and then it could not have been the *first* cause, since it would have derived its existence from something that existed before it. Consequently, this cause, which we suppose to be the first, would actually be a second cause, limited in its being and perfections as well as in its duration; it would seem to depend upon another. However, when we suppose it to be the first, all others must depend upon and be subordinate to it. From this it follows that these qualities must be inseparable from it: independence, eternity, infinity, and supreme authority. We cannot conceive of any first cause without at the same time acknowledging the existence of God.

This *first cause*, which is God, must necessarily have that *perfect unity* which allows no multiplication of either nature or perfections. Certainly, if God were not one in His being but had several natures, the number of them would have to be infinite, and

The great number, or rather the infinity, of perfections which we understand to be in the first cause is not contradictory <note>original: "repugnant"</note> to the Trinity, because the Trinity does not divide God's being. These perfections are all one and the same thing, even though we give them different names and consider them through various concepts <note>original: "ideas"</note> that we are forced to refine. Without that unity, God would necessarily be a composition of parts. Those parts would be the materials of the whole compound and would have to exist before the compound itself; therefore, they could not be the ingredients of that composition without something else intervening. Such parts could also be divided and separated; so that, by the dissolution of the parts, the compound would cease to exist. This is plainly inconsistent with the concept we have of God, who is simple <note>In philosophy, "simple" means not made of parts.</note> in His nature, independent in His will, and in every way incorruptible. 

The first cause is not only unique and without equal in its essence, but also the sole actor, without any partner, in the action by which this world was produced. For this reason, the action is called **creation**, which assumes that all things were made out of mere nothing by the power of God alone, without the help of any other being acting as either an agent or a material <note>original: "subject"</note>. 

The world, having been produced by this first cause, remains subject to His will and pleasure. In the same way it was produced by the sole act of this first cause, it is also preserved in that same state by the sole influence of the same cause. Just as He did not require any help in the creation of the universe, He does not stand in need of any assistance in the preservation <note>original: "conservation"</note> of it. 

If the first cause was free in the creation of the world, it follows that all things were made by the direction of reason and understanding, and consequently according to a certain idea and rule. Since the first cause operates in an independent manner, it could not have found the blueprint <note>original: "type"</note> of its production anywhere else but within itself; nor could it act by a rule distinct from its own being. So, in truth, God is not only the first cause but also the *exemplary cause* <term>exemplary cause: the model or pattern after which something is made</term> of all things. For the same reason, it may be said that the first cause, which is God, is the *final cause* <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or goal for which something exists</term> of all things. This is because, when the perfection of one cannot be the perfection of another, every one would stand in need of the others—that is, each would lack the specific perfection that the other beings possess. Therefore, we may add that all these supposed beings would be opposite, independent, and all supreme, which is impossible; or that all would be subject to one or another of them, which is ridiculous. 

From this, it follows that there is only one God, who is unique in His existence, incapable of being multiplied, and who is the primary and universal cause of all things. The great number, or rather the infinity, of perfections that we understand to be in the First Cause is not inconsistent with the Trinity, because the Trinity does not divide the divine being. These perfections are actually one and the same thing, even though we give them different names and consider them through different concepts (which we are forced to refine). Without that unity, there would necessarily be a composition of parts, which would be the materials of the whole compound and would have to exist before the whole; therefore, they could not be the ingredients of that composition without something else intervening. 

They might also be divided and separated, so that by the dissolution of the parts, the compound would cease to exist. This is plainly inconsistent with the idea we have of God, who is simple in His nature <note>original: "simple"; in theology, "divine simplicity" means God is not made of parts or different substances, but is a single, unified essence.</note>, independent in His will, and in every way incorruptible. 

The First Cause is not only unique and without equal in its essence, but also the sole actor, without any partner, in the act by which this world was produced. For this reason, the action is called *creation*. This implies there was nothing but mere "nothingness," out of which all things were made by the power of God alone, without help from any other, acting as either an assistant or as raw material. 

The world, having been produced by this First Cause, remains subject to His will and pleasure. Just as it was produced by the sole act of this First Cause, it is preserved in that same state by the sole influence of the same cause. Just as He did not require any help in the creation of the universe, He does not stand in need of any assistance in its preservation. 

If the First Cause was free in the creation of the world, it follows that all things were made by the direction of reason and understanding, and consequently according to a specific plan and rule. Since the First Cause operates independently, it could not have taken the blueprint for its production from anywhere else but itself; nor could it act by a rule distinct from its own being. Therefore, in truth, God is not only the first, but also the exemplary cause <note>original: "exemplary cause"; the model, pattern, or archetype after which something is created.</note> of all things. 

For the same reason, it may be said that the First Cause, which is God, is the final cause <note>original: "final cause"; the ultimate purpose or end for which a thing exists.</note> of all things. For when He, as an intelligent and free being, produced this world, He proposed for Himself an end suited to His dignity—that is, Himself and His own proper glory. So the First Cause is necessarily the

# A KEY TO MEDICINE <note>original: "PHYSIC"; in this period, physic referred to the general study of medicine and natural philosophy.</note>,

...ultimate end of all its effects. This is a subtle <note>original: "nice"</note> subject, about which all preachers and writers seem to be at a loss; but the case is clear and beautiful to those who pursue the lessons of wisdom and science.

*Second Causes* are those which derive their power or faculty of acting from the influence of the First Cause. Hence, the **Soul of the World** <note>original: *anima mundi*; a concept in ancient and Renaissance philosophy suggesting a spirit that fills all of nature</note> is the seat of all second causes. These are also termed "natural causes" because they have implanted in them, by the First Cause, the hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> power of spreading through all space and of communicating to all bodies that universal soul, or ethereal spirit, by which every particle of matter is moved and made to act upon one another. This produces the various phenomena in nature: in the animal, vegetable, and mineral worlds; in the elements; and in the firmament of heaven. 

This universal spirit or cause acts universally alongside particular causes, but in a manner that agrees with the nature of every specific thing and according to the power given to it when it was created. This power neither alters the quality of the causes nor the necessity or freedom of their actions. This power of acting, which is communicated by second causes, is not a quality distinct from the things empowered to act; thus, the power that atoms have to move in all directions does not differ from the atoms themselves. The power of burning or heating does not differ from the fire in which it is inherent—unless we are considering the way we think of things or how we speak of them according to our own perceptions. 

So it is with an action that proceeds from the cause to the effect; it is nothing more than a certain relationship, or an actual subordination, which is always found between the cause and the effect. Hence, we perceive that "second causes" are what all philosophers, ancient and modern, have debated under different forms. They are neither more nor less than that universal spirit, or inherent law, implanted in nature at the creation, by which all God's works are regulated and preserved, and the ends and purposes of that creation are directed to God's glory and manifestation, and to the good of all His creatures. 

The study of this opens our eyes to the bright beams of true wisdom: to the mutual harmony and dependence one thing has upon another; to the **sympathy and antipathy** <note>original: "sympathy and antipathy"; the belief that certain natural substances are naturally attracted to or repelled by others</note> of material bodies; to the perceptions of sense, reason, and intellectual vision; to the delicate faculties and exquisite connection of soul and body; and ultimately to the knowledge of ourselves, of our progress through this world, of our earthly <note>original: "sublunary"</note> fate and fortune, and of the things intended to preserve life or to destroy it.

*Efficient Causes* are all those actions of bodies or things which are the agents or direct means by which any effects are produced. Thus, a painter painting a picture is an efficient cause; and the picture itself, when finished, is the effect of that cause. Efficient causes include a number of compound or subordinate causes, which

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Second Causes" by detailing the specific types of causes that govern the natural and moral worlds. It transitions from the general concept of universal spirit to the specific classifications used in natural philosophy.</meta>

...also contribute towards the production of their effect. If the efficient cause acts by a power proper to itself, then it is called the **principal cause**; but, if it acts only by the force and strength of another, then it is termed the **instrumental cause**. For instance, we distinguish between the painter and the pencil, though both contribute to the production of the picture. 

Again, the subject upon which the agent works, or out of which a thing is formed, is called the *material cause*. Thus, the marble out of which a statue is carved is the material cause; similarly, the paint and canvas are the material cause of a picture, as they are the matter or materials of which it is made, while the sculptor and painter are the efficient causes. 

There is also an efficient cause found in the sun, moon, stars, and elements, by which they act upon sublunary <note>original: "sublunary"; literally "under the moon," referring to the earthly realm which is subject to change and decay, as opposed to the unchanging heavens.</note> matter and produce a variety of effects in the productivity <note>original: "fructification"</note> and natural phenomena of this world. From these arise **necessary** and **free** causes. The first of these act by necessity and without choice—such as fire, the sun, and all created beings except for angels and men. Angels and men act by free will, which is the very essence of liberty. 

The efficient cause is also either **physical** or **moral**. A *physical cause* is one that produces a perceptible bodily effect and acts directly and immediately; for example, fire is the physical cause of burning, and the sun is the physical cause of heat. A *moral cause* also produces a real effect, but in immaterial things; thus, repentance is the moral cause of forgiveness. 

Furthermore, we define a *physical cause* as that which produces its effect through a physical power <note>original: "virtue"; here meaning power or inherent capability.</note>; and a *moral cause* as that which influences the physical cause to produce an effect, though not by necessity. For example, the sun is the physical cause of light; a stone that falls from a height and fractures the skull is a physical cause of death. However, the advice, entreaty, commands, or threats <note>original: "menaces"</note> which influence us to do or not do something—though they do not force us—are moral causes. In this sense, it is obvious that a moral cause is only applicable to a free, intelligent agent; this understanding of moral and physical causes is the most accurate and clear.

Whenever the efficient cause involves a free, intelligent being acting from knowledge, all the subordinate causes work together to produce one and the same effect. For example, when a painter creates a picture: 
*   The painter is the **principal cause**.
*   The pencil <note>In this context, a "pencil" refers to a small, fine paintbrush used by artists.</note> is the **instrumental cause**.
*   The goal proposed by the painter is the **final cause**.
*   The idea directing the work is the **exemplary cause**.
*   The form and arrangement of its parts is the **formal cause**.
*   The colors and the canvas are the **material cause**, being the physical substance of the work.

Finally, if the artist improves his picture by an accidental touch—like Agillaus <note>This likely refers to the Greek painter Protogenes (or possibly Apelles), who, according to legend, became frustrated while trying to paint the foam on a horse's mouth and threw his sponge at the canvas, accidentally creating the perfect effect.</note>, who labored for many days to draw a foaming horse and could not, and in a passion threw his brush at the painting, achieving the result he wanted by chance—it is termed an **accidental cause**. Thus, we see that all subordinate causes are ultimately under the efficient cause and serve it when they are applied with reason and directed by skill.

*Form and formal cause* are one and the same thing. When we say there are two types of forms, it is only a result of how we conceptualize things; for example, we speak of two kinds of formal causes: the substantial and the accidental. However, all forms are imaginary. True philosophers do not acknowledge any substance within natural compounds other than matter (except in the case of humans), nor any form other than the arrangement of parts, because these abstract forms are completely useless. Furthermore, the *exemplary cause* <note>The "exemplary cause" refers to the model or blueprint in the mind of the creator.</note> can be categorized under the formal cause because it is the idea and internal form that we construct in our minds. For example, the formal cause of a painting is the arrangement of its parts, following the design and order previously held in the painter's mind. The same applies to all rational agents endowed with understanding.

There is no difference between matter and a material cause, and there are two types of material causes just as there are two types of matter. The "first matter" <note>original: "first matter"; in ancient and early modern physics, *materia prima* was the formless, fundamental substance underlying all physical things.</note> is that out of which all bodies are composed and into which they may be broken down through universal division. The "second matter" consists of nothing other than the specific bodies made from the first, upon which efficient causes exert their influence. Therefore, it is clear that everything in the world is a "compound" (a mixture of parts) and that no compound exists without matter. It is also certain that nothing is created without an efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary source of change; essentially, the agent or force that brings something into being.</note>. This cause acts upon compounds and breaks them down so that others may be formed from them. Because the matter of the first object serves as the material for the second, the underlying substance is the first matter (or the material cause of the compound). The specific matter that acts as the subject or "patient" <note>original: "patient"; in this context, the thing that receives an action or is acted upon.</note> for the efficient cause is called the second matter. Both can act as an efficient cause; for compounds interact with one another like the elements, pushing one another back and forth. The thing that drives another is called the **agent**, while the thing being driven is called the **patient**. If there is something that resists and pushes back against another, this reversal of motion is called **re-action**. Thus, the same object can be both the subject and the cause of motion. Since giving and receiving are the principles of the agent and the patient, both can occur simultaneously, though in different respects.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Dr. Benjamin Franklin’s experiments with oil on water, specifically detailing the physical mechanics of how oil prevents the formation of waves.</meta>

# A KEY TO PHYSIC,

On water, it instantly expands into a circle extending several feet in diameter, becoming so thin that it produces prismatic colors <note>The rainbow-like colors created by light refracting through a thin film, similar to a soap bubble or oil slick.</note> for a considerable area. Beyond those colors, it becomes so much thinner that it is invisible, except for its effect in smoothing the waves at a much greater distance. It seems, says Dr. Franklin, as if a mutual repulsion between its particles takes place as soon as it touches the water—a repulsion so strong that it acts on other bodies swimming on the surface, such as straws, leaves, etc., forcing them to recede in every direction from the drop as if from a center, leaving a large, clear space. 

In endeavoring to explain the singular effects of oil, Dr. Franklin observes that there seems to be no natural repulsion between water and air that would keep them from coming into contact with each other. Therefore, air in motion (which is wind) passing over the smooth surface of water may rub, as it were, against that surface and raise it into wrinkles. If the wind continues, these wrinkles are the "elements" of future waves. The smallest wave does not immediately subside; instead, in the process of subsiding, it raises nearly as much of the water next to it. A small power operating continually will produce a great action. Thus, the first-raised waves, being continually acted upon by the wind, increase in magnitude even if the wind does not increase in strength. They rise higher and extend their bases so as to include a vast mass of water in each wave, which, in its motion, acts with great violence. 

But if there is a mutual repulsion between the particles of oil, and no attraction between oil and water, oil dropped on water will not be held together by sticking to the spot where it falls. It will not be absorbed <note>original: "imbibed"</note> by the water, but will be free to expand itself and spread over a surface that perhaps prevents all immediate contact by repelling the oil. This expansion will continue until the mutual repulsion between the particles of oil is weakened and reduced to nothing by their distance from one another. Dr. Franklin imagines that the wind blowing over water covered with such a film of oil cannot easily "catch" upon it to raise the first wrinkles, but instead slides over it and leaves the surface as smooth as it found it. The wind does move the oil slightly, which—being between the air and the water—serves as a lubricant to slide upon and prevents friction. Hence, oil dropped on the windward side of a pond proceeds gradually to the leeward <note>The side sheltered from the wind or toward which the wind is blowing.</note> side, as can be seen by the smoothness it carries with it all the way to the opposite side. Because the wind is thus prevented from raising those first wrinkles (which he calls the "elements of waves"), it cannot produce waves, which are created by continually acting upon and enlarging those elements; thus, the whole pond is calmed. 

On the whole, there is great reason to suppose (notwithstanding the partial failure of an experiment made at Portsmouth by Dr. Franklin and others <note>Franklin conducted a large-scale test at Portsmouth, England, in 1773. While the oil smoothed the surface "choppiness," it did not stop the massive "swell" of the ocean, leading to mixed results.</note>), that seafaring people may derive advantages from using oil on particular occasions to moderate the violence of the waves or to lessen the surf, which sometimes makes landing...

Trans."; the published record of the Royal Society of London, the world's oldest scientific academy.</note> vol. 64, part 2, p. 445, etc. It is also observable on the coast of Sutherland, when the lump-fish abounds in spring and is devoured by seals, that the event may be known by the smoothness of the water above the spot, as the oil serves to still the agitation of the waves.

The term "occasional cause" is applied to the soul and body of man; these are only the occasions, not the direct causes, of their effects. The soul is not able to act on the body, nor the body reciprocally on the soul. To keep up an intercourse between them, God—on the occasion of a motion of the body—impresses a sensation on the soul; and, on the occasion of a sentiment of the soul, He impresses a motion on the body. The motions, therefore, of the soul and body are only "occasional causes" of what passes in one or the other. Thus, we say the stroke, or percussion, is only the occasional cause of the motion produced in the body that is struck; it is God who is the direct efficient cause <note>In philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; the agent that actually brings something about.</note>. And thus, the action of objects on our organs is not the efficient cause of our ideas and perceptions, but merely the occasional cause which determines God to act on the mind according to the laws of the union of soul and body.

In a medical sense, whatever produces a disease is called its cause. This operates either by inducing a new state of the solids and fluids, or by taking away something which is absolutely requisite to the exercise of some function. If a cause pre-existed in some measure in the body before the effect was produced, it is called an internal cause; but if it existed outside of the body and produced the disease by its application to it, it is called an external cause.

Internal causes generally injure first the humours <note>In historical medicine, these were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health.</note> and then the solid parts; whereas external causes affect the solids, and, in consequence of that, the humours. This holds true universally, unless perhaps in some few diseases produced by poison or contagion. The "immediate cause" is that which, taken altogether, immediately constitutes the present disease; this is always adequate and sufficient for the formation of the disease, whether it is simple or complicated. The presence of this cause constitutes and continues the disease, and the absence of it removes the disorder, being very little different from the disease itself. The investigation of this, therefore, is extremely useful and very necessary. The "remote cause" is that which changes the body in such a manner as to dispose it for the reception of a disease upon the arrival of another cause; however, it is never adequate or sufficient to produce a disease alone, nor would that other cause—the arrival of which is necessary—be of itself sufficient for the

### OF THE FIRST MATTER.

ALL philosophers agree that there is a **first matter** <note>Also known as "prima materia," the primitive, formless base of all reality in alchemy and ancient philosophy.</note>, which was produced from the beginning. Although it can never undergo any change itself, it is to be seen in all the births <note>original: "generations"</note> and decays <note>original: "corruptions"</note> found in nature. Hence it appears that the "first matter" existed before the generation of the compounds in which it is found, and that it still remains and survives the decay of them. For instance, in a fire made of wood chips, the matter of the fire was in the chips, and is found partly in the fire, partly in the smoke, and partly also in the ashes. It is agreed by all that "nothing comes from nothing" <note>original: "nothing produces nothing," or the Latin "ex nihilo nihil fit"</note>, and that there is not anything in nature that can be reduced into nothing. Instead, the first principles remain throughout all the revolutions that can happen. Therefore, in respect of matter, we may justly say that there is nothing new in the world since the creation, and that this matter in its nature is incorruptible; so, explaining the essence of this "first matter" is the only difficulty.

### ON ATOMS AND THEIR NATURE

To prove that atoms exist, we might assume that every compound substance can be divided into as many parts as it contains. Division must necessarily stop when there are no more parts left to be divided. On the other hand, there is no end to division as long as there are still particles to be divided. We must allow for one of two possibilities: either a body can never be so precisely divided that there do not always remain parts that can be further divided infinitely <note>original: "in infinitum"</note>, or there are certain parts that, after a specific number of divisions, will not allow any further splitting. Aristotle <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who believed matter was continuous and infinitely divisible.</note> holds the first view, but Pierre Gassendi <note>original: "Gassendus"; a French philosopher and scientist (1592–1655) who revived the ancient theory of atoms and tried to reconcile it with Christianity.</note> and the ancient philosophers defend the second. According to this latter doctrine, once all possible divisions are made, nothing can remain except atoms—that is, indivisible beings which are the primary elements of all natural bodies.

I admit it is hard to imagine a physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> thing being indivisible, because we see nothing in this world that cannot be broken apart. However, this does not disprove the existence of atoms. Atoms are physical because they compose larger bodies, yet they are indivisible because they are the first and most simple elements of those bodies. This leads to another difficulty: it is not easily explained how a divisible thing can be made of parts that are themselves indivisible. Unbiased minds do not find as much difficulty in understanding this as those who are swayed by their own prejudices. Some people fail to consider two points: first, that many things escape our senses but are nonetheless very real; and second, that the thing which composes a body is not itself a compound. For example, we see that "unity" (the number one) creates number, even though it is not itself a plurality of numbers. Similarly, letters form nouns and words, yet a single letter is neither a noun nor a word. The drops of water that make up rivers are not themselves rivers. In the same way, although atoms are invisible and indivisible,

Therefore, regarding matter, we may justly say that there is nothing new in the world since the creation, and that this matter is incorruptible by its very nature.

### ON THE PROPERTIES, SIZE, SHAPE, WEIGHT, AND MOTION OF ATOMS

*An atom* is a physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> entity—simple, invisible, and indivisible. Solidity constitutes its essence or essential property, which distinguishes it from spirit and vacuum <note>original: "vacuity"</note>, neither of which has the power of resistance. Atoms necessarily escape our senses because our sense organs can only perceive objects made of many distinct and substantial <note>original: "gross"</note> parts, which must be combined before they can be detected. 

However, this does not destroy the truth and reality of atoms simply because small particles <term>corpuscles</term> escape our senses. We observe this in the dust that sticks to our clothes; in the tiny particles of a stone worn hollow by drops of water; in the various hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> parts of a mite <note>a microscopic arachnid</note> that cannot be seen without a microscope; and, lastly, in the small particles seen dancing in a sunbeam within a room. We may omit many others that are even smaller, which we would undoubtedly see if our sight were sharper.

Although atoms are extremely subtle and imperceptible, they still have their own specific extension, size, and shape <note>original: "figure"</note>, which accounts for the differences between them. For instance, some are round, such as the atoms of water, oil, and mercury <note>original: "quicksilver"</note>; others have cubic shapes, such as the atoms of seawater; and others are pyramidal, like those that make up saltpeter <note>original: "nitre"</note>. Some have sharp points like needles, such as the atoms of fire. From this, we can assume there are others of various shapes. This diversity is necessary to distinguish between different compounds. Since these atoms are alike in their solidity, invisibility, and indivisibility (which are their inseparable properties), they must differ in shape and thickness; otherwise, all physical bodies would be identical.

Weight is the principle behind natural motion, insofar as it resists "violent" or forced motion. I mention this so we may determine whether the motion of atoms comes from an internal or external source, whether weight causes only one type of movement or can be inclined toward many, and whether the motion of atoms tends toward a specific center. We must also ask whether this motion is continuous or interrupted, and whether it moves perpendicularly or horizontally, in parallel or diagonally, straight, or in a parabolic or circular path.

To solve this difficulty, I propose that atoms can be considered in two states. The first state exists before they form the bodies made from them; this may be called the "state of liberty." The second state is that which they have within the bodies they compose, which may be termed the "state of obligation" or "servitude."

If atoms are considered in their original state, their motion is perpetual. An atom that is loose and free from any combination is naturally in motion, which should not be surprising at all. Motion is as essential to a free atom as understanding is to an angel; an angel is never without knowledge unless their intellect is hindered or clouded.

From this principle, it is clear that atoms are in constant motion unless they are hindered, meet an obstruction, or encounter other atoms that resist or repel them. They may also find atoms they can stick to, or they might work their way into the atoms of certain bodies or enter into a composition that stops their motion. Nevertheless, atoms within compounds are not completely motionless. They are not packed so tightly together that they lack all movement; instead, they experience motions like vibrations and palpitations, according to the space allowed to them by the tiny gaps <term>disseminated vacuities</term> <note>original: "disseminated vacuities"; the small pockets of empty space between particles in a solid object</note> spread throughout the material. In fact, some atoms occasionally attempt to escape, especially in porous bodies. This is why porous materials rot and perish sooner than other bodies that are more solid and dense. 

This is even more evident in living bodies. From these, the "animal spirits"—which are actually made of atoms and the most subtle particles <term>corpuscles</term>—are lost through the skin <term>transpiration</term> <note>original: "transpiration"; here referring to the evaporation of fluids and "spirits" through the pores</note>. Because of this, food <term>aliments</term> is necessary to resupply the spirits of the whole body that are used up by motion and activity. This motion of atoms, or the smallest particles in living bodies, can be considered a reflection of their original freedom. Although they rarely enjoy their full liberty, they are prone to causing great disturbances in order to break free. 

This is the origin of many illnesses. For example, in acute fevers, the atoms or particles of boiling blood or blocked bile <term>choler</term> <note>one of the four "humors" or bodily fluids in early medicine, believed to cause heat and irritability</note> are driven into the brain. There, they produce sleeplessness <note>original: "watchfulness"</note>, delirium, and frenzy. According to this principle, we can conclude what was said before: *That many illnesses arise from tiny particles and "freed" atoms.* When these atoms are pushed forward by others or forced back, they collide with membranes, the bone lining <term>periosteum</term>, the protective layers of the brain <term>meninges</term>, or the intestines. This causes conditions such as colic, headaches, gout, and rheumatism. Therefore, the breakdown of these particles and the freeing of atoms in our bodies are much to be feared. To prevent this danger, one must avoid all violent physical movements, as these are the external causes of the confusion of the spirits and the freeing of the atoms.

The freeing of atoms, as well as the small particles composed of those atoms, can be seen in the "great world" <note>the macrocosm or universe</note> just as much as in the "little world" <note>the microcosm or the human body</note>. For winds are nothing other than freed atoms which, driven back and forth by their own force, strike all the objects in their way.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of atomic motion and the definition of an atom as a simple, indivisible, yet physical entity. It addresses the philosophical paradox of how something can take up space without being divisible, using the soul and angels as analogies.</meta>

### A KEY TO PHYSIC,

It is these atoms that agitate the air and overturn everything that resists their motion. Therefore, the motion of atoms is not uniform or everywhere the same; instead, it varies according to the different bodies they strike, how well their shapes are suited for movement, or the proportion of empty spaces <term>vacuities</term> <note>original: "vacuities"; the voids or gaps between particles in a substance</note> scattered within those bodies. Consequently, some atoms move faster and others slower—not because some are heavier than others, but because they are pushed forward or backward, or stopped by other atoms that happen to strike them with more or less force.

An atom is not a "body" in the sense of the common notion that it is a complex, compound being; rather, it is a simple being that is also physical <term>corporeal</term> <note>original: "corporeal"; having a physical nature or body</note>. It is "simple" because it cannot be divided, and "physical" because it has a certain size <term>extension</term> <note>original: "extension"; the property of taking up space</note> and makes up the structure of larger bodies, which return to atoms when they are completely broken down.

Two other difficulties arise from this previous opinion: for if an atom cannot be divided, how can we imagine that it has size? Or how can it be an ingredient in the composition of objects that *can* be divided? To this we answer briefly: size depends on the nature of the thing that has size. For if the thing that takes up space is divisible, then its size is also divisible. 

On the other hand, consider the reasoning soul <term>rational soul</term> <note>original: "rational soul"; in early modern philosophy, the highest part of the soul responsible for human reason, thought to be distinct from the body's physical functions</note>, which possesses the whole body and performs its functions in every part of it. Nevertheless, like an atom, it is indivisible. Although it may seem divisible in relation to the space it occupies, it has an internal size that cannot be split. This is the same thing that theologians <term>divines</term> are forced to say about angels, and what some philosophers say about their physical "swollen points" <term>tumid points</term> <note>original: "tumid points"; a theoretical concept of physical points that have volume or "swelling" but are not mathematically divisible</note>. 

But some will argue that atoms are not like souls, angels, or physical points because atoms have parts and those do not; and since anything that consists of parts is divisible, it follows that an atom must also be divisible. To this difficulty I answer, along with the theologians, that angels and our souls (which are spirits), and also with the philosophers, that physical points (which are material), have no "real" parts, but only "potential" parts. That is, an angel or a reasoning soul has "parts" only in terms of the actions they perform and the space they occupy, just as "swollen points" do in terms of the space they fill. 

Indeed, an angel and the soul have two powers: the intellect and the will. These belong to a single, indivisible substance capable of both understanding and wanting. Yet no one will deny that, despite their indivisibility (which is at least equal to the indivisibility of an atom), they fill up a space that *is* divisible. Just as no one can doubt that an angel can be in the four corners and the middle of a room at the same time, thereby taking on a square shape by occupying the four corners, and can then leave that shape to take another as it pleases. This, however, cannot be said of physical points and atoms, which are <meta>The text ends here; the catchword is "destitute."</meta>

# AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES.

lacking understanding and will. The rational soul, being equally indivisible as an atom, an angel, or a single mathematical point, fully occupies a large body just as it did when the body was small. Therefore, it expands itself without being divided, because by its very nature it is simple, indivisible, and has no distinct parts. This is the opinion of *Aristotle*, and indeed it is the most common viewpoint. 

But if the soul were not extended through the whole body by its own substance, and instead had its seat only in the heart (as *Empedocles* <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that the heart was the seat of the soul.</note> believed); or in the spleen and the stomach (as *Van Helmont* <note>Jan Baptista van Helmont (1580–1644), a chemist and physician who believed the soul resided in the stomach's "vital furnace."</note> placed it); or in the *pineal gland* <note>original: "glandula pinealis"</note> of the brain (according to *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"; the Latinized name for René Descartes (1596–1650), who famously argued the pineal gland was the "seat of the soul."</note>); or in the *corpus striatum* <note>original: "striate bodies"; internal structures of the brain.</note> where the "common sense"—or the sense itself, as it is called by way of excellence—is located; and in the callous parts <note>The *corpus callosum*, the bridge of nerve fibers connecting the brain hemispheres.</note>, because there it forms and judges ideas; and in the grey matter <note>original: "cineritious part"; from the Latin *cinis*, meaning ash-colored.</note> of the brain, because there it performs the functions of memory (according to the opinion of *Duncan* <note>Likely Daniel Duncan (1649–1735), a physician who wrote on the mechanisms of the brain and soul.</note>); it is certain that all these parts, which are taken to be the seat of the soul, are divisible and have distinct parts and shapes. 

So, the soul, while indivisible, occupies a space or place that *is* divisible. From this, I conclude that indivisibility does not prevent a substance from having a certain indivisible extension, even if it is divisible in terms of the space it occupies. In other words, it may have angles and a shape in relation to its location, even though its essence remains one, simple, and indivisible.

Hence it follows that there is one universal matter, called corpuscles <term>corpuscles</term> <note>original: "corpuscles"; an early term for atoms or tiny particles of matter.</note> or atoms, filling all space. This is an extended, impenetrable, and divisible substance, common to all bodies and capable of taking any form. These particles are infinitely harder than any of the tangible, porous bodies made from them—so hard, in fact, that they never wear out or break into pieces. No other power is able to divide what God made "one" in the first creation. 

While these corpuscles remain whole, they can compose bodies of the exact same nature and texture throughout all ages. But should they wear away or break into pieces, the very nature of the things depending on them would be changed. Water and earth composed of old, worn-out particles and fragments would not have the same nature and texture today as the water and earth composed of whole particles at the beginning of time. Therefore, so that nature may be lasting, the changes we see in physical things are only the result of various separations and new associations of these permanent corpuscles. To form the vast variety of natural bodies, this matter must have motion in all its parts and act in every possible direction. These corpuscles, therefore, have not only a force of inertia <note>original: "vis inertiæ"; the resistance of matter to change its state of motion.</note>—accompanied by the passive laws of motion that naturally result from that force—but they are also moved by certain active principles, such as gravity, the process of fermentation <note>In 18th-century science, "fermentation" referred generally to internal chemical motions or reactions within a substance.</note>, and the cohesion and attraction of bodies. This happens because the spirit of the north pole enters the pores of the iron, but the southern spirit cannot; instead, it strikes against the iron and drives back its elastic particles too forcefully. I know from experience that quicksilver—prepared to be white and shining like a diamond <note>original: "adamant"</note> or polished silver—will in time become black when carried by someone who is frequently around sick people. After this, it is useless to the wearer because no small empty spaces <note>original: "vacuities"</note> are left to trap the airborne poisons. Quicksilver turns black more or less, and sooner or later, depending on the amount of malignancy in the air where the person travels. 

These antidotes can never cause harm. In fact, if prepared correctly, they not only withstand contagious air by preventing it from coming near us, but they also suppress internal vapors which, when they rise into the head, cause many illnesses. These results, strictly speaking, are the joint effects of sympathy and antipathy acting together. The bodily emissions <note>original: "animal effluvia"</note> or particles issuing from our bodies repel the malignancy of the surrounding environment through antipathy. Meanwhile, objects composed of poisonous or harmful particles draw the foul or poisonous atoms surrounding them to themselves through sympathy, just as a magnet <note>original: "loadstone"</note> draws iron. 

In this, we see (and shall later prove) that amulets or charms worn on the body—as well as electricity, animal magnetism <note>the theory that an invisible natural force flows between living things</note>, and other hidden properties acting upon our bodies—are nothing more than the natural effects of sympathy and antipathy. Aromatic herbs and sweet-smelling flowers used against infectious air act by repulsion, or antipathy. Conversely, nightshade, hemlock, and all poisonous herbs act by sympathy, drawing infectious atoms into their pores just as horseradish draws in vinegar. It follows that both of these classes of plants are useful in preserving the body's fluids <note>original: "animal juices"</note> from infection.

We may further remark that the more "signatures" or resemblances are found appearing together in a plant for the same purpose, the more powerful and effective its operation will be. In some bodies, this spirit is more abundant and active; in others, it is more sparse and weakened. Therefore, the more that same spirit produces a suitable form and figure in various subjects under the same climate, the more those subjects are enabled to sympathize with and assist each other. For sympathy is

...by the spirit; and resemblance <note>original: "similitude"</note> points out the things that act by sympathy. Hence it is that a similarity of nature <note>original: "similitude of affection"</note> increases strength, while the contrary—hatred—weakens it. Thus it is that plants with parts resembling a scorpion—such as leopard's bane <note>original: "libards-bane"</note>, hellebore, and aconite <note>original: "aconitum"</note>—will cure the bite of that reptile. Likewise, the flowers of plants that resemble butterflies promote fertility and virility, such as the early purple orchid <note>original: "gandergoose"</note>, bean flowers, honeysuckle <note>original: "woodbine"</note>, and ragwort. 

Plants spotted like snakes, such as crow garlic <note>original: "cow-garlic"</note>, cuckoopint <note>original: "wake robin"</note>, dragonwort, sea-dragon, etc., are healing <note>original: "sanative"</note> against the bites of serpents. Plants which resemble the head of such animals are also effective against their poison; for example, Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> affirms that the flowers of wild bugloss, which look like the head of a viper, are a certain cure.

The medicinal properties <note>original: "virtues"</note> of plants and herbs are, however, variable and liable to be damaged by changes in climate. This can alter or destroy them, as we see in many of the medical plants brought into England from other countries. Although they seem to thrive here, they never possess their healing powers to the same excellent degree as in their native climate. This is the reason that Culpeper <note>Nicholas Culpeper (1616–1654), a famous English botanist and herbalist</note> recommends English herbs for an English constitution. 

The bodies of different animals also cause the same plant to have different effects. The tithymals <note>original: "tythmals"</note> or spurges <note>Plants of the genus Euphorbia</note> are all very violent laxatives <note>original: "cathartics"</note> when taken by humans. Yet, they are eaten by goats and several other animals without any purgative effect, and they even seem to give those animals a particular boost of vigor and energy. Fish, on the contrary, are more strongly affected by them than we are; the juice of spurge, made into a paste with flour and honey, will intoxicate them so much that they may be picked out of the water by hand. Similarly, bitter almonds cause no ill effects for us, yet they kill all sorts of birds that touch them.

These ideas may be ridiculed for their extreme simplicity. Yet, where is the man familiar with science <note>original: "natural philosophy"</note> and medicine <note>original: "physic"</note>, and possessed of an impartial mind, who would dare to dispute these facts? Every traveler knows something of the herbs I have mentioned and is capable of judging their resemblance and connections <note>original: "similitude and sympathy"</note>. Let him apply them for the purposes I have pointed out, and their hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> properties will soon be apparent to his senses. The path of nature is a plain and obvious road, full of the most pleasing views and the most reliable guides. God, in the fullness of His all-knowing wisdom <note>original: "omniscience"</note> and mercy, seems to have set a mark on the smallest particles of His creation for humanity's information and benefit. In the study of these marks, both our happiness and our health will always be found.

<page-num>89</page-num>
<header>AND OCCULT SCIENCE <note>Occult here refers to "hidden" or "inner" natural processes not immediately visible to the eye</note>.</header>

# THE OCCULT PROPERTIES OF REPRODUCTION <note>original: "GENERATION"</note>
## IN PLANTS AND HERBS.

All plants are produced from seeds, just as all animals are produced from eggs, and the process of nature is very similar in both types of reproduction. Even the smallest vegetables have seeds, though they are often not discoverable by the naked eye. Mistletoe is also known to be produced from seed; and the flat, stalkless <note>original: "sessile"</note> fungi <note>original: "funguses"</note>, which some consider to be diseased growths <note>original: "morbid excrescences"</note>, are actually true species of those mushrooms <note>original: "agarics"</note> that have caps and stems and grow on the ground. When their seeds fall on a moist tree, they produce, as it were, half-caps without stems. 

Furthermore, the fact that seeds are the "eggs" of plants is shown by this: just as every egg produces an offspring similar to the parent, so do the seeds of vegetables; therefore, they are also eggs. A seed resembles a hen’s egg; like the egg, a seed has a shell, an external membrane or film, a membrane that contains the yolk, the yolk itself, and the germinal spot <note>original: "scar or point of life"</note>. In seeds, the egg-white is missing because the moisture of the earth takes its place and nourishes the plant embryo. 

When the flower begins to fade, the seed starts to swell. On the outside, a small sac <note>original: "vesicle"</note> is seen, which is the amnion <note>The innermost membrane surrounding an embryo</note>, equipped with an umbilical cord <note>original: "chord or navel-string"</note> that is introduced through the chorion <note>The outermost membrane surrounding an embryo</note> to the opposite side of the egg. While the amnion grows within the egg, another small body is observed on its top. This also grows continually until it has filled the entire chorion and egg; eventually, the amnion and chorion are turned into the external shell or coat of the seed. Thus, as the same changes occur in the seed as in the egg, seeds must be the eggs of plants. 

Furthermore, it is plain that plants spring from eggs because of their lobes <note>Now known as cotyledons, the first "seed leaves" of a plant</note>. When we speak of cows and similar four-legged animals, these lobes are nothing other than several fetal membranes <note>original: "secundines"</note> that always adhere to the fetus, drawing their supply of fluids from the womb <note>original: "matrix"</note>, which they prepare for the nourishment of the tender fetus. It is very well known that most plants have these seminal leaves or lobes. These seminal leaves once constituted the entire seed, except for the hilum <note>The "eye" of the seed, or the point where it was attached to the plant</note> or "little heart," which contains the point of life. These lobes prepare the nourishment for the very tender plant until it is able to strike root in the earth. This is the same way the yolk in an egg becomes the placenta, preparing the nourishment and sending it through the umbilical cord to the chick, after which the lobes drop off. 

Hence, it appears that the seminal leaves are the lobes; but since all lobes proceed from the egg or seed, we may fairly conclude that plants are produced from eggs. However, as no egg can produce an animal until it is fertilized <note>original: "impregnated or fecundated"</note> by the male, it will be necessary to investigate the placement of the reproductive organs designed by nature for this purpose in plants.

# A KEY TO PHYSIC <note>Physic refers to the art of healing or the study of natural medicine</note>

It is clear that the reproductive organs of plants must be located where the seeds are produced. Since seeds are produced where the flower and fruit are, the reproductive organs must be found within the flower and fruit. No clear or obvious example has ever been found of a plant that lacks flowers and fruit, even if they are sometimes too small to see clearly. Therefore, we can rightly say that the essence of plants lies in their reproduction <note>original: "fructification"</note>. 

Furthermore, just as conception <note>original: "generation"</note> precedes birth in animals, the flower in plants always precedes the fruit. We are therefore naturally led to credit the flower with fertilization <note>original: "fecundation"</note>, and the ripe fruit with the "birth" or release of the seed. The flower may, consequently, be defined as the reproductive organs of a plant used for fertilization, and the fruit as the reproductive organs used for the birth or ripening of the seed. 

We know that there are many plants which lack certain parts—some lack the <term>calyx</term> <note>the green outer leaves that protect a bud</note>, others the <term>corolla</term> <note>the petals of a flower</note>, others the filaments of the <term>stamens</term>, and others the <term>style</term> <note>the stalk of the female organ</note>. However, all flowers, except for **mosses**, are equipped with **anthers** <note>original: "antheræ"</note>, **stigmas** <note>original: "stigmata"</note>, or both. Therefore, these parts must be the essential core of the flower. If we find a flower with anthers but no stigmas, we will surely find another flower—either on the same plant or a different plant of the same species—which has stigmas, either with anthers or without them. 

The act of fertilization is performed in the flower; therefore, the reproductive organs of both sexes must be present there. They do not, however, always have to be in the same individual flower. It is sufficient for the male organs to be in one flower and the female organs in another. These reproductive organs are the **anthers** and the **stigmas**. 

The **anthers**, or male organs of reproduction in flowers, are nothing more than the bodies that prepare and contain the male sperm. Therefore, these anthers are the testicles and seminal vesicles, and their dust <note>pollen</note> is the true male sperm of plants. This dust corresponds to the particles called "little animals" <note>original: "animalcules"; referring to the microscopic sperm cells discovered in the 17th century</note> in the male sperm of animals. 

This argument is proven by the following facts: the anthers and their dust always appear before the fruit. Once they shed their dust—which they do before the flower has reached its full strength—they have finished their job; they then drop off and become useless. Furthermore, the anthers are positioned in the flower so that their dust (the male sperm) can reach the **pistil**, or female organ. In most flowers, the stamens surround the pistil. If the pistil leans toward the upper side of the flower, the stamens do the same; if the pistil hangs down <note>original: "nods"</note>, the stamens grow upward to reach it.

Furthermore, the anthers and stigmas are at their peak at the same time, whether they are in the same flower or in separate ones. Moreover, if we cut open the anthers before they have shed their dust, their internal structure will be found to be just as wonderful and intricate as that of the seed-

And, if we cut off the **anthers** <note>original: "antheræ"</note> of any plant which bears only one flower—taking care at the same time that no other plant of the same species is near it—the fruit fails to develop <note>original: "proves abortive"</note>, or at least produces seeds which will not grow. Finally, the shape of the fertilizing dust will clearly convince anyone that this fine powder is not gathered by chance, or from the dryness of the anthers.

The powder of the anthers, in terms of fertilization <note>original: "fecundation"</note>, corresponds to the sperm cells <note>original: "animalcules in the male sperm"</note> in animals; and the **stigma**, which receives this dust, is always somewhat moist so that the dust may instantly stick to it. That the **stigmas** <note>original: "stigmata"</note>, which are the other essential parts of the flower, are the female organs of reproduction <note>original: "generation"</note>, may be proved by the following considerations: the parts of the **pistil** <note>original: "pistillum"</note> are the **ovary** <note>original: "germen"</note>, the **style**, and the **stigma**. The ovary (or seed-bud), while the plant is in flower, is always imperfect and immature, being only the starting point for the future embryo <note>original: "fœtus"</note>. The style is not an essential part, for it is missing in many species of plants; but the ovary can never bring the fruit to maturity unless it is within the flower along with the stigma. 

Hence it follows that the stigma is that part of the flower which receives the fertilizing dust. This will further appear if we consider that the stigma is always situated so that the anthers, or their fertilizing dust, can reach it. Moreover, it always has a shape unique to itself, so that in most (though not all) plants it is double when the fruit consists of two cells; triple when the seed-vessel has three cells; quadruple when it has four cells, and so on. Again, the stigmas are always at their strongest at the same time as the anthers. Besides, the stigmas in most plants, when they have fulfilled their purpose, drop off in the same way as the anthers do; which proves that the stigmas contribute nothing to the ripening of the fruit, but serve only for the purpose of reproduction. 

If the stigmas are cut off before they have received the fertilizing dust of the anthers, the plant is sterilized <note>original: "castrated"</note> in its female organs, and the fruit perishes. The stigma of the flower has, besides, two other unique properties: namely, that it is always stripped of the <term>cuticle</term> <note>the thin, protective outer skin or film of a plant</note>, nor does it have any bark as the other parts have, and it is always covered with moisture.

On the whole, it appears that the reproduction of plants is accomplished by the anthers shedding their dust on the stigmas. In the reproduction of animals, we are certain that the male sperm must come in contact with the female organ for any fertilization to occur. In the vegetable kingdom, the reproductive dust is carried by the air to the moist stigmas, where the particles burst and discharge their exceedingly fine or
