The **stamens** <note>original: "stamina"</note> and **pistil** <note>original: "pistillum"</note> are generally the same height so that the male dust may more easily reach the stigma. In those plants where this is not the case, a singular process of fertilization <note>original: "fecundation"</note> may be observed. 

For example, in the African tree crane’s-bill, or *geranium inquinans*, where the pistil is shorter than the stamens, the flowers hang down <note>original: "are pendulous"</note> before they bloom. However, upon opening, they stand upright so that the powder may fall onto the stigma. After this happens, they droop again until the fruit is ripe, and then they stand upright a second time so that their seeds may be more easily scattered. In some varieties of pinks, the **stigmas** <note>original: "pistilla"</note>, which are longer than the stamens, are bent back like rams' horns toward the anthers.

Furthermore, the stamens for the most part surround the pistil, so that some of the dust is always blown by the wind onto the stigma. Moreover, the stamens and pistil develop at the same time—not only within the same flower but also in cases where some flowers are male and others female on the same plant, with very few exceptions.

In almost all types of flowers, we see how they expand or open in the heat of the sun; but in the evening, or when the air is moist, they close or contract their petals. This prevents moisture from reaching the dust of the anthers, which would cause it to clump <note>original: "coagulate"</note> and make it impossible to be blown onto the stigma. But once the fertilization is over, the flowers no longer contract in the evening or even when it rains. 

The wind frequently serves as a vehicle for bringing the **pollen** <note>original: "farina"</note> of the male plants to the females. M. Geoffroy <note>Étienne François Geoffroy, a French botanist</note> cites a story from Jovius Pontanus <note>Giovanni Gioviano Pontano, an Italian humanist poet</note>, who relates that in his time there were two palm trees: a male tree cultivated at Brindisi and a female tree in the wood of Otranto, fifteen leagues <note>approximately 45 miles</note> apart. This female tree went several years without bearing any fruit; finally, after rising above the other trees of the forest so that it might "see" (as the poet says) the male palm tree at Brindisi, it began to bear fruit in abundance. M. Geoffroy has no doubt that the tree only began to bear fruit because it was then high enough to catch the pollen of the male tree on its branches, brought there by the wind. 

In the male and female versions of the **pistachio nut tree** <note>original: "pistachia-nut-tree"</note>, they observe the same method as in the date tree. We may also observe that since male dust is generally heavier than the air <note>original: "of greater specific gravity"</note>, in most plants where the pistil is longer than the stamens, the all-wise Creator has made the flowers "nodding" (drooping) so that the powder may more easily fall onto the stigma. Plants that grow underwater, around the time of flowering, raise their reproductive <note>original: "genital"</note> stems above the water; these stems sink again as soon as the time of reproduction is over. A similar conclusion may be further established from the consideration of all sorts of flowers; but enough has been said to prove that the reproduction of plants is performed by the reproductive dust <note>original: "genital dust"</note> of the **anthers** <note>original: "antheræ"</note> falling on the moist **stigma** (the female organ). This dust, with the help of the moisture, adheres and bursts, discharging its contents. The subtle particles of this dust are then absorbed by the **style** and carried into the **ovary** <note>original: "ovarium"</note>, **germen**, or seed-bud. However, the dust of the anthers does not penetrate through the style to the germen and the beginnings of the seed, as some writers have supposed. The contrary appears to be the case from opening the large flower of an oriental rough poppy and cutting its **pistil** <note>original: "pistillum"</note> perpendicularly downwards; the **lamellae** <note>original: "lamellæ," meaning thin plates or folds</note>, the **placentas** <note>original: "placentæ," the part of the ovary where seeds attach</note>, and the small seeds sticking to them will be found to be a pure white color, even though at the same time the style and the entire stigma are completely stained with a purple hue from the dust of the anthers. Hence, we conclude that not one grain or particle of the **pollen** <note>original: "farina," literally "flour"</note> enters the folds of the receptacle or the seeds themselves.

We may close this account by observing, overall, that the **calyx** <note>the green outer leaves of a flower</note> is the marriage-bed in which the **stamens** <note>original: "stamina"</note> and **pistils** <note>original: "pistilla"</note>—the male and female organs—celebrate the nuptials of plants, and where they are cherished and defended from external injuries. The **corolla** or petals are the curtains closely surrounding the reproductive organs in order to keep off storms, rain, or cold; but when the sun shines bright, they freely expand, both to give access to the sun’s rays and the fertilizing <note>original: "fecundating"</note> dust. 

The **filaments** are the spermatic vessels by which the juice, secreted from the plant, is carried to the anthers. The **anthers** <note>original: "antheræ"</note> are the testicles and may not improperly be compared to the soft roe or milt of fishes. The dust of the anthers corresponds to the sperm and seminal microscopic organisms <note>original: "animalcules"</note>; for though it is dry so that it may be more easily carried by the wind, it becomes moist upon touching the stigma. The **stigma** is that external part of the female organ which receives the male dust and on which the male dust acts. The **style** is the vagina or tube through which the essence <note>original: "effluvia"</note> of the male dust passes to the germen or seed-bud. The **germen** is the ovary, for it contains the unimpregnated or unfertilized seeds. The stomach of plants is the earth, from which they receive their nourishment, and the finest and most subtle parts of its soil is their **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid containing nutrients that is absorbed during digestion</term>. The root, which carries the chyle from the stomach to the body of the plant, is analogous to the **lacteals** or **chyliferous vessels** <term>vessels that carry nutrients to the bloodstream</term> of animals. The trunk, which supports and gives strength to the whole plant, is analogous to the bones. The leaves, by which plants **transpire** <note>original: "transpire," meaning to release moisture</note>, serve as lungs. They may also be compared to the muscles of animals, for by their movement in the wind, the plant is put in motion. For this reason, herbs with leaves cannot thrive unless they have air; however, succulent plants which have no leaves thrive very well even when shut up in greenhouses and quite deprived of external air. 

Heat is to plants what the heart is to animals; for they have no heart, nor do they have any need for one, because they live like **polyps** <note>original: "polypes," simple aquatic organisms</note> in the animal kingdom. Their juices, mixed with air, are propelled through their vessels but are not circulated back again by returning vessels. Plants generally have their reproductive organs <note>original: "genital organs"</note> placed at their branches <note>original: "ramifications"</note>, just as animals have theirs at the branching of the **iliac vessels** <note>the major blood vessels of the pelvis</note>, with this difference: the branches of plants grow upward, whereas those of animals go downward or backward. Because of this, the ancients called a plant an "inverted animal." Pliny observes that there is a natural instinct for reproduction in plants, and that the males, by a certain gust of wind and subtle powder, consummate the "marriage" with the females.

Regarding the manner in which the pollen <note>original: "farina," literally "flour"</note> fertilizes <note>original: "fecundifies"</note>, Mr. Geoffroy <note>Etienne François Geoffroy (1672–1731), a French chemist and physician</note> proposes two opinions:

1. That the pollen, being always composed of sulfurous elements and full of subtle, penetrating parts (as appears from its sharp odor), falls on the **pistils** of the flowers and dissolves there. The subtlest of its parts then penetrate the substance of the pistil and the young fruit, causing a **fermentation** <note>here meaning a chemical or biological trigger</note> to open and unfold the young plant already enclosed in the **embryo** <note>the ovule or immature seed</note> of the seed. In this hypothesis, the seed is supposed to contain the plant in miniature, only needing a proper juice to unfold its parts and make them grow.

2. The second opinion is that the pollen of the flower is the first germ or bud of the new plant, and needs nothing to unfold it and enable it to grow except the juice it finds prepared in the embryos of the seed. 

The reader will observe that these two theories of vegetable reproduction bear a strict analogy to the two theories of animal reproduction: namely, either that the young animal is in the male seed <note>original: "semen masculinum"</note> and only needs the juice of the womb <note>original: "matrix"</note> to cherish and bring it forth; or that the animal is contained in the female egg <note>original: "ovum"</note> and needs only the male seed to trigger a fermentation, etc. Mr. Geoffroy prefers the idea that the actual seed is in the pollen, because even the best microscopes do not discover the least appearance of any bud in the little

# AND OCCULT SCIENCES.

The embryos of the grains, when examined before the **apices** <term>apices: the tips of the stamens, now called anthers, which produce pollen</term> have shed their dust. In leguminous plants <note>plants in the pea and bean family</note>, if the leaves and **stamens** <note>original: "stamina"</note> are removed and the pistil (the part that becomes the pod) is viewed with a microscope before the flower has opened, the little green transparent **vesicles** <note>original: "vesiculæ," small sac-like structures</note> that will become the grains will appear in their natural order; but they still show nothing but the mere coat or skin of the grain. If the observation is continued for several days in other flowers as they advance, the vesicles will be found to swell and gradually become filled with a clear liquid. Once the **pollen** <note>original: "farina," literally 'flour,' used historically to describe pollen dust</note> is shed and the petals fall, we observe a little greenish speck or globule floating around in this liquid. At first, there is no sign of organization in this little body; but in time, as it grows, we begin to distinguish two little leaves like two horns. The liquid gradually disappears as the little body grows, until at length the grain becomes quite opaque. Upon opening it, we find its cavity filled with a young plant in miniature, consisting of a little germ or **plumule** <note>original: "plumula," the embryonic shoot</note>, a little root, and the lobes of the bean or pea, etc.

The way this germ from the apex enters the vesicle of the seed is not very difficult to determine. Besides the fact that the cavity of the pistil reaches from the top down to the embryos of the grains, those grains or vesicles have a little aperture corresponding to the end of the pistil’s cavity. Thus, the small dust or **pollen** <note>original: "farina"</note> may easily fall through the opening into the mouth of the vesicle, which is the embryo of the grain. This cavity, or **cicatricula** <term>cicatricula: a small scar or opening on a seed, such as the hilum of a bean, where it was attached to the plant</term>, is much the same in most grains and is easily observed in peas and beans without a microscope. The root of the little germ is positioned right against this opening, and it is through this that it passes out when the grain begins to germinate.

From what has been said, it is evident that unless the female plant is impregnated by the male, it can produce no fruit or seed that will grow. This holds true throughout the entire system of vegetation. But since trees and plants are immovably fixed and cannot roam about like animals in search of a mate, the all-wise Creator has compensated for this by means of little insects like the bee and the winds. These undoubtedly carry the pollen, or fertilizing matter of the male, to the **pistils** <note>original: "pistilla"</note> of the female, resulting in impregnation and generation. However, in the production of fruit, this is often a chance event which sometimes happens in abundance and at other times only sparingly. Therefore, those who cultivate fruit have been led by art to assist nature in this necessary contact of the sexes. While in Arabia, I was taken to see this curious operation performed on the date tree, by which the Arabs always ensure a plentiful harvest of that fruit. This crop is of great importance to their trade, and this art appears to have been known among them long before any...

### A KEY TO PHYSIC.

In the flower, these parts are also revealed; so that within the blossom, we find all the internal structures of a plant laid open.

The stomach of plants is the earth, from which they receive their nourishment, and the finest and most subtle parts of its soil constitute their **chyle** <term>chyle: a milky fluid containing nutrients, formed during digestion</term>. The root, which carries the chyle from the stomach to the body of the plant, is analogous to the **lacteals** <term>lacteals: vessels that carry nutrients from the intestines into the bloodstream</term> or chyle-bearing vessels of animals. The trunk, which supports and gives strength to the whole plant, is analogous to the bones. The leaves, through which plants transpire, serve as the lungs; they may also be compared to the muscles of animals, for by their movement in the wind, the plant is put into motion. For this reason, leafy herbs cannot thrive unless they have access to air; however, succulent plants which have no leaves can thrive very well even when shut up in greenhouses and completely deprived of external air. 

Heat is to plants what the heart is to animals; for plants have no heart, nor do they have any need for one. This is because they live like **polyps** <note>original: "polypes," simple aquatic organisms like corals or jellyfish which were then thought to bridge the gap between plants and animals</note> in the animal kingdom; their juices, mixed with air, are propelled through their vessels but are not circulated back again by returning vessels <note>The author correctly notes that plants lack a circulatory system like that of animals, where blood returns to a heart</note>. Plants generally have their reproductive organs located where their branches divide, just as animals have theirs at the division of the **iliac vessels** <term>iliac vessels: large blood vessels in the pelvic area where the body branches into the legs</term>, with this difference: the branches of plants grow upward, whereas those of animals go downward or backward. Because of this, the ancients called a plant an "inverted animal." Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (23–79 AD), a Roman naturalist</note> observes that there is a natural instinct for reproduction in plants, and that the males, by a certain breeze and subtle powder, complete the marriage with the females.

Regarding the manner in which the **pollen** <note>original: "farina," literally 'flour'</note> fertilizes the plant, **Mr. Geoffroy** <note>Etienne François Geoffroy (1672–1731), a French chemist and physician who studied plant reproduction</note> proposes two opinions:

1.  That the pollen, being always composed of a sulfurous substance and full of subtle, penetrating parts (as evidenced by its sharp odor), falls on the pistils of the flowers. There it dissolves, and its most subtle parts penetrate the substance of the pistil and the young fruit. This triggers a fermentation that opens and unfolds the young plant enclosed within the embryo of the seed. In this hypothesis, the seed is supposed to contain the plant in miniature, only needing a proper fluid to unfold its parts and make them grow.

2.  The second opinion is that the pollen of the flower is the first germ or bud of the new plant. It needs nothing to unfold it and enable it to grow except the juice it finds prepared in the embryos of the seed. 

The reader will observe that these two theories of vegetable reproduction bear a strict analogy to the two theories of animal reproduction: namely, either that the young animal is in the **male seed** <note>original: "semen masculinum"</note> and only needs the fluids of the **womb** <note>original: "matrix"</note> to nourish and bring it forth; or that the animal is contained in the female **egg** <note>original: "ovum"</note> and only needs the male seed to trigger fermentation, etc. Mr. Geoffroy tends to believe the actual seed is in the pollen, because even the best microscopes do not discover the slightest appearance of a bud in the little...

The liquid diminishes imperceptibly as the little body grows, until at length the grain becomes quite opaque. Upon opening it, we find its cavity filled with a young plant in miniature, consisting of a little shoot <note>original: "germ or plumula"</note>, a little root, and the lobes of the bean or pea.

The way in which this germ from the tip enters the vesicle <note>original: "vesicula"</note> of the seed is not very difficult to determine. no botanist had dreamed of the difference of sexes in vegetables. The gardener informed me of this, but was surprised to find I knew the circumstance already; for, he says, all who come from Europe to this country have regarded this operation as a fable. When they observe a tree where the spadix <note>a spike of flowers</note> has female flowers, they search on a tree that has male flowers (which they know by custom and experience) for a male spadix which has not yet burst out of its spatha <note>a large sheath or leaf-like bract</note> or husk. This they open, take out the spadix, and cut it lengthwise into several pieces, taking care not to hurt the flowers. These pieces of the male spadix they put lengthwise between the small branches of the spadix which has female flowers, and then cover them over with a palm leaf. In this situation, the pistils <note>original: "pistilla"</note> of the female flower become impregnated by the male, which soon after withers and dies; unless the natives "marry" and fertilize <note>original: "fecundate"</note> the female date tree in this way, it bears no fruit. 

Even if they allow the spadix of the male flower to burst or come out before it is taken, it is useless for fertilization; for this purpose, it must have its *maidenhead*, as the Arabs term it, or it will not work; and this is lost the moment the blossoms burst out of their case. From this curious process of nature in the generation of vegetables, and from a contemplation of the apparatus she has contrived for that purpose, many useful hints may be derived on how to alter, improve, enrich, and vary the taste, form, and quality of fruits, etc., by impregnating the flower of one with the pollen <note>original: "farina"</note> of another of the same class. It is to this artificial coupling and mixing that we attribute the numberless varieties of new fruits, flowers, etc., produced every year by our nurserymen and gardeners, along with many other phenomena in the vegetable kingdom.

In the cultivation of many of our home plants, we sometimes meet with circumstances not unlike those of the date tree, which become barren when deprived of the males. Thus, if the flowers of the male hemp are pulled off before those of the female are fully expanded, the females do not produce fertile seeds. However, as a male flower is sometimes found upon a female plant, this may be the reason why fertile seeds are sometimes produced even after this precaution has been observed. The tulip affords another experiment for the same purpose: cut off all the anthers <note>original: "antheræ"</note> of a red tulip before the pollen is released; then take the ripe anthers of a white tulip and throw the white pollen upon the stigma of the red. The seeds of the red tulip, being thus impregnated by one of a different color <note>original: "complexion"</note>, will produce some red, some white, but mostly variegated flowers the next season.

On account of its similarity to the toadflax in every part but the flower, Linnaeus imagined it to have been produced by a chance mixing <note>original: "fortuitous commixture"</note> of the toadflax with some other plant. From this doctrine, he supposes that only two species of each genus of plants existed *from the beginning* <note>original: "ab origine"</note>, and that all the variety of species which now appear have been produced by "unnatural embraces" between species of different genera. In support of this theory, he defends the case of Richard Baal, a gardener at Brentford. This Baal sold a large quantity of the seeds of the cauliflower <note>original: "brassica florida"</note> to several gardeners in the suburbs of London. These gardeners, after sowing their seeds in the usual manner, were surprised to find them turn out to be plants of a different species from that which Baal made them believe they had purchased; for, instead of the cauliflower, the plants turned out to be long-leaved cabbage <note>original: "brassica longifolia"</note>. The gardeners, upon making this discovery, began a prosecution for fraud against Baal in Westminster Hall. The court found Baal guilty of fraud and ordered <note>original: "decerned"</note> him not only to return the price of the seeds, but also to pay the gardeners for their lost time and the use of their ground.

> "Had these judges (says Linnaeus) been acquainted with the sexual generation of plants, they would not have found Baal guilty of any crime, but would have attributed the accident to the chance impregnation of the cauliflower by the pollen of the long-leaved cabbage."

With respect to the nourishment of plants, we need only look to the analogy that is known to exist between plants and animals. It is highly probable that the root fibres of plants take up their nourishment from the earth in the same manner that the lacteal vessels <note>small vessels that absorb fats from the digestive tract</note> absorb nutrients from the intestines. As the oily and watery parts of our food are perfectly united into a milky liquid by means of saliva <note>original: "spittle"</note>, pancreatic juice, and bile before they enter the lacteals, we have every reason to maintain the analogy and suppose that the oily <note>original: "oleaginous"</note> and watery parts of the soil are also blended together before they are taken up by the absorbing vessels of the plant. To form a perfect judgment of this, we must consider that every soil, in its natural state, contains enough absorbent earth to blend its inherent oil and water. However, when we load the soil with "fat" manures <note>manures high in organic matter or oils</note>, it becomes essential to provide it with something at the same time to help mix <note>original: "assimilate"</note> the parts. Lime, soap-ashes, kelp, marl, and all alkaline substances perform that office. In order to make this process visible to the senses, dissolve one dram of Russian potash in four ounces of water; then add one spoonful of oil. # A KEY TO PHYSIC,

...a familiar experiment is a clear <note>original: "just"</note> representation of what happens after the process of paring and burning the turf <note>original: "burn-baking"</note>, and consequently, may be considered as a confirmation of the hypothesis proposed. In this process, as the grassy surface <note>original: "sward"</note> is reduced to ashes, a fixed alkaline salt <note>Potash or wood ash residue</note> is produced. The moisture of the atmosphere soon dissolves that salt into a liquid state; this liquid, mixing with the soil, brings about a union of the oily and watery parts, in the manner demonstrated in the experiment. 

When the underlying layer <note>original: "under stratum"</note> consists of a rich vegetable compost <note>original: "mould"</note>, the effects of paring and burning will be long-lasting. However, when the soil happens to be thin and poor, the first crop frequently suffers before it reaches maturity. The farmer, therefore, who goes to the expense of paring and burning a thin soil should provide it with a portion of rotten dung or slaughterhouse manure <note>original: "shambles manure"</note> before the ashes are spread. This is necessary to supply the lack of oily particles; in this way, the crop will be supported during its growth, and the land will be preserved in health and vigor. 

But plants do not only receive nourishment through their roots; they also receive it through their leaves. Vegetables that have a succulent leaf—such as vetches <note>a type of legume</note>, peas, beans, and buckwheat—draw a great part of their nourishment from the air. On that account, they deplete <note>original: "impoverish"</note> the soil less than wheat, oats, barley, or rye, the leaves of which have a firmer texture. Rape and hemp are oil-bearing plants and, consequently, they deplete the soil; however, rape does so less than hemp because of its more succulent leaf. The leaves of all kinds of grain are succulent for a time, during which period the plants take little from the earth; but as soon as the ear begins to form, they lose their softness and their power of attraction diminishes. The root fibers <note>original: "radical fibres"</note> are then more vigorously employed in extracting the oily particles of the earth for the nourishment of the seed. 

The leaves of plants serve not only as discharge pores <note>original: "excretory ducts"</note> to separate and carry off the excess watery fluid (which, if held too long in the plants, would turn rancid and harmful to them), but they also serve to absorb the dew and rain, which contain salt, sulfur, etc. In this way, leaves serve the same purpose for plants that the lungs do for animals. But, as plants do not have a chest <note>original: "thorax"</note> that expands and contracts, their "breathing in" and "breathing out" <note>original: "inspirations and expirations"</note> are not as frequent as those of animals. Instead, they depend entirely on the alternating changes from hot to cold for "breathing in," and the other way around <note>original: "vice versa"</note>—from cold to hot—for "breathing out." 

However, the greater part of their nourishment is derived from the roots. These, therefore, are found to be quite large in proportion to the body of the plant above ground; the surface area <note>original: "superficies"</note> of the roots is more than four-tenths of the surface area of the plant above. This explains the necessity of cutting off many branches from a transplanted tree; because, in digging it up, a great part of its roots is inevitably cut off. 

It is a curious, hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> fact regarding vegetables that they thrive best from decay <note>original: "putrefaction"</note> and flourish most in putrid air. Manure, though it has a stench almost...

Plants, when forced from their natural position, are endowed with a power to restore themselves. A hop-plant, twisting <note>The original text uses "twifting," an OCR error for the archaic "twisting," where the "long s" (ſ) was mistaken for an "f."</note> around a stick, directs its course from south to west, just as the sun does. If you untwist it and tie it in the opposite direction, it dies. If you leave it loose in the wrong direction, it recovers its natural direction in a single night. Twist a branch of a tree so as to invert its leaves and fix it in that position; if left in any degree loose, it untwists itself gradually until the leaves are restored to their natural position. What better can an animal do for its own welfare?

A root of a tree, meeting with a ditch in its progress, is laid open to the air. What follows? It alters its course like a rational being; it dips into the ground, undermines the ditch, rises on the opposite side to its usual distance from the surface, and then proceeds in its original direction. Lay a wet sponge near a root exposed to the air; the root will direct its course toward the sponge. Change the place of the sponge, and the root varies its direction. Put a pole into the ground at a moderate distance from a climbing <term>original: "scandent"</term> plant; the plant directs its course to the pole, lays hold of it, and rises to its natural height. 

A honeysuckle <note>original: "honeyfuckle"</note> proceeds in its course until it is too long to support its own weight, and then it strengthens itself by growing into a spiral. If it meets with another plant of the same kind, they merge for mutual support—the one spiraling to the right, the other to the left. If a honeysuckle twig meets with a dead branch, it spirals from the right to the left. The tendrils <term>original: "claspers"</term> of bryony <note>original: "briony"</note> grow into a spiral and lay hold of whatever comes in their way for support. If, after completing a spiral of three rounds, they find nothing, they then try again for further support by altering their course.

By comparing these and other instances of seemingly voluntary motion in plants with the degree of life endowed to some of the lower kinds of animals, we can scarcely hesitate to ascribe superiority to the former—that is, if we set the question of sensation aside. Mussels <note>original: "muscles"; the author refers to the shellfish</note>, for instance, are fixed to one place as much as plants are; nor do they have any power of motion besides that of opening and shutting their shells. In this respect, they have no superiority over the motion of the sensitive plant <note>Mimosa pudica, a plant famous for folding its leaves when touched</note>; nor does their action reveal more intelligence <term>original: "sagacity"</term>—or even as much—as the roots of the plane tree or the actions of other vegetables.

A simple experiment accurately represents what happens during the process of "burn-baking" <term>paring and burning the top layer of soil to create fertilizer</term> and can be seen as confirming the theory presented. In this process, the sod <note>original: "sward"</note> is burned to ashes, producing a concentrated alkaline salt <note>Potash, used as a fertilizer</note>. Moisture from the air soon dissolves that salt into a liquid, which, when mixing with the soil, causes the oily and watery components to bond together, just as shown in the experiment. When the layer beneath consists of a rich organic soil <note>original: "vegetable mould"</note>, the effects of burn-baking will be lasting. However, if the soil is thin and poor, the first crop often struggles before it even reaches maturity. Therefore, a farmer who goes to the expense of paring and burning thin soil should also add a portion of rotten dung or slaughterhouse manure <note>original: "shambles manure"</note> before the ashes are spread. This provides the necessary oily particles the soil lacks. By doing this, the crop is supported throughout its growth, and the land remains healthy and productive.

But plants do not only receive nourishment through their roots; they also take it in through their leaves. Vegetables with fleshy <note>original: "succulent"</note> leaves—such as vetches, peas, beans, and buckwheat—draw much of their nourishment from the air. Because of this, they deplete the soil less than wheat, oats, barley, or rye, which have leaves with a tougher texture. Rape and hemp are oil-bearing plants and, as a result, they drain the soil of nutrients; however, rape does this less than hemp because its leaves are meatier. The leaves of all grains are fleshy for a while, and during this time, the plants take very little from the earth. However, as soon as the grain head begins to form, the leaves lose their softness and their ability to draw nutrients from the air decreases. The root fibers <note>original: "radical fibres"</note> then work more intensely to extract oily particles from the earth to nourish the developing seeds. 

The leaves of plants serve not only as drainage channels <note>original: "excretory ducts"</note> to remove excess water—which would become rancid and harmful to the plant if kept inside too long—but also to absorb dew and rain, which contain salt, sulfur, and other minerals. In this way, they serve the same purpose for plants that lungs do for animals. However, because plants do not have a chest <note>original: "thorax"</note> that expands and contracts, they do not "breathe" as frequently as animals. Instead, their inhalation and exhalation depend entirely on temperature changes: they inhale when the temperature changes from hot to cold, and the other way around <note>original: "vice versa"</note> when it changes from cold to hot. 

Despite this, the majority of their nourishment comes from the roots. Consequently, roots make up a large portion of the plant's total structure; the surface area <note>original: "superficies"</note> of the roots is more than four-tenths the size of the plant above ground. This explains why it is necessary to prune many branches when transplanting a tree: because digging it up removes a large portion of its roots.

A honeysuckle proceeds in its course until it is too long to support its own weight, and then strengthens itself by shooting into a spiral. If it meets with another plant of the same kind, they coalesce <note>grow together or unite</note> for mutual support—the one screwing to the right, the other to the left. If a honeysuckle twig meets with a dead branch, it screws from the right to the left. The tendrils <note>original: "claspers"</note> of briony shoot into a spiral and lay hold of whatever comes in their way for support. If, after completing a spiral of three rounds, they meet with nothing, they then try again for further support by altering their course.

By comparing these and other instances of seeming voluntary motion in plants with that share of life with which some of the inferior kinds of animals are endowed, we can scarcely hesitate to ascribe the superiority to the former—that is, putting sensation out of the question. Mussels <note>original: "muscles"</note>, for instance, are fixed to one place as much as plants are; nor have they any power of motion besides that of opening and shutting their shells. In this respect, they have no superiority over the motion of the sensitive plant <note>Mimosa pudica, known for folding its leaves when touched</note>; nor does their action discover more sagacity—or even as much—as the roots of the plane-tree or the action of other vegetables.

M. Buffon <note>Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon (1707–1788), a famous French naturalist</note>, who seems to be desirous of confounding the animal and vegetable kingdoms, denies sensation to be any essential distinction. "Sensation," says he, "more essentially distinguishes animals from vegetables; but sensation is a complex idea..."

A familiar experiment provides a fair representation of what happens after the operation of paring and burning <note>original: "burn-baking"</note> the soil, and consequently may be considered as a confirmation of the hypothesis advanced. In this process, the turf <note>original: "sward"</note> being reduced to ashes, a fixed alkaline salt <note>This refers to potash, a chemical found in wood and plant ashes that acts as a fertilizer.</note> is produced; the moisture of the atmosphere soon reduces that salt into a fluid state, which, mixing with the soil, brings about a union of the oily and watery parts, in the manner demonstrated in the experiment. When the lower layer <note>original: "under stratum"</note> consists of a rich soil <note>original: "vegetable mould"</note>, the effects of paring and burning will be lasting; but when the soil happens to be thin and poor, the first crop frequently suffers before it arrives at maturity. The farmer, therefore, who goes to the expense of paring and burning a thin soil, should provide it with a portion of rotten dung, or manure from slaughterhouses <term>shambles manure</term>, before the ashes are spread, in order to supply the deficiency of oily particles. In this way, the crop will be supported during its growth, and the land will be preserved in health and vigor. 

But plants receive nourishment not only by their roots, but also by their leaves. Vegetables that have a fleshy <note>original: "succulent"</note> leaf, such as vetches, peas, beans, and buckwheat, draw a great part of their nourishment from the air, and for that reason impoverish the soil less than wheat, oats, barley, or rye, the leaves of which have a firmer texture. Rape and hemp are oil-bearing plants and, consequently, they drain the soil of its nutrients; however, rape does so less than hemp because of its leafier, more succulent nature. The leaves of all kinds of grain are succulent for a time, during which period the plants take little from the earth; but as soon as the ear begins to form, they lose their softness and their power to attract nourishment from the air diminishes. The root fibers <note>original: "radical fibres"</note> are then more vigorously employed in extracting the oily particles of the earth for the nourishment of the seed. 

The leaves of plants serve not only as channels <note>original: "excretory ducts"</note> to separate and carry off excess water—which, if held too long in the plants, would turn rancid and harmful to them—but also to soak up dew and rain, which contain salt, sulfur, etc. In this way, leaves serve the same purpose for plants that the lungs do for animals. But as plants do not have a chest <term>thorax</term> that expands and contracts, their "breathing" <note>original: "inspirations and expirations"</note> is not as frequent as those of animals; instead, it depends entirely on the alternating changes from hot to cold for inhalation, and the other way around <note>original: "vice versa"</note> for exhalation. 

However, the greater part of their nourishment is derived from the roots. These, therefore, are found to be quite large in proportion to the body of the plant above ground; the surface area <note>original: "superficies"</note> of the roots is more than four-tenths that of the plant above. This explains the necessity of cutting off many branches from a transplanted tree; because when it is dug up, a great portion of its roots is inevitably cut off.

It is a curious hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> fact regarding vegetables that they thrive best from rotting matter <note>original: "putrefaction"</note> and flourish most in putrid air. Manure, though it has a stench almost...

Plants, when forced from their natural position, are endowed with a power to restore themselves. A hop plant, twisting around a pole, directs its course from south to west, just as the sun does. If you untwist it and tie it in the opposite direction, it dies. If you leave it loose in the wrong direction, it recovers its natural direction in a single night. It is no doubt, however, just as much a responsibility for those who take the contrary side of the question to prove that vegetables are not endowed with sensation as it was necessary for Monsieur Buffon to prove that they are. But a little attention will show us that the difficulty here proceeds entirely from our inability to see the principle of sensation. We perceive this principle in ourselves, but no man can perceive it in another. Why then does every individual of mankind conclude that his neighbor has the same sensations as himself? It can only be from analogy. Every man perceives his neighbor formed in a manner similar to himself; he acts in a similar manner on similar occasions, and so on. Just so it is with non-human animals. It is no more doubtful that they have sensations than that we have them ourselves. If a man is wounded with a knife, for instance, he expresses a sense of pain and endeavors to avoid a repetition of the injury. We must further take notice that there are sensations essentially distinct from one another; and in proportion as an animal is endowed with more or fewer of these different species, it is more or less perfect as an animal. But as long as only one of them remains, it makes not the least approach to the vegetable kingdom; and when they are all taken away, it is so far from becoming a vegetable that it is only a mass of dead matter. The senses of a perfect animal, for instance, are five in number. Take away one of them—suppose sight—he becomes then a less perfect animal, but remains as unlike a vegetable as before. Suppose him next deprived of hearing; his resemblance to a vegetable would be as little as before because a vegetable can neither feel, taste, nor smell, and we suppose him still to enjoy these three senses. Let us, lastly, suppose him endowed only with the sense of feeling—which, however, seems to include that of taste—and he is no more a vegetable than formerly, but only an imperfect animal. If this sense is then taken away, we connect him not with the vegetable kingdom, but with what <term>M. Buffon</term> <note>original: "M. It is to this kingdom, and not to the vegetable, that animals plainly approximate as they descend in complexity. 

Indeed, to suppose an approximation between the vegetable and animal kingdoms is very absurd; for, at that rate, the most imperfect animal ought to be the most perfect plant, but we observe no such thing. Although all animals are possessed of vegetable life, these two seem to be as perfectly distinct and incommensurate to one another as any two things we can possibly imagine.

It is this principle of self-preservation in animals which, being the most powerful one in their nature, is generally taken—and with very good reason—as the true characteristic of animal life. This principle is undoubtedly a consequence of sensation; and, as it is never observed to take place in vegetables, we have a right to say that the foundation of it, namely, sensation, does not belong to them. If we had been told this by God himself, we might have known that he gave plants <note>original: "them"; referring to the "vegetables" or plants discussed on the previous page.</note> to animals for food; in this case, to have endowed plants with sensation <note>The ability to feel or perceive.</note> would have been cruelty. Though countless animals prey upon one another, all of them possess some means of defense. From this, we justly conclude that their mutual destruction was not an original appointment of the Creator. Instead, it was something that followed from the Fall of Adam, which God foresaw would happen over the course of time and for which he gave every animal some means of guarding against.

It may, no doubt, be objected here that giving some means of self-defense to every animal cannot be considered sufficient proof that the Creator did not originally intend for them to be destroyed, seeing as these means are not always effective for their preservation. This objection, however, cannot be completely resolved without solving the question concerning the origin of evil among the works of a perfectly good being. But whatever difficulty there may be in solving that question, it is certain that because some means of self-defense is given to every animal, it was the original design of the Creator that, in all cases, one species of animal should not be destroyed at the mere pleasure or will of another. Conversely, as no means of self-defense is given to any plant, it is plain that they were destined to be prey for every species of animal that had access to them.

Philosophers have insisted much on the necessity of one animal devouring another so that there might be sufficient room for all. However, far from being a system worthy of divine wisdom, this seems to be a criticism of it—as if the Author of Nature could not have found means to preserve the life of one part of his creatures without the destruction and misery of the rest. The sacred writings leave us at no loss to see how this carnivorous nature began; and in the next world, this "piece of perfection" (as the bloodthirsty <note>original: "sanguinary"</note> philosophers mentioned above would have it) seems to be left out. For there, it is said, "They shall not hurt nor destroy; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and there shall be no more pain." <note>A reference to the prophecy of the Peaceable Kingdom in Isaiah 11 and 65.</note>

### ON ANIMAL FLOWERS.

The primary argument for plants possessing animal life was inferred from the curious construction of the freshwater hydra <note>original: "polypus"; a tiny aquatic animal capable of regenerating parts of its body.</note> and the *actinia* genus, called animal flowers, sea-anemones, sea-sunflowers, and so on. These indeed have the external form and figure of plants, with scarcely any movement from place to place <note>original: "progressive motion"</note>, and might easily deceive superficial observers. But when examined more minutely, the hydra and the entire *actinia* class turn out to be absolute animals of the viviparous kind <note>Giving birth to live young; while anemones can reproduce this way, they are now known to be invertebrates rather than mammals.</note> that feed on fish. They are called flower-fish <note>An early term for sea anemones, which were often seen as a "link" between the plant and animal kingdoms.</note>. There is one species of them in which the purest white, carmine, and ultramarine are scarcely sufficient to express their brilliance. The bodies of some of them are hemispherical, of others cylindrical, and of others shaped like a fig. Their substance likewise differs; some are stiff and gelatinous, others fleshy and muscular; but all of them are capable of altering their figure when they extend their bodies and claws <note>referring to their tentacles</note> in search of food. They are found on many of the rocky coasts of the West India islands, and on some parts of the coast of England. They have only one opening, which is in the center of the uppermost part of the animal; round this are placed rows of fleshy claws; this opening is the mouth of the animal, and is capable of great extension. The animals themselves, though exceedingly voracious, will bear long fasting. They may be preserved alive a whole year, or perhaps longer, in a vessel of seawater, without any visible food; but, when food is presented, one of them will successively devour two mussels <note>original: "muſcles"</note> in their shells, or even swallow a whole crab as large as a hen's egg. In a day or two the crab shell is voided at the mouth, perfectly cleared of all the meat. The mussel shells are likewise discharged whole, with the shells joined together, but entirely empty, so that not the least particle of fish is to be perceived on opening them. An anemone of one species will even swallow an individual of another species; but, after retaining it ten or twelve hours, will throw it up alive and uninjured. Through this opening also it produces its young ones alive, already furnished with little claws, which, as soon as they fix themselves, they begin to extend in search of food. One of the extremities of the sea anemone exactly resembles the outward leaves of that flower; while its limbs are not unlike the shag <note>The fuzzy or fibrous inner part of a flower.</note> or inner part of it. By the other extremity it fixes itself, as by a sucker, to the rocks or stones lying in the sand; but it is not totally deprived of the power of locomotion <note>original: "progreſſive motion"</note>, as it can shift its situation, though very slowly.

A peculiar species of animal-flowers, called the clustered animal-flower, has been found in some of the West India islands, an account of which was published in the *Philosophical Transactions* <note>The scientific journal of the Royal Society of London.</note>, volume 57 <note>original: "vol. lvii."</note>, by Mr. Ellis, in a letter to Lord Hillsborough. This compound animal, which is of a tender fleshy substance, consists of many tubular bodies, swelling gently towards the upper part, and ending like a bulb or very small onion; on the top of each is its mouth, surrounded by one or two rows of tentacles, or claws, which when contracted look like circles of beads. The lower part of all these bodies has a communication with a firm fleshy wrinkled tube, which sticks fast to the rocks, and sends forth other fleshy tubes, which creep along them in various directions. ### OF THE POLYPUS.

The Polype, or Polypus, which for so long divided the opinions of naturalists as to whether it was of a vegetable or animal nature, is a freshwater insect of the *Hydra* genus, in the class of worms and the order of *zoophytes* <note>original: "zoophytes"; a historical term for animals that look like plants, such as coral or sponges</note>, according to the Linnæan system <note>The biological classification system developed by Carl Linnaeus</note>. It has a cylindrical shape, though this varies, and possesses very long tentacula <note>original: "tentacula"; tentacles</note>, or claws. Hardly any animal in the world is more difficult to describe than this surprising insect; it changes its entire shape at will and is frequently found covered with young in such a way that it appears branched and forked <note>original: "ramose and divaricated"</note>. These young ones cling to it so closely that they seem to be part of its own body.

When it is in a simple and moderate state of contraction or expansion <note>original: "dilatation"</note>, it is oblong, slender, translucent <note>original: "pellucid"</note>, and of a pale reddish color. Its body is somewhat smaller toward the tail, by which it attaches itself to some solid object, and larger toward the other end. There it has a large opening called its mouth, around which are the <term>tentacula</term>, or claws. These are eight in number and are usually extended to about half the length of its body. By means of these tentacles—or arms, as they are commonly called—which can expand into a circle more than six inches <note>original: "half a foot"</note> in diameter, the creature feels everything that might serve as food. Seizing the prey with one of them, it calls upon the assistance of the others, if necessary, to guide the food to its mouth.

The way it produces its young differs from the common course of nature in other animals. A young one emerges from the side of its parent in the form of a small bump <note>original: "pimple"</note> which, growing longer every hour, becomes a complete animal in about two days and drops off its parent to fend for itself. However, before it detaches, it often has another young one growing from its own side, and sometimes a third growing from that one, even before the first has separated from the parent. What is very extraordinary is that no distinction of sex or evidence of mating <note>original: "copulation"</note> has ever been discovered among them. Every individual of the species is fertile, and remains so whether kept separate or allowed to live among others. But what is even more surprising is the regeneration <note>original: "reproduction"</note> of its various parts when cut off; for when it is cut into a number of separate pieces, it becomes as many distinct and separate animals in a day or two. Each piece has the ability to grow a head, a tail, and the other organs necessary for life and all animal functions.

There is no specific place on the body of the polyp from which the young are born; they sprout out like shoots or branches of a tree from all external parts of their bodies. Mr. <term>Trembley</term> <note>Abraham Trembley (1710–1784), a Genevan naturalist famous for his pioneering studies on Hydra and their regenerative abilities</note>, who had heard much of this creature and was determined to prove to himself through actual experiments whether it was a plant or an animal, cut one in the middle. Each of these provides nourishment not only for itself, but for the whole colony; an increase in the size of one polyp by its feeding contributes to the growth of the rest. Thus, a freshwater polyp becomes like a branched plant, or a creature composed of many bodies. Each of these has this singular characteristic: if one of them is cut in half, the separated part becomes a complete animal. ## OF THE POLYP.

The Polyp (or *Polypus*), which for a long time divided naturalists' opinions on whether it was a plant or an animal, is a freshwater insect of the *Hydra* genus. In the Linnæan system, it is classified as a worm in the order of *zoophytes* <note>original: "zoophytes"; a historical term for "animal-plants," organisms like coral or anemones that appear to have characteristics of both kingdoms</note>. It has a cylindrical shape that can change, with very long tentacles or claws. Scarcely any animal in the world is more difficult to describe than this surprising creature; it changes its entire shape at will and is often found covered with young in such a way that it appears <term>branched and spread out</term> <note>original: "ramose and divaricated"</note>. These young ones cling to it so closely that they seem to be parts of its own body.

When it is alone and in a normal state—neither contracted nor stretched—it is oblong, slender, <term>translucent</term> <note>original: "pellucid"</note>, and pale reddish in color. Its body is slightly narrower toward the tail, which it uses to attach itself to some solid object, and larger toward the other end, where it has a large opening called its mouth. Surrounding the mouth are eight tentacles (or claws), which are usually extended to about half the length of its body. By means of these tentacles—or arms, as they are commonly called—expanded into a circle more than six inches in diameter, the creature feels everything that can serve as food. Seizing the prey with one of them, it calls in the assistance of the others, if necessary, to pull it into its mouth.

->Of <term>ANIMALCULES</term>.<-
<note>original: "Animalcules"; an archaic term for microscopic organisms, literally meaning "little animals."</note>

The next most surprising part of animal nature is that of animalcules—a vast tribe of living beings that are entirely invisible to the naked eye. They cannot even be perceived to exist without the assistance of microscopes. The smallest living creatures our instruments can show are those that inhabit the water. While it is possible that animalcules just as tiny—or perhaps even more so—may fly in the air or crawl upon the earth, it is nearly impossible to bring such creatures under our examination. However, because water is transparent and confines the creatures within it, we are able to discover everything it contains down to a certain degree of smallness by applying a drop of it to our lenses <note>original: "glasses"</note>. Some of the most curious of these animalcules described by microscopic observers are as follows:

1. *The Hair-like Insect.* This is so named on account of its shape; it is extremely slender and is frequently a hundred and fifty times as long as it is wide. The body or middle part, which is nearly straight, appears in some to be composed of rings like the windpipe <note>original: "windpipe"; meaning the trachea</note> of land animals; in others, it seems instead to be scaled, or made up of rings that cross one another diagonally. Its two ends are hooked or bent to nearly the same degree, but in opposite directions. Since no eyes...

The hair-like insect was first discovered in a ditch at Norwich, where one end connects to the river and the other end to a second ditch into which several drains <note>original: "kennels" — open gutters or street drains</note> empty themselves. Even assuming only half or a quarter of it was composed of them, according to these dimensions, their numbers must exceed all imagination.

## 2. *Eels in paste, etc.* 

When paste is allowed to stand until it becomes sour, it is then found to be the home of countless microscopic organisms <term>animalcules</term>, which can be seen by the naked eye. Although their form cannot be perfectly distinguished, their motion is very noticeable, and the whole paste will seem to be alive. No. 3 represents one of these little eels <note>original: "anguillæ"</note> magnified. The most remarkable property of these insects is that they give birth to live young <term>viviparous</term>. 

If one of them is cut through near the middle, several oval bodies of different sizes will be seen to come out. These are young eels <note>original: "anguillæ"</note>, each of them coiled up and enclosed in its own membrane. This membrane is so extremely delicate that it is hardly visible even with the strongest magnifier while it encloses the embryo animal. The largest and most developed immediately break through this covering, unfold themselves, and wriggle about nimbly in the water; others get out, uncoil, and move themselves about more slowly; and the least mature remains entirely without motion. 

The **uterus**, or vessel that contains all these oval bodies, is composed of many small rings, not unlike the windpipe <note>original: "aspera arteria"</note> of land animals, and seems to be considerably elastic. As soon as the microscopic creature is cut in two, the oval bodies are pushed out with some force by the recoil of this organ <note>original: "bowel" — used here in a general sense for an internal duct or vessel</note>. A hundred or more of the young have been seen to come from the body of a single eel, which explains their enormous rate of reproduction, as several such large generations are likely produced in a short time. Microscopic organisms of a similar kind are also found in vinegar and, like those already described, are found to give birth to live young. But it is not only in acidic substances that such things are observed. In some fields of wheat, many grains...

3. The ***Proteus***, so named because it assumes a great number of different shapes, making it difficult to recognize as the same animal throughout its various transformations. Indeed, unless it is carefully watched while changing from one shape to another, it will often seem to become suddenly invisible. When water in which any sort of vegetable has been steeped <note>original: "infused"</note>, or in which animals have been preserved, has stood quietly for some days or weeks in a glass or other vessel, a slimy substance will collect on the sides. If some of this is taken up with the point of a penknife, placed on a slip of glass in a drop of water, and examined through a microscope, it will be found to harbor several kinds of tiny organisms <note>original: "animalcules"</note> that are seldom found swimming about in open water; the *Proteus* is one of these. 

Its shape is better understood from the following plate <note>This refers to an engraved illustration in the original book.</note> than from any description that could be given. Its substance and color seem to resemble that of a snail, and its overall shape bears a considerable resemblance to that of a swan. It swims back and forth with great vivacity but will now and then stop for a minute or two. During this time, its long neck is usually moved as far as it can reach—forwards and on every side—with a somewhat slow but steady <note>original: "equable"</note> motion like that of a snake, frequently extending to three times the length of its body, seemingly in search of food. 

No eyes or mouth-like openings can be seen in the head, but its actions plainly prove it to be an animal that can see. For although multitudes of different microscopic organisms <note>original: "animalcules"</note> swim about in the same water, and its own forward motion is very swift, it never strikes against any of them. Instead, it directs its course between them with a dexterity that would be wholly unaccountable if we supposed it lacked sight. When it is alarmed, it suddenly draws in its neck (as shown in the Plate at numbers 4 and 5), transforming itself into the shape shown at number 6. 4. ***The Wheel-animal, or Vorticella.*** <note>original: "Vorticella" is Latin for "little whirlpool." This organism is now known to modern science as a rotifer.</note> This wonderful microscopic organism <note>original: "animalcule"</note> is found in rainwater that has stood for some days in lead gutters, or in hollows of lead on the tops of houses, or in the slime or sediment left by such water; it may perhaps also be found in other places. In this dry state, it is globular in shape and no larger than a grain of sand, showing no signs of life. But when put into water, within half an hour a slow <note>original: "languid"</note> motion begins; the globule turns itself about, lengthens itself by slow degrees, and takes on the form of a lively maggot <note>The author uses "maggot" to describe the larva-like, elongated body of the rotifer.</note>. Numbers 10, 11, 12, and 13 show the different appearances of its wheels, and Numbers 14 and 15 show its globular form. 

The most remarkable part of this organism is its wheel-work. This consists of a couple of semicircular instruments around the edges of which many little fibers <note>original: "fibrillæ"; these are cilia, hair-like structures used for swimming and feeding</note> move themselves very briskly, sometimes with a kind of rotation and sometimes in a trembling or vibrating manner. When in this state, it sometimes unfastens its tail and swims along with great swiftness, seemingly in pursuit of its prey. Sometimes the wheels seem to be entire circles armed with small teeth, like those of the balance-wheel of a watch, appearing projected forward beyond the head and extending sideways somewhat wider than its diameter. The teeth or cogs of these wheels seem to stand very regularly at equal distances, but their shape varies according to their position, the degree of their protrusion, and perhaps the will of the animal itself. All the actions of this creature seem to imply intelligence <note>original: "sagacity"</note> and quickness of sensation. At the least touch or motion in the water, they instantly draw in their wheels. Their eyes seem to be located somewhere near the wheels because, while in the "maggot" state, its motions are slow and blundering; but after the wheels are pushed out, they are performed with great regularity, swiftness, and steadiness.

It may be observed that some grains appear blackish on the outside, as if they were scorched. However, when opened, they are found to contain a soft white substance. Upon close inspection, this appears to be nothing more than a <term>congeries</term> <note>original: "congeries"; a cluster or collection.</note> of threads or fibers lying close together in a parallel direction. They much resemble the unripe down of certain thistles if you were to cut open the flower-heads before they begin to bloom <note>original: "blow".</note>. This fibrous matter shows not the slightest sign of life or motion unless water is applied. But immediately upon wetting—provided the grains of wheat have been newly gathered—the supposed fibers separate and appear to be living creatures. Their motions at first are very slow <note>original: "languid".</note>, but they gradually become more active and vigorous, twisting and wriggling themselves much like the "eels in paste," <note>original: "eels in paste"; these are "vinegar eels" (Turbatrix aceti), tiny nematodes often found in unpasteurized vinegar or flour paste, a common reference in early microscopy.</note> though always slower and with less regularity.

3. The ***Proteus***, <note>original: "Proteus"; named after the Greek sea-god who could change his shape. In early microscopy, this name was applied to various organisms that shifted forms, such as certain ciliates or amoebas.</note> so called because it assumes a great number of different shapes, is so changeable that it is scarcely recognizable as the same animal in its various transformations. Indeed, unless it is carefully watched while passing from one shape to another, it will often seem to become suddenly invisible. When water—in which any sort of vegetable has been infused or animals preserved—has stood quietly for some days or weeks in a glass or other vessel, a slimy substance will collect on the sides. If some of this is taken up with the point of a pen-knife, placed on a slip of glass in a drop of water, and looked at through the microscope, it will be found to harbor several kinds of little animals <note>original: "animalcules".</note> that are seldom found swimming about in the open water; among these, the *Proteus* is one. Its shape is better understood from the following plate than from any description that could be given. Its substance and color seem to resemble that of a snail, and its whole shape appears to bear a considerable resemblance to that of a swan. It swims back and forth with great vivacity, but will now and then stop for a minute or two. During this time, its long neck is usually employed as far as it can reach—forwards and on every side—with a somewhat slow but steady motion like that of a snake. It frequently extends to three times the length of its body, seemingly in search of food. 

No eyes, nor any opening in the head like a mouth, can be discerned; however, its actions plainly prove it to be an animal that can feel. For, although multitudes of different <term>animalcules</term> <note>original: "animalcules"; an early term for microscopic organisms, literally meaning "little animals."</note> swim about in the same water and its own forward motion is very swift, it never strikes against any of them. Instead, it directs its course between them with a skill <note>original: "dexterity".</note> that would be wholly unaccountable if we supposed it lacked the sense of sight. When it is alarmed, it suddenly draws in its neck (as represented in the Plate at No. 4 and 5), transforming itself into the shape shown at No. 6. In this state, it becomes more opaque and moves about very slowly with the large end foremost. In addition to those mentioned above, several other species of animals equipped with "wheels" can be found in our waters; some of which appear to have a rotating motion, and others a vibrating one. Number 16 represents a type found in the ditch at Norwich where the "hair-like insect" is produced. These differ from the previous ones only by having very long tails. Numbers 17, 18, and 19 represent a species of wheel-animals that are also covered with shells. The body of this species consists of three parts, just like the others; however, in this case, the thorax <note>the chest or middle section of an insect or crustacean</note> and abdomen are not separated by any gut or middle vessel, but are joined directly together. The heart is clearly visible, having a regular rhythm of contraction and expansion <note>original: "systole and diastole"</note> at *a a a*, as in the previous species. 

These creatures occasionally pull themselves entirely inside their shells; the shell then appears to end in six short spikes on one side and two on the other. The young of this species are carried in small oval sacs <note>original: "sacculi"</note> or protective coverings <note>original: "integuments"</note> fastened to the outside of the lower part of their shells, somewhere near the tail. When a young one is about to break out of its covering, the parent assists it significantly by wagging its tail and striking the oval bag. This forces the young one’s head into the water, although its tail cannot be freed as quickly. In this state, the young one starts its wheels spinning and tries its hardest to free itself from its confinement. Once it has gotten clear, it swims away, wagging its tail just like the parent, and leaving the empty covering attached to the parent's shell. 

These wheel-animals are great pests to the water-flea, a diagram of which is shown in the following plate. Number 20 shows it magnified, with some wheel-animals attached to it. Number 21 shows the flea's natural size. These insects are often found in large numbers in the same water; in such cases, it is common to find five or six of these shelled wheel-animals <note>likely referring to "loricate" rotifers, which have a stiffened outer wall</note> fastened by their tails to the shell or antennae <note>original: "horns"</note> of the flea. This appears to cause the flea a great deal of distress; it cannot drive them away or shake them off, no matter how hard it tries.

### 6. *The Globe-animal*
This microscopic creature <term>animalcule</term>, represented at Number 24, appears exactly spherical <note>original: "globular"</note>, having no appearance of a head, tail, or fins. 7. **The Pipe-animal.** These creatures are found on the coast of Norfolk, living in small tubes or cases made of sandy matter, in such multitudes that they compose a mass sometimes three feet in length. Number 25 shows a piece of such a cluster <note>original: "congeries"</note> broken off, where *a a a a* represent the mouths or openings of the pipes where the little animals make their home. This body is composed of muscular rings <note>original: "ringlets"</note> like those of a worm, and is capable of great extension or contraction. The front <note>original: "anterior"</note> end or head, *d*, is exceedingly beautiful, having around it a double row of little arms arranged in a very regular order, which are likely used to catch its food and bring it to its mouth. Some of these tubes are found fossilized <note>original: "petrified"</note> and constitute one species of *syringoides* <note>original: "syringoides," a Latin term for tube-like fossils</note>.

8. **An Insect with net-like arms.** The properties and shape of this little animal are very extraordinary. It is found only in cascades where the water runs very fast. There, these insects are found in clusters, standing upright on their tails; when grouped together, they resemble the honeycombs of bees at the time they are filled with their pupae <note>original: "aureliæ"</note>. On being taken out of the water, they spin threads by which they hang exactly in the same manner as a garden spider. Number 27 shows one of these insects magnified. Its body appears curiously turned, as if on a lathe; at the tail are three sharp spines on which it raises itself and stands upright in the water. 

However, the most curious apparatus is around its head, where it is equipped with two instruments like fans or nets which serve to provide its food. These it frequently spreads out and draws in again; when drawn up, they are folded together with the utmost precision <note>original: "nicety and exactness"</note>, so as to be invisible when brought close to the body. At the base of these fans, a couple of claws are fastened to the lower part of the head; every time the nets are drawn in, these claws conduct whatever is caught in them to the animal's mouth. 

Some of these creatures were kept with water in a vial, but most of them died in two days. The rest, having spun themselves transparent cases (which were fastened either to the sides of the glass or to pieces of grass put into it), seemed to be changed into a kind of pupa <note>original: "chrysalis"</note>. None of them lived above three days; and though fresh water was given to them two or three times a day, within a few hours it would stink to an almost inconceivable degree—even at several yards' distance—even though, in proportion to the water, the total number of insects was no more than one to one million, one hundred and fifty thousand...

10. ***Spermatic Animals and Microscopic Organisms in Liquids.*** <note>original: "Animalcula Infusoria," referring to microorganisms found in infusions of organic matter</note>. The discovery of living microscopic organisms in the semen of most animals is claimed by Mr. Leeuwenhoek <note>original: "Lewenhoek"</note>. According to this naturalist, these organisms are found in the male seed of every kind of animal; their general appearance is much the same, nor does their size differ in proportion to the total size <note>original: "bulk"</note> of the animal to which they belong. The bodies of all of them seem to be of an elongated oval shape, with long, tapering, slender tails issuing from them. Because of this shape, they resemble tadpoles and have been frequently called by that name, though their tails are much longer in proportion to their bodies than those of tadpoles. It is also observable that the organisms in the seed of fishes have tails much longer and more slender than those in other animals—so much so that the tips of them cannot be seen without the best glasses and the closest attention. Figures 29, *a, b, c, d,* represent the spermatic organisms of the rabbit; and Figures 30, *e, f, g, h,* represent those found in the seed of a dog. 

The numbers of these organisms are inconceivable. On viewing the milt <term>milt</term> <note>the seminal fluid of fish</note> or seed of a male codfish through a microscope, innumerable multitudes of organisms are found within it. They are of such a tiny size that at least ten thousand of them could be contained within the volume of a single grain of sand. From this, it is concluded that the milt of this single fish contained more living microscopic creatures than there are people living in the whole world. To find the comparative size of these organisms, Mr. Leeuwenhoek placed a hair from his head near them. Through his microscope, the hair appeared an inch in width, and he was satisfied that at least sixty such organisms could easily lie across that diameter. He observed that when the water with which he had diluted the semen <note>original: "seed"</note> of a codfish evaporated <note>original: "exhaled"</note>, the little bodies of the microorganisms <term>animalcules</term> burst into pieces. This did not happen to those in the semen of a ram, and this is attributed <note>original: "imputed"</note> to the greater firmness and consistency of the latter, just as the flesh of a land animal is more compact than that of a fish. These microorganisms appear to be very vigorous and tenacious of life, for they may be observed to move long after the animal from which they are taken is dead. They also have this peculiarity: they are continually in motion without the least rest or intermission, provided there is enough fluid for them to swim about in. These microorganisms are found only in the semen; nothing showing the least sign <note>original: "token"</note> of life can be discovered by the best microscopes <note>original: "glasses"</note> in the blood, saliva <note>original: "spittle"</note>, urine, bile <note>original: "gall"</note>, or chyle <note>chyle: a milky fluid produced in the small intestine during digestion</note>. The **Microscopic Organisms in Liquids** <note>original: *Animalcula Infusoria*</note> take their name from being found in all kinds of either vegetable or animal infusions. Indeed, there is scarcely any kind of water—unless it is saturated <note>original: "impregnated"</note> with some mineral substance—that will not reveal living creatures. Mr. Leeuwenhoek <note>original: "Lewenhoek"</note> says that at first he could discern no living creatures in rainwater; but after it had stood for some days, he discovered innumerable microorganisms, many thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand, and as small in proportion to a mite as a bee is to a horse. In other rainwater, which had likewise stood for some time, he found the smallest sort he had ever seen; and in a few more days, he found others eight times as large as these and almost round. 

In another quantity of rainwater that had been exposed like the former, he discovered a type of microorganism with two little horns in continual motion. The space between the horns was flat, though the body was roundish but tapering a little toward the end; there, a tail appeared that was four times as long as the body and only as thick as a spider’s web. He observed several hundreds of these within the space a single grain of sand would occupy. If they happened upon the smallest filament or string, they became entangled in it; they would then stretch their bodies into an oblong shape and struggle hard to free their tails. 

He observed a second sort, which was oval-shaped, and he imagined the head to be at the pointed <note>original: "sharpest"</note> end. The body was flat, with several small feet moving exceedingly quickly, though they were not detectable <note>original: "discernible"</note> without a great deal of attention. Sometimes they changed their shape into a perfect circle, especially when the water began to dry up. Nor do the usual methods of killing animals seem effective at destroying their life force <term>vital principle</term>. For example, hot mutton gravy was sealed in a vial with a cork and then placed among hot ashes to kill every living creature that might exist in it as effectively as possible. > "On May 25, 1768, when the Fahrenheit thermometer read seventy degrees, I boiled a potato in New River water <note>The New River was a man-made canal opened in 1613 to supply London with fresh drinking water.</note> until it reached a mealy consistency. I put part of it, with an equal proportion of the boiling liquid, into a cylindrical glass jar that held a little less than half a pint, and covered it tightly with a glass lid. At the same time, I sliced an unboiled potato and put roughly the same quantity into a similar glass jar with the same proportion of unboiled New River water. I covered it with a glass lid and placed both vessels next to each other. 
> 
> On May 26, twenty-four hours later, I examined a small drop of each using the highest magnifier of a Wilson microscope <note>A popular 18th-century handheld microscope designed by James Wilson.</note>, which has a focal distance of one-fiftieth of an inch. To my amazement, both were full of rod-shaped <note>original: "linear shape"</note> microscopic organisms. They were clearly visible and moved back and forth with great speed; there appeared to be more animal life than vegetable particles in each drop. 
> 
> I have tried this experiment repeatedly and found it always succeeds in proportion to the heat of the surrounding <note>original: "circumambient"</note> air. Even in winter, if the liquids are kept properly warm, the experiment will succeed in two or three days. The organisms I observed are infinitely smaller than sperm cells <note>original: "spermatic animals"</note> and have a very different shape. Any careful observer who compares them will be convinced they are not related.
