Thus we have given as full an account as our limits allow of the most curious kinds of microscopic organisms <note>original: "animalcules"</note> that have been observed so far. We cannot, however, leave this subject without discussing the microscopic organisms found in human semen <note>original: "seed of man"</note>.

Before the invention of microscopes, the doctrine of spontaneous generation <note>original: "equivocal generation"</note>—regarding both certain kinds of animals and plants—was universally accepted. But this instrument soon convinced every intelligent person that those plants previously thought to be produced by spontaneous generation actually grew from seeds, and animals, in the same way, came from a male and female. However, as the microscope shed light on one part of nature, it left another involved in darkness. The origin of infusion microbes <note>original: "animalcula infusoria"</note> or of the sperm cells <note>original: "spermatic animals"</note> already mentioned remains just as unknown as many other kinds were when the doctrine of spontaneous generation was fully accepted.

The discovery of sperm cells was thought to shed some light on the mysterious process of reproduction <note>original: "generation"</note> itself, and these tiny creatures were imagined to each be individuals of the same species as the parent. In this theory, the infinite number of these organisms was an objection, and the difficulty remained as great as before. Monsieur <note>original: "M."</note> Buffon, however, as far as human reproduction is concerned, has given such a detailed account of the microscopic organisms <term>animalcules</term> <note>The term "animalcules" was used in the 18th century to describe any microscopic life; here, Buffon is describing spermatozoa.</note> in human semen <note>original: "seed of man"</note>, that we shall state it here for the information of the curious.

Having obtained the genitals <note>original: "private parts"</note> of a man who died a violent death, he extracted all the semen from them while they were still warm. Having examined a drop of it with a double microscope, it had the appearance shown in the illustration at No. 31. Large filaments appeared, which in some places spread out into branches and in others intermingled with one another. These filaments clearly appeared to be agitated by an internal wavy motion, like hollow tubes containing some moving substance. He distinctly saw this appearance change into the one shown at No. 32. Two of these filaments, which were joined lengthwise, gradually separated from each other in the middle, alternately approaching and receding like two tight cords fixed by the ends and pulled apart in the middle. These filaments were composed of globules that touched one another and resembled a string of beads <note>original: "chaplet of beads"</note>. After this, he observed that the filaments swelled in several places and perceived small globular bodies emerge from the swollen parts, which had a vibrating motion like a pendulum. These small bodies were attached to the filaments by small threads, which gradually lengthened as the bodies moved. At last, the small bodies detached themselves entirely from the filaments, pulling behind them the small thread, which looked like a tail. When a drop of the seminal fluid was diluted, these small bodies moved very briskly in all directions. The seminal matter was at first too thick, but it gradually became more fluid; as its fluidity increased, the filaments disappeared, but the small bodies became exceedingly numerous. Each of them had a long thread or tail attached to it, from which it clearly tried to get free. Their forward motion was extremely slow, during which they vibrated to the right and left, and at each vibration, they had a rolling, unsteady motion in a vertical direction.

At the end of two or three hours, as the seminal matter became even more fluid, a greater number of these moving bodies appeared. They were then freer from obstructions; their tails were shorter; their forward motion was more direct, and their side-to-side <note>original: "horizontal"</note> motion was greatly diminished. In five or six hours, the semen had acquired almost all the fluidity it could without decomposing. Most of the small bodies were now disengaged from their threads; their shape was oval. They moved forward with considerable speed, and, by their irregular motions backward and forward, they looked more like animals than ever before.

An objection has, however, been made to the existence of microscopic organisms <term>animalcules</term> in the semen, or in any other part of animal bodies, based on the total exclusion of air, which is found to be so necessary to the life of larger animals. Many instances, however, have been observed of large animals being found in such situations that they could not possibly have enjoyed the least benefit from the air for a great number of years; and in this state, they have not only lived but lived much longer than they would otherwise have done.

In Toulon harbor and the surrounding waters <note>original: "the road"</note> are found solid, hard stones that are perfectly intact, yet contain several living shellfish of an exquisite taste in different cells, secluded from all communication with the air. These are called *Dactyli*—that is, "Dates" <note>original: "i. e. Dates"</note>. To reach these fish, the stones must be broken with heavy hammers <note>original: "mauls"</note>. Also, along the coast of Ancona <note>original: "Anconia"</note> in the Adriatic, there are stones usually weighing about fifty pounds and sometimes even more; the outside is rugged and easily broken, but the inside is so hard as to require a strong arm and an iron hammer to break them. Within them, in separate niches, are found small shellfish, quite alive and very palatable, called *solenes* <note>Latin: razor clams</note> or *cappe lunghe* <note>Italian: "long clams," also referring to razor clams</note>. These facts are attested by Pierre Gassendi, Blondel, Mayol (the learned bishop of Sulturara), and more particularly by Ulisse Aldrovandi <note>original: "Aldrovandus"</note>, a physician of Bologna. The two latter speak of it as a common fact which they themselves saw.

<meta>This page continues a series of anecdotal reports regarding "entombed" animals—creatures found alive inside solid substances like wood or stone—used as evidence in the study of natural history and occult science.</meta>

### AND OCCULT SCIENCE.

“In the trunk of an elm, about the size of a fairly stout man, three or four feet above the root and exactly in the center, a live toad was found. It was medium-sized but lean, and it filled up the entire vacant space. As soon as an opening was made by splitting the wood, it scuttled away very hastily. A firmer and sounder elm never grew, so it cannot be supposed that the toad had crawled into it later. The egg or spawn from which it was formed must, by some very singular accident, have been lodged in the tree when it first began to grow. There the creature had lived without air, feeding on the substance of the tree, and growing only as the tree grew. This is attested by Mr. Hubert, a professor of philosophy at Caen.”

The volume for the year 1731 contains a similar observation, expressed in these words: “In 1719, we gave an account of a fact which, though improbable, was well attested: that a toad had been found living and growing in the stem of a medium-sized elm, without any way for the creature to come out or to have gotten in. M. Seigne, of Nantes, has laid before the academy a fact of the exact same nature, except that instead of an elm it was an oak, and larger than the elm, which increases the wonder. He judges, by the time required for the growth of the oak, that the toad must have survived in it without air or any <term>external nourishment</term> <note>original: "adventitious aliment"</note> for eighty or one hundred years. M. Seigne seems to have known nothing of the fact reported in 1719.”

With the two previous stories may be grouped a narrative by Ambroise Paré, chief surgeon to Henry III, King of France. Paré, who was a very sensible writer, relates the following fact, of which he was an eyewitness:

> “While I was (he says) at my country house near the village of Meudon, I was watching a quarryman whom I had set to break some very large and hard stones. In the middle of one, we found a huge toad, full of life, and without any visible opening by which it could have entered. I began to wonder how it was born, grew, and lived; but the laborer told me it was not the first time he had met with a toad and similar creatures within huge blocks of stone where there was no visible opening or crack.”

Observations of living toads found in very hard and solid stones occur in the works of several authors, particularly Baptist Fulgosa <note>Battista Fregoso (c. 1440–1504), a Doge of Genoa</note>, the famous physicians Agricola and Horstius, and Lord Verulam <note>Francis Bacon (1561–1626), a foundational figure in the scientific method</note>. Others give very <term>convincing</term> <note>original: "specious," here meaning plausible or fair-seeming</note> accounts of snakes, frogs, crabs, and lobsters being found alive, enclosed within blocks of marble, rocks, and large stones.

An instance similar to these, the truth of which we have no reason to doubt, was observed in this country in the year 1773, where a large toad was found in the middle of a piece of coal that did not have the slightest visible crack or fissure.

On the whole, though philosophers are not yet able to discover how these minute creatures are produced, it is clear that there really are animals much smaller than...

# A KEY TO PHYSIC.

...what we can see with our naked eye seems to be indisputable. And the subject evidently requires the utmost attention of philosophers, as well as further improvements in the construction of microscopes, to investigate and explain it fully. Most naturalists suspect another species or order of invisible microorganisms <note>original: "animalcules"</note>—those that escape the detection even of the best microscopes—and they offer many probable theories about them. Reason and analogy support the existence of infinite, imperceptible microorganisms. The naked eye can see everything from an elephant to a mite; but there, a new order begins, visible only through the microscope. This order includes all those from the size of a mite down to those twenty-seven million times smaller; and this category cannot yet be said to be fully understood, as the microscope has not yet reached its ultimate perfection.

Microorganisms are the cause of various disorders. The itch <note>likely referring to scabies</note>, according to several experiments, is a disorder arising from the irritation of a species of microorganism found in the blisters <note>original: "pustules"</note> of that condition. This makes it easy to understand how the disease is spread by contact from one person to another, as well as why the cure is achieved through external applications. Many other skin <note>original: "cutaneous"</note> eruptions, often supposed to originate in the blood, are nothing more than settlements made by colonies of these invisible beings. A swarm of them lands upon the skin and, finding a comfortable home in its pores, soon produces a puncture, along with scabs and irritation. 

But this is not the worst. Observation has long convinced me that a variety of internal complaints in the stomach, pancreas, lungs, liver, and intestines are brought on by swallowing millions of these and other imperceptible living creatures that inhabit raw vegetables and dirty <note>original: "foul"</note> water. Finding the heat and food of the stomach suitable <note>original: "congenial"</note> for their growth, they become a new species of an alarming size and prey upon the vital organs, to the great detriment of the patient’s health and often at the expense of his life, before the malady can be known or even suspected.

A patient of mine, a young man nearly eighteen years old, had been in a wasting condition <note>original: "consumptive habit"</note> for a considerable time and suffered from a stomach disorder. Even though he had consulted several eminent physicians and had taken various medicines, he never found the slightest relief <note>original: "alleviation"</note> from his pain. It appeared further that these tentacles or claws had been so strongly attached to the intestines or the lining of the stomach that they had resisted the power of all common remedies to remove them. The patient happily found immediate relief and is now healthy and robust.

From several other patients—who appeared to be in a "decline" <note>original: "consumptions"; a general term for wasting diseases</note>, or were afflicted with nausea or unusual sensations in the stomach and intestines—I have extracted living animals that would terrify many people to look upon. These must have come from the spawn or eggs of tiny creatures <note>original: "animalcules"</note> taken in with food. For this reason, I would advise all my readers to take the utmost care in washing and cleaning salads, watercress, and all raw vegetables. One should particularly guard against the long red worm which almost always lies concealed in the very heart or center of a head of celery. The same caution is necessary when eating all kinds of fruit, since nothing more abounds with microscopic organisms <note>original: "animalcules"</note> and various living creatures. Cold raw water, especially when stagnant, ought never to be drunk. It is always the safest way to boil your water before it is used in any kind of drink, or even if it is to be drunk alone.

I might here provide many other instances of persons who have developed living creatures in their bowels by swallowing the eggs or spawn of the parent animal. A young man, a servant to Lord Stawell <note>Henry Stawell Bilson-Legge, 2nd Baron Stawell (1757–1820)</note> at Holt Park near Farnham, Surrey, had eaten ravenously of watercress. Some time afterward, his health began to fail, and he complained of a constant sensation of pain at the pit of his stomach which no medicine could remove. His lordship, valuing the man, sent him to London for the advice of the most capable physicians, but still to no avail. In this state, he was sent home to his friends and given up as a lost and incurable case. At this stage, some strong emetics <note>medicines used to induce vomiting</note> were given to him by a country apothecary. To the amazement of everyone in the surrounding countryside, he threw up an incredible number of small tadpoles. These were evidently produced from spawn attached to the watercress, which had been eaten without care and perhaps without washing. The patient recovered rapidly, and in less than a month, he was able to resume his former occupation.

The form, arrangement, and order of the teeth are admirable and provide us with a noble example of the wisdom and goodness of the Creator. The front teeth are weaker and further from the center of the jaw, as they only prepare the food for the rest. The others, intended to grind and masticate <term>chew</term> the food, are accordingly stronger and placed near the center of motion. Their peculiar hardness is very remarkable, considering the tender substances from which they are formed. 

Furthermore, their various shapes in different creatures are equally noteworthy, as they are all carefully adapted to the specific food and needs of different species. In predatory animals <note>original: "the rapacious"</note>, they are designed for catching, holding, and tearing prey. In plant-eaters <note>original: "herbaceous"</note>, they are meant for gathering and the comminution <term>grinding into small pieces</term> of vegetables. In creatures without teeth, such as birds, the bill makes up for the defect. 

Additionally, the temporary absence of teeth is just as observable in certain stages of life. For instance, children have no teeth while they are unable to use them, preventing them from hurting themselves or their mothers. Yet, at the very age when they can begin to eat more substantial food and live without nursing—and when they begin to need teeth to help with speech—their teeth start to appear and grow gradually as they need them. When this first set is worn out or decayed, they are succeeded by a new set, which is firmer and more durable than the first.

## OF INSTINCT.

Instinct is a hidden <term>occult</term> power or disposition of the mind by which animals are unerringly directed to do spontaneously whatever is necessary for the preservation of the individual or the continuation of the species. Because of this, all the actions of animals <note>original: "brutes"</note>, or inferior creatures, are said to be directed by *instinct*, but those of man by *reason*. Philosophers, however, have greatly differed in their opinions concerning this subject, and modern authors are extremely at a loss where to draw the line. Some maintain that man is endowed with a greater number of instincts than any species of animal whatever. Others insist that in human nature there is no power or propensity at all which can properly be called instinctive. Some contend that animals are guided wholly by an invariable instinct, without the smallest power of memory or of any intellectual faculty; while others insist that they possess a vegetative soul <note>In historical philosophy, the "vegetative soul" was the basic life force responsible for growth and reproduction, shared by plants, animals, and humans.</note>, directed by a certain instinct, and are capable of reason, memory, and experience.

With respect to man, nothing can be more apparent than that—as he is the microcosm <term>a miniature version of the universe</term>, or the epitome of all created nature—he must of necessity partake of all its essential properties, of which *reason* and *instinct* rank among the foremost.

Upon the slightest reflection, it will be obvious to every reader that reason can never be exercised except through experience; consequently, until man has arrived at a certain degree of maturity, he must be directed in most of the leanings of nature by mere instinct. Thus an infant, a few moments after its birth, is directed by an instinctive impulse for its preservation to seek the breast and to suck it. To the same cause—in the earlier stages of life and in all savage, uneducated countries—are attributed the first sensations or desires for sexual intercourse <note>original: "copulation"</note>; these arise not from the pleasures of enjoyment, for they are then unknown, but from an impulsive instinct for the propagation of the species. ...is most suitable, both for convenience and strength. Bees, as if they knew this, make their cells in the shape of regular hexagons. As the honeycombs have cells on both sides, the cells may either be exactly opposite—having wall against wall <note>original: "partition against partition"</note>—or the bottom of a cell may rest upon the walls between the cells on the other side, which acts as a buttress to strengthen it. The latter method is best for strength; accordingly, the bottom of each cell rests against the point where three walls meet on the opposite side, which provides the greatest possible stability. The bottom of a cell may either be one flat surface <note>original: "plane"</note> perpendicular to the side walls, or it may be composed of several surfaces meeting at a solid angle in the center point. It is only in one of these two ways that all the cells can be identical without wasting room. And for the same purpose, if there is more than one surface at the bottom, there must be exactly three. It has been demonstrated that by making the bottoms of the cells consist of three surfaces meeting at a point, there is a significant saving of material and labor.

The bees, as if they were acquainted with these principles of solid geometry, follow them most accurately; the bottom of each cell is composed of three surfaces which make obtuse angles with the side walls and with one another, meeting in a point in the middle of the bottom. The three angles of this bottom are supported by three walls on the other side of the comb, and its center point is supported by the common intersection of those three walls. One more instance of the mathematical skill displayed in the structure of a honeycomb deserves to be mentioned. It is a curious mathematical problem to determine at what precise angle the three surfaces which compose the bottom of a cell ought to meet in order to achieve the greatest possible saving of material and labor. This is one of those problems belonging to the higher branches of mathematics called "maxima and minima" problems. The celebrated Colin Maclaurin <note>original: "M'Laurin"</note> solved it by a calculation using fluxions <note>A fluxion is an early term for a derivative in calculus, a method developed by Isaac Newton.</note>, which can be found in the *Transactions of the Royal Society of London*, and he determined the precise angle required. 

Upon the most exact measurement <note>original: "mensuration"</note> that the subject would allow, Maclaurin afterwards found that this is the very angle at which the three surfaces in the bottom of a honeycomb cell actually meet. If a honeycomb were a work of human art, every person of common sense would conclude, without hesitation, that the person who invented the design must have understood the principles on which it was constructed. We need not say that bees know none of these things. They work most geometrically without any knowledge of geometry—somewhat like a child who, by turning the handle of a barrel organ, makes good music without any knowledge of music. The art is not in the child, but in the person who made the organ. In like manner, when a bee makes its comb so geometrically...

...instinct of the parent wasp is the more remarkable because she does not feed upon flesh herself <note>original: "parent-waſp"; many species of wasps hunt insects to feed their larvae, even though the adults eat nectar</note>. Birds of the same species, unless restrained by peculiar circumstances, uniformly build their nests of the same materials, and in the same form and situation, though they inhabit very different climates; and the form and situation are always exactly suited to their nature, and calculated to afford them shelter and protection.

When danger, or any other circumstance peculiar to certain countries, renders a deviation from the common form or situation of nests necessary, that deviation is made in an equal degree, and in the very same manner, by all the birds of one species; and it is never found to extend beyond the limits of the country where alone it can serve any good purpose. When removed by necessity from their eggs, birds return to them with haste and anxiety, and shift them so as to heat them equally; and it is worthy of observation that their haste to return is always in proportion to the cold of the climate. Thus the ostrich in Senegal, where the heat is excessive, neglects her eggs during the day but sits upon them in the night. At the Cape of Good Hope, however, where the degree of heat is less, the ostrich, like other birds, sits upon her eggs both day and night. In countries infested with monkeys, many birds, which in other climates build in bushes and clefts of trees, suspend their nests upon slender twigs, and thus elude the rapacity of their enemies.

The following is remarkable. A cat frequented a closet, the door of which was fastened by an iron latch. A window was situated near the door. When the door was shut, the cat gave herself no uneasiness. As soon as she was tired of her confinement, she mounted on the sill of the window, and with her paw dexterously lifted the latch and came out. This practice, which we are told continued for years, must have been the consequence of reasoning in particular ideas. It could not be the effect of instinct; for instinct is adapted only to a state of nature, in which cats have neither latches to lift nor doors to open. And as it is not said that the animal attempted to lift the latches of other doors, we are not authorized to infer that this particular action was the consequence of reasoning in ideas enlarged by abstraction <note>original: "abstraction"; the author distinguishes between the cat learning a specific mechanical task and the human ability to understand the general concept of a "latch"</note>: the cat had repeatedly seen one door opened by an exertion which she was capable of imitating.

From the time of her appearance until after the middle of summer, the nests of the birds selected to receive her egg are to be found in great abundance; but, like other migrating birds, she does not begin to lay until some weeks after her arrival. It is widely acknowledged that the cuckoo does not hatch its own eggs. The hedge-sparrow <note>now commonly known as the Dunnock</note>, the water-wagtail, the titlark <note>the Meadow Pipit</note>, the red-breast <note>the Robin</note>, the yellow-hammer, the green-linnet, or the whinchat is generally the nurse of the young cuckoo. Among the birds mentioned above, she generally selects the first three, but shows a much greater preference for the hedge-sparrow. This last bird commonly takes four or five days to lay her eggs. During this time (generally after she has laid one or two), the cuckoo contrives to deposit her egg among the rest, leaving its future care entirely to the hedge-sparrow. When the hedge-sparrow has sat for her usual time and helped the young cuckoo and some of her own offspring hatch from their shells, her own young ones—and any eggs that remain unhatched—are soon turned out of the nest. The young cuckoo remains as the possessor of the nest and the sole object of the sparrow's future care. The young birds are not killed beforehand, nor are the eggs smashed; instead, they are all left to perish together, either caught in the bush that holds the nest or lying on the ground beneath it. 

"The early fate of the young hedge-sparrows," says Mr. Jenner <note>Edward Jenner (1749–1823), the physician who pioneered the smallpox vaccine, was also a respected naturalist who first correctly described this cuckoo behavior</note>, who conducted these experiments, "is a circumstance that has been noticed by others but attributed to the wrong causes; however, the true cause we shall presently explain." A variety of theories have been formed about it. For example, a cuckoo laid her egg in a water-wagtail's nest in the thatch of an old cottage. The wagtail sat for her usual time and then hatched all the eggs but one; that egg, along with all the young birds except the cuckoo, was turned out of the nest. The young birds, five in total, were found upon the rafter that projected from under the thatch, and with them was an egg that was not damaged in the least. The cuckoo was reared by the wagtails until it was nearly capable of flying, at which point it was killed by an accident.

In another instance, a hedge-sparrow built her nest in a hawthorn bush in a timber yard. After she had laid two eggs, a cuckoo dropped in a third. The sparrow continued laying as if nothing had happened until she had laid five, her usual number, and then began to sit.

The method of accomplishing this was very curious. It is wonderful to see the extraordinary exertions of the young cuckoo when it is only two or three days old, especially if a bird too heavy for it to lift out is put into the nest with it. In this state, it seems constantly restless and uneasy. 

The singularity of its shape is well adapted to these purposes; for, unlike other newly-hatched birds, its back from the shoulder blades <note>original: "scapulæ"</note> downward is very broad, with a significant depression in the middle. This depression seems formed by nature for the purpose of giving a more secure placement to the egg of the hedge-sparrow <note>The hedge-sparrow is the Dunnock (*Prunella modularis*).</note>, or its young one, when the young cuckoo is employed in removing either of them from the nest. When it is about twelve days old, this cavity is quite filled up, and the back then assumes the shape of nestling birds in general.

It appears a little extraordinary that two cuckoo eggs should ever be deposited in the same nest, as the young one produced from one of them must inevitably perish; yet two instances of this kind fell under our author’s observation, one of which he relates as follows: Two cuckoos and a hedge-sparrow were hatched in the same nest this morning (June 27, 1787); one hedge-sparrow’s egg remained unhatched. A few hours later, a contest began between the cuckoos for the possession of the nest. This continued undecided until the next afternoon, when one of them, which was somewhat larger in size, turned out the other, along with the young hedge-sparrow and the unhatched egg. This contest was very remarkable. The combatants alternately appeared to have the advantage, as each carried the other several times nearly to the top of the nest and then sank down again, oppressed by the weight of its burden; until at length, after various efforts, the strongest prevailed and was afterwards raised by the hedge-sparrows.

But the principal circumstance that has puzzled the minds of naturalists <note>Early scientists who studied biology and the natural world.</note> respecting the cuckoo is why, unlike other birds, it does not build a nest, incubate its eggs, and rear its own young. The most probable suggestion is the short stay this bird is allowed to make in the country where it is destined to breed, and the demand nature places upon it during that stay to produce a numerous offspring. The cuckoo’s first appearance here is about the middle of April, commonly on the 17th. Its egg is not ready for incubation <note>The process of sitting on eggs to hatch them using body heat.</note> until some weeks after its arrival, seldom before the middle of May. Two weeks are taken up by the sitting bird in hatching the egg. The young bird generally stays three weeks in the nest before it flies, and the foster-parents feed it for more than five weeks after this period. Therefore, if a cuckoo should be ready with an egg much sooner than...

Among the many peculiarities of the young cuckoo, there is one that shows itself very early. Long before it leaves the nest, it frequently, when irritated, assumes the manner of a bird of prey: it looks ferocious, throws itself back, and pecks at anything presented to it with great intensity <note>original: "vehemence"</note>, often making a chuckling noise like a young hawk at the same time. This is likely the source of the common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> opinion that this bird changes into a hawk and devours its nurse upon quitting the nest; which also gives rise to the French proverb, "Ungrateful as a cuckoo" <note>original: *Ingrat comme un coucou*</note>. Sometimes, when disturbed to a lesser degree, it makes a kind of hissing noise accompanied by a heaving motion of the whole body. 

From what has been said, it becomes evident that the same instinctive impulse which directs the cuckoo to lay <note>original: "deposit"</note> her eggs in the nests of other birds also directs her young one to throw out the eggs and young of the owner of the nest. The scheme of nature would be incomplete without it; for it would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, for the little birds destined to provide care <note>original: "succour"</note> for the cuckoo to also find enough for their own young after a certain period; nor would there be enough room for them to inhabit the nest. 

Cuckoos may be, and often are, raised as pets <note>original: "brought up tame"</note> so as to become familiar with humans. In this state, they will eat bread and milk, fruits, insects, eggs, and meat, either cooked or raw; but in nature, they chiefly live on caterpillars. When fat, they are said to be as good for eating as a corncrake <note>original: "land-rail"</note>; the French and Italians eat them to this day. The ancient Romans admired them greatly as food: Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> says that there is no bird which can be compared to them for delicacy. In migrating, the majority of these birds are supposed to go to Africa, since they are observed to visit the island of Malta twice a year during their passage back and forth, as is supposed, to that part of the world.

The instinct discovered in ants, beavers, etc., is too well known and admired to need any mention here; we see in a great variety of birds, insects, and quadrupeds a similar economy in laying up stores of provisions in times of plenty so that they might have access to them in times of need. The common jackdaw <note>original: "daw"</note> has a peculiar knack for this; in houses where they have been raised as pets, they have frequently been known to hide—along with their food—money, rings, seals, lockets, and other small trinkets, thereby causing hurtful suspicions of theft toward servants or others who are perfectly innocent.

...natural planters of all kinds of wood and trees. He says, “About twenty-five years ago, while coming from Rosecastle <note>Rose Castle was the traditional home of the Bishop of Carlisle.</note> early in the morning, I observed a great number of crows very busy at work on a sloping hillside with a mossy surface. I went out of my way specifically to watch their labor, and I found they were planting a grove of oaks. The way they planted was like this: they first made little holes in the earth with their beaks <note>original: "bills"</note>, turning round and round until the hole was deep enough; then they dropped in the acorn and covered it with earth and moss. The season was late autumn, when all seeds are fully ripe.” Mr. Robinson seems to think that divine Providence <note>Providence: the protective care of God or nature</note> gave the crows this instinct solely for the reproduction <note>original: "propagation"</note> of trees. However, I imagine it was given to them mainly for their own survival <note>original: "preservation"</note>, by hiding food <note>original: "provision"</note> during times of plenty to supply them during times of scarcity. In this way, such an instinct in these birds may serve a double purpose: both their own support in times of need and the reproduction of the trees they plant. For wherever they hide a great number of nuts or grains in the earth, we cannot expect them to find all of them again; instead, many will remain in the patch of ground they use, growing alongside one another.

A wonderful spirit of sociability <note>original: "sociality"</note> among animals <note>original: "the brute creation"</note>, independent of sexual attraction, has often been noted. Many horses, though calm when with others, will not stay a single minute in a field by themselves; the strongest fences cannot keep them in. One horse was known to leap out of a stable window (used for shoveling out manure) just to follow its companions, even though it was remarkably quiet in every other respect. Oxen and cows will not grow fat when kept alone; they will ignore the finest pasture if it is not made appealing by the company of others. There is no need to give the example of sheep, which constantly flock together. 

However, this tendency <note>original: "propensity"</note> does not seem to be limited to animals of the same class or species. Even a great difference in type and size does not always prevent social advances and mutual friendship. The following remarkable example is given of this: A gentleman who kept only one horse also happened to have one solitary hen. These two mismatched <note>original: "incongruous"</note> animals spent much of their time together in a lonely orchard, where they saw no other creatures but each other. Gradually, an obvious affection began to develop between these two isolated <note>original: "sequestered"</note> individuals. The hen would approach the horse <note>original: "quadruped"</note> with sounds of contentment <note>original: "complacency"</note>, rubbing herself gently against his legs. Meanwhile, the horse would look down with satisfaction and move with the greatest care and caution <note>original: "circumspection"</note> to avoid trampling his tiny companion. Through these mutual acts of kindness, each seemed to comfort the other during their lonely hours.

In the *Gentleman's Magazine* for March 1788, we find the following anecdotes regarding a raven. The raven mentioned “lives, or did live three years ago, at the Red Lion inn at Hungerford; his name, I believe, is Rafe. You should know that when I arrived at that inn, my carriage <note>original: "chaise"</note> ran over and bruised the leg of my Newfoundland dog. While we were examining the injury to the dog's foot, Rafe was clearly a concerned observer. From the moment the dog was tied up under the manger with my horse, Rafe not only visited him, but brought him bones and attended to him with frequent and specific marks of kindness.

The bird's attention to the dog was so noticeable that I mentioned it to the ostler <note>original: "hostler"; a person who looks after horses at an inn</note>, for I had not heard a word before about the history of this benevolent creature. John then told me that Rafe had been raised from the time he was a fledgling <note>original: "pin-feather"</note> in close friendship with a dog. He said that the affection between them was mutual and that the entire neighborhood had often witnessed the countless acts of kindness they had shown each other. Rafe's poor dog friend, after a while, unfortunately broke his leg; during the very long time the dog was confined, Rafe waited on him constantly, carried him his daily provisions, and scarcely ever left him alone! 

One night, the ostler accidentally shut the stable door, and Rafe was deprived of his friend’s company for the whole night. In the morning, however, the ostler found the bottom of the door so pecked away that if it had not been opened, Rafe would have created his own entrance within another hour. I then questioned my landlady (a sensible woman) and heard everything I have related confirmed by her, along with several other singular examples of the kindness this bird shows to all dogs in general, but particularly to maimed or wounded ones. I hope and believe the bird is still living, and any traveler will find I have not overrated his merit."

To these instances of attachment between mismatched animals—arising from a spirit of sociality or feelings of sympathy—we may add the following instance of fondness born from a different motive, as recounted by Mr. White in his *History of Selborne*.

"A friend of mine had a little, helpless young hare <note>original: "leveret"</note> brought to him, which the servants fed with milk from a spoon. Around the same time, his cat had kittens, but the young were killed <note>original: "dispatched"</note> and buried. The young hare was soon lost and was supposed to have gone the way of most foundlings, or perhaps been killed by a dog or cat. However, two weeks later, as the master was sitting in his garden in the dusk of the evening, he observed his cat trotting toward him with her tail erect. She was calling with little, short, inward notes of satisfaction, such as cats use toward their kittens. Something was gamboling after her, which proved to be the young hare; the cat had nourished it with her milk and continued to support it with great affection. Thus was a plant-eating <note>original: "graminivorous"</note> animal nurtured by a meat-eating and predatory one! Why would so cruel and bloodthirsty a beast as a cat—of the ferocious genus *Felis* <note>original: "felis"</note>, the 'lion of mice' <note>original: "murium leo"</note>—

As Linnaeus <note>Carl Linnaeus (1707–1778), the Swedish botanist and zoologist who established the modern system of biological classification.</note> calls it, why a cat should be moved with any tenderness toward an animal that is its natural prey is not so easy to determine. This strange affection was probably caused by that *longing* <note>original Latin: *desiderium*; here referring to a maternal yearning or a sense of loss.</note>—those tender maternal feelings—which the loss of her kittens had awakened in her breast. It likely also came from the comfort and relief she gained by allowing her teats to be suckled, as they were over-filled with milk. Through this habit, she became as delighted with this foundling as if it had been her real offspring. 

This incident is a good explanation for those strange circumstances which serious historians as well as poets assert: that abandoned children are sometimes nurtured by female wild beasts that had probably lost their young. For it is not at all more marvelous that Romulus and Remus <note>The legendary twin brothers and founders of Rome who, according to myth, were abandoned as infants and suckled by a she-wolf.</note>, in their infant state, should be nursed by a she-wolf, than that a poor little nursing leveret <term>leveret: a young hare</term> should be fostered and cherished by a fierce cat <term>original: "grimalkin"; an old term for a female cat, often implying one that is territorial or fierce.</term>

That brute animals possess reflection and sentiment, and are capable of kind as well as hot-tempered passions—independent of sexual attachment and natural affection—and that they have a great share of fidelity, pride, and even a sense of glory, may be demonstrated by the elephant, the horse, and the dog. 

Elephants, even in a wild state, are peaceful and gentle creatures. They never use their weapons except in defense of themselves or their companions. Their social dispositions are so strong that they are seldom found alone, but always march in large troops. The oldest and most experienced lead the front; the younger or lame ones stay in the middle; and those of middle age walk in the rear. The females carry their young on their tusks, embracing them at the same time with their trunk. 

They seldom march in this regular order except when they consider the journey dangerous, such as an expedition to cultivated lands where they expect to meet with resistance. On other occasions, they are less cautious; some of them fall behind or separate from the rest, but seldom so far as to be out of the reach of help by alarming and gathering their companions. It is dangerous to offer them the least injury, for they run straight toward the offender. Although the weight of their body is great, their steps are so large that they easily outrun the swiftest man. They either pierce the victim with their tusks or seize them with their trunk, hurl them into the air like a stone, and then trample them under their feet. However, they never attack any person unless they are provoked. Because they are extremely sensitive and reactive regarding injuries, it is always prudent to keep out of their way. Travellers who frequent those countries kindle large fires and beat drums during the night in order to prevent their approach. After being once attacked by men or falling into an ambush, they are said never to forget

the injury, but search for every opportunity of getting revenge. As they are endowed perhaps with a more exquisite sense of smell than any other animal—owing to the great size of their nose—they can scent a man at a very great distance and trace him by his footsteps.

The elephant, when tamed, is the most friendly and obedient of all animals; he is entirely attached to the person who feeds and takes care of him. In a short time, he understands signs and the sound of his master's voice. He distinguishes the language of passion, of command, and of satisfaction, and acts accordingly. He receives his orders with attention and executes them with prudence and readiness, but without reckless haste. He easily learns to bow his knees and lower his body for the convenience of those who mount him. He caresses his friends with his trunk. He lifts burdens with his trunk and assists those who are loading him by helping place them on his back. He delights in shining harness and decorative trappings. When yoked to a cart or wagon, he pulls equally and cheerfully, unless he is abused by unwise punishment. His guide is generally mounted on his neck, holding a small iron rod, sharp at the point, in his hand; he directs the elephant's motion by pricking him on the ears and head, but for the most part, a word is sufficient. 

A tame elephant will do more labor than six horses, but then he requires a proportional quantity of food. They are the principal beasts of burden in many parts of Africa and the East Indies. They carry sacks and bundles of all kinds on their necks, backs, and tusks. They never lose or damage anything committed to their care: they will stand on the edge of a river, take bundles off their necks and tusks, and lay them carefully in a boat whenever they are desired, then try with their trunks to see whether they are properly situated. If they are loaded with casks <term>casks: large wooden barrels used for transporting liquids or dry goods</term>, they go in search of stones to prop them up and prevent them from rolling. 

The elephant is not only the most manageable, but the most intelligent of animals; sensible of benefits and resentful of injuries. In India, they were once employed in the launching of ships: one was directed to force a very large vessel into the water, but the work proved superior to his strength. His master, with a sarcastic tone, bade the keeper take away this "lazy beast" and bring another; the poor animal instantly repeated his efforts, fractured his skull, and died on the spot. In Delhi, an elephant passing along the streets put his trunk into a tailor’s shop where several people were at work; one of them pricked the end of it with his needle. The beast passed on, but at the next dirty puddle he filled his trunk with water, returned to the shop, and, squirting every drop among the people who had offended him, spoiled their work. An elephant in Ajmer <note>original: "Adſmeer"</note>, which often passed through the bazaar <note>original: "bazar"</note> or market, always received a mouthful of greens from a certain herb-woman as he went by. Eventually, he was seized by one of his periodic fits of rage, broke his chains, and ran through the market, causing the crowd to flee. Another elephant, in his madness, killed his <term>cornac</term> <note>an elephant driver or mahout</note> or keeper. The wife, seeing the tragedy, took her two children and threw them before the elephant, saying, "Now that you have destroyed their father, you may as well end their lives and mine too." It immediately stopped and relented. It took the oldest child, placed him on its neck, adopted him as its <term>cornac</term>, and never again allowed anyone else to mount it. 

A soldier at Pondicherry <note>a city in India</note> was accustomed to sharing a portion of his rations with one of these animals. One day, after drinking a bit too much and finding himself pursued by the guards who were going to take him to prison, he took refuge under the elephant’s body and fell asleep. The guards tried in vain to force him from this sanctuary, as the elephant protected him with its trunk. The next morning, when the soldier recovered from his drunken state, he shuddered with horror to find himself lying under the belly of this massive animal. The elephant, who undoubtedly sensed the man’s distress, caressed him with his trunk to give him courage and make him understand that he could now leave safely. 

A painter wanted to draw the elephant kept in the menagerie at Versailles in an unusual pose: holding its trunk high in the air with its mouth open. The duration of an elephant's pregnancy has been determined to be slightly less than two years, as an elephant gave birth to a young one 21 months and three days after she was captured. All dogs, from the fearsome boar-hound to *Pompey the Little* <note>A reference to a popular 1751 satirical novel, *The History of Pompey the Little*, which follows the life of a lapdog.</note>, were the same in the beginning. All the variety we see in them is produced by changes in climate, the accidental effects of soil, food, or environment, or the results of human care, experimentation, or whims <term>caprice</term>. Every huntsman knows what a huge difference can be made in dogs by diligently improving the breed over twenty or thirty years. 

Nature wisely tends to make every creature suited to the country where it lives or works; this is why hounds and all other animals decline <note>original: "degenerate"</note> when moved to very different climates. This is clear from the following experiment: if a pair of true Southern Hounds are moved to the North and allowed to breed naturally without intermixing with other types, their bodies will gradually become lighter and their barks higher-pitched <note>original: "shriller accents"</note>. All dogs change in the same way when moved from one country to another. 

However, the greatest human efforts and ingenuity—whether aided by climate change or cross-breeding—could never add a single new species to the works of creation. Nature remains fundamentally consistent and does not allow the Almighty Creator to be imitated by short-sighted mortals. Despite our skills, mules are always sterile; nor can the most inquisitive experimenter <term>projector</term> produce a single cross-bred <term>amphigeneous</term> animal that is able to reproduce. 

There appears to be a distinct difference between species in all living creatures. The horse, dog, bear, and goat—no matter how much they are changed by breeding, mating, or climate in size or shape—will always reveal characteristics that belong to their specific species. Above all, their unique instinct and drive for reproduction will lead them to recognize and show their kinship. Animals of truly different species will never mate with one another. This is one of the strongest arguments that wolves, foxes, and dogs are originally the same species: not only are they physically joined in the same way during mating <term>coition</term>, but there are frequent instances of hybrid litters from a dog and a fox, or a dog and a wolf. Because of these extraordinary abilities shown by animals of different countries and species, some philosophers have argued that animals are endowed with a soul, though one essentially inferior to that of humans; and to this soul they have granted immortality. Father Bougeant <note>Guillaume-Hyacinthe Bougeant (1690–1743), a French Jesuit author whose work on animal language was highly controversial.</note>, a Jesuit, has lately published a treatise specifically on this subject, titled *A Philosophical Amusement on the Language of Brutes* <note>Originally published in French as "Amusement philosophique sur le langage des bêtes" in 1739.</note>. "Reason," he says, "naturally inclines us to believe that beasts have a spiritual soul; the only thing that opposes this view is the consequences that might be inferred from it. You dare not say it is matter, because you must then necessarily suppose matter is capable of thinking. Nor will you say that it is spirit, as this opinion brings with it consequences contrary to the principles of religion—including the idea that man would differ from beasts only by degrees of 'more or less' <note>original: "plus and minus"</note>, which would demolish the very foundation of all religion.

And if these proud spirits know their own dismal state, what a humiliation must it be for them to see themselves reduced to the condition of animals! But whether they know it or not, such a shameful degradation is still, regarding them, the primary effect of the divine vengeance I just mentioned; it is an anticipated hell."

The first proposition is hard to accept and explicitly contradicts the Holy Scriptures, which state that everything God created was good—indeed, very good. This might, at most, be said of animals that interact with humans, but not at all of birds, fish, and insects, which have no relationship to him.

All that can be reasonably inferred from the greater prevalence of malicious passions among animals than among men is that the former have less rationality than men. Accordingly, it is found that among savages <note>This term reflects the 18th-century colonial perspective that non-European peoples were less "rational" or "civilized" than Europeans.</note>, who exercise their reason less than other men, every species of barbarity is practiced without being deemed a crime.

Upon the whole, it is impossible to deduce this variety of action in animals from a general and uniform instinct only. For they accommodate their operations to times and circumstances. They combine; they choose the favorable moment; they avail themselves of the occasion, and seem to receive instruction by experience. Many of their operations demonstrate reflection: the bird repairs a shattered nest instead of instinctively constructing a new one; the hen, who has been robbed of her eggs, changes her place in order to lay the remainder with more security; the cat discovers both care and artifice in concealing her kittens. Again, it is evident that on many occasions animals know their faults and mistakes and correct them; they sometimes contrive the most ingenious methods of obtaining their ends, and when one method fails, they have recourse to another. They have, without doubt, a kind of language for the mutual communication of their ideas.

How is all this to be accounted for, unless we suppose them endowed with the powers of perceiving, thinking, remembering, comparing, and judging? They certainly have these powers, in a degree inferior to the human species, and form classes below them in the graduated scale of intelligent beings; but, their actions not being directed to moral ends, they are consequently not accountable and are not proper subjects for reward or punishment in a future world.

After all, it does not appear upon what principle of reason and justice it is that mankind has founded their right over the lives of every creature that is placed in a subordinate rank of being to themselves. Whatever claim they may have based on the right of food and self-defense—if they extended their privilege no further—numberless beings might enjoy their lives in peace who are now hurried out of them by the most wanton and unnecessary cruelties. It is surely difficult to discover why it should be thought less inhuman to crush to death a harmless insect, whose single offense is that he eats that food which nature has prepared for his sustenance, than it would be were we to kill any bulky creature for the same reason. There are few tempers so hardened against the impressions of humanity as not to shudder at the thought of the latter; and yet the former is universally practiced without the least check of compassion. ### AND OCCULT SCIENCE.

...with a body infinitely out of proportion to our own, not considering that "great" and "little" are merely relative terms. But the inimitable Shakespeare would teach us, that

> ———the poor beetle that we tread upon,
> In corporal suffering feels a pang as great
> As when a giant dies.———

And, indeed, there is every reason to believe that the sensations of many insects are as necessary as those of creatures of far larger dimensions—perhaps even more so. The millipede <note>original: "millepede"</note>, for instance, rolls itself up at the slightest touch, and the snail pulls in her horns at the least approach of our hand. Are not these the strongest indications of their sensibility <note>sensibility: the capacity to feel or perceive physical sensations</note>? And is it any evidence of our own sensibility that we are not moved to treat them with a more sympathetic tenderness?

I cannot conclude these observations on the instinct and economy <note>original: "œconomy"—here meaning the natural organization and lifestyle of an animal</note> of brute animals without reciting the following most remarkable account of the land-crab, which inhabits the Bahama Islands, as well as most parts in the tropics, and feeds upon vegetables. These creatures live not only in a kind of orderly society in their retreats in the mountains, but regularly, once a year, march down to the seaside in a body of some millions at a time. As they multiply in great numbers, they choose the month of April or May to begin their expedition; they then sally out by the thousands from the stumps of hollow trees, from the cracks in rocks, and from the holes which they dig for themselves under the surface of the earth. At that time the whole ground is covered with this band of adventurers; one cannot set down a foot without treading upon them. The sea is their destination, and they direct their march toward it with straight-line precision. No mathematician <note>original: "geometrician"</note> could send them to their destined station by a shorter course; they turn neither to the right nor left, whatever obstacles intervene. Even if they meet with a house, they will attempt to scale the walls to keep the uninterrupted course <note>original: "unbroken tenor"</note> of their way.

However, though this is the general order of their route, they are obliged on other occasions to conform to the layout of the country; if it is cut through by rivers, they are then seen to wind along the course of the stream. The procession sets forward from the mountains with the regularity of an army under the guidance of an experienced commander. They are commonly divided into three battalions; the first of these consists of the strongest and boldest males, which, like pioneers <note>pioneers: in a military context, soldiers who march ahead of the main army to clear paths and build defenses</note>, march forward to clear the way and face the greatest dangers. These are often obliged to halt for want of rain, and to go into the most convenient encampment until...

The main body of the army is composed of females, who never leave the mountains until the rain has set in for some time, and then descend in a regular battle formation <note>original: "battalia"</note>, being formed into two columns fifty paces broad and three miles deep, and so close together that they almost cover the ground. The night is their primary time for traveling; however, if it rains during the day, they do not fail to take advantage of the occasion, continuing to move forward in their slow, uniform manner. When the sun shines and is hot upon the surface of the ground, they make a universal halt and wait until the cool of the evening. When they are terrified, they march back in a confused, disorderly manner, holding up their nippers, with which they sometimes tear off a piece of the skin and then leave the weapon <note>The author refers to the crab's ability to "drop" a claw (autotomy) to escape a threat</note> where they inflicted the wound. They even try to intimidate their enemies, for they often clatter their nippers together as if to threaten those who come to disturb them. 

But, although they strive to be formidable to humans, they are much more so to each other; they possess one most unsocial quality: if any of them is accidentally maimed in such a manner that they are incapable of proceeding, the rest fall upon and devour them on the spot, then pursue their journey. 

When, after a fatiguing march and escaping a thousand dangers (for they are sometimes three months in reaching the shore), they have arrived at their destined port, they prepare to cast their spawn. The eggs <note>original: "peaſe"</note> are still within their bodies and not yet released <note>original: "excluded"</note> under the tail, as is usual in animals of this kind; for the creature waits for the benefit of seawater to help the delivery. For this purpose, as soon as the crab has reached the shore, it eagerly goes to the edge of the water and lets the waves wash over its body two or three times. This seems only a preparation for bringing their spawn to maturity; for, without further delay, they withdraw to seek a lodging upon land. 

In the meantime, the spawn grows larger, is released from the body, and sticks to the barbs under the flap—or more properly, the tail. This bunch is seen to be as big as a hen's egg and looks exactly like herring roe. In this state of pregnancy, they seek the shore once more for the last time; shaking off their spawn into the water, they leave chance <note>original: "accident"</note> to bring it to maturity. shore, and slowly traveling up to the mountains. The older crabs, however, are not as energetic during the return journey; they have become so feeble and lean that they can hardly creep along, and their flesh changes color at that time. Most of them, therefore, are forced to stay in the flat parts of the country until they recover, digging holes in the earth and covering the openings with leaves and dirt so that no air can enter. There they shed their old shells, which they leave behind appearing almost entirely whole; the place where the shell opened on the belly is nearly invisible. At that time they are quite naked and remain almost motionless for six days, during which they become so fat that they are considered delicious food. At this stage, they have four large white stones <note>These are gastroliths, often called "crab's eyes," which are calcium deposits the crab uses to harden its new shell</note> under their stomachs, which gradually decrease in size as the shell hardens; by the time the shell is fully formed, these stones disappear. When this animal has retreated to the mountains, it is nearly unreachable. Because it survives only on vegetables, it seldom ventures out; and since its home is in the most inaccessible places, it remains in perfect security for a great part of the season. It is only when it is driven by the desire to spawn, or compelled to descend into the flat country, that it is captured. At those times, the natives wait for its descent in eager expectation and destroy thousands of them. However, disregarding the crabs' bodies, they only seek the small spawn <note>original: "spawn"; referring to the eggs or roe</note> that lies on each side of the stomach within the shell, which is about as thick as a man’s thumb.

The crabs are much more valuable upon their return after they have shed their shells; for, being covered with a skin resembling soft parchment, almost every part except the stomach may be eaten. They are captured in their holes by feeling for them with an instrument, or they are hunted at night with torches <note>original: "flambeaux"</note> while they are on their journey. The instant the animal perceives it is being attacked, it throws itself on its back and pinches most terribly with its claws whatever it happens to grab. But the skilled crab-catcher takes them by the hind legs in such a way that the pincers cannot touch him, and then he throws them into his bag. Sometimes they are also caught when they take refuge in the bottom of holes in the rocks by the seaside; the hunters place a stick at the mouth of the hole to prevent them from escaping, and soon after, the incoming tide enters the hole. Upon the tide's retreat, the animal is found drowned in its lair. These crabs come in various sizes, the largest being about six inches wide. They walk sideways like sea crabs and are shaped like them; some are black, some are yellow, some red, and others are variegated <note>term: variegated; streaked or spotted with different colors</note> with a mix of red, white, and yellow. Some of these are poisonous, and several people have died from eating them, particularly the black variety.

->## OF SCENT.<-

Nothing more clearly demonstrates the doctrine of atoms <note>the theory that all matter is composed of tiny, invisible particles</note> than *scent*. It is an <term>effluvium</term> <note>a gaseous emission or odor</note> continually arising from the <term>corpuscles</term> <note>tiny particles</note> that issue out of all bodies. Being infused with the particular state and quality of the blood and juices of the specific animal from which they flow, these particles cause the vast variety of smells or scents recognized by the olfactory nerves, or organs of smelling. 

This explains why one person differs from another in scent, and why a dog will track the footsteps of his master for a hundred miles, follow him into any house, church, or other building, and distinguish him from every other person, even if surrounded by ten thousand others. When the faithful animal has thus diligently sought out and recognized his master, he is seldom willing even to trust the evidence of his own eyes until, with his hackles raised <note>original: "erected crest"</note>, he has taken a few reassuring <note>original: "cordial"</note> sniffs to convince himself he is right. 

From this, we also see how a pack of hounds is able to pursue a hare, fox, stag, or any other animal they are trained to hunt, following the scent even through the presence of others of the same species, without being distracted from the pursuit of the very same animal they *first* started tracking. Furthermore, we discover how it is possible for birds and beasts of prey to be guided to their food from such vast distances. These corpuscles, emitted from decaying <note>original: "putrid"</note> bodies and floating in the air, are carried by the wind in different directions. When they strike the olfactory nerves of whatever animals they meet in their path,* <margin>*It is by this means that smallpox, measles, putrid fevers <note>historical term for typhus or similar infections</note>, and all epidemic illnesses are communicated, and the plague and pestilence are carried from one place to another.</margin> they immediately lead them to the spot. 

It does not matter how much the effluvia may have dissipated, so long as enough remains to stimulate the olfactory organ. Whether it is a bird or a beast, they test the scent in all directions until they eventually discover the path where the scent becomes stronger and stronger as they proceed. Nature has taught them that this is the direct and obvious road to their prey, and it prevents them from following the opposite course, where the scent grows weaker and weaker—what in hunting is termed <term>heel</term>. This observation is confirmed by the increased eagerness we see in all animals the closer they approach the object of their pursuit, as we see with hounds and spaniels while hunting and

-># AND OCCULT SCIENCE.<-

...following, they become more eager in proportion to how fresh the scent is and how much closer they get to the game. Among four-legged animals <note>original: "quadrupeds"</note>, whether domestic or wild, this same sense directs the male to the female that is ready for mating; we see the dog, the boar, the bull, and the stallion, when turned loose, sniff the surrounding air and proceed accordingly. By this same medium, the pests <note>original: "vermin"</note> that infest our dwellings know how to direct their movements—whether to undermine walls, eat through solid boards, cross rivers, or climb drainpipes <note>original: "spouts"</note>. This shows how much more strongly the faculty of smelling is possessed by animal species than by humans. This was wisely ordained by nature to enable them to seek their food and reproduce their species; without it, they would often perish or would have long ago become extinct.

There are wonderful examples of animal carcasses that, though covered with lime and buried ten feet underground, have sent forth so strong a scent that they attracted dogs to the spot, who eagerly endeavored to dig away the earth to get at them. A tragic instance happened only a few years ago at Petersfield in Hampshire, where an unfortunate woman, having privately given birth to two children, buried them in a deep hole in a nearby cellar. Within three days, some dogs were attracted to the spot by the scent, dug them up, and had partly devoured them before the shocking circumstance was discovered. It is no wonder, then, that a pack of hounds that has caught the scent of a polecat or weasel will pursue them into the thickest forest and assemble around the very tree up which they ran for shelter. Nor is it strange that bloodhounds, as in times of old, should trace out fugitives and robbers in underground caverns, in trees, caves, or forests, or in the crevices of inaccessible rocks, of which examples are given by the most reputable historians. It is, however, to be remarked that just as all animals hunt for and pursue their prey by its scent, they also seem instinctively to know that they themselves are hunted and pursued by means of the scent issuing from their own bodies. But, as this subject allows for so much curious and <term>occult</term> <note>In historical science, "occult" refers to "hidden" natural forces—like magnetism or scent—that act at a distance without a visible connection.</note> speculation, I shall give a few examples of the effects of scent upon different animals and the sense and sagacity they display in the management of it.

First, let us consider the hare.

The hare is naturally a timid animal but gives off a very strong scent. It sleeps in its <term>form</term> <note>the shallow depression or "seat" where a hare hides and rests</note> during the day, and it feeds and mates at night. On a moonlight evening, a number of them are sometimes seen playing together, leaping and pursuing each other; but the slightest motion, even the falling of a leaf, alarms them. Then they all run off separately, each taking a different route. They are extremely swift in their motion, which is a kind of gallop or a succession of quick leaps. ## Of SCENT.

Nothing more clearly demonstrates the "theory of atoms" than scent. It is a vapor <note>original: "effluvium"</note> continually rising from the tiny particles <note>original: "corpuscles"</note> that come out of all bodies. Because these particles are filled with the specific state and quality of the blood and juices of the particular animal they flow from, they create the vast variety of smells or scents detectable by the olfactory nerves, or organs of smelling. 

This is the reason why one person differs from another in *scent*, and why a dog will trace the footsteps of his master for a hundred miles, follow him into any house, church, or other building, and distinguish him from every other person, even if surrounded by ten thousand others. When the faithful animal has thus diligently sought out and recognized his master, he is seldom willing even to trust the evidence of his own eyes until, with his head held high, he has taken a few reassuring sniffs to convince himself he is right. 

This also explains how a pack of hounds is able to pursue a hare, fox, stag, or any other animal they are trained to hunt, following the scent even through the presence of other animals of the same species, without being distracted from the pursuit of the very same animal they *first* started. It also shows how birds and beasts of prey can be directed to their food from such great distances; for these particles, rising from rotting bodies and floating in the air, are carried by the wind in different directions. When they hit the olfactory nerves of whatever animals they meet in their way,* they immediately lead them to the spot. 

It does not matter how much the vapor has dissipated, as long as enough remains to stimulate the smelling organs. Whether it is a bird or a beast, they test the scent in all directions until they finally discover the path where it grows stronger and stronger as they proceed. Nature has taught them to know that this is the direct and obvious road to their prey, and it prevents them from following the opposite direction, where the scent naturally grows weaker—what in hunting is called the *heel* <note>The reverse of the trail left by the prey</note>. This observation is confirmed by the increased excitement we see in all animals the closer they approach the object they are chasing; as we see in hounds and spaniels while hunting and—

hunting <note>original: "shooting"</note> are all the more eager <note>original: "earnest"</note> in proportion to how fresh the scent is and how close they get to the game. Among four-legged animals <term>quadrupeds</term>, whether wild or domestic, this same sense directs the male to a female in heat <note>original: "in season for love"</note>. This is why we see dogs, boars, bulls, and stallions, when turned loose, sniff the surrounding <term>ambient</term> air and proceed accordingly toward her. 

Through this same medium, the vermin that infest our homes know how to direct their movements—whether to undermine walls, gnaw through solid boards, cross rivers, or climb drainpipes. This shows how much more powerful the sense of smell is in animal species <note>original: "brute species"</note> than in humans. This was wisely ordained by nature to enable them to seek their food and reproduce; without it, they would often perish or would have long ago become extinct.

There are amazing examples of animal carcasses that, even when covered with lime <note>A chemical used to speed decomposition and mask odors</note> and buried ten feet underground, have emitted such a strong scent that dogs were attracted to the spot and tried to dig them up. A tragic case occurred only a few years ago in Petersfield, Hampshire, where a woman, having secretly given birth to two children, buried them in a deep hole in a nearby <unclear>field</unclear> <note>OCR: "i;"—likely field or inclosure</note>. However, within three days, dogs were attracted to the spot by the scent, dug them up, and had partially eaten them before the shocking discovery was made. 

It is no wonder, then, that a pack of hounds can track a polecat or weasel into the densest forest and gather around the exact tree where it has hidden. Nor is it surprising that bloodhounds, as they did in ancient times, can track down fugitives and robbers in underground <term>subterraneous</term> caverns, trees, caves, forests, or cracks in inaccessible rocks. Historians of high repute have recorded many such instances. 

However, it should be noted that just as animals hunt their prey by scent, they also seem to know instinctively that they are being hunted by the scent coming from their own bodies. Because this subject involves so much fascinating and hidden <term>occult</term> speculation, I will provide a few examples of how scent affects different animals and the intelligence they show in managing it—starting with the hare.

The hare is naturally a timid animal, but it gives off a very strong scent. It sleeps in its "form" <note>A hare's shallow nest or resting place</note> during the day, and it feeds and mates <note>original: "copulates"</note> at night. On moonlit evenings, hares are sometimes seen playing together, leaping and chasing one another. Yet the slightest movement—even a falling leaf—alarms them, causing them to scatter in different directions. They are extremely fast, moving in a series of quick leaps or a gallop. higher grounds. Because their front feet are much shorter than their hind ones, they run with more ease uphill than downhill. The hare is endowed with all those instincts which are necessary for its own preservation. In winter, it chooses a **form** <term>the resting place or nest of a hare</term> exposed to the south, and in summer to the north. It has a thousand contrivances to elude the vigilance of its pursuers and to break its scent from the hounds. 

If it is rainy, the hare usually takes to the highways. If she comes to the side of a young grove or spring, she seldom enters, but **squats down** <note>crouches low to the ground to hide</note> until the hounds have over-shot her; then she will return the very way she came, for fear of the wet and dew that hangs on the boughs. When she comes near brook-sides and **plashes** <note>original: "plashes"—shallow pools or puddles</note>, she will make all her crossings, **doublings** <term>the act of a hunted animal turning back on its own path to confuse hounds</term>, and maneuvers. 

Some hares have been so crafty that as soon as they heard the sound of a hunting horn, they would instantly start out of their form—even if it were at a distance of a quarter of a mile—and go swim in some pool, resting upon a rush-bed in the middle of it. They would not stir from there until they heard the sound of the horn again, and then would start out, swimming to land. They have stayed ahead of the hounds for four hours before being caught, swimming and using all sorts of cunning and crossings in the water. 

Indeed, such is the natural craft and cunning of the hare that sometimes, after she has been hunted for three hours, she will drive up a fresh hare and squat in that hare's form herself. Others, having been hunted for a considerable time, will creep under the door of a **sheep-cot** <note>a small shelter or fold for sheep</note> and hide themselves among the sheep; or, when they have been hard-hunted, they will run in among a flock of sheep and will by no means be driven out from among them until the hounds are tied up and the sheep driven into their pens. Some of them will take to the ground like a rabbit, or run up a wall and hide in the grass on top of it. Some hares will go up one side of a hedge and come down the other, with only the thickness of the hedge being the distance between their paths. 

A hare that has been exhausted by hunting has been known to get upon a **quickset hedge** <term>a hedge made of living plants, usually hawthorn, planted closely together</term> and run a good distance along the top of it, and then leap off onto the ground. They will also frequently retreat to furze bushes and leap from one to the other to cut off the scent, which frequently causes the hounds to lose the trail. 

In the springtime or summer, a hare will not sit in bushes because they are frequently infested with **pismires** <note>original: "pismires"—an archaic term for ants</note>, snakes, and adders; instead, they will sit in cornfields and open places. In the wintertime, they sit near towns and villages in tufts of thorns and brambles, especially when the wind is northerly or southerly. It is remarkable that the hare, although so frequently pursued by dogs, seldom leaves the place where she was born, or even the form in which she usually sits.
