Females are larger <note>original: "grosser"</note> than the males and have less strength and agility; they are also more timid and never allow the dogs to approach as near to their **form** <term>the resting place or nest of a hare</term> before rising as the males do. They also practice more tricks <note>original: "arts"</note> and **double** <term>turn back on their own tracks to confuse hounds</term> more frequently than the males. The hare is found in almost every climate; and, even though they are hunted everywhere, their species never diminishes. They are able to breed during the first year of their lives; the females are pregnant for about thirty days and produce four or five young at a time. As soon as they have given birth, they mate again; so it may be said that they are almost always pregnant. The eyes of the young are open at birth; the mother suckles them for about twenty days, after which they separate from her and find their own food. The young never go far from the place where they were born, yet they still live solitary lives and make forms about thirty paces distant from each other. Thus, if a young hare is found anywhere, you can be almost certain of finding several others within a very small distance.

The fertility <note>original: "fecundity"</note> of the rabbit is even greater than that of the hare. They will breed seven times in a year, and the female sometimes brings eight young ones at a time. Supposing this to happen regularly for four years, the number of rabbits from a single pair would amount to one million, two hundred seventy-four thousand, eight hundred and forty. They are able to breed when they are six months old; and, like the hare, the female is almost constantly in season; she is pregnant for about thirty days and gives birth to between four and eight in a litter. A few days before giving birth, she digs a hole in the earth—not in a straight line, but in a zig-zag shape. She enlarges the bottom of this hole in every direction and then pulls a great quantity of hair from her own belly to make a kind of bed for her young. During the first two days after birth, she never leaves them except when pressed by hunger, and then she eats quickly and returns; in this manner, she suckles and attends to her young for six weeks. All this time, both the hole and the young are hidden from the male. Sometimes, when the female goes out, she fills the mouth of the hole with earth mixed with her own urine to deceive the male. But when the young ones begin to come to the mouth of the hole and to eat the herbs the mother brings them, the father seems to recognize them; he takes them between his paws, smooths their hair, and caresses them with great fondness.

The fox fixes his home on the edge of a wood, near cottages; he listens for the crowing of the rooster <note>original: "cock"</note> and the cries of the poultry. He smells them from a distance; he chooses his time wisely <note>original: "with judgment"</note>; he hides his path as well as his plan; he creeps forward cautiously, sometimes even dragging his body, and rarely makes a failed mission. In this way, he has been seen on a moonlight night entering a pasture where several hares were feeding. Lying down and taking his tail in his mouth, he has dragged himself along like a rolling stone, unsuspected by his prey, until he had gotten too close for any of them to escape. If he can leap the wall or crawl underneath, he ravages the courtyard, kills everything, and then retreats quietly with his prey, which he either hides under the plants <note>original: "herbage"</note> or carries off to his den <note>original: "kennel"</note>. He returns in a few minutes for another, which he carries off or hides in the same way, but in a different place. He continues this until the rising sun or movement in the house warns <note>original: "advertise"</note> him that it is time to stop his work and retreat to his den. 

He plays the same game with those who catch thrushes, woodcocks, etc. He visits the nets and birdlime <term>a sticky substance spread on branches to trap birds</term> very early in the morning, carries away the birds that are caught one after another, and hides them in various places—especially near roadsides, in furrows, or under plants or brushwood—where they sometimes lie for two or three days. However, he knows exactly where to find them when he is hungry. He hunts young hares in the fields, catches older ones in their resting places <note>original: "seats"</note>, never misses those that are wounded, digs rabbits out of their burrows <note>original: "warrens"</note>, discovers the nests of partridges and quails, catches the mothers on their eggs, and destroys a huge amount of game. 

The fox is extremely greedy <note>original: "voracious"</note>; besides all kinds of meat, he eats eggs, milk, cheese, fruit, and especially grapes with equal hunger. When young hares and partridges are unavailable, he hunts rats, field mice, snakes <note>original: "serpents"</note>, lizards, toads, etc. He destroys vast numbers of these, which is the only service he provides to mankind. He is so fond of honey that he attacks wild bees, wasps, and hornets. At first, they drive him away with a thousand stings, but he only retreats to roll on the ground and crush them. He returns to the attack so often that he forces them to abandon the hive, which he then uncovers to devour both the honey and the wax. He will also eat fish, lobsters, grasshoppers, and so on. 

Foxes only breed once a year, and the litter usually consists of four or five—rarely six and never fewer than three. When the female is pregnant <note>original: "full"</note>, she retreats and rarely leaves her hole, where she prepares a bed for her young. When she senses that her den has been discovered and her young have been disturbed, she carries them off one by one in search of another home. The fox, as well as the related <note>original: "congenerous"</note> wolf, can breed with dogs, as mentioned before. Crows, magpies, and other birds—who view the fox as a common enemy—will often reveal his hiding place <note>original: "retreat"</note> with their angry calls.

The stag or buck is the most clever <note>original: "crafty"</note> of all deer species. He does not wait to use his defensive tricks until his strength fails him. Instead, as soon as he realizes that the first burst of a fast chase has not worked, he repeatedly retraces his steps. Their mating season <note>original: "season of love"</note> begins about the end of August or the beginning of September, when they leave the coppice <note>a thicket of small trees</note>, return to the forests, and search for the hinds <note>female deer</note>. They cry with a loud voice; their neck and throat swell; they become perfectly restless and cross the fields and the fallow grounds in broad daylight. They strike their horns against the trees and hedges; in a word, they seem to be transported with fury and run from country to country until they find the hinds or females, whom they pursue and compel into submission. For the female at first avoids and flees from the male, and never submits to his embraces until she is fatigued with the pursuit. The old hinds also come into season before the younger ones. When two bucks approach the same hind, they must fight before they mate <note>original: "enjoy"</note>. If they are nearly equal in strength, they threaten, paw the ground, set up terrible cries, and attack each other with such fury that they often inflict mortal wounds with the strokes of their horns. The combat never ends except in the defeat or flight of one of the rivals. The conqueror loses not a moment in enjoying his victory, unless another rival approaches, whom he is again obliged to attack and repel. 

The oldest stags are always masters of the field because they are stronger and more furious than the young ones, who must wait patiently until their superiors tire and leave their mates. Sometimes, however, the young stags accomplish their purposes while the old ones are fighting and, after a hasty gratification, flee. The hinds prefer the old stags, not because they are most courageous, but because they are much more ardent. It has been alleged that, attracted by the scent of the hinds, the stags in the mating <note>original: "rutting"</note> season throw themselves into the sea and pass from one island to another at the distance of several leagues. They leap even more nimbly than they swim; for, when pursued, they easily clear a hedge or a pale fence <note>a fence made of wooden stakes</note> six or seven feet high, and on all pressing occasions show astonishing sense and wisdom <note>original: "sagacity"</note>.

Wolves have been known to follow armies and to come in packs to battlefields where bodies are poorly buried, tearing them up and devouring them with insatiable greed. Once they are accustomed to human flesh, they will attack people ever after, preferring the shepherd to the flock, devouring women, and carrying off children. 

The wolf, unlike the dog, is an enemy to all society and keeps no company even with those of his own species. When several wolves unite, it is not for a peaceful society but for war; it is accompanied by noise and dreadful howling, signaling an attack upon some large animal, such as a stag, an ox, or a formidable mastiff <note>mastiff: a large, powerful breed of dog often used for guarding or hunting</note>. This military expedition is no sooner finished than they separate, and each returns in silence to his solitude. There is very little interaction even between males and females: they feel the mutual attraction of mating <note>original: "love"</note> only once a year and never remain together for long. 

The females come into heat <note>original: "in season"</note> in winter. Many males follow the same female, and this gathering is more violent <note>original: "bloody"</note> than the hunting pack; for they growl, chase, fight, and tear at one another, and often kill the male that is preferred by the female. The female usually runs away for a long time, tiring out her admirers, and then slips away while they sleep with the most alert or favored male. 

Wolves mate like dogs and have a bony <note>original: "osseous"</note> penis containing a structure that swells and prevents them from separating during the act. When the females are about to give birth, they search for a hidden place in the deepest parts of the forest. The puppies are born blind, like dogs; the mother nurses them for several weeks and soon teaches them to eat meat, which she prepares for them by tearing it into small pieces. Sometime after, she brings them field mice, young hares, partridges, and live poultry. The young wolves begin by playing with these animals and finally kill <note>original: "worry"</note> them; then the mother pulls off the feathers, tears them to pieces, and gives a portion to each of her young. They never leave their den until they are six weeks or two months old. Then they follow their mother, who leads them to drink from the hollow trunk of a tree or a nearby pool. She leads them back to the den, or, if she senses danger, she makes them hide elsewhere. Although the she-wolf is naturally more timid than the male, like most females, she defends her young with great courage when they are attacked; she loses all sense of danger and becomes completely furious. She never leaves them until their upbringing is complete—until they are so strong as to need no further help or protection.

He carries a sheep in his mouth and at the same time outruns the shepherds; so he can only be stopped or deprived of his prey by dogs. His bite is cruel, and always more stubborn <note>original: "obstinate"</note> in proportion to how little the victim resists; for, when an animal can defend itself, the wolf is cautious and wary <note>original: "circumspect"</note>. He never fights except out of necessity, and not from motives of courage. When wounded with a musket ball, he cries out; and yet, when men are killing <note>original: "dispatching"</note> him with bludgeons, he does not complain. When he falls into a snare, he is so overcome with terror that he may be either killed or taken alive without resistance; he allows himself to be chained, muzzled, and led wherever you please without showing the least symptom of resentment or discontent. 

Wolves are now so rare in the populated parts of America that the inhabitants leave their sheep unguarded the whole night. Yet the governments of Pennsylvania and New Jersey did some years ago allow a reward of twenty shillings—and the latter even thirty shillings—for the killing of every wolf. History <note>original: "Tradition"</note> informed them what a plague <note>original: "scourge"</note> those animals had been to the colonies, so they wisely determined to prevent such an evil. In their early days <note>original: "infant state"</note>, wolves came down in multitudes from the mountains, often attracted by the smell of the corpses of hundreds of Indians who died of smallpox, which was brought among them by the Europeans. But the animals did not limit their attacks <note>original: "insults"</note> to the dead; they even devoured the sick and dying in their huts. 

Britain, a few centuries ago, was much infested by them. As recorded by Holinshed <note>original: "Hollingshead"; referring to Raphael Holinshed (c. 1525–1580), author of the *Chronicles*</note>, the wolf was very harmful <note>original: "noxious"</note> to the flocks in Scotland in 1577; nor was it entirely wiped out until about 1680, when the last wolf fell by the hands of the famous Sir Ewen Cameron. King Edward I issued his royal command to Peter Corbet to oversee and assist in their destruction in the several counties of Gloucester, Worcester, Hereford, Salop <note>Salop: the historical name for Shropshire</note>, and Stafford. In the neighboring county of Derby, certain persons at Wormhill held their lands by the duty of hunting and capturing the wolves that infested the country, which is why they were called "wolf-hunters" <note>original: "wolve-hunt"</note>. 

Looking back to Saxon times, we find that in King Athelstan’s reign wolves were so numerous in Yorkshire that a shelter <note>original: "retreat"</note> was built at Flixton in that county “to defend travelers <note>original: "passengers"</note> from the wolves, so that they should not be devoured by them.” Such ravages did these animals make during winter—particularly in January, when the cold was most severe—that the Saxons named that month "wolf-month" <note>Old English: *Wulf-monath*</note>. At the Cape of Good Hope, there is a species called the tiger-wolf <note>tiger-wolf: an archaic name for the spotted hyena</note>, which is actually gifted with the ability to imitate the cries of other animals to some extent. By this means, this master-deceiver is sometimes lucky enough to trick and attract calves, foals, lambs, and other animals. Near some of the larger farms, where there is a great deal of cattle, this ravenous

This beast is to be found almost every night; and at the same time, by frequently betraying itself from one hour to another with its howling, it gives the dogs the alarm. This is done with the intent to give the rest of the wolves an opportunity to come out from their ambush <note>original: "ambuscade"</note> and, without meeting the least resistance, carry off enough booty for themselves and their fleeing brothers. 

The tiger-wolf <note>original: "tiger-wolf"; a historical name for the spotted hyena (*Crocuta crocuta*)</note>, though a much larger and stronger animal, does not venture—unless driven to the utmost necessity—to measure its strength with a common dog, which is certainly clear proof of its cowardice. Notwithstanding this, the Hottentots <note>A historical name for the Khoekhoe, the indigenous nomadic pastoralists of South Africa</note> inform us that it is still within living memory that the tiger-wolf was bold enough to steal upon them and molest them in their huts, particularly by carrying off their children. This, however, is now no longer the case—a circumstance, perhaps, resulting from the introduction of firearms into the country. This invention has, in recent times, caused this as well as other wild beasts to stand in greater awe of man than they did formerly. I have heard the following story of the tiger-wolf mentioned, which is laughable enough, though perhaps not quite so probable:

> "At a feast near the Cape <note>The Cape of Good Hope, South Africa</note> one night, a trumpeter who had drunk his fill was carried outdoors so that he might cool himself and become sober again. The scent of him soon drew a tiger-wolf there, which threw him on its back and dragged him along like a corpse up toward Table Mountain. During this, however, the drunken musician woke up enough to realize the danger of his situation and sounded the alarm with his trumpet, which he carried fastened to his side. The wild beast, as may easily be imagined, was no less frightened in its turn."

Any person other than a trumpeter would, in such circumstances, undoubtedly have been nothing more than wolf’s meat.

The jackal appears to have a sense of smell equal to a dog, of which it seems to be a wild species. They go in packs of forty, fifty, and even two hundred, and hunt like hounds in full cry from evening until morning. They destroy flocks and poultry, but to a lesser degree than the wolf or fox; they ravage the streets of villages and gardens near towns, and will even destroy children if left unprotected. They will enter stables and outhouses and devour skins or anything made of that material. They will familiarly enter a tent and steal whatever they find from a sleeping traveler. In the absence of living prey, they will feed on roots and fruits, and even on the most infected carrion; they will greedily dig up <note>original: "disinter"</note> the dead and devour putrid carcasses. They attend caravans and follow armies in hopes that death will provide them a banquet. Their natural voice is a howl. **PATHOLOGICALLY.**—Remember that you must die! <note>original: "Memento mori!"</note> The life of man resembles a bubble ready to burst; his fate is suspended by a hair and is dependent on the uncertain passage of time. "The earth contains nothing more fragile than man:" *Homer.*—"Nothing is weaker than human life: to what dangers, and to how many diseases, is it not exposed! Hence the whole period of a man's life is but a span: half of it is necessarily spent in a state resembling death; without including the years of infancy, in which there is no judgment; or the period of old age, fertile in sufferings, during which the senses are blunted, the limbs become stiff, and the faculties of sight and hearing, the power of walking, and the teeth—the instruments of nourishment—fail before the rest of the body:" *Pliny.*—"Thus a considerable part of death is suffered during life; and death possesses all that belonged to the times which are past. Finally, nature will speedily recall and destroy all the beings which you see, and all that your imagination can suppose to exist hereafter; for death calls equally upon all, whether they be good or whether they be evil:" *Seneca.*

**NATURALLY.**—Live innocently, for God is present! <note>original: "Innocui vivite, Numen adest!"</note> Man, the prince of living beings, who is a miracle of nature and for whom all things on this earth were created, is an imitative animal—weeping, laughing, singing, speaking; manageable, sensible, inquisitive, and most wise. He is weak and naked, unprovided with natural weapons, exposed to all the injuries of fortune, in need of assistance from others, possessed of an anxious mind, eager for protection, continually complaining, changeable in temper, stubborn in hope, and slow in the acquisition of wisdom. He despises the time which is past, abuses that which is present, and sets his affections on the uncertain future; thus continually neglecting winged time, which, though infinitely precious, can never be recalled. For thus the best and swiftest time, in every age, flies on with miserable mortals. Some it summons to attend their daily and burdensome labors; some it confines to luxurious inaction, pampered even to suffocation with excesses; some it lures into the ever-restless paths of ambition; some it renders anxious for the acquisition of wealth, and distresses by the possession of the thing desired; some it condemns to solitude, and others to have their doors continually crowded with visitors. Here one bewails the conduct of his children; there one grieves their loss. Tears will fail us sooner than their causes, which only oblivion can remove. "On every hand our evils outweigh our advantages; we are surrounded with dangers; we rush forward into untried situations; we are enraged without having received provocation; like wild beasts, we destroy those we do not hate; we wish for favorable winds <note>original: "gales"</note>, which lead us only to destruction; the earth opens wide, ready for our death:" *Seneca.*—"Other animals unite together against enemies of a kind different from their own, while man suffers most injuries from his own species:" *Pliny.*

**POLITICALLY.**—*Be of ancient virtue and faith!* <note>original: "Esto antiqua virtute et fide!"</note> Man, instead of following that which is right, is subjected to the guidance of obvious error; this shrouds all his faculties under the thick veil of custom as soon as he is born. According to its dictates, he is fed, educated, brought up, and directed in all things; and by its arbitrary rules, his honesty, courage, wisdom, morality, and religion are judged. Thus, governed by opinion, he lives according to custom instead of being guided by reason. Though sent into the world as a mortal being (for all are evidently born to suffer), instead of endeavoring to secure those things which are most advantageous and truly beneficial, he—infatuated by the smiles of fortune—anxiously collects her gaudy trifles for future enjoyment and neglects her real benefits. He is driven to madness by envious critics; he persecutes the truly religious with hatred for differing from himself in theoretical opinions; he excites countless quarrels <note>original: "broils"</note>, not so that he may do good, but for a purpose that even he himself is ignorant of. He wastes his precious and irrecoverable time on trifles; he thinks lightly of immortal and eternal concerns while regulating the inheritance of his descendants. Perpetually entering into new projects and forgetful of his real condition, he builds palaces instead of preparing his grave, until at length, in the midst of his schemes, death seizes him. Then, first opening his eyes, he perceives, O man, that all is an illusion.

**MORALLY.**—*Do good and rejoice!* <note>original: "Benefac et lætare!"</note> Man is composed of a living inner substance <note>original: "animated medullary substance," likely referring to the brain or the nervous system as the seat of the soul</note> which prompts him to that which is right, and of a bodily frame liable to impressions which instigate him to the enjoyment of pleasure. In his natural state, he is foolish, reckless, a thoughtless follower of examples, ambitious, wasteful, dissatisfied, cunning, irritable, envious, malicious, and greedy. By the influence of just morals, he is transformed to be attentive, chaste, considerate, modest, temperate, quiet, sincere, mild, charitable, grateful, and contented.

He was endowed with wise <note>original: "sapient"</note> reason and made capable of drawing conclusions from the impressions of his senses so that, from a consideration of created objects, he might know their Creator as the Almighty, the Infinite, the All-knowing, the Eternal God. So that we may live morally under His governing care, it is necessary that we have a thorough conviction of His existence and must keep it ever in our memory.

In the *System of Nature* <note>original: "*Systema Naturæ*," the landmark work by Carl Linnaeus</note>, MAN (*Homo*) is ranked as a distinct genus of the order *Primates* or "Chiefs," belonging to the *Mammalia* class of animals, or those which nourish their young by means of milk-producing teats or breasts. Of this genus, he is the only species; and is denominated *Sapiens* ("Wise"), as being endowed with wisdom far superior to—or rather to the exclusion of—all other animals. He varies according to climate, education, and habits; and the following varieties, exclusive of *wild men* <note>Historical accounts often included "feral children" or "wild men" as a sub-category of humanity.</note>, are enumerated by Linnaeus:

**Americans.** "Of copper-colored complexion, <term>choleric</term> <note>One of the four humors, associated with an irritable or ambitious temperament.</note> constitution, and remarkably erect." Their hair is black, lank, and coarse; their nostrils are wide; their features harsh, and the chin is scantily supplied with a beard. They are obstinate in their tempers, free and satisfied with their condition, and are regulated in all their proceedings by traditional customs. They paint their skin with red streaks.

**Europeans.** "Of fair complexion, <term>sanguine</term> <note>Associated with a hopeful, social, and active temperament.</note> temperament, and brawny form." The hair is flowing and of various shades of brown; the eyes are mostly blue. They are of gentle manners, acute in judgment, quick of invention, and governed by fixed laws. They dress in close-fitting garments.

**Asiatics.** "Of sooty complexion, <term>melancholic</term> <note>Associated with a pensive, analytical, or somber temperament.</note> temperament, and rigid fiber." The hair is strong, black, and lank; the eyes are dark brown. They are of grave, haughty, and covetous manners, and are governed by opinions. They dress in loose garments.

**Africans.** "Of black complexion, <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>Associated with a calm, stoic, or sluggish temperament.</note> temperament, and relaxed fiber." The hair is black and frizzy; the skin soft and silky; the nose flat; the lips are thick; and the female has a natural apron <note>A historical reference to the "Hottentot apron," an anatomical feature of certain Southern African women that fascinated 18th-century naturalists.</note> and long, loose breasts. They are of crafty, indolent, and careless dispositions, and governed in their actions by caprice. They anoint the skin with grease.

The following arrangement of the varieties in the human species is offered by Dr. Gmelin <note>Johann Friedrich Gmelin (1748–1804), a German naturalist who edited an influential edition of Linnaeus's work.</note> as more convenient than that of Linnaeus:

**a. White (*Homo albus*).** Formed by the rules of symmetrical elegance and beauty—or at least what we consider as such. This division includes almost all the inhabitants of Europe; those of Asia on this side of the Ob River <note>original: "Oby"</note>, the Caspian Sea, Mount Imaus <note>The Himalayas or Hindu Kush mountain range.</note>, and the Ganges; likewise the natives of northern Africa, of Greenland, and the Inuit <note>original: "Esquimaux"</note>.

Those characteristics in the human form by which man is distinguished from non-human <note>original: "brute"</note> animals, can be reduced to two main points. The first is the strength of the leg muscles, by which the body is supported in a vertical position above them; the second consists in the jointing <note>original: "articulation"</note> of the head with the neck at the middle of its base. <meta>This page continues from a classification of human varieties and "monsters," transitioning into a comparative anatomical study of human bipedalism versus the anatomy of other primates and quadrupeds.</meta>

<page-num>128</page-num>

# A KEY TO PHYSIC,

...we are supported in these various positions. This power resides chiefly in the muscles that make up the main part of the calf of the leg. Their exertion is felt, and their motion is visible externally, when we stand upright and bend our body backward and forward. This power is just as great when we walk, even on a horizontal plane. When climbing a height, the weight of the body is felt more noticeably than when descending. All these motions are natural to humans. Other animals, on the contrary, when placed on their hind legs, are either incapable of performing them at all, or do it partially, with great difficulty, and for a very short time.

The gibbon, and the jocko <note>An archaic term used by naturalists like Buffon to refer to the chimpanzee.</note> or orangutan <note>original: "ourang-outang"</note>, are the animals that most resemble humans in their physical build. They can stand upright with much less difficulty than other animals <note>original: "brutes"</note>; but the strain they experience in this position clearly shows that it is not natural to them. The reason is that the muscles in the back part of the leg in the gibbon and the jocko are not large enough to form a calf, as they are in humans. Consequently, they are not strong enough to support the thighs and body in a vertical line or to keep them in that position.

The postures proper to humans and to other animals are indicated by the different ways in which the head is joined <note>original: "articulated"</note> to the neck. The two points where the bony <note>original: "osseous"</note> part of the head connects to the first vertebra of the neck—allowing every movement of the head to be made with great ease—are located at the edge of the large opening <note>original: "great foramen"</note> of the occipital bone. In humans, this opening is situated near the center of the base of the skull <note>original: "cranium"</note>. It provides a passage for the spinal cord <note>original: "medullary substance"</note> into the vertebrae and determines where the head joins the neck.

Since the body and neck are naturally held in a vertical direction, the head must be balanced on the vertebrae as if on a pivot or point of support. The face is on a vertical line, almost parallel to that of the body and neck. The jaws, which are very short compared with those of most other animals, extend very little further forward than the forehead.

No other animal has hind legs as long as the body, neck, and head combined (measured from the top of the head to the pubic bone <note>original: "os pubis"</note>) as humans do.

In the frame of the human body, the principal parts are nearly the same as those of other animals; however, there is as great a difference in the connection and shape of the bones as there is in the postures proper to each species. If a person were to assume the natural posture of four-legged animals <note>original: "quadrupeds"</note> and try to walk using both hands and feet, they would find themselves in a very unnatural position. They could move their feet and head only with the greatest difficulty and pain; no matter how much effort they made, they would find it impossible to maintain a steady and continuous pace. The main obstacles they would encounter would arise from the structure of the pelvis, the hands, the feet, and the head.

The plane of the large opening in the back of the skull <note>original: "great occipital foramen"</note>, which is almost horizontal in humans, places the head in a state of balance upon

...the neck when we stand upright in our natural posture. However, when we are in the posture of four-legged animals (quadrupeds), this structure prevents us from raising our head to look forward. This is because the movement of the head is stopped by the protrusion of the back of the skull (the occiput), which then comes too close to the vertebrae of the neck.

In most animals, the *foramen magnum* <note>original: "foramen magnum"; the large opening at the base of the skull through which the spinal cord passes.</note> of the occipital bone is located at the back of the head. Their jaws are very long, and the back of the skull has no protrusion beyond this opening. The plane of this opening is vertical or tilted slightly forward or backward. Consequently, the head hangs down and is joined to the neck at its back part. This position of the head allows four-legged animals to face their muzzle forward even though their bodies are oriented horizontally. They can raise it to reach above them or touch the ground with the tips of their jaws when they lower their neck and head to their feet. In the posture of a four-legged animal, a human could only touch the ground with the forehead or the top of the head.

When a human stands, the heel rests on the ground along with the rest of the foot. When walking, the heel is the first part to touch the ground. Humans can also stand on one foot. These are unique features of our physical structure and movement that are not found in other animals. We may therefore conclude that humans cannot be classified as quadrupeds. 

We may add that in humans, the brain is much larger and the jaws much shorter than in any other animal. Because of its large size, the brain forms the protrusion of the back of the skull (the occiput), the forehead, and the entire part of the head above the ears. In other animals, the brain is so small that most of them have no protruding back-skull, and the forehead is either missing or very low. In animals with large foreheads—such as the horse, the ox, or the elephant—the forehead is positioned as low as, or even lower than, the ears. These animals also lack a protruding back-skull, and the top of the head is very small. The jaws, which make up the largest part of the muzzle, are large compared to the small size of the brain. The length of the muzzle varies: in single-hoofed <note>original: "solipede"</note> animals, it is very long; it is short in the orangutan <note>original: "ourang-outang"</note>; and in humans, it does not exist at all. Furthermore, no beard grows on a muzzle; this human feature is missing in every other animal.

Anatomists have taken great pains to study the physical nature of humanity and the biological organization that determines our place in the animal kingdom. By tracing and comparing various external parts—observing that the human body is covered with hair in some places; that humans can walk on hands and feet simultaneously like four-legged animals; that, like certain animals that hold food in their paws, humans have two collarbones (clavicles); and that females give birth to live young and provide milk from their breasts—one might be tempted to classify humans as live-bearing <note>original: "viviparous"</note> quadrupeds. However, in truth, such a classification would be flawed, arbitrary, and absurd. Man is

Most animals are blind for some days after birth. Infants open their eyes to the light the moment they enter the world, but their eyes are dull, fixed, and commonly blue. The newborn child cannot distinguish objects because they are incapable of focusing their eyes upon them. The organ of sight is still imperfect; the cornea is wrinkled, and perhaps the retina is too soft to receive the images of external objects or to communicate the sensation of clear vision. At the end of forty days, the infant begins to hear and to smile. About the same time, it begins to look at bright objects and frequently turns its eyes toward a window, a candle, or any light. Now it also begins to weep, for its earlier cries and groans were not accompanied by tears. 

Smiles and tears are the result of two internal sensations, both of which depend on the functions of the mind. Thus, they are unique to the human race and serve to express mental pain or pleasure, while the cries, movements, and other signs of physical pain and pleasure are common to humans and most other animals. Considering the subject as philosophers <term>original: metaphysicians</term>, we find that pain and pleasure are the universal powers that set all our passions in motion.

The size of an infant born at full term is commonly twenty-one inches. The head is large in proportion to the body; this disproportion, which is even greater in the early stages of the fetus, continues throughout infancy. The skin of a newborn child is a reddish color because it is so thin and transparent that it allows a slight tint of the blood's color to show through. The form of the body and limbs is by no means perfect in a child soon after birth; all the parts appear to be swollen. This swelling decreases as the child grows.

Otherwise, there is a great risk of disorienting <note>original: confusing</note> the infant’s brain and causing a total physical breakdown <term>original: derangement</term>. It is necessary for their health that their sleep be long and natural. 

It is possible, however, that they may sleep too much and thereby endanger their health <term>original: constitution</term>. However robust and healthy a child may be, they may be exposed to great danger and inconvenience if any other food <note>original: aliment</note> is given before the end of the first month. In Holland, Italy, Turkey, and throughout the Middle East <note>original: the whole Levant</note>, the food of children is limited to the nurse’s milk for an entire year. The indigenous people <note>original: savages</note> of Canada nurse their children for four, five, and sometimes even seven years. In this country, as nurses generally do not have a sufficient quantity of milk to satisfy the appetites of their children, they commonly supply the lack of it with <term>panada</term>—a dish made of bread crumbs boiled in water or milk—or other light preparations.

Teeth usually begin to appear around the age of seven months. Teething <note>original: the cutting of these</note>, although a natural process, does not follow the common laws of nature, which usually act on the human body without causing the slightest pain or even producing any sensation. In this case, a violent and painful effort is made, accompanied by cries and tears. At first, children lose their cheerfulness and energy; they become sad, restless, and fretful. The gums are red and swollen, but they later become white when the pressure of the teeth is so great that it stops the circulation of the blood. Children put their fingers in their mouths to remove the irritation they feel there. Some relief is provided by putting a piece of ivory, coral, or some other hard and smooth object into their hands, which they use to rub the affected part of the gums. This pressure, being opposite to that of the teeth, calms the pain for a moment, helps thin the membrane of the gum, and makes it easier for the tooth to break through. Nature here acts against herself, and sometimes the gum must be lanced <note>original: an incision of the gum must take place</note> to allow the tooth to pass.

When children are allowed to cry for too long and too often, hernias <term>original: ruptures</term> are sometimes caused by the strain they exert. These may easily be cured by the prompt application of bandages; but if this remedy is delayed too long, the condition may continue through life. Children are also very susceptible to worms. Some of the bad effects caused by these parasites might be prevented by giving them a little wine every now and then, for fermented liquors have a tendency to prevent their growth <note>original: generation</note>.

Although the body is very delicate in the state of infancy, it is less sensitive to cold then than at any other time of life. Internal heat appears to be greater: the pulse in children is much faster than in adults, from which we are certainly entitled to conclude that internal heat is greater in the same proportion. For the same reason, it is evident that small animals have more heat than large ones, for the beating of the heart and the pulse are always faster in proportion to the smallness of the animal. The heartbeats of a sparrow follow one another so rapidly that they can scarcely be counted.

Until three years of age, the life of a child is very uncertain <note>original: precarious</note>. In the following two or three years, it becomes more stable; and at six or seven years of age, a child has a better chance of living than at any other period of life. From the **bills of mortality** <term>bills of mortality</term> <note>Weekly mortality statistics published in London, which listed the numbers and causes of deaths.</note> published in London, it appears that, of a certain number of children born at the same time, half of them die within the first three years. According to this, half of the human race is cut off before they are three years old. However, the mortality rate among children is not nearly as high everywhere as it is in London. M. Dupré de Saint Maur <note>Nicolas-François Dupré de Saint-Maur (1695–1774), a French statistician known for his work on population and economics.</note>, based on a great number of observations made in France, has shown that half of the children born at the same time do not pass away until seven or eight years have elapsed.

The period of infancy is followed by that of adolescence. This begins, together with puberty, at the age of twelve or fourteen, and commonly ends in girls at sixteen, and in boys at eighteen; but sometimes it does not end until twenty-one, twenty-three, or even twenty-five years of age. According to its etymology—being derived from the Latin word *adolescentia* <note>Latin: "the state of growing up."</note>—this stage is completed when the body has attained its full height. Thus, puberty accompanies adolescence and precedes youth. This is the spring of life; this is the season of pleasures, of loves, and of graces. But alas! This smiling season is of short duration. 

Hitherto, nature seems to have had nothing in view but the preservation and growth of her work. She has made no provision for the infant except what is necessary for its life and development. The child has lived, or rather enjoyed, a kind of **vegetable existence** <note>In this context, a life focused purely on physical growth and survival without social, rational, or reproductive drives.</note> which was contained within itself and which it was incapable of sharing with others. In this first stage of life, reason is still asleep. But the principles of life soon multiply, and man possesses not only what is necessary for his own existence, but what enables him to give existence to others. This **redundancy of life** <note>An overflow or excess of vital energy beyond what is needed for one's own survival.</note>, this source of health and vigor, can no longer be confined, but endeavors to diffuse and expand itself.

The age of puberty is announced by several marks. The first symptom is a kind of numbness and stiffness in the groins, accompanied by a new and peculiar sensation in those parts which distinguish the sexes. There, as well as in the armpits, small white protuberances appear, which are the germs of a new production: a kind of hair by which these parts are afterwards to be veiled. The voice, for a considerable time, is rough and uneven; after which it becomes fuller, stronger, and deeper than it was before. This change may easily be distinguished in boys, but less so in girls because their voices are naturally higher <note>original: sharper</note>. These marks of puberty are common to both sexes, but there are marks peculiar to each: such as the discharge of the **menses** <term>menses</term> <note>Menstruation.</note> and the growth of the breasts in girls; the beard and the emission of **semen** in boys. Females arrive at puberty sooner than males, but the age of puberty differs among different nations and seems partly to depend on the temperature of the climate and the quality of food. But in northern regions and in the countryside, girls hardly reach puberty until they are fourteen or fifteen, and boys not until they are sixteen or seventeen. In our climate, girls, for the most part, have attained complete maturity at eighteen, and boys at twenty years of age.

During adolescence and puberty, the body commonly reaches its full height. Around that time, young people grow several inches almost all at once. But there is no part of the human body which increases more quickly and more perceptibly than the **reproductive organs** <term>organs of generation</term> <note>Archaic term for the biological organs used for reproduction.</note> in both sexes. In males, this growth is nothing but an unfolding of the parts and an increase in size; but in females, it often causes a shrinking and contraction, which have been given various names by those who have written about the signs of virginity.

Marriage is a state suitable to humanity, wherein one must make use of those new faculties acquired at puberty. At this period of life, the desire to produce a being like oneself is strongly felt. The external form and the compatibility of the sexual organs undoubtedly cause that irresistible attraction which unites the sexes and continues the human race. By connecting pleasure with the propagation of the species, nature has provided most effectively for the continuation of her work. *"Be fruitful and multiply"* <note>original: "Increase and multiply"</note> is the express command of the Creator and one of the natural functions of life. 

We may add that at the age of puberty, a thousand impressions act upon the nervous system. These place a person in such a situation that he feels his existence only through that voluptuous sense, which then appears to become the seat of his soul. This sense engrosses the entire range of feelings of which he is capable, and it eventually reaches such a height that its intensity cannot long be sustained without a general disruption of the whole physical system. The persistence of such a feeling may sometimes indeed prove fatal to those who indulge in excessive enjoyment; but it is equally dangerous to those who stubbornly persist in **celibacy** <note>The state of abstaining from marriage and sexual relations.</note>, especially when strongly urged by nature. 

The semen, being confined too long in its vessels, may—by its stimulating properties—cause diseases in both sexes and excite irritations so violent as to reduce a person to the level of a brute animal. Until three years of age, the life of a child is very precarious. In the two or three following years, it becomes more certain; and at six or seven years of age, a child has a better chance of living than at any other period of life. From the bills of mortality <note>Records of deaths and their causes published by parishes.</note> published in London, it appears that, of a certain number of children born at the same time, half of them die within the first three years: according to which, half of the human race are cut off before they are three years of age. But the mortality among children is not nearly so great everywhere as in London. Monsieur <note>original: "M."</note> Dupré de Saint Maur, from a great number of observations made in France, has shown that half of the children born at the same time are not extinct <note>meaning deceased or no longer living.</note> until seven or eight years have elapsed.

The period of infancy is followed by that of adolescence. This begins, together with puberty, at the age of twelve or fourteen, and commonly ends in girls at sixteen, and in boys at eighteen, but sometimes not until twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-five years of age. According to its etymology (being derived from the Latin word *adolescentia* <note>meaning "the state of growing up."</note>), it is completed when the body has attained its full height. Thus, puberty accompanies adolescence and precedes youth. This is the spring of life; this is the season of pleasures, of loves, and of graces: but alas! this smiling season is of short duration. Until now, nature seems to have had nothing in view but the preservation and increase of her work: she has made no provision for the infant except what is necessary for its life and growth. It has lived, or rather enjoyed, a kind of vegetative existence <note>original: "vegetable existence"; in 18th-century science, this referred to the biological functions of nutrition and growth shared with plants, before the development of reason.</note>, which was shut up within itself, and which it was incapable of communicating. In this first stage of life, reason is still asleep: but the principles of life soon multiply, and man has not only what is necessary to his own existence, but what enables him to give existence to others. This overflow of life, this source of health and vigor, can no longer be confined, but endeavors to diffuse and expand itself.

The age of puberty is announced by several marks. The first symptom is a kind of numbness and stiffness in the groin, accompanied by a new and peculiar sensation in those parts that distinguish the sexes. There, as well as in the armpits, small bumps of a whitish color appear, which are the seeds of a new growth <note>original: "germs of a new production"</note>, a kind of hair by which these parts are afterward to be covered <note>original: "veiled"</note>. The voice, for a considerable time, is rough and unequal; after which it becomes fuller, stronger, and deeper <note>original: "graver"</note> than it was before. This change may easily be distinguished in boys; but less so in girls, because their voices are naturally higher <note>original: "sharper"</note>. He stands upright; his posture is that of command; his majestic countenance, which is turned toward heaven, bears the impressions of his dignity. The image of his soul is painted in his face; the excellence of his nature shines through the physical organs and gives a fire and animation to the features of his face. His majestic manner, his firm and confident walk, announce the nobility of his rank. He touches the earth only with his feet; he views it only at a distance and seems to look down upon it. 

It has been rightly observed that the face of man is the mirror of his mind. In the looks of no other animal are the expressions of passion painted with such energy and speed, and with such gentle transitions and shades, as in those of man. We know that in certain emotions of the mind, the blood rises to the face and produces blushing; and that in others, the face turns pale. These two symptoms—the appearance of which depends on the structure and transparency of the skin's membrane <note>original: "reticulum"; likely referring to the *rete mucosum*, the layer of skin responsible for pigmentation and where blood flow is most visible.</note>, especially redness—constitute a unique beauty. 

In our climates, the natural color of the face of a man in good health is white, with a lively red spread across the cheeks. Paleness of the face is always a suspicious symptom. A color that is shaded with black is a sign of melancholy <note>In the medical theory of the time, "melancholy" was caused by an excess of "black bile."</note> and of impaired bile; and constant, universal redness is proof that the blood is being carried with too much force to the brain. A bluish <note>original: "livid"</note> color is a diseased and dangerous symptom; and a yellowish tint is a sign of jaundice or an overabundance of bile. The color of the skin is frequently altered by lack of sleep or nourishment, or by digestive issues <note>original: "looseness and diarrhoea."</note>.

Despite the general similarity of faces within nations and families, there is a wonderful diversity of features. No one, however, is at a loss to recognize the person to whom he intends to speak, provided he has once fully seen him. One man has liveliness and joy painted in his face, and announces beforehand—by the cheerfulness of his appearance—the character he will maintain in society. The tears which wet the cheeks of another man would excite compassion in the most unfeeling heart. Thus, the human face is the meeting point for the symptoms of both his moral and physical conditions:
*   Tranquillity and anger
*   Threatening and joy
*   Smiles and laughter
*   Malice, love, and envy
*   Jealousy, pride, and contempt
*   Disdain or indignation
*   Irony and arrogance
*   Tears, terror, and astonishment
*   Horror, fear, and shame
*   Humiliation, sorrow, and affliction
*   Compassion and meditation
*   Particular convulsions, sleep, death, etc. 

The differences between these expressions are important enough to form a primary subject in the study of human nature.

When the mind is at ease, all the features of the face are in a state of profound peace. Their proportion, harmony, and union point out the serenity of the thoughts. But when the soul is agitated, the human face becomes a living canvas, where the passions are represented with equal delicacy and energy, where every emotion...

### AND OCCULT SCIENCE.

Every emotion of the soul is expressed by some feature, and every action by some mark; the vivid impression of these features anticipates our will and reveals, through expressive <note>original: "pathetic"; here meaning full of pathos or emotion rather than "pitiful."</note> signs, our secret agitation and those intentions which we are anxious to conceal. It is particularly in the eyes that the soul is painted in the strongest colors and with the most delicate shades.

The different colors of the eyes are dark hazel, light hazel, green, blue, gray, and whitish-gray. The most common of these colors are hazel and blue, both of which are often found in the same eye. Eyes which are commonly called black are actually only dark hazel; they appear black because they are contrasted with the white of the eye. Wherever there is a tint of blue, however slight, it becomes the prevailing color and outshines the hazel with which it is intermixed to such a degree that the mixture cannot be perceived without a very close examination. The most beautiful eyes are those which appear black or blue. In the former, there is more expression and vivacity; in the latter, more sweetness and perhaps delicacy. Next to the eyes, the parts of the face by which the <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of judging a person’s character or personality from their outer appearance, especially the face.</note> is most strongly marked are the eyebrows. Being of a different nature from the other parts, their effect is increased by contrast. They are like a shadow in a picture, which gives relief <note>A term from art referring to the appearance of three-dimensional depth or "standing out" from the background.</note> to the other colors and forms.

The forehead is one of the largest parts of the face and contributes most to its beauty. Everybody knows how great an importance hair has in the physiognomy, and that baldness is a very great defect. When old age begins to approach, the hair which first falls off is that which covers the crown of the head and the parts above the temples. We seldom see the hair of the lower part of the temples, or of the back of the head, completely fall off. Baldness is peculiar to men; women do not naturally lose their hair, though it becomes white—as does that of men—at the approach of old age.

The nose is the most prominent feature of the face. But as it has very little motion, and that only during the most violent passions, it contributes less to expression than to the beauty of the countenance. The nose is seldom perfectly centered <note>original: "perpendicular to the middle of the face"</note>, but for the most part is turned to one side or the other. The cause of this irregularity—which, according to painters, is perfectly consistent with beauty and the absence of which would even be a deformity—appears to be the frequent pressure on one side of the child's nose cartilage against the mother's breast during breastfeeding. At this early period of life, the cartilages and bones have acquired very little solidity and are easily bent, as may be observed in the legs and thighs of some individuals who have been injured by the bandages of <term>swaddling clothes</term>. <note>Long strips of cloth formerly wrapped around infants to restrict movement, which the author suggests could cause physical deformities if applied incorrectly.</note>

# A KEY TO PHYSIC, <note>original: "Physic"; here referring to the art of healing and the study of natural science and the human body.</note>

Next to the eyes, the mouth and lips have the greatest motion and expression. These motions are under the influence of the passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to any strong emotions or states of mind, such as anger, joy, or sorrow.</note>. The mouth, which is set off by the vermilion <note>A bright red color.</note> of the lips and the enamel of the teeth, marks their different characters by the various forms which it assumes. The organ of the voice likewise gives animation to this feature, and communicates to it more life and expression than is possessed by any of the rest. The cheeks are uniform features and have no motion or expression except from that involuntary redness or paleness with which they are covered in different passions—such as shame, anger, pride, and joy on the one hand, and fear, terror, and sorrow on the other.

In different passions, the whole head assumes different positions and is affected with different motions. It hangs forward during shame, humility, and sorrow; it inclines to one side in languor and compassion; it is elevated in pride, and held erect and fixed in obstinacy <note>Stubbornness.</note> and self-conceit; in astonishment, it is thrown backwards; and it moves from side to side in contempt, ridicule, anger, and indignation. In grief, joy, love, shame, and compassion, the eyes swell and the tears flow. The effusion <note>The outward flow.</note> of tears is always accompanied by an extension of the muscles of the face, which opens the mouth.

In sorrow, the corners of the mouth are depressed, the under-lip rises, the eyelids fall down, and the pupil of the eye is raised and half-conceled by the eyelid. The other muscles of the face are relaxed, so that the distance between the eyes and the mouth is greater than ordinary; and consequently, the countenance <note>A person's face or facial expression.</note> appears to be lengthened. 

In fear, terror, consternation, and horror, the forehead is wrinkled, the eyebrows are raised, and the eyelids are opened as wide as possible; the upper lid uncovers a part of the white above the pupil, which is depressed and partly concealed by the under lid. At the same time, the mouth opens wide, the lips recede from each other, and reveal <note>original: "discover"</note> the teeth both above and below. 

In contempt and derision, the upper lip is raised at one side and exposes the teeth, while the other side of the lip moves a little and has the appearance of a smile. The nostril on the elevated side of the lip shrivels up, and the corner of the mouth falls down. The eye on the same side is almost shut, while the other is open as usual; but the pupils of both are depressed, as when one looks down from a height. 

In jealousy, envy, and malice, the eyebrows fall down and are wrinkled; the eyelids are elevated, and the pupils are depressed. The upper lip is elevated on both sides, while the corners of the mouth are a little depressed, and the under lip rises to join the middle of the upper. 

In laughter, the corners of the mouth are drawn back and a little elevated; the upper parts of the cheeks rise; the eyes are more or less closed; the upper lip rises, and the under one falls down; the mouth opens; and, in cases of immoderate <note>Excessive or extreme.</note> laughter, the skin of the nose wrinkles. That gentler and more gracious kind of laughter which is called *smiling*, is seated wholly

...is expressed entirely in the parts of the mouth. The lower lip rises; the corners of the mouth are drawn back; the cheeks are puffed up; the eyelids move closer together; and a small twinkling is observed in the eyes. It is very extraordinary that laughter may be excited either by a psychological <note>original: "moral"; here referring to internal emotional or mental triggers.</note> cause without the immediate action of external objects, or by a particular irritation of the nerves without any feeling of joy. Thus, an involuntary laugh is excited by a slight tickling of the lips, of the palm of the hand, of the sole of the foot, of the armpits, and below the middle of the ribs. We laugh when two different ideas, whose combination was unexpected, are presented to the mind at the same time, and when one or both of these ideas, or their union, include some absurdity which excites an emotion of contempt <note>original: "disdain."</note> mingled with joy. In general, striking contrasts never fail to produce laughter.

A change is produced in the features of the face by weeping as well as by laughing. When we weep, the lower lip is separated from the teeth, the forehead is wrinkled, the eyebrows are lowered, and the dimple, which gives a gracefulness to laughter, leaves the cheek. The eyes are more compressed and almost constantly soaked in tears, which in laughter flow more seldom and less abundantly.

The arms, hands, and every part of the body contribute to the expression of the passions <note>original: "passions"; here meaning strong emotions or states of feeling.</note>. In joy, for instance, all the parts of the body are moved with quick and various motions. In listlessness <note>original: "languor."</note> and sorrow, the arms hang down, and the whole body remains fixed and immovable. In admiration and surprise, this total suspension of motion is likewise observed. In love, desire, and hope, the head and eyes are raised to heaven and seem to seek <note>original: "solicit."</note> the desired good; the body leans forward as if to approach it; the arms are stretched out and seem to seize the beloved object beforehand. On the contrary, in fear, hatred, and horror, the arms seem to push backward and repel the object of our dislike <note>original: "aversion."</note>; we turn away our head and eyes as if to avoid the sight of it; we recoil in order to shun it.

Although the human body is externally much more delicate than that of any other animal, yet it is very vigorous <note>original: "nervous"; in this context, meaning strong, sinewy, or full of physical energy.</note> and perhaps stronger in proportion to its size than that of the strongest animals. We are assured that the porters at Constantinople <note>Now known as Istanbul, Turkey.</note> carry burdens of nine hundred pounds weight, yet drink nothing but water. A thousand wonderful stories are related of the Hottentots <note>A historical name for the Khoekhoe people of Southern Africa, now considered offensive.</note> and other peoples concerning their agility in running. Civilized man does not know the full extent of his powers, nor how much he loses by that softness <note>original: "effeminacy"; here meaning physical weakness or lack of vigor due to a comfortable lifestyle.</note> and inactivity by which they are weakened and destroyed. He is even content to be ignorant of the strength and vigor which his limbs are capable of acquiring through motion and by being accustomed to severe exercises, as is observed in runners, tumblers, and rope-dancers. The conclusion is, therefore, founded on the most just and indisputable reasoning <note>original: "induction."</note> and—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of human physiology, transitioning from the physical expression of emotions to the mechanics of movement (walking, running, and jumping), the restorative nature of sleep, and the onset of physical decline in middle and old age.</meta>

...analogy. The posture of walking is less tiring for a person than the posture assumed when running. With every step, a person covers more ground; the body leans forward, and the arms move in the same direction; respiration increases, and breathing becomes difficult. Jumping <note>original: "leaping"</note> begins with a deep bending of the limbs; the body crouches down, but then immediately extends itself with great effort. The movements involved in jumping make it very exhausting.

It is observed that simply stopping exercise is not enough to restore the body's energy when it is exhausted by fatigue. Like a mechanical clock, the body's "springs"—even when not in motion—remain wound up as long as we are awake, even if every movement is suspended. In sleep, nature finds the rest it requires, and the various organs enjoy a healthy <note>original: "salutary"</note> relaxation. This is that remarkable state in which a person—unconscious of their own existence and appearing almost dead—repairs the damage their faculties have sustained and seems to take on a new life. In this state of drowsiness and rest, the senses stop acting, bodily functions are suspended, and the body seems left to itself. The outward symptoms of sleep, which are our primary focus, are easily recognized. As sleep approaches, the eyes begin to blink, the eyelids droop, and the head starts to nod and hang down. This sudden drop startles the sleeper; he jumps and tries to fight off sleep, but in vain. A new urge, stronger than the first, takes away his ability to lift his head; his chin rests upon his chest, and in this position, he enjoys a peaceful sleep.

The period of physical decline generally spans from age forty or forty-five to sixty or sixty-five. At this stage of life, the loss of body fat causes those wrinkles that begin to appear on the face and other parts of the body. Because the skin is no longer supported by the same amount of fat and has lost its elasticity, it cannot tighten and instead sags into folds. During this decline, a significant change also occurs in one's vision. In our youth <note>original: "vigour of our days"</note>, the crystalline lens—which is thicker and more transparent <note>original: "diaphanous"</note> than the fluids <note>original: "humours"</note> of the eye—allows us to read small print from a distance of eight or ten inches. However, as decline sets in, the volume of the eye's fluids decreases, they lose their clarity, and the transparent cornea becomes less curved <note>original: "convex"</note>. To compensate for this, we hold reading material further away from our eyes; however, this does little to help because the image of the object then appears smaller and more blurred <note>original: "obscure"</note>. Another sign of aging is a weakened stomach and indigestion, which occurs in most people who do not exercise enough relative to the amount and richness <note>original: "quality"</note> of the food they eat. By age sixty, sixty-three, or sixty-five, the signs of decline become more and more visible,

visible, and indicate *old age*. This period commonly extends to the age of seventy, sometimes to seventy-five, but seldom to eighty. When the body is weakened <note>original: "extenuated"</note> and bent by old age, man then becomes *infirm* <note>original: "crazy," which in this period meant physically broken or full of cracks, rather than mentally ill</note>. *Infirmity* therefore is nothing but *a frail old age*. The eyes and stomach then become weaker and weaker; leanness increases the number of wrinkles; the beard and the hair become white; the strength and the memory begin to fail. After seventy, or at most eighty years of age, the life of man is nothing but labor and sorrow: such was the language of David <note>A reference to Psalm 90:10</note> nearly three thousand years ago. Some men of strong constitutions, and in good health, enjoy old age for a long time without falling into decrepitude; but such instances are not very common. The infirmities of decrepitude continually increase, and at length death concludes the whole. This fatal end is uncertain. The only conclusions which we can form concerning the duration of life must be derived from observations made on a great number of men who were born at the same time, and who died at different ages.

The signs of decrepitude form a striking picture of weakness and announce the approaching breakdown <note>original: "dissolution"</note> of the body. The memory totally fails; the nerves become hard and dull; deafness and blindness take place; the senses of smell, touch, and taste are destroyed; the appetite fails; the necessity of eating, and more frequently that of drinking, are all that is felt. After the teeth fall out, chewing <term>mastication</term> is imperfectly performed, and digestion is very bad; the lips fall inward; the edges of the jaws can no longer approach one another; the muscles of the lower jaw become so weak that they are unable to raise and support it; the body sinks down; the spine is bent outward; and the vertebrae grow together at the front; the body becomes extremely lean; the strength fails; the decrepit wretch is unable to support himself; he is obliged to remain on a seat, or stretched in his bed. The bladder becomes paralytic; the intestines lose their elasticity <note>original: "spring"</note>; the circulation of the blood becomes slower; the beats of the pulse no longer reach eighty in a minute, as in the vigor of life, but are reduced to twenty-four, and sometimes fewer. Respiration is slower; the body loses its heat; the circulation of the blood ceases; death follows; and the dream of life is no more.

Man, however, has no right to complain of the shortness of life. Throughout all living beings, there are few who possess to a greater degree all the internal causes which tend to prolong its different stages. The term of pregnancy <term>gestation</term> is very significant; the development of the teeth is very late; his growth is slow and is not completed until about twenty years have elapsed. The age of puberty, also, is much later in man than in any other animal. In short, the parts of his body, being composed of a softer and more flexible substance, are not...

[The bones of humans are not] so soon hardened as those of inferior animals. Man, therefore, seems to receive at his birth the seeds of a long life: if he does not reach the distant period which nature seemed to promise him, it must be owing to accidental or acquired causes, foreign to himself. Instead of saying that he has finished his life, we ought rather to say that he has not completed it. The natural and total duration of life is in some measure proportioned to the period of growth. A tree or an animal, which soon acquires its full size, decays much sooner than another which continues to grow for a longer time. If it be true that the life of animals is eight times longer than the period of their growth, we might conclude that the boundaries of human life may be extended to a century and a half <note>150 years</note>.

It does not appear that the life of man becomes shorter in proportion to the length of time the world has existed. In the days of the Psalmist <note>A reference to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms, who wrote that a typical life lasts 70 or 80 years</note>, the ordinary limits of human life did not exceed seventy or eighty years. No king of Judah lived beyond that period. When the Romans, however, were numbered by Vespasian, there were found in the empire—even in that age of effeminacy <note>original: "effeminacy," here referring to a period of luxury and physical softness</note>—ten men aged a hundred and twenty and upwards. Stanislaus, King of Poland and Duke of Lorraine, exceeded that age. Pope Clement XII lived to the age of 80. George I of Britain attained the age of 83. Cramers, physician to the emperor, saw at Temeswar two brothers, one aged 110 and the other 112, both of whom were fathers at that age. Saint Paul the hermit was 113 at his death. Before we proceed to identify the common causes of longevity, it is proper to examine the lifestyle and circumstances of those who have enjoyed it. We find that those who have lived to the greatest age were generally people who did not reach their full physical growth until very late in life. They were also individuals who kept their appetites and passions under complete control. In short, those who have lived past 100 years have generally been strong, hard-working, temperate, and careful to follow a strict <term>regimen</term> <note>A systematic plan for diet and lifestyle</note>. Born with naturally good constitutions, they were seldom or never subject to disease. They enjoyed excellent health and vigor, retaining the use of their senses until the very last moment of their lives.

## AND OCCULT SCIENCE.
<page-num>147</page-num>

Among those who have led a life of contemplation and study, many have reached a very advanced age. Longevity is common among the different religious orders, who by their rules are restricted to a moderate diet and obliged to abstain from wine and meat. Some famous anchorites <term>religious hermits</term> have lived to a great age while feeding on nothing but the wild roots and fruits they found in the deserts where they had retired. The philosopher Xenophilus, who lived to the age of 106, belonged to the Pythagorean sect. It is well known that those philosophers who believed in the transmigration of souls <note>original: "transmigration of souls"; the rebirth of a soul into a new body, or reincarnation</note> refused to eat meat because they imagined that killing an animal would be the same as murdering another person. 

A country life has produced many healthy and vigorous old men. It is generally thought that a happy old age is harder to achieve in towns than in the country. However, Sir Hans Sloane, Duverney, and Fontenelle are examples of men whose lives were spent in cities and yet extended to a very great length. It has also been observed that people who have lost their reason live a very long time; this is attributed to their being free from those anxieties <note>original: "inquietudes"</note> which are a most deadly poison to the body. People possessing a good enough understanding, but lacking ambition, have been found to enjoy very long lives. Men who are without pretension—who are free from the cares brought on by a desire to show off their talents or to acquire dignity and power—who feel no regret for the past or anxiety about the future—are strangers to those torments of the mind that waste and consume the body. To that tranquility of soul, which is such an excellent privilege of childhood, they add the benefit of being "young for a long time" due to their physical constitution, upon which their mental state has a striking and powerful influence.

Precocious wisdom and early talents are often more likely to cause astonishment than to fulfill long-term expectations. The rapid development of mental faculties, by shortening the period of youth, seems to decrease the total duration of life proportionally. We knew of a young lady of seventeen who could speak seven languages very correctly; she translated and wrote Latin, Greek, Italian, Spanish, German, English, and French, but she died at the age of eighteen. The young man who proposed to marry her, having been told that he could not win her hand until he had made himself worthy of her by reaching the same level of talent and knowledge, died the same year and at the same age.

From these observations, Dr. Haller has attempted to determine the reasons why a few men are spared longer than others from the common fate of death. The circumstances that work against a long life are often independent of our will, such as the devastation of epidemic diseases <note>original: "distempers"</note>, mental trouble and anxiety (which create diseases in the body), or the torments of ambition. To live long, it is necessary to live in a healthy <note>original: "salubrious"</note> climate and to enjoy a fortune easy enough to exclude those uneasy desires which

Among every ten persons who have lived to the age of a hundred, eight or nine will be found to have lived in the north.

According to the bills of mortality <term>official records of deaths</term>, it appears that after women have passed a certain age, they live much longer than men who have reached the same age. Similarly, it is found by experience that for women, the age of youth is shorter and happier than for men, but the period of old age is longer and attended with more trouble. They reach maturity sooner, and they age sooner. <note>original: "Citius pubescunt, citius senescunt."</note>

After death, the organization of the body begins to dissolve, and all its parts relax, decay, and separate. This is produced by an internal fermentation which causes putrefaction <term>rotting</term> and reduces the body to ammonia <note>original: "volatile alkali"</note>, foul-smelling oil, and earth.

The desire for self-preservation and for extending the short span of life is so intimately interwoven with our constitution that it is rightly esteemed one of the first principles of our nature. In spite of even pain and misery, it seldom leaves us until the last moments of our existence. It seems, therefore, to be no less our duty than our interest to examine minutely the various means that have been considered conducive to health and long life; and, if possible, to distinguish those circumstances that are essential to that great end from those which are merely accidental.

It has long been known that fresh air is more immediately necessary to life than food; for a person may live two or three days without food, but not many minutes without air. The life-giving principle contained in the atmosphere—so essential to the support of fire as well as animal life, concerning which authors have proposed so many theories—is nothing else but that pure oxygen <note>original: "oxygenated fluid"</note> lately discovered by that brilliant philosopher Lavoisier <note>Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794) was a chemist who identified and named oxygen.</note>. The common atmosphere may well be supposed to be more or less healthy in proportion to how much it abounds with this animating principle. As this flows in large amounts from the green leaves of all kinds of vegetables—even from those of the most poisonous kind—may we not, in some measure, explain why instances of longevity <term>long life</term> are so much more frequent in the country than in large cities? In cities, the air, instead of sharing so largely in this healthy quality, is daily contaminated with harmful animal waste and odors <term>effluvia</term>.

With respect to climate, various observations combine to prove that those regions located within the temperate zones are best calculated to promote long life. This perhaps explains why Italy has produced so many long-lived people, and why islands in general are healthier than continents; of which Bermuda and some others afford examples. It is a pleasing circumstance that our own island [Britain] appears to contain far more instances of longevity than could well be imagined.
