It is generally accepted that the human constitution is adapted to the specific state and temperature of each respective climate, so that no part of the habitable globe can be declared too hot or too cold for its inhabitants. Yet, in order to promote a friendly intercourse between the most remote regions, the Author of nature <note>A common Enlightenment-era term for God or the Creator.</note> has wisely enabled humans to endure great and surprising changes of temperature without harm.

Though food and drink of the simplest kinds are considered the best for supporting the health of the body, it can hardly be doubted that variety may be safely enjoyed occasionally, provided men restrain their appetites within the bounds of temperance. We cannot suppose that bountiful Nature poured forth such a rich profusion of provisions merely to tease the human species; to do so would be to attribute to her the role of a cruel stepmother <note>original: "step-dame"</note> instead of that of a kind and indulgent parent. 

Besides, we find that through the wonderful powers of the digestive organs, a variety of animal and vegetable substances with very different principles are happily assimilated into one mild, uniform chyle <term>a milky fluid drained from the intestines during digestion</term>. Therefore, it seems natural to distrust those cynical writers who would rigidly confine mankind to one simple dish and restrict their drink to the mere water of the brook. Nature, it is true, has pointed out that mild, flavorless fluid as the universal diluent <note>A substance used to thin or dissolve others; here, the primary liquid for hydration.</note> and therefore most admirably adapted for our daily beverage. 

But experience has equally proved that wine and spirituous liquors are no less healthy and beneficial on certain occasions, whether it is to support strength against sickness or bodily fatigue, or to cheer the mind under the pressure of heavy misfortunes. But, alas! What Nature intended as innocent and useful cordials <term>medicinal beverages intended to stimulate the heart or spirits</term>—to be used only occasionally and according to the direction of reason—custom and whim have, by degrees, made habitual to the human frame and liable to the most enormous and destructive abuses. Hence, it may be justly doubted whether gluttony and intemperance have not depopulated the world more than even the sword, pestilence, and famine. Therefore, the old maxim is true: "The manner of use makes a medicine out of poison, and a poison out of medicine." <note>original: "*Modus utendi ex veneno facit medicamentum, ex medicamento venenum*"</note>

It is accepted by everyone that alternating motion and rest, and sleep and staying awake <note>original: "watching"</note>, are necessary conditions for health and longevity. These ought to be adapted to age, temperament, constitution, the temperature of the climate, and so on; but the errors which mankind daily commit in these respects become a fruitful source of diseases. While some are bloated and weakened by ease and laziness, others are emaciated and become stiff through hard labor, staying awake, and fatigue. From this, it appears that nutrition is one of the final and most perfect actions of the body; for this to be healthy <note>original: "laudable"</note>, all the preceding actions must necessarily have been so as well. Therefore, the chyle <term>a milky fluid produced in the intestines during digestion</term>—which some consider the immediate substance of nutrition—is indeed suited to fill the larger vessels, but it cannot nourish or restore them. Once this fluid is thinned, changed, and more thoroughly mixed in the lungs through breathing, and thus prepared to pass through certain vessels, it is indeed made more suitable, yet it is still far from being completely ready to serve as the substance of nutrition. 

However, through the repeated action of the lungs, the internal organs <term>viscera</term>, and the vessels, a soft, sticky, molding <term>plastic</term>, and tasteless fluid <term>humor</term> is formed from this substance. This serum <note>The clear, yellowish part of blood</note>, when thickened by heat, becomes exactly like the white of an egg. This fluid, therefore, contains all the conditions found in the substance from which we know, by certain experience, all the solid parts of an animal arise through simple incubation <note>The process by which an embryo develops in an egg</note>. It is, therefore, a step closer, but it is not yet fully prepared for nutrition; much less is the *cruor* <term>the thick, red, globular part of the blood</term>. 

Neither of these is yet ready to enter the smallest vessels, although various authors have identified both as the "nutritive juice." Just as heat acts during incubation, the action of the internal organs and vessels on the serum introduces various changes until, at last, a portion of it is made refined <note>original: "subtile"</note> enough for the required purpose. As this substance is used up, it is instantly replaced; thus, we have the true, immediate material of nutrition.

Now that the substance of nutrition has been identified, the way it works and the causes behind it are as follows: when a fluid is driven through a full canal—whether it be cone-shaped or cylindrical, elastic or rigid—if it moves from a wider to a narrower section, or if it meets any resistance, it will attempt to stretch the walls of that canal along the direction of its length. This must happen everywhere in the body, except perhaps in the veins and storage areas <note>original: "receptacles"</note>. Through this *nisus* <term>a physical effort or internal striving</term>, however weak it may be, the vessels will be gradually and imperceptibly lengthened. As they lengthen, they will become increasingly slender. 

Consequently, the furthest ends of the vessels, which are extremely small in humans, are continually stretched and made less and less solid—that is, they move closer and closer to breaking down. Eventually, they will hold together so weakly that they are barely distinguishable from fluids. While this motion and propulsion continue, two things must necessarily happen. First, the outermost particles of the smallest tubes will be torn off and converted back into a type of fluid <term>humor</term>, regardless of where in the body they are located. Secondly, the smallest particles that joined together to form the thinnest fibers <term>fibrillae</term> will be pulled apart, leaving open gaps <term>interstices</term> where they previously held together. Furthermore, it is evident that the newer, more tender, and nearer to the cause of motion these vessels are, the more easily they will be lengthened, stretched, destroyed, and repaired. From the combination of these causes arise the strength, hardness, rigidity, and thickness of the solid parts. Hence, the number of vessels is greatest in embryos, and as age comes on, it noticeably diminishes; and hence it is that their weakness constantly declines while their strength and firmness increase. In young people, therefore, the quantity of fluids <note>original: "humours"</note> is excessive and greatly exceeds the solids; in old men, the solids exceed the fluids. And here we see the reason, manner, and appearance of growth, maturity, decline, and, at length, death from pure old age.

Dr. Priestley <note>Joseph Priestley (1733–1804), a chemist who discovered oxygen</note> concludes, from experiments intended to discover the principle of nutrition in plant and animal substances, that this principle is phlogiston <note>an obsolete chemical theory that a fire-like element was contained within combustible bodies</note>. This nutritional principle is immediately dissolved by the gastric juice and the chyle <term>a milky fluid formed in the small intestine during digestion</term> created from it. When it has entered the circulation along with the chyle and served its purpose in the animal economy <note>original: "œconomy"; the functional system of a living organism</note>, it is expelled again by the blood through the lungs and released into the air, which becomes saturated with it <note>original: "phlogisticated"</note>.

## OF FOOD, OR ALIMENT.

From aliment, or food, through the process of digestion, a very mild, sweet, and whitish liquid is prepared. This resembles milk and is known as *chyle*. Once it is absorbed by the lacteal veins <term>vessels that carry chyle to the bloodstream</term>, it is conveyed into the circulation and converted into blood. This provides the supply of nutrition which, as we have seen above, is required to replace the constant waste produced by the body. 

Food is the most necessary thing for the preservation of our bodies. Since our health depends greatly on our choice of food, it is very important to understand, in general, what is most proper for our nourishment, and, in cases of illness, what is best adapted to restore us. Our blood and fluids <note>original: "juices"</note> naturally tend to become decayed and bitter <note>original: "acrimonious"</note>; fresh chyle, properly received, prevents this destructive tendency and maintains that mild state which is essential for health. 

A diet consisting of meat <note>original: "animal diet"</note> provides the most of this mild, nutritious fluid <note>original: "mucilage"</note>. Watery fluids thin out the parts that are too thick and carry away what is no longer useful. It is only the small amount of gelatinous material <note>original: "jelly"</note> separated from the starchy <note>original: "farinaceous"</note> parts of vegetables that, after being highly processed by the body, is con-

Foods of these three different qualities, when properly mixed with one another, provide proper nourishment for the human body. ### OF AIR.

It is no easy task to describe the nature and origin of air, as it is a fluid that cannot be perceived by any of our senses except for touch. Indeed, from the resistance and pressure it exerts, we know that such a substance exists, which surrounds our earth everywhere. It is of the utmost importance, not only for the progress of many useful arts but also as an absolute necessity for the preservation of health and life.

Whether air is healthy or unhealthy depends on the different vapors <note>original: "effluvia"</note> it contains, and this should be closely watched by the chronically ill <term>valetudinarian</term> <note>a person who is constantly anxious about their health or who has a weak constitution</note>. ...houses owned by the poor in large towns, which are often no better than jails <note>original: "gaols"</note>. These low, dirty dwellings are the primary breeding grounds for bad air and contagious diseases. Those who live in them seldom enjoy good health, and their children often die young. In the choice of a house, those who have the means should always pay the greatest attention to open, fresh air. The various methods that luxury has invented to make houses airtight and warm contribute significantly to making them unhealthy. No house can be healthy <note>original: "wholesome"</note> unless the air has a free passage through it. For this reason, houses should be ventilated daily by opening opposite windows and admitting a current of fresh air into every room. Beds, instead of being made up as soon as people get out of them, should be turned down and exposed to the fresh air from the open windows throughout the day. This would drive out any harmful vapors <note>original: "noxious vapour"</note> and would certainly promote the health of the residents.

In hospitals, jails, ships, etc., where that cannot be conveniently done, ventilators should be used. The method of removing foul air and introducing fresh air by means of ventilators is a very beneficial <note>original: "salutary"</note> invention and is indeed the most useful of all our modern medical improvements. It can be applied universally and offers numerous advantages to both those in health and those in sickness. In all places where large numbers of people are crowded together, ventilation becomes absolutely necessary.

Air that stagnates in mines, wells, cellars, etc., is extremely harmful <note>original: "noxious"</note>. That kind of air is to be avoided like the most deadly poison. It often kills almost as quickly as lightning. For this reason, people should be very cautious when opening cellars that have been shut for a long time, or when descending into deep wells or pits, especially if they have been kept tightly covered. We see daily accounts of people who lose their lives by going down into deep wells and other places where the air stagnates; all these accidents could be prevented simply by lowering a lighted candle before entering and stopping if the flame goes out. Yet this precaution, simple as it is, is seldom used.

If fresh air is necessary for those in health, it is even more so for the sick, who often lose their lives for want of it. The idea that sick people must be kept very warm is so common that one can hardly enter a patient’s room without feeling faint from the hot, suffocating smell. Anyone can judge how this must affect the sick. No medicine is as beneficial to the sick as fresh air. It is the most reviving of all tonics <note>original: "cordials"</note> if it is administered with care. We should not, however, throw open doors and windows at random upon the sick. Fresh air should be let into the room gradually and, if possible, by opening the windows in a different room.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of air quality and chemistry from the previous page, specifically categorizing and defining the different types of "airs" (gases) recognized in late 18th-century science, transitioning between the older "phlogiston" theory and the "new chemistry" of Antoine Lavoisier.</meta>

# A KEY TO PHYSIC,

*Dephlogisticated air* <note>original: "Dephlogisticated air"</note>—known as oxygen gas or "vital air" in the new chemistry—is a gas naturally released by plants. It can be produced artificially from saltpeter <note>original: "nitre"</note>, red lead <note>original: "minium"</note>, magnesia, water, and other substances. This gas is exceptionally good at supporting fire and animal life, and it is one of the primary components of our atmosphere.

*Phlogisticated air*, or nitrogen gas <note>original: "azotic gas"</note>, is produced in large amounts during decay <note>original: "putrefaction"</note> and fermentation. It is also obtained by heating metals <note>original: "calcination"</note> and through other chemical processes involving combustion <note>original: "phlogistic processes"</note>. It kills animals and puts out flames, but it is very beneficial to plant life and is another major component of our atmosphere.

*Fixed air*, or carbon dioxide gas <note>original: "carbonic acid gas"</note>, gets its name because it tends to attach to and stay "fixed" within certain substances. It consists of oxygen <note>original: "dephlogisticated air"</note> combined with charcoal. It is created through fermentation and all combustion processes, and it shows the properties of an acid. It extinguishes flames and kills animals.

*Inflammable air* (hydrogen gas) consists entirely of charcoal and water thinned by heat <note>note: This was an early, incorrect theory of hydrogen's composition; hydrogen is actually an element.</note>. It is notable for being the lightest of all physical substances. It is produced naturally from all stagnant, decaying water and can be made artificially from certain metal solutions, by passing steam over red-hot iron, or by distilling wood and coal with intense heat. It can also be produced by focusing a magnifying lens on charcoal in a vacuum <note>original: "in vacuo"</note>. It puts out flames unless it is mixed with a certain amount of regular air or oxygen, in which case it explodes violently. It kills animals but helps plants grow.

*Nitrous air*, or nitric oxide gas <note>original: "nitrous gas"</note>, is made artificially by dissolving metals or other substances in nitric acid. When mixed with oxygen, both gases lose their form and produce a small amount of nitric acid. It instantly kills animals and puts out flames. When combined with some metals, it turns into ammonia <note>original: "volatile alkali"</note>. In some cases, it can be made to support fire and even life. Because it shrinks <note>original: "condensing"</note> when combined with oxygen, it is used as a test for the healthiness <note>original: "salubrity"</note> of the air.

*Marine acid air*, known as hydrochloric acid gas <note>original: "muriatic acid gas"</note> in the new chemistry, is simply hydrochloric acid turned into a vapor and stripped of most of its water.

*Dephlogisticated marine acid air*, or chlorine gas <note>original: "oxygenated muriatic acid gas"</note>, is thought by some to be hydrochloric acid with its "phlogiston" removed; others believe it is the same acid with pure air added to it. It bleaches <note>original: "destroys"</note> many kinds of colors and, when combined with hydrogen <note>original: "inflammable air"</note>, turns back into common hydrochloric acid <note>original: "marine acid"</note>.

*Alkaline air*, or ammonia gas, is the same as pure ammonia <note>original: "volatile alkali"</note> and is formed by combining nitrogen <note>original: "phlogisticated air"</note> and hydrogen <note>original: "inflammable air"</note>.

*Hepatic air*, or sulfurous acid gas <note>note: Likely hydrogen sulfide, which smells like rotten eggs</note>, is produced when "liver of sulfur" <note>term: a mixture of potassium sulfides</note> is broken down by acids. In normal air, it is flammable but does not explode when it burns.

*Atmospheric air is composed of oxygen <note>original: dephlogisticated air</note> and nitrogen <note>original: phlogisticated air</note>, and thus it supports and sustains both animal life and plant growth.*

The outer part of our habitable world is the air or atmosphere. This is an elastic <note>original: springy</note> body that surrounds the solid earth on all sides and is nearly a thousand times lighter than water. The higher one goes, the less the air is compressed by the weight of the air resting above it; consequently, being an elastic body, it becomes thinner. 

Since a column of air of any diameter is equal in weight to a column of mercury <note>original: quicksilver</note> of the same diameter between twenty-nine and thirty inches high, we can conclude that the top of the atmosphere is not very close to the surface of the solid earth. Now, since mercury is nearly fourteen times heavier than water, the atmosphere will support a column of water about fourteen times higher than the column of mercury—which is about thirty-four feet. If we consider that air is a thousand times lighter than water, then a column of air equal in weight to a thirty-inch column of mercury would be 36,800 feet <note>The OCR text reads "six thousand eight hundred," but the author's subsequent calculation of "near seven miles" and the physics involved suggest thirty-six thousand eight hundred feet was intended.</note>. By this, we know that the air or atmosphere is at least seven miles high, and probably much more. 

If we consider that air is an elastic body and that the air nearest the earth is compressed by the weight of the entire atmosphere above it, we find that the air near the earth's surface is much denser and thicker than it is in the upper regions. This theory explains why great cities are not as healthy to live in as small towns and country villages. London, in particular, is much more harmful to health because of the many industrial works that release harmful vapors <note>original: noxious effluvia</note> composed of the various "airs" mentioned previously. Consequently, this creates an atmosphere for breathing that is not well-suited to human life.

### OF EXERCISE.

Exercise may be described as either active or passive. Active exercise includes walking, hunting, dancing, playing lawn bowls <note>original: bowls</note>, and similar activities, as well as speaking and other physical or mental labor. Passive exercise includes riding in a carriage <note>original: coach</note>, on horseback, or in any other similar manner. 

Exercise should be continued until one just begins to feel tired and ought to be performed before dinner in pure, clear air. For this reason, journeys and trips into the country contribute greatly to preserving and restoring health. Exercise increases the circulation of the blood, thins and breaks down the bodily fluids, and promotes regular perspiration as well as the proper secretion of all the humors <note>term: humors; the various fluids of the body thought to determine health and temperament.</note>. It also stimulates the animal spirits <note>In historical medicine, "animal spirits" were believed to be a subtle fluid that traveled through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note> and helps distribute them into all the fibers of the body; it strengthens the limbs, creates an appetite, and aids digestion. For these reasons, those who accustom themselves to exercise are generally very robust and seldom suffer from diseases.

Boerhaave <note>Herman Boerhaave (1668–1738) was a famous Dutch physician and botanist whose teachings dominated European medicine in the 18th century.</note>

Boerhaave <note>Herman Boerhaave (1668–1738) was a world-renowned Dutch physician and botanist known as the "father of physiology."</note> recommends bodily exercise for diseases characterized by a weak and loose <note>original: lax</note> fiber. By riding on horseback, the hanging internal organs <note>original: pendulous viscera</note> of the abdomen are shaken every moment and gently rubbed against one another, while the pure air acts on the lungs with greater force. However, it should be noted that a weak man should not ride on a full stomach. He should ride either before dinner or after digestion is nearly finished. When the stomach is full and stretched <note>original: distended</note>, weak people cannot easily handle the jolting of the horse. But when the primary passages <note>original: primæ viæ; the digestive tract, including the stomach and intestines</note> are nearly empty, the remaining waste <note>original: fæces</note> is discharged by this vibration. Sailing in a ship is also an exercise of great use to weak people. If the vessel moves with an even motion, the increase in perspiration usually creates a wonderful sense of energy <note>original: alacrity</note>, stimulates an appetite, and promotes digestion. These exercises are especially helpful to weak people; however, to strengthen the body through muscle movement, running and other physical exercises should be used. In these, we should begin with the most gentle, such as walking, and increase the intensity by degrees until we reach running. Those exercises of the body that also delight the mind are especially beneficial, such as tennis, fencing, etc. For this reason, the wisdom of antiquity appointed rewards for those who excelled in these gymnastic exercises, so that the bodies of their youth might be hardened for the toils of war.

As nothing is more beneficial to health than moderate exercise, so violent exercise drains the energy <note>original: spirits</note>, weakens the body, destroys the elasticity of the fibers, and exhausts the fluid parts of the blood. It is no wonder, then, that intense and deadly fevers often arise from too much violent exercise. This occurs because the flow of blood through the veins toward the heart is quickened by the contraction of the muscles. As the veins are emptied, the arteries more easily push their fluids through the smallest vessels into the veins, which now offer less resistance. Consequently, the speed of the circulation will increase through all the vessels. But this cannot happen without the humors <note>The body's vital fluids in historical medical theory</note> being applied more often, or in greater quantity, to the secretory organs. Because of this, the more fluid parts of the blood are lost, and what remains becomes thickened <note>original: inspissated</note>. By the increased action of the vessels on their fluids, and the reaction of the fluids back upon the vessels, the blood acquires an inflammatory density. Additionally, through the violent friction <note>original: attrition</note> of the solids and fluids, along with the resulting heat, all the humors will tend toward a greater sharpness <note>original: acrimony</note>, and the salts and oils of the blood will become more irritating and volatile. Therefore, those fevers which arise from too much exercise or motion are cured by resting the body and mind, along with such foods and medicines that moisten, dilute, and soften or soothe this sharpness.

Frequent repetitions of this, performed early and before the sun grows hot, will be more beneficial than repeating it seldom and staying out for a long time; for, since a camp offers little convenience for refreshment, all unnecessary fatigue is to be avoided. 

As for the second article—cutting branches for shading the tents, digging trenches around them to carry off water, airing the straw bedding, cleaning clothes and equipment <note>original: "accoutrements"</note>, and helping with the duties of the communal mess—these should not be disagreeable exercises for the men during some part of the day. Lastly, regarding recreations, the men must be encouraged to participate either by the example of their officers or by small prizes <note>original: "premiums"</note> given to those who excel in the kinds of sports judged most conducive to health. However, great caution is necessary here not to allow them to exhaust themselves too much, especially in hot weather or during times of sickness; but above all, their clothes must be kept dry, as wet clothes are frequent causes of disease and death.

Exercise, above all, is especially necessary for the philosopher, the student, and young gentlemen at school. However useful or agreeable study may be to the mind, it is far from being equally healthy <note>original: "salutary"</note> for the body. Everyone observes that the Creator has formed an intimate connection between the body and the mind—a perpetual action and reaction by which the body instantly feels the disorders of the mind, and the mind feels those of the body. The delicate mechanisms <note>original: "springs"</note> of our frail physical machines lose their activity and become weakened <note>original: "enervated"</note>, and the vessels are blocked by obstructions when we completely stop exercising; the consequences necessarily affect the brain. A highly studious and sedentary <note>original: "sedentary"; a lifestyle involving much sitting and little physical activity</note> life is therefore equally harmful <note>original: "prejudicial"</note> to both the body and the mind. 

The limbs likewise become stiff; we develop an awkward, forced manner; a certain unpleasant <note>original: "disgustful"</note> air accompanies all our actions, and we come very near to being as disagreeable to ourselves as we are to others. An inclination toward study is highly commendable, but it should not, however, inspire us with a dislike for society. The natural destiny of man is to live among his fellows; and whatever the status of our birth or our situation in life may be, there are a thousand occasions where a man must naturally desire to make himself agreeable: to be active and skillful; to dance with grace; to control a spirited horse <note>original: "command the fiery steed"</note>; to defend himself against a brutal enemy; or to preserve his life through agility, such as by leaping, swimming, etc. Many rational causes have therefore given rise to the practice of specific exercises; and the wisest and most kind-hearted legislators have established, in their academies and universities, proper methods for enabling youth who devote themselves to study to also become expert in praiseworthy athletic exercises.

# A KEY TO PHYSIC,

Anyone who considers the structure of the human body will soon be convinced of how necessary exercise is for the health of children. The body is composed of a countless number of vessels, whose fluids cannot be circulated without the action and pressure of the muscles. But, if the fluids remain inactive, blockages must occur, and the <term>humours</term> <note>original: "humours"; in early medicine, these were the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to regulate health and temperament.</note> will, of course, be corrupted <note>original: "vitiated"</note>, which cannot fail to cause diseases. Nature has equipped both the vessels that carry the blood and the lymph with numerous valves, so that the action of every muscle might push their contents forward; but, without action, this admirable design can have no effect. 

This part of the <term>animal economy</term> <note>The "animal economy" refers to the internal organization and functional systems of a living body.</note> demonstrates the necessity of exercise for the preservation of health. Without exercise, the circulation of the blood cannot be properly maintained, nor can the different secretions be duly performed; without exercise, the fluids cannot be properly prepared, nor the <term>solids</term> <note>In this context, "solids" refers to the firm parts of the body, like muscles, fibers, and organs, as opposed to the fluids.</note> made strong or firm. The beating of the heart, the movement of the lungs, and all vital functions are greatly supported by exercise. To explain the exact manner in which these effects are produced would lead us further into the mechanics of the human body than most of those for whom this book is intended would be able to follow. We shall, therefore, only add that when exercise is neglected, none of the bodily functions can be properly performed; and when that is the case, the entire physical health <note>original: "constitution"</note> must collapse.

The love of activity shows itself very early in humans. This principle is so strong that a healthy youth cannot be restrained from exercise even by the fear of punishment. Our love of motion is surely a strong proof of its usefulness. Nature implants no disposition in vain. It seems to be a <term>universal</term> <note>original: "catholic"</note> law throughout the whole animal creation that no creature can enjoy health or find food without exercise. Every creature, except man, takes as much of it as is necessary. He alone, and the animals under his care, deviate from this original law; and they suffer accordingly. 

Inactivity never fails to cause a universal <term>weakening</term> <note>original: "relaxation"</note> of the body’s tissues, which leaves the body vulnerable to countless diseases. When the tissues are weakened, neither digestion nor any of the secretions can be properly carried out. In this case, the worst consequences must follow. How can people who lounge all day in easy chairs and sleep all night on soft down beds fail to be weakened? Nor do those greatly improve the situation who never go outdoors except in a coach or a <term>sedan chair</term> <note>A sedan chair was an enclosed seat carried on poles by two men, a common luxury for the wealthy.</note>. These fashionable luxuries have become so common that the inhabitants of great towns seem to be in some danger of losing the use of their limbs altogether. It is now considered beneath anyone to walk if they can afford to be carried. How ridiculous it would seem to a person unacquainted with modern luxury to see the young and healthy being carried along on the shoulders of their fellow humans! Or to see a bloated body <note>original: "fat carcase"</note>, riddled with diseases caused by laziness, being dragged through the streets by six horses!

# AND OCCULT SCIENCE.

Glandular blockages <note>original: "obstructions"</note>, which are now so common, generally result from inactivity. These are the most stubborn of illnesses. As long as the liver, kidneys, and other glands properly perform their functions, health is seldom impaired; but when they fail, nothing can restore it. Exercise is almost the only cure we know for glandular blockages; indeed, it does not always work as a remedy, but there is reason to believe that it would seldom fail to prevent these complaints if it were practiced in a timely manner. One thing is certain: among those who take sufficient exercise, glandular diseases are very little known, whereas the lazy and inactive are seldom free from them. Weak nerves are the constant companions of inactivity. Nothing but exercise and open air can invigorate <note>original: "brace"</note> and strengthen the nerves, or prevent the endless train of diseases which result from a weakened <note>original: "relaxed"</note> state of these organs. We seldom hear active or hard-working people complain of nervous diseases; these are reserved for the children of ease and wealth <note>original: "affluence"</note>. Many have been completely cured of these disorders by being reduced from a state of wealth to laboring for their daily bread. This plainly points out the sources from which nervous diseases flow, and the means by which they may be prevented. It is absolutely impossible to enjoy health when perspiration is not properly carried out; but that can never happen where exercise is neglected. When the matter which ought to be thrown off by perspiration is kept in the body, it corrupts <note>original: "vitiates"</note> the <term>humours</term> <note>The "humours" were the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that ancient and early modern medicine believed governed health.</note> and causes the gout, fevers, rheumatism, and so on. Exercise alone would prevent many of those diseases which cannot be cured, and would remove others where medicine proves ineffective.

No habit of laziness hurts health more than the modern custom of staying in bed too long in the morning. This is the general practice in great towns. The inhabitants of cities seldom rise before nine or ten o'clock; but the morning is undoubtedly the best time for exercise, while the stomach is empty and the body refreshed with sleep. Besides, the morning air invigorates and strengthens the nerves and, in some measure, serves the same purpose as a cold bath. Let anyone who has been accustomed to staying in bed late rise by six or seven, spend a couple of hours in walking, riding, or any active diversion outdoors, and he will find his spirits cheerful and calm through the day, his appetite sharp, and his body invigorated and strengthened. Habit soon renders early rising agreeable, and nothing contributes more to the preservation of health. The inactive are continually complaining of stomach pains, gas <note>original: "flatulencies"</note>, indigestion, and so on. These complaints, which pave the way to many others, are not to be removed by medicines. They can only be cured by a vigorous course of exercise, to which they seldom fail to yield.

Exercise, if possible, ought always to be taken in the open air. When that cannot be done, various methods may be devised for exercising the body indoors.

# A KEY TO MEDICINE <note>original: "PHYSIC"</note>.

It is not necessary to adhere strictly to any particular kind of exercise. The best way is to take them by turns, and to use that longest which is most suitable to one's strength and constitution. Those kinds of exercise which give action to most of the bodily organs are always to be preferred, such as walking, running, riding, digging, swimming, and such like. It is much to be regretted that active and athletic <note>original: "manly"</note> recreations <note>original: "diversions"</note> are now so little practiced. Recreations make people take more exercise than they otherwise would do, and are of the greatest service to such as are not under the necessity of laboring for their bread. As active recreations lose ground, those of a sedentary kind seem to prevail. Sitting hobbies <note>original: "sedentary diversions"</note> are of no other use but to consume time. Instead of relieving the mind, they often require more thought than either study or business. Everything that induces people to sit still, unless it be some necessary employment, ought to be avoided.

The recreations which afford the best exercise are hunting, shooting, playing at cricket, lawn bowls, etc. These exercise the limbs and promote perspiration and the other bodily secretions. They likewise strengthen the lungs and give firmness and agility to the whole body. Those who can ought to spend two or three hours a day on horseback; those who cannot ride should employ the same time in walking. Exercise should never be continued too long. Over-fatigue prevents the benefit of exercise, and instead of strengthening the body, it tends to weaken it. Every man should place himself under some sort of necessity to take exercise. Laziness <note>original: "indolence"</note>, like other vices when indulged, gains ground and at length becomes agreeable. Hence many who were fond of exercise in the early part of life become quite averse to it afterwards. This is the case with most <term>hypochondriac</term> <note>In this period, "hypochondriac" referred to a physical digestive and nervous disorder, not just health anxiety.</note> and <term>gouty</term> <note>Gout: a painful form of arthritis often associated with a rich diet and lack of exercise.</note> people, which renders their diseases in a great measure incurable. Laziness not only causes diseases and renders men useless to society, but promotes all manner of vice. To say a man is lazy is little better than calling him vicious. The mind, if not engaged in some useful pursuit, is constantly in quest of imaginary <note>original: "ideal"</note> pleasures or impressed with the fear of some imaginary evil. From these sources proceed most of the miseries of mankind. Certainly, man was never intended to be idle. Inactivity frustrates the very design of his creation; whereas an active life is the best guardian of virtue and the greatest preservative of health.

### Of SLEEP.

SLEEP, as well as food, ought to be duly regulated. Too little sleep weakens the nerves, exhausts the spirits, and causes diseases; and too much renders the mind dull, the body heavy <note>original: "gross"</note>, and disposes one to <term>apoplexies</term> <note>Apoplexy: a sudden loss of consciousness or movement, similar to a stroke.</note>, <term>lethargies</term> <note>Lethargy: then considered a specific medical state of morbid drowsiness or prolonged sleep.</note>, and other complaints of a similar nature. Besides, the actual amount of sleep cannot be measured by time alone; one person may be more refreshed by five or six hours of sleep than another is by eight or ten. Children may always be allowed to sleep as much as they please; however, for adults, six or seven hours is certainly sufficient, and no one should exceed eight. Those who stay in bed for more than eight hours may slumber, but they can hardly be said to sleep; they generally toss and dream away the first part of the night, fall asleep toward morning, and doze until noon. The best way to make sleep sound and refreshing is to rise early <note>original: "betimes"</note>. The habit of staying in bed for nine or ten hours not only makes sleep less refreshing but also weakens the constitution <note>The physical health and strength of a person's body.</note>. Nature designates the night as the proper time for sleep. Nothing destroys the constitution more certainly than staying awake all night <note>original: "night-watching"</note>. It is a great pity that a practice so destructive to health has become so fashionable. How quickly the lack of rest at the proper time can wither the most blooming complexion or ruin the best constitution is evident from the ghastly faces <note>original: "countenances"</note> of those who, as the phrase goes, "turn day into night and night into day." To make sleep refreshing, the following things are required: first, get enough exercise in the open air; next, avoid strong tea or coffee; then, eat a light supper; and finally, go to bed with a mind as cheerful and calm as possible.

It is certain that too much exercise can prevent sleep just as much as too little. However, we rarely hear active and hard-working people complain of restless nights. It is generally the idle and lazy who suffer from these issues. Is it any wonder that a soft down bed is not refreshing to someone who sits in an easy chair all day? A great part of life's pleasure consists of alternating between rest and movement; but those who neglect movement can never truly enjoy rest. The laborer enjoys more true luxury in plain food and sound sleep than can be found at lavish tables or on soft pillows when exercise is lacking. The idea that light suppers lead to sound sleep is a well-known proverb. Many people, if they overeat even slightly at that meal, are sure to have uneasy nights; and if they do fall asleep, the heavy burden on their stomach and spirits causes frightening dreams, broken and disturbed rest, the nightmare, and so on. If those same people went to bed with a light supper, or stayed up until that meal was well digested, they would enjoy sound sleep and wake up refreshed and cheerful. There are, indeed, some people who cannot sleep unless they have some solid food at night, but this does not mean a heavy supper is necessary.

...reason why everyone should endeavor to be as calm in their mind as possible when they go to rest. Many, by indulging in grief and anxious thoughts, have lost the ability to sleep soundly for so long that they could never afterwards enjoy it. Sleep, when taken in the early part of the night, is generally considered most refreshing. Whether this is the result of habit or not is difficult to say; but, as most people are accustomed to going to bed early when young, it may be assumed that sleep at this time will prove most refreshing to them for the rest of their lives. Whether the early part of the night is best for sleep or not, surely the early part of the day is fittest both for business and amusement; and we hardly ever find an early riser who does not enjoy a good state of health.

Experience proves that the more a person sleeps, the more they are inclined to sleep. If in the morning we sleep an hour beyond our custom, the consequence is that we shall be dull and sluggish all day; and regarding these facts, there are some very remarkable cases. 

— A youth in Germany, of immense wealth, was summoned by his prince to receive a title of nobility. On this occasion, he drank to such an excess that the prince, in order to cure him of such a scandalous vice, had him carried into a dark and remote place where he slept for three days and three nights; for whenever he awoke, believing it to be the middle of the night, he went back to sleep again. 

— The memoirs of the Academy of Sciences at Paris mention a sleep of two months caused by catalepsy, a disease by which the patient is instantly rendered as motionless as a statue. 

— Samuel Chilton, a laborer in Somersetshire, fell into a profound sleep without any visible cause, out of which no means could recover him until, after a month's time, he woke up on his own. His mother, fearing he would starve in that "sullen mood" <note>original: "humour"; here meaning a stubborn or morbid state of mind.</note>, as she called it, put bread, cheese, and small beer <note>A weak beer with low alcohol content, commonly drunk at the time instead of water.</note> by him, and it was consumed daily. On the ninth of April, 1696, he was seized with a similar sleeping fit which lasted until the seventh of August, when he awakened without knowing he had slept more than a single night. He occasionally used the food set by him and had bowel movements until, about the tenth week, his jaws seemed to be set and his teeth clenched so close together that his mouth could not be opened. All the nourishment he received during those seven weeks was about three pints of tent <note>original: "tent"; a deep red Spanish wine often used for medicinal purposes.</note> poured through a cavity in one of his teeth. He had urinated only once and never had a stool the entire time. On the 17th of August, 1697, his fit returned, and Dr. Oliver, the author of the memoir, went to the house in order to test whether there might be some deception <note>original: "imposture"</note> in this extraordinary phenomenon. He put his mouth to Chilton's ear and called him several times by his name as loud as he could; he pulled him by the shoulders, pinched his nose, and stopped his mouth and nose at the same time. He lifted up his eyelids and found the eyeballs drawn up under the brows; furthermore, he held a vial of spirit of sal ammoniac <note>original: "spirit of sal ammo-"; a solution of ammonia used as smelling salts to provoke a physical reaction.</note>...

## OF DREAMS.

Hardly any part of nature is less open to our observation than the human mind in this state. The dreamer himself cannot easily observe the manner in which dreams arise or disappear. When he wakes, he cannot recollect the circumstances of his dreams with sufficient accuracy. Even if we were to watch over him with the most vigilant attention, we could not perceive with certainty what emotions are excited in his mind, or what thoughts pass through it, during his sleep. 

But even if we could determine these phenomena, many other difficulties would still remain. What parts of a human being are active, and what are dormant, when he dreams? Why does he not always dream while asleep? Or why does he dream at all? Do any circumstances in our physical constitution, situation, and peculiar character determine the nature of our dreams? We may lay before the reader such facts as have been established concerning dreaming, and the most plausible theories that have been offered to explain those particulars about which we can only speculate—or at least for which we have so far obtained nothing more certain than conjecture.

In dreaming, we are not conscious of being asleep. This is well known from a thousand circumstances. When awake, we often recollect our dreams; and we remember on such occasions that, while those dreams were passing through our minds, it never occurred to us that we were separated by sleep from the active world. We are often observed to act and talk in dreaming as if we were busily engaged in the interactions of social life. In dreaming, we do not consider ourselves to be witnessing or bearing a part in a fictional scene. We do not seem to be in a situation similar to the actors in a dramatic performance, or the spectators before whom they perform, but rather engaged in the business of real life. All the varieties of thought that pass through our minds when awake may also occur in dreams; all the images which

All the same emotions can be triggered, and we are often driven by an equal intensity of passion; none of the activities we are capable of engaging in while awake are impossible in dreams. In short, our range of action and observation is just as wide in one state as in the other; and while dreaming, we do not perceive any distinction between our dreams and the events and transactions we actually experience in our daily lives.

Though in dreams imagination appears to be free from all restraint and indulges in the wildest whims <note>original: "wanton freaks"</note>, it is generally agreed that the imaginary activities of the dreamer always bear some relation to their particular character in the world, their habits, and the circumstances of their life. The lover, we are told, dreams of his mistress; the miser of his money; the philosopher renews his research in sleep, often with the same pain and fatigue as when awake; and even the merchant, at times, returns to balance his books and calculate the profits of a business venture while slumbering on his pillow. *And not only do the more general circumstances of a person's life influence his dreams; his passions and habits are the same when asleep as when awake. A person whose habits of life are virtuous does not in his dreams plunge into a series of crimes; nor are the vicious reformed when they pass into this imaginary world.* An irascible man <note>original: "choleric man"</note> finds himself offended by slight provocations in his dreams just as he does in his ordinary interactions with the world, and a mild temper remains peaceful in sleep. 

The character of a person's dreams is influenced by their waking circumstances in a much more mysterious <note>original: "unaccountable"</note> manner. Certain dreams usually arise in the mind after a person has been in certain situations. Dr. Beattie <note>James Beattie (1735–1803), a Scottish philosopher and poet who wrote "Dissertations Moral and Critical," which included an essay on dreaming.</note> relates that he once, after riding thirty miles in a strong wind, spent part of the following night in dreams that were indescribably terrible. The state of a person's health, and the way in which the vital functions are carried on, have a considerable influence in determining the character of dreams. After a meal that is too heavy, or after eating an unusual kind of food, a person always has dreams of a certain nature. 

In dreaming, the mind for the most part has no interaction through the senses with surrounding objects. If you touch a person gently who is asleep, they do not feel the sensation. *You may awake him by a sharp blow; but, when the stroke is not sufficiently violent to awake him, he* [is unaware of it], unless the light is so strong as to rouse him from sleep. Yet there is one remarkable fact concerning dreaming which may seem to contradict what has been asserted here. In dreams, we are prone not only to speaking aloud because of the suggestions of our imagination, but even to getting up, walking about, and engaging in small tasks without waking. Now, since we are so active in these instances, it seems we cannot be entirely unaware <note>original: "insensible"</note> of the presence of surrounding objects. The sleepwalker is actually aware, to a certain degree, of the objects around him; however, he does not pay attention to all their details, nor do they trigger the same emotions in him as they would if he were awake. He feels no terror on the roof of a house or at the edge of a cliff; consequently, because he is free from fear, he is also safe in such situations—unless he is suddenly awakened. This is one of the most inexplicable phenomena of dreaming. 

There is also another fact that does not quite align with what was previously stated. It is said that while sleeping, a person will continue to hear the noise of a nearby waterfall <note>original: "cataract"</note>, or the regular strokes of a hammer, or any similar sound that is loud enough and has continued without interruption since before they fell asleep. We do not know whether the person wakes up if the noise suddenly stops. This fact is supported by enough evidence to be considered true; it is quite curious. Even when awake, if we are deeply focused on a study or busy with work, we might not notice the sound of a nearby clock striking or a drum beating. Therefore, it is even more surprising that we should remain aware of sounds while asleep. 

Not only do a person’s general character, habits of life, and state of health influence his dreams, but those matters in which he has been most deeply interested during the preceding day—and the thoughts that have occupied his imagination most frequently—often provide the subjects of his dreams. When I look forward with anxious expectation toward any future event, I am likely to dream of either the disappointment or the fulfillment of my wishes. If I have been engaged throughout the day in business or amusements that I found exceedingly agreeable, or if I have been extremely unhappy, either my happiness or my misery is likely to be renewed in my dreams. 

Though dreams have been regarded by almost all nations throughout the world (at least during some periods of their history) as prophetic of future events, it does not appear that this popular opinion has been established on solid grounds. Christianity, indeed, teaches us to believe that the Supreme Being can and does work upon our minds, influencing our choices <note>original: "determinations of our will"</note> at times without making us aware of the influence <note>original: "restraint"</note> being placed upon us. It is, therefore, by no means impossible, or inconsistent with the general patterns of nature, for dreams to relate to the future. We have no reason to doubt that the dreams described in the Bible <note>original: "Holy Scriptures"</note> were prophetic of future events and inspired by heaven, nor should we laugh at the idea of a prophetic dream as being absurd or ridiculous.

We know of no other facts that have been fully proven concerning dreaming. However, we are not yet sufficiently acquainted with this important phenomenon in the history of the mind. We cannot say by what laws of our nature <note>original: "constitution"</note> we are so frequently drawn into these imaginary events, nor what specific means are used to create the delusion. The delusion is, indeed, remarkably strong. A person will sometimes see a book in a dream and believe they are reading it; they may even understand the nature of the writing and remember, after waking, what they believed they were reading. Can this really be a delusion? If it is a delusion, how and for what purpose is it produced? It appears that the mind does not become inactive during sleep like the body—or at least it is not always inactive while we are asleep. When we do not dream, the mind must either be inactive, or the connection between the mind and the body must be suspended in some way. When we do dream, the mind probably works in concert with the body, but it does not act in the same way as when we are awake. It seems to be clouded or bewildered because it is temporarily deprived of the use of the senses. Imagination becomes more active and more unpredictable <term>capricious</term>, while all other faculties—especially judgment and memory—become disordered and irregular in their operation.

Various theories have been proposed to explain what seems so inexplicable here. The clever Mr. Baxter, in his treatise *On the Immateriality of the Human Soul* <note>Andrew Baxter (1686–1750) was a Scottish philosopher who argued that dreams were caused by external spirits acting upon the soul.</note>, tries to prove that dreams are produced by the agency of spiritual beings. He suggests these spirits either amuse themselves or work seriously by involving mankind in all those imaginary events we experience while dreaming. This theory, however, is far from being believable. It leads us entirely beyond the limits of our knowledge. It requires us to believe without evidence. It is not supported by any similar examples in nature. It creates difficulties even more mysterious than those it was intended to solve. Until it appears that our dreams cannot possibly be produced without the interference of other spiritual agents—who would need to possess enough influence over our minds to deceive us with imagined joys and involve...

Besides, from the facts which have been stated as well known concerning dreams, it appears that their nature depends both on the state of the human body and on that of the mind. But, if they were caused by the agency of other spiritual beings, how could they be influenced by the state of the body? Those would be a curious set of spiritual beings who depend in such a manner on the state of our corporeal frame <note>the physical body</note>. It is better not to believe in their existence at all than to place them in such a state of dependency.

Wolfius <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a prominent German philosopher who sought to explain all things through reason</note>, and after him Mr. Formey <note>Jean Henri Samuel Formey (1711–1797), a philosopher known for popularizing Enlightenment ideas</note>, have supposed that dreams never arise in the mind except as a consequence of some of the organs of sensation having been previously excited. They argue that either the ear, the eye, or the organs of touch, taste, or smell communicate information somehow in a quiet, secret manner. Thus, they partly rouse the mind's faculties from the lethargy in which they are buried during sleep, engaging them in a series of confused and imperfect exertions. 

But what passes in dreams is so very different from all that we do when awake that it is impossible for the dreamer himself to distinguish whether his powers of sensation play any part in the experience. It is not necessary that the imagination be always excited by sensation. Fancy <note>the creative imagination</note>, even when we are awake, often wanders from the present scene. Absentmindedness is common among the studious; poets and mathematicians many times forget where they are. We cannot discover, from anything a dreaming person displays to an observer, that their organs of sensation take any part in the imaginary transactions in which they are occupied. In those rare instances where sleeping persons are said to hear sounds, those sounds are also said to influence the nature of their dreams in some way. But such instances are unique <note>original: "singular"</note>. 

Since it appears that the dreamer is himself incapable of distinguishing—either during his dreams or by recollection when awake—whether any new impressions are communicated to him by his organs of sensation; since even by watching over him and comparing our observations of his emotions in his dreams with what he remembers after waking, we cannot (except in one or two rare instances) confirm this fact; and since the mind is capable of acting while the organs of sensation are at rest and on many occasions refuses to listen to the information they convey; we may, without hesitation, conclude that the theory of Wolfius and Formey has been advanced too hastily and incautiously.

Other physiologists tell us that the mind, when we dream, is in a state of delirium. Sleep, they say, is attended with what is called a "collapse of the brain." During this state, either the whole or a part of the nerves of which it consists are in a condition where they cannot carry on the usual intercourse between the mind and the organs of sensation. As for physiology, the connection between mind and body must undoubtedly remain unknown. The delusions produced in dreams are, in all probability, due to something mysterious in the nature of that connection.

Amid this uncertainty regarding how our powers of mind and body function during dreaming, it is pleasing to find that we can, however, apply our imperfect knowledge of these phenomena to useful purposes. Our dreams are affected by the state of our health, by how we spent the previous day, by our general habits of life, and by the hopes we most fondly indulge or the fears that most often overcome our courage when we are awake. By remembering our dreams, therefore, we may learn to correct many improper behaviors; we may learn to refrain from physical exercises, or from certain foods and drinks that have unfavorable effects on our constitution; we can resist evil habits that are creeping up on us in time; and we can guard against hopes and fears that distract us from our proper concerns and make us unfit for the duties of life. Instead of wondering what our dreams might foretell, we should, with much better reason, reflect on what caused them and look back to the circumstances in our past life to which they are owed. The sleep of innocence and health is sound and refreshing, and its dreams are delightful and pleasing. Conversely, a diseased <note>original: "distempered"</note> body and a polluted or troubled mind are haunted in sleep by frightful, impure, and unpleasant dreams.

### OF INTEMPERANCE.

It is universally agreed that temperance <note>moderation, particularly in eating and drinking</note> and exercise are the two best physicians in the world. If these were properly respected, there would be little need for any others. Temperance may justly be called the parent of health; yet many people act as if they thought disease and death were too slow in their progress. Through intemperance and debauchery, they seem to actually invite their arrival. The danger of intemperance is clear from the very construction of the human body. Health depends on a state of the solids and fluids that allows them to perform vital functions properly. While these functions proceed regularly, we are sound and well; but whatever disturbs them necessarily impairs our health. Intemperance never fails to disorder the entire bodily system <note>original: "animal œconomy"; an 18th-century term for the organized physical functions of a living being</note>. It hurts digestion, relaxes the nerves, makes the different secretions irregular, corrupts the bodily fluids <note>original: "humours"; in pre-modern medicine, these were the four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament</note>, and causes countless diseases.

The analogy between the nourishment of plants and animals provides striking proof of the danger of intemperance. Moisture and manure greatly promote growth in plants, yet an excessive amount of either will entirely destroy them. Even the best things become hurtful, and even destructive, when carried to excess. From this we learn that—

The highest degree of human wisdom consists in regulating our appetites and passions so as to avoid all extremes. This is primarily what entitles us to be called rational beings. A person who is a slave to their appetite will always be a disgrace to human nature. The Supreme Being has endowed <note>original: "endued"</note> us with various passions for the continuation <note>original: "propagation"</note> of the species and the preservation of the individual. Intemperance is the abuse of these passions, while moderation consists in their proper regulation. 

Humanity, not content with satisfying the simple needs of nature, creates artificial wants and is perpetually searching for something to gratify them; however, imaginary wants can never be satisfied. *Nature is content with little, but luxury knows no bounds.* Consequently, the gourmet <note>original: "epicure"</note>, the drunkard, and the lecher <note>original: "debauchee"</note> seldom stop their pursuits until their money or their health <note>original: "constitution"</note> fails. At that point, they usually see their error when it is too late.

It is impossible to establish fixed rules regarding diet because of the different physical makeups of mankind. However, even the most ignorant person certainly knows what is meant by excess, and it is in every person's power, if they choose, to avoid it. The great rule of diet is to strive for simplicity. Nature delights in the most plain and simple food, and every animal except man follows her dictates. Man alone riots without restraint and ransacks the whole of creation in search of luxuries, leading to his own destruction. An elegant writer of the last age <note>Likely referring to Joseph Addison in "The Spectator."</note> speaks of intemperance in diet this way:

> “For my part, when I behold a fashionable table set out in all its splendor <note>original: "magnificence"</note>, I fancy that I see gout and dropsy <note>Dropsy is an archaic term for edema, or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note>, fevers and lethargies, with countless other diseases, lying in ambush among the dishes.”

Nor is intemperance in other matters less destructive than in diet. How quickly the immoderate pursuit of sexual <note>original: "carnal"</note> pleasures, or the abuse of intoxicating liquors, ruins the best health! Indeed, these vices generally go hand in hand. This is why we so often see the devotees of Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine.</note> and Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love, here representing sexual excess.</note>—even before they have reached the prime of life—worn out with disease and hurrying at a swift pace toward an untimely grave. If men reflected on the painful diseases and premature deaths daily caused by intemperance, it would be enough to make them shrink back with horror from indulging even their favorite pleasures.

Intemperance does not hurt its practitioners alone; the innocent too often feel its dreadful effects. How often do we see a miserable mother with her helpless infants pining in want while the cruel father indulges his insatiable appetites? unhappy people fly to it for relief. It affords them indeed a temporary ease. But, alas! this solace is short-lived; and when it is over, the spirits sink as much below their usual tone as they had before been raised above it. Hence a repetition of the dose becomes necessary, and every fresh dose makes way for another, till the unhappy wretch becomes a slave to the bottle, and at length falls a sacrifice to what at first perhaps was taken only as a medicine. No man is so dejected as the drunkard when his debauch has worn off. Hence it is, that those who have the greatest flow of spirits while the glass circulates freely, are of all others the most melancholy when sober, and often put an end to their own miserable existence in a fit of depression <note>original: "spleen"</note> or ill humor.

*Drunkenness not only proves destructive to health, but likewise to the faculties of the mind.* It is strange that creatures who value themselves on account of a superior degree of reason to that of animals <note>original: "brutes"</note> should take pleasure in sinking so far below them. Were those who voluntarily deprive themselves of the use of reason to continue ever after in that condition, it would seem like a just punishment. Though this is not the consequence of one act of intoxication, it seldom fails to follow a course of it. By a habit of drinking, the greatest genius is often reduced to a mere idiot. Intoxication is peculiarly hurtful to young persons. It heats their blood, impairs their strength, and obstructs their growth; besides, the frequent use of strong liquors in the early part of life destroys any benefit that might arise from them afterwards. *Those who make a practice of drinking fine spirits <note>original: "generous liquors"</note> when young, cannot expect to reap any benefit from them as a restorative <note>original: "cordial"</note> in the decline of life.* Drunkenness is not only in itself a most abominable vice, but is an inducement to many others. There is hardly any crime so horrid that the drunkard will not commit for the love of liquor. We have known mothers sell their children's clothes, the food that they should have eaten, and afterwards even the infants themselves, in order to purchase the accursed draught.

It is amazing that our improvements in arts, learning, and politeness, have not put the barbarous custom of drinking to excess out of fashion. It is indeed less common in Southern Britain <note>England</note> than it was formerly: but it still prevails very much in the North <note>Scotland</note>, where this relic of barbarity is mistaken for hospitality. In Ireland, no man is supposed to entertain his guests well, who does not make them drunk. Forcing people to drink is certainly the greatest piece of rudeness that any man can be guilty of. Bravado, a desire to please <note>original: "complaisance"</note>, or mere good-nature, may induce a man to take his glass, if urged to it, at a time when he might as well take poison. The custom of drinking to excess has long been out of fashion in France; and, as it begins to lose ground among the more polite part of the English, we hope it will soon be banished from every part of the United Kingdom.

### ON THE PASSIONS.

The passions have a great influence on both the cause and the cure of diseases. How the mind affects the body will, in all probability, always remain a secret. It is sufficient for us to know that there is an established mutual influence between the mental and physical parts of our being, and that whatever harms one disorders the other.

**ON ANGER.** — The passion of anger disturbs the mind, distorts the face, speeds up the circulation of the blood, and disrupts all vital and bodily <note>original: "animal"</note> functions. It often causes fevers and other sudden <note>original: "acute"</note> diseases, and sometimes even sudden death. This passion is particularly harmful to those who are delicate or have weak nerves. I have known such persons to frequently lose their lives from a violent fit of anger, and I would advise them to guard against the excess of this passion with the utmost care. It is not, indeed, always in our power to prevent becoming angry; but we can surely avoid holding onto resentment in our hearts. Resentment eats away at the mind and causes the most stubborn long-term <note>original: "chronical"</note> disorders, which gradually wear down the constitution. Nothing shows true greatness of mind more than forgiving injuries: it promotes social peace and greatly contributes to our own ease, health, and happiness. Those who value their health should avoid violent outbursts of anger as they would the most deadly poison. Neither should they indulge in resentment, but instead they should endeavor at all times to keep their minds calm and serene. Nothing contributes so much to the health of the body as a constant peace of mind. Added to this is the unseemliness <note>original: "indecency"</note> of extreme anger; how, while it lasts, it makes us the object of scorn and mockery to all those around us, and leaves us, when it passes, feeling aware of it and ashamed. We should also consider the inconveniences and irreversible misconduct into which our quick tempers have sometimes betrayed us; the friendships it has cost us; the distress and embarrassment in which we have been involved by it; and the painful regret which, for one reason or another, it always costs us.

Physicians and naturalists <note>original: "naturalists" — researchers of the natural world and biology</note> provide examples of very extraordinary effects of this passion. Borrichius <note>Olaus Borrichius (1626–1690), a Danish polymath and physician</note> cured a woman of a stubborn tertian ague <note>A fever, often malarial, that returns every third day</note>, which had defeated the art of medicine, by putting the patient into a furious fit of anger. Valeriola <note>François Vallériole (1504–1580), a noted French physician</note> used the same method with similar success in a quartan ague <note>A fever that returns every fourth day</note>. This same passion has been equally beneficial to those who are paralyzed, suffering from gout, or even mute; to the latter, it has sometimes restored the use of speech. Etmuller <note>Michael Ettmüller (1644–1683), a famous German physician</note> gives various examples of very remarkable cures performed by anger; among others, he mentions a person confined to bed with the gout who, being provoked by his physician, attacked him and was cured. It is true that the remedy is somewhat dangerous in its application, especially when a patient does not know how to use it with moderation. We find several instances...

## OF THE PASSIONS.

### ON THE PASSIONS.

The passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to strong emotions or states of mind.</note> have great influence on both the cause and cure of diseases. How the mind affects the body will, in all probability, always remain a secret. It is sufficient for us to know that there is an established mutual influence between the mental and physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> parts, and that whatever injures the one disorders the other.

**ON ANGER.**—The passion of anger agitates the mind, distorts the face, accelerates the circulation of the blood, and disorders all vital and bodily <note>original: "animal"</note> functions. It often causes fevers and other sudden <note>original: "acute"</note> diseases, and sometimes even sudden death. This passion is peculiarly hurtful to the delicate and those with weak nerves. I have known such persons frequently lose their lives from a violent fit of anger, and I would advise them to guard against the excess of this passion with the utmost care. It is not, indeed, always in our power to prevent being angry; but we can surely avoid harboring resentment in our breast. Resentment preys upon the mind and causes the most stubborn chronic <note>original: "chronical"</note> disorders, which gradually waste away the constitution. Nothing shows true greatness of mind more than forgiving injuries; it promotes the peace of society and greatly contributes to our own ease, health, and happiness. Those who value health should avoid violent outbursts of anger as they would the most deadly poison. Neither should they indulge in resentment, but should endeavor at all times to keep their minds calm and serene. Nothing tends as much to the health of the body as a constant tranquility of mind. Add to this the indecency of extravagant anger: how it renders us, while it lasts, the scorn and sport of all around us; how it leaves us, when it ceases, sensible of our behavior and ashamed; the inconveniences and irreversible misconduct into which our irritability <note>original: "irrascibility"</note> has sometimes betrayed us; the friendships it has lost us; the distresses and embarrassments in which we have been involved by it; and the bitter repentance which, for one reason or another, it always costs us.

Physicians and naturalists provide examples of very extraordinary effects of this passion. Borrichius cured a woman of a persistent tertian ague <note>A fever that returns every third day, often associated with malaria.</note>, which had defied the art of medicine, by putting the patient into a furious fit of anger. Valeriola made use of the same means, with similar success, in a quartan ague <note>A fever that returns every fourth day.</note>. The same passion has been equally beneficial to paralytic, gouty, and even mute persons; to these last, it has sometimes restored the use of speech. Etmuller gives several examples of very singular cures performed by anger; among others, he mentions a person confined to bed with the gout who, being provoked by his physician, flew at him and was cured. It is true, the remedy is somewhat dangerous in its application when a patient does not know how to use it with moderation. We meet with several in—

It is also certain that this passion, by the spasmodic constriction it produces in the organs, exerts its power principally on the stomach and intestines, which are highly nervous and membranous parts. Because of this, the symptoms are more dangerous in proportion to the greater "consent" <note>An archaic medical term for the physiological connection or "sympathy" between different parts of the body.</note> of the stomach and intestines with the other nervous parts, and almost with the whole body. 

The unhappy influence of anger on the biliary and hepatic <note>Relating to the liver.</note> ducts is also very surprising; since, by an intense constriction of these, the liver is not only rendered hardened <note>original: "scirrhous"</note>, but stones are also often generated in the gallbladder and bile ducts. These accidents have scarcely any other origin than an obstruction of the free motion and outflow of the bile by means of this violent constriction. From such a constriction of these ducts also proceeds the jaundice, which in process of time lays a foundation for stone-like deposits <note>original: "calculous concretions"</note> in the gallbladder. Lastly, by increasing the motion of the fluid or the spasms of the fibrous parts through anger, a larger quantity of blood is propelled with force to certain parts. This results in them being too much distended, and the openings of the veins distributed there are opened too wide. It is evident from experience that anger has a great tendency to excite hemorrhages, whether from the nose, the opening of the pulmonary artery <note>likely referring here to coughing up blood</note>, the veins of the anus <note>hemorrhoids</note>, or in women, from the uterus—especially in those previously accustomed and disposed to such evacuations.

**Of Fear.**—The influence of fear, both in causing and aggravating diseases, is very great. No man should be blamed for a reasonable concern for life; but too great a desire to preserve it is often the cause of losing it. Fear and anxiety, by depressing the spirits, not only make us susceptible to diseases, but often render those diseases fatal which a brave mind would overcome. Sudden fear generally has violent effects. Epileptic fits and other convulsive disorders are often caused by it. Hence the danger of that practice, so common among young people, of frightening one another. Many have lost their lives, and others have been rendered miserable, by pranks of this kind. It is dangerous to play with the human passions. The mind may easily be thrown into such disorder that it never again acts with regularity.
