But the gradual effects of fear prove most hurtful. The constant dread of some future evil, by dwelling upon the mind, often occasions the very evil itself. Hence it comes to pass that so many die of those very diseases which they long had a dread of, or which had been impressed on their minds by some accident or foolish prediction. This, for example, is often the case with women in childbirth <note>original: "child-bed"</note>. Many of those who die in that situation are impressed with the notion of their death a long time before it happens; and there is reason to believe that this impression is often the cause of it. The methods taken to impress the minds of women with the apprehensions of the great pain and peril of childbirth are very hurtful. Few women die in labor, though many lose their lives after it; which may be accounted for in this way: a woman after delivery, finding herself weak and exhausted, immediately fears she is in danger, and this fear seldom fails to obstruct the necessary discharges <note>original: "evacuations"; in this context, it refers to the natural postpartum bleeding and fluids known as lochia, which 18th-century doctors believed must flow freely to prevent fever.</note> upon which her recovery depends. Thus women <note>original: "the sex"</note> often fall victim to their own imaginations, when there would be no danger if they feared none. It seldom happens, when two or three women in a great town die in childbirth, that their deaths are not followed by many others. Every woman of their acquaintance who is pregnant dreads the same fate, and the disease becomes epidemic <note>original: "epidemical"</note> by the mere force of imagination. This should induce pregnant women to despise fear, and by all means to avoid those tattling gossips who are continually buzzing in their ears the misfortunes of others. Everything that may in the least alarm a patient, or a woman in childbirth, ought to be guarded against with the greatest care.

In general, the effects of terror are a contraction of the small vessels and a repulsion of the blood into the large and internal ones; from this proceed a suppression of perspiration, a general oppression, trembling, and anguish of the heart and lungs, which become overcharged with blood. Frights often occasion incurable diseases, such as epilepsy, stupor, madness, and so on. In acute diseases, they have evidently killed many by the agitation into which they have thrown the "spirits" <note>original: "spirits"; referring to the "animal spirits," a contemporary medical term for the fluid or energy thought to flow through the nerves.</note>, which are already too much disordered. We also have accounts of persons absolutely killed by terrors when in perfect health at the time of receiving the shock: people ordered to be executed, but with private orders for a reprieve, have expired at the block without a wound.

When a person is affected with terror, the principal effort should be to restore the circulation to its proper order, to promote perspiration, and to calm the agitation of the patient. For these purposes, he may drink a little warm liquor, such as camomile tea, etc.; the feet and legs may be put into warm water, the legs rubbed, and the camomile tea repeated every six or eight minutes. "Charles Gustavus (the successor of Christina of Sweden) was besieging Prague when a peasant <note>original: 'boor'; a term for a crude or unrefined rural person.</note> of most extraordinary face <note>original: 'visage'</note> desired admittance; and, being allowed entrance, offered, by way of amusing the king, to devour a whole hog of one hundred pounds weight in his presence. 'Sir,' said the fellow, irritated at the remark, 'if your master will but make that old gentleman take off his sword and his spurs, I will eat him immediately, before I begin the hog.' General Koningsmark (who had, at the head of a body of Swedes, performed wonders against the Austrians, and who was looked upon as one of the bravest men of the age) could not stand this proposal, especially as it was accompanied by a most hideous and supernatural <note>original: 'preternatural'</note> expansion of the frightful peasant’s jaws. Without uttering a word, the veteran suddenly turned around, ran out of the court, and did not think himself safe until he had arrived at his quarters; where he remained for over twenty-four hours locked up securely before he got rid of the panic which had so severely affected him."

Fear should not rise higher than to make us attentive and cautious; when it gains an ascendancy in the mind, it becomes an unbearable <note>original: 'insupportable'</note> tyranny and renders life a burden. The object of fear is evil; and to be exempt from fear, or at least not enslaved to it, gives dignity to our nature and invigorates all our faculties. Yet there are evils which we ought to fear. Those that arise from ourselves, or which it is in our power to prevent, it would be madness to despise and audacity not to guard against. External evils, which we cannot prevent, or could not avoid without a breach of duty, it is manly and honorable to bear with fortitude. Insensibility to danger is not fortitude, any more than the incapacity of feeling pain can be called patience; and to expose ourselves unnecessarily to evil is worse than folly, and very blameworthy presumption.

### Of IMPOTENCY OCCASIONED BY FEAR.

It has been proved by Dr. Hunter <note>Likely Dr. John Hunter (1728–1793), a pioneering Scottish surgeon and anatomist.</note> that impotency is frequently the result of fear. That is, there must be both a power of body and disposition of mind; for the mind is subject to a thousand alarms which affect the actions of these parts. A conscientious man has been known to lose his powers upon finding the woman he was going to be connected with was unexpectedly a virgin. 

Shedding tears arises entirely from the state of the mind, although it is not as much a compound action as the act in question. As these cases do not arise from a real physical inability, they must be carefully distinguished from those that do. We see cases of this kind every day. I shall relate one as an illustration of this subject and its method of cure: A gentleman told me that he had lost his virility <note>original: "virility"; here meaning his physical ability to perform sexually.</note>. After more than an hour of investigating the case, I identified the following facts: he had strong erections at unnecessary times, which showed that he naturally possessed this power; these erections were accompanied by desire, which are all the natural powers required. However, there was still a defect somewhere, which I suspected came from the mind. I asked if all women were the same to him. It appeared there was only one woman who caused this inability, and it arose from his intense desire to perform well with her. This desire produced a doubt or fear of failure <note>original: "want of success"</note> in his mind, which was the cause of his inability to perform. 

As this arose entirely from a mental state produced by a particular circumstance, the mind had to be the focus of the cure. I told him that he could be cured if he could perfectly rely on his own power of self-denial. When I explained what I meant, he told me that he could depend on his own willpower and resolution. I then told him that if he had perfect confidence in himself in that regard, he was to go to bed with this woman, but first promise himself that he would not have any sexual intercourse with her for six nights, regardless of his desires or physical abilities. He agreed to do this and promised to let me know the result. 

About a fortnight <note>A period of two weeks.</note> later, he told me that this resolution had produced such a total change in his state of mind that his physical power soon returned. Instead of going to bed with the fear of inability, he went with the fear that he would be possessed by too much desire and too much power, to the point that it might become uncomfortable for him. This actually happened; he would have been happy to shorten the time. Once he had "broken the spell," his mind and physical powers worked together again, and his mind never returned to its former state of anxiety.

The organs of reproduction <note>original: "generation"</note> may be divided into two categories: the essential and the accessory. The testicles are the essential parts; the penis and its related structures are the accessory parts. Since this division is based on how these parts function in a healthy state—where their actions perfectly align—any lack of coordination or responsiveness between them can also be divided into two types. 

The first type is where the actions are out of sync: the accessory part functions without the primary or essential part. An example is an erection of the penis occurring even when neither the mind nor the testicles have been stimulated. The second type is where the testicles produce fluid <note>original: "perform the action of secretion"</note> too quickly for the penis, which does not have a matching erection. The first condition is called <term>priapism</term> <note>A persistent and often painful erection unrelated to sexual desire.</note>, and the second is what should be called <term>seminal weakness</term> <note>A condition involving involuntary or premature discharge of semen.</note>. 

The mind significantly influences how these two parts coordinate. However, in many cases, it seems that erections depend more on one's mental state than the production of <term>semen</term> does. Many men experience the secretion of fluid without the erection; in these cases, the lack of an erection appears to be caused by mental anxiety <note>original: "fears of the mind"</note> alone.

<term>Priapism</term> often happens spontaneously, or it can result from visible irritation of the penis, as seen in cases of venereal <term>gonorrhea</term>, especially when the infection is severe. The sensation of such erections is uncomfortable rather than pleasant. Furthermore, the feeling in the head of the penis <note>original: "glans"</note> during these episodes is not like the sensation caused by sexual desire; instead, it feels more like the state of the organs immediately after sexual intercourse <note>original: "coition"</note>. 

Cases that arise spontaneously are more serious than those caused by inflammation, as they likely stem from underlying causes that are not easily cured by known methods. Priapism caused by inflammation, as in <term>gonorrhea</term>, shares similar symptoms, but the sensation is generally painful, resulting from the inflammation of the tissue. It should be noted that these observations only apply to priapism when it is a primary condition, not when it is merely a symptom of another disease, which frequently happens.

<term>Seminal weakness</term>—which is the discharge <note>original: "secretion and emission"</note> of <term>semen</term> without an erection—is the opposite of priapism and is by far the more serious of the two conditions. There are many degrees of this condition, ranging from near-perfect coordination of the parts to the testicles acting entirely on their own. In every instance of this disease, the production and release of semen happens too quickly. 

Like priapism, it does not stem from healthy desire or physical capability. Although mild cases may involve both, they are not in the proper balance; even a very slight desire often triggers a full release. The release of semen can be so rapid that a mere thought or light physical contact <note>original: "toying"</note> causes it to flow. Dreams can trigger this release multiple times in a single night. Sometimes the dreams are so faint that the person is not even aware of them, even when they are woken up by the act of discharge <note>original: "emission"</note>. ### ON GRIEF.

**GRIEF** is the most destructive of all the emotions <note>original: "passions"; in historical medicine, passions were strong internal movements or states of mind that could affect physical health.</note>. Its effects are permanent, and when it sinks deep into the mind, it generally proves fatal. Anger and fear, being of a more violent nature, seldom last long; but grief often changes into a fixed melancholy, which preys upon the spirits and wastes the constitution. This emotion should not be indulged. It can generally be conquered at the beginning, but once it has gained strength, all attempts to remove it are in vain. No person can prevent misfortunes in life, but it shows true greatness of mind to bear them with serenity. Many people make a virtue out of indulging in grief, and when misfortunes happen, they obstinately refuse all consolation until the mind, overwhelmed with melancholy, sinks under the weight. Such conduct is not only destructive to health but inconsistent with reason, religion, and common sense.

A change of ideas is as necessary for health as a change of posture. When the mind dwells long upon one subject, especially one of a disagreeable nature, it harms all the functions of the body. Therefore, indulged grief spoils the digestion and destroys the appetite. By these means, the spirits are depressed, the nerves relaxed, the bowels inflated with gas <note>original: "wind"</note>, and the <term>humors</term> <note>In early medicine, the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—thought to determine health.</note> are corrupted <note>original: "vitiated"</note> for want of fresh supplies of <term>chyle</term> <note>A milky fluid produced during digestion that eventually enters the bloodstream.</note>. In this way, many an excellent constitution has been ruined by a family misfortune or anything that causes excessive grief. It is utterly impossible for any person with a dejected mind to enjoy health. Life may indeed be dragged out for a few years, but whoever wishes to live to a good old age must be good-humored...

We can either choose to spend time with cheerful or melancholy companions, engage in the amusements and duties of life, or sit still and brood over our calamities, as we choose.

These, and many such things, are certainly in our power, and from these, the mind generally takes its character <note>original: "cast"</note>. The variety of scenes that we experience through our senses was certainly designed to prevent our attention from being fixed too long upon any one object. Nature abounds with variety, and the mind, unless held down by habit, delights in contemplating new objects. This at once points out the method of relieving a distressed mind. Turn the attention frequently to new objects; examine them for some time. When the mind begins to pull back <note>original: "recoil"</note>, shift the scene. By this means, a constant succession of new ideas may be kept up until the disagreeable ones entirely disappear. Thus, traveling, the study of any art or science, and reading or writing on subjects that deeply engage the attention will expel grief sooner than the most lighthearted entertainments.

It has already been observed that the body cannot be healthy unless it is exercised; neither can the mind. Inactivity <note>original: "indolence"</note> nourishes grief. When the mind has nothing else to think of but calamities, it is no wonder that it dwells there. Few people who pursue business with focus are hurt by grief. Therefore, instead of withdrawing ourselves from the world or from business when misfortunes happen, we ought to engage in them with more than usual attention, to perform the duties of our position <note>original: "functions of our station"</note> with double diligence, and to socialize with friends of a cheerful and social temperament. Innocent amusements are by no means to be neglected. These, by leading the mind gradually to the contemplation of agreeable objects, help to dispel the gloom that misfortunes cast over it. They make time seem less tedious and have many other happy effects. Some persons, when overwhelmed with grief, turn to drinking. This is making the cure worse than the disease. It seldom fails to end in the ruin of fortune, character, and health <note>original: "constitution"</note>.

### OF LOVE.

**LOVE** is perhaps the strongest of all the passions <note>original: "passions"; in historical medicine, this refers to powerful emotions or internal drives that influence physical health.</note>; at least, when it becomes violent, it is less subject to the control of either the understanding or the will than any of the rest. Fear, anger, and several other passions are necessary for the preservation of the individual, but love is necessary for the continuation of the species itself. It was therefore proper that this passion should be deeply rooted in the human breast. Though love is a strong passion, it is seldom as rapid in its progress as several of the others. With regard to love, in its usual and more appropriate meaning, it may be defined as, “that affection which, being compounded of animal desire, esteem, and benevolence, becomes the bond of attachment and union between individuals of different sexes; and makes them feel in the society of each other a species of happiness which they experience nowhere else.” We call it an *affection* rather than a passion because it involves a desire for the happiness of its object. Mere animal desire considers nothing but the species and the sex of its object; before it can make a specific choice, it must be combined with sentiments very different from itself. 

The first sentiment with which it is combined—and by which a man is prompted to prefer one woman to another—seems to be the delight we take in gracefulness of person, regularity of features, and beauty of complexion. To give an example from a specific human feature: the line forming the ridge of the nose is considered beautiful when it is straight. This straightness is also the central form, which is found more often than any one specific degree of concave, convex, or any other irregular shape that might be suggested. The man, being more robust, is suited for hard labor and outdoor activities; the woman, being more delicate, is suited for indoor <note>original: "sedentary"</note> work and especially for nursing children. The man, bold and vigorous, is qualified to be a protector; the woman, delicate and timid, requires protection. Because of this, a man never admires a woman for her physical strength or personal courage, and women always despise men who lack those qualities. The man, as a protector, is directed by nature to lead; the woman, recognizing her position <note>original: "conscious of inferiority"</note>, is inclined to obey. 

Their intellectual powers match nature’s intent. Men have the insight and solid judgment needed to lead; women have the understanding to be charming under good leadership. A greater degree of intellect in women might cause dangerous rivalry between the sexes, which nature has avoided by giving them different talents. Women possess more imagination and sensitivity <note>original: "sensibility"</note> than men, which makes their enjoyments more intense; at the same time, this makes them better at sharing that enjoyment with others. Consider another major difference in temperament: the gentle and persuasive <note>original: "insinuating"</note> manners of women tend to soften the roughness of men. Wherever women are granted freedom, they become refined <note>original: "polish"</note> sooner than men do.

These are not the only details that distinguish the sexes. Regarding the ultimate goal of love, it is the privilege of the man—as the superior and protector—to choose. The woman, once chosen, has only the privilege of either consenting or refusing. Whether this distinction is the direct result of the different natural temperaments of the sexes, or simply the effect of social habits <note>original: "associations"</note> that are inevitably formed,

## OF MELANCHOLY.

The causes <note>original: "pathology"</note> of melancholy and mania are very obscure, as they occur without any fever or disturbance in the blood's motion. Often they are also hereditary, depending on the original structure of the body, especially of the brain; the faults of which, however, cannot be detected by even the most meticulous <note>original: "nicest"</note> anatomist. But it is well known that various diseases of the brain—obstructions, tumors (either of the brain itself or of the skull <note>original: "cranium"</note> pressing upon it), any injury done to the head, and, as some physicians report, the hardness and dryness of the brain, and certain peculiar irritations affecting the nervous system—are capable of bringing on this malady. And indeed, the irritations affecting the nervous system in mad people are so great that they often sleep little or not at all for a long time. 

Yet even this very defective and imperfect knowledge of the diseases of the brain and nerves is by no means free from difficulties. For, though we know that the brain, or a certain part of it, is hurt or irritated by a swelling or a pointed bone growing into it, nobody can foretell how great the malady may be, or what its nature from such an injury. Examples are not lacking of people who, after losing a large part of the brain, have recovered and lived a long time; or of those who have felt no inconvenience from a large portion of that organ <note>original: "viscus"</note> being corrupted, until at length they have fallen suddenly down and died in convulsions.

Many persons of a religious turn of mind behave as if they thought it a crime to be cheerful. They imagine the whole of religion consists in certain mortifications, or denying themselves the smallest indulgence, even of the most innocent amusements. A perpetual gloom hangs upon their countenances, while the deepest melancholy preys upon their minds. Eventually, the fairest prospects vanish, everything takes on a dismal appearance, and those very objects which ought to give delight afford nothing but disgust. Life itself becomes a burden, and the unhappy wretch, persuaded that no evil can equal what he feels, often puts an end to his own miserable existence. It is a great pity that religion should ever be so far perverted as to become the cause of those very evils which it was designed to prevent. Nothing can be better calculated than true religion to raise and support the mind of its followers <note>original: "votaries"</note> under every affliction that can befall them. It teaches them that even the sufferings of this life are preparatory to the happiness

### OF THE PROGNOSTICS OF DISEASES; WITH RULES FOR PRESERVING HEALTH.

A PROGNOSTIC <note>original: "prognostic"; a prediction of the likely course and outcome of a disease</note> is a judgment of the outcome <note>original: "event"</note> of either a state of health or of a disease; such as whether it shall end in life or death, be long or short, mild or malignant, etc., based on <note>original: "taken from"</note> certain symptoms. When a person judges what disorder is coming upon them or is already present based on the following remarks, a safe and effective remedy will generally be found in the Medical Part of the Herbal <note>An "Herbal" is a reference book describing plants and their medicinal properties</note>. However, whenever that work is not sufficiently detailed for the purpose, I shall add such occasional observations for prevention and cure as have occurred to me in my recent practice.

Hippocrates <note>A famous Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> was the first who treated medicine in a regular and rational manner, and he is therefore justly considered the father of medicine <note>original: "phyfic"</note>. Hippocrates noted <note>original: "remarked"</note> four stages in illnesses <note>original: "distempers"</note>: the beginning of the disease, its increase <note>original: "augmentation"</note>, its peak <note>original: "state or height"</note>, and its decline <note>original: "declination"</note>. In such diseases that end fatally, death takes the place of decline. In the third stage, therefore, the change is most significant <note>original: "considerable"</note>, as it determines the fate of the sick person; and this is most commonly done by means of a *crisis*. By this word, he understood any sudden change in sickness, whether for better or worse, and whether health or death follows immediately. Such a change, he says, is made at that time by nature, either acquitting <note>original: "absolving"</note> or condemning the patient. Hence we may conclude that Hippocrates imagined diseases to be only a disturbance of the bodily functions <note>original: "animal economy"</note>, with which Nature was perpetually at odds <note>original: "at variance"</note>, using her utmost efforts <note>original: "endeavours"</note> to expel the cause of the illness <note>original: "offending cause"</note>. Her manner of acting on these occasions is to return the humors <note>original: "humours"; in ancient medicine, these were the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament</note> to their natural state. It is the discord of these humors—whether in relation to their quantity, quality, mixture, motion, or any other way in which they become harmful <note>original: "offensive"</note>—that causes the disturbance of the whole body. The principal means employed by nature for this...

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Hippocratic medicine, moving from the definition of a prognostic to the specific process of how a disease "ripens" and reaches a turning point, or crisis.</meta>

<header>A KEY TO PHYSIC,</header>

The goal is what Hippocrates calls *concoction* <note>original: "concoction"; the process of ripening or "digesting" the diseased humors so they can be expelled</note>. By this, he understood the bringing of the disease-causing <note>original: "morbific"</note> matter lodged in the humors <note>the body's primary fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to control health</note> to such a state that it is easily prepared for expulsion by whatever means nature might think most proper. When matters are brought to this stage, whatever is superfluous or harmful immediately empties itself, or nature points out to physicians the way by which such an evacuation is to be accomplished. 

The crisis <note>the turning point of a disease, leading to either recovery or death</note> takes place either by bleeding, bowel movements <note>original: "stool"</note>, vomiting, sweating, urination, tumors or abscesses, scabs, pimples, spots, etc. However, these evacuations are not to be looked upon as the effects of a true crisis unless they occur in a considerable quantity; small discharges are not sufficient to make a crisis. On the contrary, small discharges are a sign that nature is depressed by the load of humors, and that she lets them go only through weakness and continual irritation. What comes forth in this manner is "crude" <note>unprocessed or premature</note> because the distemper is still too strong; while matters remain in this state, only a bad or imperfect crisis is to be expected. This shows that the disease triumphs, or at least is equal in strength to nature, which predicts death or a prolongation of the disease. In this last case, however, nature often has an opportunity of attempting a new crisis more successful than the former, after having made fresh efforts to advance the maturation of the humors.

It must be observed here, however, that according to Hippocrates, this maturation cannot be achieved except within a certain time, just as every fruit has a limited time to ripen; for he compares the humors which nature has digested to fruits that have come to maturity. The time required for this maturation depends on the differences among the diseases mentioned above. In those which Hippocrates calls "very acute," the digestion or crisis happens by the fourth day; in those which are only "acute," it happens on the seventh, eleventh, or fourteenth day. This last is the longest period generally allowed by Hippocrates in diseases that are truly acute, though in some places he stretches it to the twentieth or twenty-first—even sometimes to the fortieth or sixtieth—days. 

All diseases that exceed this last term are called *chronic* <note>original: "chronical"</note>. And while in those diseases that exceed fourteen days he considers every fourth day as "critical"—or at least remarkable, by which we may judge whether the crisis on the fourth day will be favorable or not—in those which run from twenty to forty days, he reckons only by the seventh days. In those that exceed forty days, he begins to reckon by twenty-day periods. Beyond the hundred and twentieth day, he thinks that the number of days has no power over the crisis. They are then referred to the general changes of the seasons; some terminating about the equinoxes, others about the solstices, and others about the rising or setting of the stars of certain constellations. Or, if numbers still have any place, he reckons by months or even whole years. Thus, he says, certain diseases in children have their crisis in the seventh month after their birth, and others in their seventh or even their fourteenth year.

<summary>This page explains the Hippocratic theory of "concoction" (the maturation of disease) and the "crisis" (the turning point), detailing the specific timelines and methods by which the body expels harmful matter.</summary>

<header>AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES.</header>

Although Hippocrates mentions the twenty-first day as one of the critical days in acute illnesses <note>original: "distempers"</note>, as already noted, in other parts of his works he also mentions the twentieth. The reason he provides in one of those passages is that the days of sickness were not always full twenty-four-hour periods. In general, however, he is very attached to the odd-numbered days. In one of his aphorisms, he tells us:

> "The sweats that occur on the third, fifth, seventh, ninth, eleventh, fourteenth, seventeenth, twenty-first, twenty-seventh, thirty-first, or thirty-fourth days are beneficial. However, those that occur on other days suggest that the patient will be weakened, that the disease will be very long-lasting, and that they will be prone to relapses."

He further says that:

> "the fever which leaves the patient on any day other than an odd one is usually likely to return."

Occasionally, however, he admits that it is otherwise; he gives an example of a healthy <note>original: "salutary"</note> crisis happening on the sixth day. But these are very rare instances and, in his opinion, cannot disprove the general rule. Besides the crisis—the change that decides the patient's fate—Hippocrates often speaks of another kind of shift that only changes the type of the disease without restoring the patient to health. This happens when a <term>vertigo</term> <note>a sensation of spinning or dizziness</note> turns into <term>epilepsy</term> <note>a neurological disorder marked by seizures</note>, or when a <term>tertian fever</term> <note>a fever that returns every third day, often associated with malaria</note> becomes a <term>quartan</term> <note>a fever that returns every fourth day</note> or a continuous fever.

What primarily earned Hippocrates the immense respect he received was his accuracy in <term>prognostics</term> <note>the art of predicting the likely course and outcome of a disease</note>. He did not just distinguish one disease from another by the signs that specifically belonged to each; by comparing the same disease across different people and observing the symptoms that usually appeared before and after, he could often predict an illness before it arrived and later give a correct judgment on its outcome. Because of this skill in predicting, he was greatly admired. He brought this to such a height that it may justly be called his masterpiece. Celsus, who lived after him, remarked that later physicians—though they discovered several new things about managing diseases—were still indebted to the writings of Hippocrates for everything they knew about diagnostic signs. We might add that we are indebted to Celsus for a true understanding of Hippocrates' work.

The first thing Hippocrates considered when called to a patient was their appearance. To him, it was a good sign if the patient's face looked like it did when they were healthy, or as it looked before the disease began. The more it differed from this, the more danger was suspected. The following is the description he gives of a dying man's appearance:

> "When a patient," he says, "has a sharp nose, sunken eyes, hollow temples, and cold, drawn-in ears; when the skin of the forehead is tight and dry, and the color of the face is pale green or leaden, one can be certain that death is very near. This is true unless the patient’s strength has been suddenly drained by long periods of sleeplessness <note>original: "watchings"</note> or by a <term>looseness</term> <note>original: "looseness," meaning diarrhea</note>."

<summary>This page explains Hippocrates' theories on "critical days" and his legendary skill in medical prognostics, including the famous description of the "Hippocratic face" as a sign of approaching death.</summary>
<keywords>Hippocrates, Celsus, critical days, acute distempers, aphorisms, crisis, prognostics, vertigo, epilepsy, tertian fever, quartan fever, Facies Hippocratica, medical history</keywords>

--- Page 284 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Hippocrates' medical observations, moving from the timing of "critical days" to the physical signs (prognostics) that indicate a patient's recovery or approaching death.</meta>

<header>A KEY TO MEDICINE,</header>

"...diarrhea <note>original: "looseness"</note>, or having gone a long time without eating." This observation has been confirmed by the findings of succeeding physicians, who have, following his lead, named it the **Hippocratic face** <note>a clinical term for the facial changes—such as sunken eyes and pinched nose—observed in someone close to death</note>. The lips hanging loose and cold are also viewed by this author as a confirmation of the previously mentioned prognosis. He also derived signs from the specific condition of the eyes. When a patient cannot tolerate light; when they shed tears involuntarily; when, in sleep, some part of the white of the eye is visible (unless they usually sleep that way, or are suffering from diarrhea): these signs, as well as the previous ones, predict danger. Eyes that appear dull <note>original: "deadened"</note>, with a blurred appearance <note>original: "mist before them"</note>, or that have lost their brightness, predict death or great weakness. Eyes that are sparkling, fierce, and fixed indicate that the patient is delirious, or that they soon will be seized with a frenzy. When the patient sees anything red, or sparks of fire and lightning passing before their eyes, you may expect a hemorrhage; this often happens before those crises which involve a loss of blood. 

The condition of the patient is also shown by their posture in bed. If you find them lying on one side, with the body, neck, legs, and arms slightly bent <note>original: "contracted"</note>—which is the posture of a healthy person—it is a good sign. On the contrary, if they lie on their back with their arms stretched out and legs hanging down, it is a sign of great weakness; and particularly when the patient slides or lets themselves fall down toward the foot of the bed, it indicates that death is near. When a patient in a burning fever is continually fumbling with their hands and fingers, moving them up before their face and eyes as if to brush away something passing before them; or picking at the bed-covers as if searching for small straws, removing dirt, or plucking at bits of wool <note>these behaviors are known medically as carphology and floccillation; they are often involuntary signs of a serious brain disturbance or approaching death</note>; all this is a sign that they are delirious and will die. 

Among the other signs of a current or approaching delirium, he also adds this: when a patient who naturally speaks little begins to talk more than they used to do, or when one who talks much becomes silent, this change is to be considered a sort of delirium, or is a sign that the patient will soon fall into one. The frequent trembling or twitching of the tendons in the wrists <note>original: "starting of the tendons of the wrists"; medically known as subsultus tendinum</note> likewise predicts a delirium. As for the different types of delirium, Hippocrates is much more afraid of those that dwell on mournful subjects than those accompanied by mirth.

When a patient breathes rapidly and feels oppressed, it is a sign that they are in pain and that the organs above the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>the muscle separating the chest from the abdomen</note> are inflamed. Taking a long time between breaths <note>original: "breathing long"</note> shows the patient to be delirious, but easy and natural <term>respiration</term> <note>breathing</note> is always a good sign in acute diseases. Hippocrates relied heavily on respiration in making his prognoses, and therefore took care in several places to describe the different ways a patient might breathe. Constant wakefulness <note>original: "watchings"</note> in acute diseases are signs of current pain or a delirium near at hand.

In his opinion, the patient's urine is best when the sediment is white, soft to the touch, and of a consistent texture <note>original: "equal consistence"</note>. If it remains this way throughout the course of the illness <note>original: "distemper"</note>, and until the time of the crisis <note>the turning point of a disease</note>, the patient is in no danger and will soon be well. This is what Hippocrates called "concocted" <note>digested or ripened</note> urine, which indicates the successful processing <note>original: "concoction"</note> of the bodily humors. He observed that this "concoction" of the urine seldom appeared fully except on the days of the crisis, which happily put an end to the disease. 

"We ought," said Hippocrates, "to compare the urine with the pus <note>original: "purulent matter"</note> that drains from ulcers. Just as white pus, which has the same quality as the urine sediment we are now discussing, is a sign that an ulcer is about to heal <note>original: "on the point of closing"</note>, so urine that is clear, of a color other than white, or has a foul smell, is a sign that the ulcer is infectious <note>original: "virulent"</note> and therefore very difficult to cure. The types of urine similar to the healthy one we described are the only ones that may be called 'good'; all the rest are bad, and differ from one another only by degree. The first type never appears until nature has overcome the disease; they are a sign of the processing <note>original: "concoction"</note> of humors, without which you cannot hope for a certain cure. On the contrary, the latter types are produced as long as the 'crudity' <note>undigested or raw state of bodily fluids</note> remains and the humors continue unprocessed."

Among the urines of this last sort, the best are reddish with a sediment that is soft and of a consistent texture; this indicates that the disease will be somewhat long-lasting <note>original: "tedious"</note>, but without danger. The worst are those which are very red and, at the same time, clear and without sediment; or those that are muddy and cloudy <note>original: "troubled"</note> when passed. In urine, there is often a sort of cloud hanging in the vessel in which it is collected. The higher this cloud rises, or the further it is from the bottom, or the more its color differs from the healthy sediment mentioned above, the more "crudity" <note>unprocessed illness</note> is present. 

Urine that is yellow or a sandy color indicates an abundance of bile. Black urine is the worst, especially if it has a foul smell and is either entirely muddy or entirely clear. Urine with sediment like large ground wheat, or little flakes or scales layered one upon another, or like bran, is a bad sign—especially the last one. The fat or oil that sometimes floats on top of the urine, appearing like a spider's web, is a sign of a wasting away <note>original: "consumption"</note> of the flesh and solid parts of the body. 

Passing a large quantity of urine is the sign of a crisis, and sometimes the quality of the urine shows how the bladder is affected. We must also observe that Hippocrates compared the state of the tongue with the urine; that is to say, when the tongue was yellow and coated with bile, he knew the urine must naturally be the same color; and when the tongue was red and moist, the urine was its natural color.

It should be taken as a good prognosis when some worms, both round and long, are evacuated at the same time as the stool. 

The prognosis, however, may still be favorable even if the matter excreted is thin and liquid, provided it does not make too much noise while being passed, and the evacuation is not too small in quantity or too frequent, which might cause the patient to faint. All matter that is watery, white, pale green, red, frothy, or viscous is bad. Waste that is blackish or of a livid <note>bluish or lead-colored</note> hue is the most dangerous. That which is pure black—being nothing but a discharge of black bile—always predicts a very poor outcome; this humor, from whatever part of the body it comes, shows the diseased condition of the intestines. 

Excrement consisting of several different colors indicates that the illness will be long and may have dangerous consequences. Hippocrates classifies bilious or yellow stools mixed with blood, green, or black matter, or matter resembling the scrapings of the intestines, in the same dangerous category. He also considers stools consisting of pure bile or entirely of phlegm to be very bad. 

Matter brought up by vomiting should ideally be a mixture of bile and phlegm; where only one of these humors is observed, the condition is worse. Vomit that is black, livid, green, or the color of a leek indicates alarming consequences. The same is true for vomit that smells very foul; if it is also livid at the same time, death is not far off. The vomiting of blood is very often fatal. 

The spittings <note>expectoration or phlegm</note> that provide relief in lung diseases and pleurisies <note>inflammation of the membrane surrounding the lungs</note> are those that come up easily and without difficulty. It is a good sign if they are mixed with much yellow at the beginning; but if they appear of the same color, or are red, a long time after the start of the illness, or if they are salty and acrimonious <note>biting or irritating</note> and cause violent coughing, they are not a good sign. Purely yellow spittings are bad, and those that are white, viscous, and frothy provide no relief. 

Whiteness is a good sign of concoction <note>original: "concoction"; the process of the body "ripening" or digesting the diseased humors</note> in regards to phlegm; but it should not be entirely viscous, nor too thick, nor too clear. We may make the same judgment of nasal discharge according to its concoction or crudity <note>the state of being "raw" or unprocessed by the body’s heat</note>. Phlegm that is black, green, or red is of bad consequence. In inflammations of the lungs, those mixed with bile and blood are a good omen if they appear at the beginning, but are bad if they do not arise until around the seventh day.

When the patient sweats nowhere but on the head and neck, it is a sign that the disease will be long and dangerous. A gentle sweat in some particular part—of the head and breast, for instance—gives no relief, but instead indicates the location of the disease <note>original: "distemper"</note> or the weakness of that specific part. This kind of sweat was called by Hippocrates *ephidrosis* <note>original: *ephidrosis*; a Greek term for a localized or moderate sweat</note>. The hypochondria <note>original: "hypochondria"; in historical medicine, this refers to the regions of the upper abdomen just below the ribs</note>, or the abdomen in general, ought always to be soft and even, as well on the right side as on the left. When there is any hardness or unevenness in those parts, or heat and swellings, or when the patient cannot bear to have it touched, it is a sign the intestines are unwell <note>original: "indisposed"</note>.

Hippocrates also inquired into the state of the pulse, or the beating of the arteries. The most ancient physicians, however, and even Hippocrates himself for a long time, understood this word to mean the violent pulsation that is felt in an inflamed part without even putting the fingers to it. It is observed by Galen and other physicians that Hippocrates touches on the subject of the pulse more briefly than any other topic on which he treats. But that our celebrated physician understood something even on this subject is easily gathered from several passages in his writings; as when he observes that in acute fevers the pulse is very quick and very large; and when he makes mention, in the same place, of trembling pulses and those that beat slowly; and when he observes that in some diseases incident to women, when the pulse strikes the finger faintly and in a languishing manner, it is a sign of approaching death. He remarks also, in the *Coan Prognostics* <note>original: *Coacæ Prænotiones*; a collection of medical observations from the school of Hippocrates on the island of Cos</note>, that he whose vein—that is to say, whose artery at the elbow—beats, is just about to go mad, or else that the person is at that time very much under the influence of anger. Many other variations of the pulse are listed by physicians, but most of them are uncertain and not confirmed by experience. See the article "Pulse" in the Medical Part of the *Herbal*, page 106, where the subject is more fully treated.

It may even skip beats <note>original: "intermitting"</note>, then—with a sudden flush in the face—immediately become very quick, and perhaps soon after surprisingly calm and steady; it continues in this alternating pattern.

***Prognostics of a scarlet fever.*** With various general symptoms of fever, the patient at first complains of low spirits <note>original: "dejection of spirits"</note>, a slight soreness or rather stiffness in the neck, and a sense of tightness in the muscles of the neck and shoulders, as if they were bound with cords. On the second day of the fever, this soreness in the throat increases, and the patient finds it difficult to swallow. However, the difficulty seems less caused by the pain of the attempt or the narrowness of the passage than by an inability to move the necessary muscles into action. 

The skin feels hot and dry, but not hard, and the patient experiences frequent small, sharp pains, as if touched with the point of a needle. The breath is hot and burning to the lips, and thirst makes them wish to drink; but the tendency toward nausea and the effort required for swallowing <note>original: "deglutition"</note> are so unpleasant that they seldom care to drink much at a time. They also experience much uneasiness from a lack of rest during the night. On the morning of the third day, the face, neck, and breast appear redder than usual; in a few hours, this redness becomes universal and increases to such a degree of intensity that the face, body, and limbs resemble a boiled lobster in color and are clearly swollen.

A *delirium* <note>a state of mental confusion and emotional disruption</note> accompanies many different kinds of fevers. Sometimes it is slight, easily resolved, and hardly considered a bad sign. The fierce delirium is preceded and accompanied by a redness of the face, head pain, a great pounding of the arteries, and noise in the ears. The person's usual manners change, and an unusual irritability and ill-nature prevail. The impairment of judgment is first observed when the patient is between sleep and waking; they believe their own imagination while ignoring their actual senses, and their memories occur in a random, irregular manner. Fury at last takes hold, sometimes with an unusual and incredible degree of physical strength, so that several people can scarcely keep a single patient in his bed. 

The mild delirium, on the contrary, is often accompanied by a weak pulse, a pale and sunken <note>original: "collapsed"</note> face, and vertigo when the patient sits in an upright posture. He is seldom angry but often unresponsive, and sometimes remarkably grieved and fearful. The loss of judgment, as in the former kind, is first noticed when the patient is half awake, but a temporary recovery follows once light is admitted and friends begin to speak. The patient mutters much to himself and pays little attention to things around him. At last, becoming quite unresponsive, he feels neither hunger nor thirst, nor any other natural urges <note>original: "propensities of nature"</note>, which results in urine and excrement being voided involuntarily. # A KEY TO PHYSIC,

As the disorder increases, it ends in <term>subsultus tendinum</term> <note>original Latin: "jumping of the tendons"; involuntary twitching of the tendons, usually a sign of extreme physical exhaustion or approaching death</note>, tremors, convulsions, fainting, and death. The other species of delirium also frequently ends in this way when the vitality <note>original: "spirits"</note> and strength of the patient begin to fail. The symptoms accompanying either of these kinds of delirium show an unusual <note>The OCR reads "uſual," but in the medical context of the 18th century, "unusual" or "inordinate" (disordered) was the standard description for the blood flow in delirium</note>, disordered, and unequal motion of the blood through the brain, and a great change in that state which is necessary for the exercise of the mental powers. It is likely enough that an inflammation of the brain, more or less violent and widespread, sometimes occurs, although the signs of general inflammation are frequently slight. This we learn from the dissection of deceased bodies, which often show a general redness of the brain or some of its parts, or sometimes an effusion <note>an escape of fluid into a body cavity</note> or the formation of pus <note>original: "suppuration"</note>.

The outlook <note>original: "prognostics"</note> for the malignant, putrid, or ulcerous sore throat <note>Historical terms for severe throat infections like diphtheria or streptococcal infections that caused tissue death</note> vary greatly between different people. Sometimes a shivering fit <note>original: "rigour"</note>, with a feeling of fullness and soreness of the throat and a painful stiffness of the neck, are the first symptoms reported. Sometimes alternating chills and fever, with some degree of dizziness, drowsiness, or headache, introduce the disease. In others, it begins with much more severe feverish symptoms: great pain in the head, back, and limbs; a vast oppression of the <term>praecordia</term> <note>the region of the body just in front of the heart and stomach</note>, and constant sighing. Some adults go about for several days in a weakened, drooping state, with much uneasiness and anxiety, until at last they are forced to take to their beds. Thus, the disease is quite varied at its onset. 

But it commonly begins with chills and fever, a feeling of heaviness and pain in the head, a sore throat, and hoarseness; some coughing, nausea, and frequent vomiting and diarrhea <note>original: "purging"</note>, especially in children, where it is sometimes very severe, though the opposite condition <note>constipation</note> is more common in adults. There is usually a very great loss of spirit, sudden weakness, a great heaviness on the chest, and faintness from the very beginning. The pulse is generally quick, small, and fluttering, though sometimes heavy and undulating. The eyes appear heavy, reddish, and tearful <note>original: "weeping"</note>; the face is often full, flushed, and bloated, though sometimes pale and sunken. 

The following are the signs for predicting the course of the disease: If a gentle, easy sweat begins on the third or fourth day; if the pulse becomes slower, firmer, and more regular; if the dead tissue <note>original: "sloughs"</note> in the <term>fauces</term> <note>the back of the throat</note> peels off naturally and the area beneath appears reasonably clean and healthy red <note>original: "florid"</note>; if the breathing becomes softer and easier, and some strength and alertness return to the eyes—then all is well. A healthy turning point <note>original: "salutary crisis"</note> soon follows, marked by continued sweating and a cloudy urine that leaves a mealy sediment <note>original: "turbid, subsiding, farinaceous urine"</note>, plenty of phlegm being coughed up <note>original: "expectoration"</note>, and a very large peeling of the skin <note>original: "desquamation of the cuticle"</note>. 

But if a shivering fit <note>original: "rigour"</note> occurs and the <term>exanthemata</term> <note>skin rashes or eruptions</note> suddenly disappear or turn a bruised, leaden color <note>original: "livid"</note>; if the pulse grows very small and quick, and the skin remains hot and seemingly parched; if breathing becomes more difficult, the eyes appear dead and glassy, and the urine is pale and clear—then a state of delirium <note>original: "phrenzy"</note> or a coma may be expected to follow,

Symptoms of the croup, or inflammation of the glottis <note>the part of the larynx consisting of the vocal cords and the opening between them</note>: A hoarseness, with some shrillness and a ringing sound in both speaking and coughing, as if the noise came from a brass <note>original: "brazen"</note> tube. At the same time, there is a sense of pain around the larynx, some difficulty breathing, with a whizzing sound during inhalation <note>original: "inspiration"</note>, as if the passage of air were narrowed <note>original: "straitened"</note>. The cough which accompanies it is commonly dry; and, if anything is coughed up, it is pus-like <note>original: "purulent"</note> matter, and sometimes films resembling portions of a membrane. Along with all these symptoms, there is a frequent pulse, restlessness, and an uneasy sense of heat. When the back of the throat <note>original Latin: "internal fauces"</note> is viewed, it sometimes shows no appearance of inflammation; but frequently redness, and even swelling, appears. Sometimes there is an appearance of matter like that coughed up, together with the symptoms now described—particularly great difficulty breathing and a sense of strangling in the throat <note>original Latin: "fauces"</note>, by which the patient is sometimes suddenly killed.

In a pleurisy <note>inflammation of the pleurae, which impairs lubrication in the chest cavity and causes pain when breathing</note>, the <term>pathognomonic</term> <note>signs specifically characteristic of a particular disease</note> signs are a cough, difficulty breathing, pain in the side, and a continued fever; the additional signs are the various types of matter coughed up <note>original: "expectorated"</note>, which are sometimes bloody, sometimes bilious, etc. When the pains, which at first affected only one side, afterwards spread to the other, or when they leave the side first affected and pass entirely into the other, these are always marks of a dangerous disease. A delirium occurring during a lung <note>original: "pneumonic"</note> inflammation is always a symptom indicating much danger. Bloodletting <note>original: "bleeding"</note> is the remedy chiefly to be relied upon; it may be performed in either arm, as the surgeon finds most convenient, and the quantity of blood taken away should generally be as large as the patient's strength will allow. Yet the patient must stay out of bed as much as he can bear; he must have plenty of warm, diluting drinks mixed with vegetable acids, accompanied by nitre <note>potassium nitrate, used as a cooling medicine</note> or some other cooling neutral salt; and the bowels <note>original: "belly"</note> should also be kept open by soothing <term>clysters</term> <note>enemas</note> or cooling laxative medicines. Vomiting in the beginning is dangerous; but in a somewhat advanced state of the disease, emetics <note>medicines that induce vomiting</note> have been found the best means of promoting the clearing of the lungs <note>original: "expectoration"</note>. Warm, moist applications <note>original: "fomentations"</note> and poultices to the painful part have been found useful, but <term>blistering</term> <note>the application of an irritating plaster to the skin to create a blister, intended to "draw out" internal inflammation</note> is found to be much more effective. A blister, however, should not be applied until at least one bloodletting has been performed, as <term>venesection</term> <note>bloodletting</note> is less effective when the irritation of a blister is present. If the disease is moderate, a blister may be applied immediately after the first bloodletting; but in violent cases, where it may be assumed that a second bloodletting may soon be necessary after the first, it

<meta>This page continues the discussion of treating inflammations of the chest (specifically pleurisy), focusing on the timing of medical interventions like bloodletting and blistering. It then details the transition of the disease into empyema (pus in the chest cavity) and concludes with the symptoms of heart inflammation.</meta>

# A KEY TO PHYSIC,

It will be proper to delay the blister <note>a plaster used to irritate the skin and draw out "humors"</note> until after the second bloodletting, when it may be supposed that the irritation caused by the blister will be over before a third bloodletting becomes necessary. It may frequently be useful in this disease to repeat the blistering; in that case, the plasters should always be applied somewhere on the chest <term>thorax</term>, for when applied to more distant parts they have little effect. Keeping the blistered parts open, and making what is called a "perpetual blister," has much less effect than repeated blistering. 

When this disease terminates unfavorably, it often ends in an accumulation of pus in the chest <term>empyema</term>, which is caused by the discharge <note>original: "effusion"</note> of a quantity of pus-like <term>purulent</term> matter into the cavity of the chest, producing a lingering and painful disorder that is very often incurable. The first sign of an empyema is a cessation of the pain in the breast which was previously constant; this is followed by a sensation of weight on the diaphragm and a shifting movement of matter <note>original: "fluctuation of matter"</note>, sometimes making a noise that may be heard by those standing nearby. The acute fever changes into a wasting fever <term>hectic fever</term>, with the symptoms worsening <note>original: "exacerbation"</note> at night, and a continual, troublesome dry cough remains. 

Breathing <note>original: "respiration"</note> is exceedingly difficult because the lungs are prevented by the accumulated matter from fully expanding. The patient can lie easily on the side where the matter is collected, but not on the other side, because then the weight of the matter presses on the central partition of the chest <term>mediastinum</term>, producing unease. The more the wasting <note>original: "hectic"</note> heat increases, the more the body becomes emaciated and its strength declines. In some patients, there is a danger of suffocation when they stoop down, which goes away when they change their posture; and in some, there is a coughing up of pus <note>original: "purulent spitting"</note>. 

These symptoms are accompanied by great anxiety, palpitations of the heart, and fainting. Very few recover after an empyema has once formed, especially if the operation of surgical drainage <term>paracentesis</term> is neglected. After this operation is performed, there is no hope if a great quantity of bloody, foul-smelling <term>fetid</term> pus is discharged, if the fever continues, and if the patient spits up pus-like, pale, frothy, grayish-blue <term>livid</term>, or green matter along with a decay of strength. 

However, when a small quantity of white pus (not very foul-smelling) is discharged, there is then hope of a perfect recovery; particularly when the fever and thirst quickly cease, the appetite returns, and bowel movements <note>original: "faeces"</note> of a good consistency are passed, with strength also returning to some degree. If the matter is not dried up within seven weeks, the disease readily changes to a tube-like ulcer <term>fistulous ulcer</term>, which is very difficult to cure. An empyema affecting both sides of the chest is more dangerous than one affecting only one side.

The *inflammation of the heart* is attended with all the symptoms mentioned before, but in a higher degree. It is besides sometimes accompanied with a fear of swallowing liquids <note>original Latin: "hydrophobic symptoms"</note>, fainting, palpitations of the heart, a seeming madness, a weak <note>original: "sunk"</note> and irregular pulse, watery eyes, and a dejected countenance, with a dry, black tongue.

<meta>This page continues the medical descriptions of internal inflammations, shifting from the chest (pleurisy and heart inflammation mentioned on the previous page) to the digestive organs, specifically the stomach, intestines, and liver.</meta>

## AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES.

The signs of an *inflammation of the stomach* are intense heat and pain in the <term>epigastric region</term> (the upper-middle part of the abdomen), extreme anxiety, nearly constant and painful hiccups, and most painful vomiting of everything taken into the stomach. This disease is always very dangerous, and the outlook <note>original: "prognosis"</note> is uncertain; it must always be judged in proportion to the severity of the symptoms. A sudden stop in pain, coldness around the <term>precordia</term> (the area of the chest over the heart and lower stomach), great weakness, a faint and irregular pulse, and a decrease in hiccups indicate <term>gangrene</term> (tissue death) and approaching death. 

Because the stomach is so sensitive and so closely connected with the rest of the body's systems, it is obvious that an inflammation there, whatever the cause, can have fatal consequences. In particular, because of the great weakness it produces, it may prove suddenly fatal without running through the usual stages of inflammation. A likelihood of recovery <note>original: "tendency to admit of resolution"</note> may be recognized if the disease did not arise from a violent cause, if the symptoms are moderate, and if they gradually fade during the first or, at most, the second week of the illness. 

The risk of gangrene may be suspected if the symptoms continue with unremitting violence despite the use of proper remedies. A gangrene that has already begun may be identified by the symptoms mentioned above, particularly great weakness and a sudden end to the pain. The tendency toward the formation of pus <note>original: "suppuration"</note> may be recognized if the symptoms continue in only a moderate degree for more than one or two weeks, and if the pain lessens considerably while a sense of weight and anxiety remains. When an <term>abscess</term> (a collection of pus) has formed, the rapid pulse first slows down, but soon after it increases again, accompanied by frequent cold shivering and a worsening of symptoms in the afternoon and evening. This is followed by night sweats and other symptoms of a wasting <term>hectic fever</term>. These eventually prove fatal, unless the abscess opens into the cavity of the stomach, the pus is vomited up, and the ulcer is quickly healed.

An inflammation of the intestines shows itself by a steady pain in the abdomen, accompanied by fever, vomiting, and constipation <note>original: "costiveness"</note>. The pain is often felt in different parts of the abdomen, but more frequently spreads over the whole area and is particularly violent around the navel. Inflammations of the intestines may arise from the same causes as those of the stomach, though commonly the former will occur more easily from cold applied to the legs or to the belly itself. It is also found occurring alongside spasmodic colic, an <term>incarcerated hernia</term> (where part of the intestine is trapped), or a <term>volvulus</term> (a twisted loop of intestine). Inflammations of the intestines have the same endings as those of the stomach, and the outlook in both cases is much the same.

*Inflammation of the liver* is accompanied by considerable fever, a frequent, strong, and hard pulse, dark-colored <note>original: "high-coloured"</note> urine, and an acute pain in the <term>right hypochondrium</term> (the upper right area of the abdomen under the ribs), which increases when pressing upon the part. The pain is very often in a part of the side that makes it appear like <term>pleurisy</term> (inflammation of the chest lining), and like that, it is frequently increased when breathing in.

suppuration. The disease is also commonly accompanied by a cough, which is generally dry but sometimes moist. When the pain resembles that of <term>pleurisy</term> (inflammation of the chest lining), the patient cannot lie down comfortably except on the side that is affected. The pain often extends to the <term>clavicle</term> (collarbone) and to the top of the shoulder; it is sometimes accompanied by hiccups and sometimes by vomiting. Like other inflammations, an inflammation of the liver may end in resolution (recovery), <term>suppuration</term> (the formation of pus), or <term>gangrene</term> (tissue death). The likelihood of any of these outcomes can be determined by the signs already mentioned.

*Inflammation of the spleen* begins with a notable fit of shivering, followed by intense heat and very great thirst. Pain and a <term>tumor</term> (swelling) are felt in the left <term>hypochondrium</term> (the upper region of the abdomen below the ribs), and the <term>paroxysms</term> (sudden attacks) for the most part follow a <term>quartan form</term> <note>original: "quartan form"; a pattern where symptoms recur every four days, or every 72 hours, often associated with malaria</note>. When patients are exposed to fresh air for even a short time, their hands and feet immediately become very cold. If a hemorrhage occurs, the blood flows from the left nostril.

It is often very difficult to distinguish rheumatism from gout. However, in *rheumatism*, there is generally much less involvement of the stomach. It primarily affects the larger joints—and often several of them at the same time. It occurs earlier in life than gout; it is not known to be hereditary; and it can usually be traced to some obvious cause, particularly exposure to cold. 

To distinguish chronic rheumatism from the acute form: when the pains are prone to shifting their location; when they are especially severe at night; and when they are accompanied by some degree of <term>pyrexia</term> (fever), swelling, and particularly redness of the joints, the disease should be considered acute rheumatism. 

However, the case should be considered purely chronic rheumatism when there is no longer any fever; when the pained joints are not red, but are cold and stiff; and when they do not easily sweat. In some chronic cases, while a free and warm sweat breaks out on the rest of the body, the sweat is only clammy and cold on the pained joints. Furthermore, the pain in these joints is increased by cold and relieved by the application of heat. Perhaps more accurately, the first condition (acute) may be called a state of irritability, and the second (chronic) a state of <term>atony</term> <note>original: "atony"; a lack of physiological tone or muscular strength</note>. 

Chronic rheumatism—or rather, the atonic type—can affect various joints, but it is especially likely to affect those surrounded by many muscles or those where the muscles are used in constant and vigorous activity. This is the case with the vertebrae of the lower back, an ailment called *lumbago*; or the hip joint, where the disease is called *ischias* or *sciatica*. Violent strains and spasms, occurring during sudden and forceful exertion, can trigger rheumatic conditions that initially resemble chronic rheumatism. These include lumbago and other issues that seem to be located more in the muscles than in the joints. The distinction between rheumatic pains and the similar pains found in syphilis and scurvy...

### AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES.

It must be obvious, either from the location of the pains or from the accompanying symptoms peculiar to those diseases.

What we call a flare-up <note>original: "paroxysm"</note> of the gout is principally characterized by an inflammatory affection of some of the joints. This sometimes comes on suddenly, without any warning, but is generally preceded by several symptoms: such as the ceasing of the foot-sweating that usually affected the patient; an unusual coldness of the feet and legs; a frequent numbness alternating with a sense of pricking along the whole of the lower limbs; frequent cramps of the leg muscles; and an unusual swelling <note>original: "turgescence"</note> of the veins. While these symptoms occur in the lower limbs, the body is affected with some degree of sluggishness and tiredness <note>original: "torpor and languor"</note>, and the functions of the stomach in particular are more or less disturbed. The appetite is diminished, and gas <note>original: "flatulency"</note> or other symptoms of indigestion are felt. These symptoms occur for several days, sometimes for a week or two, before a flare-up occurs; but commonly, on the day immediately preceding it, the appetite becomes hungrier than usual. It is commonly supposed that there are some cases of rheumatism which are scarcely to be distinguished from the gout. However, Dr. Cullen <note>Dr. William Cullen (1710–1790) was a famous Scottish physician whose system of classifying diseases was widely used in the 18th century</note> thinks these cases are few, and that the two diseases may for the most part be distinguished with great certainty by observing the patient's predisposition, the preceding circumstances, the parts affected, the recurrence of the disease, and its connection with the rest of the body's systems; these circumstances usually appear very differently in the two diseases.

Signs <note>original: "Prognostics"</note> that a person is infected with the plague:
1. Great loss of strength.
2. Sluggishness, giddiness, and consequent staggering which resembles drunkenness, or a headache and various states of delirium.
3. Anxiety, heart palpitations, fainting <note>original: "syncope"</note>, and especially the weakness and irregularity of the pulse, denoting a considerable disturbance in the action of the heart.
4. Nausea and vomiting, particularly the vomiting of bile, which shows an accumulation of "vitiated" <note>meaning corrupted or unhealthy</note> bile in the gallbladder and bile ducts, which has moved into the intestines and stomach. This also indicates a significant spasm and loss of "tone" <note>In historical medicine, "tone" referred to the healthy tension or vigor of the muscles and vessels</note> in the small blood vessels on the surface of the body.

The smallpox begins with an inflammatory fever <note>original: "synocha"</note>. It generally comes on about midday, with some symptoms of a cold stage, and commonly with a significant tiredness and drowsiness. A hot stage is soon formed and becomes more intense on the second and third day. During this course, children are liable to frequent twitching <note>original: "startings"</note> from their sleep; and adults, if they are kept in bed, are prone to heavy sweating. On the third day, children are sometimes affected with one or two seizures <note>original: "epileptic fits"</note>. Towards the end of the third day, the rash <note>original: "eruption"</note> commonly appears.

The principal marks by which the chickenpox may be distinguished from the smallpox are:
1. The appearance, on the second or third day of the rash, of a blister <note>original: "vesicle"</note> full of clear fluid <note>original: "serum"</note> upon the top of the sore.
2. The crust, which covers

# A KEY TO PHYSIC,

the pustules on the fifth day; at which time those of the <term>smallpox</term> are not yet at the height of their suppuration <note>original: "suppuration"; the process of forming pus</note>. Foreign medical writers hardly ever mention the name of the <term>chicken-pox</term>, and the writers of our own country scarcely mention anything more of it than its name. Morton <note>Richard Morton (1637–1698), an English physician who specialized in pulmonary diseases and fevers</note> speaks of it as if he supposed it to be a very mild version of genuine <term>small-pox</term>. 

But these two diseases are surely totally different from one another, not only because of their different appearances mentioned above, but because those who have had the <term>small-pox</term> are still capable of being infected with the <term>chicken-pox</term>. Furthermore, those who have once had the <term>chicken-pox</term> are not capable of having it again, though to those who have never had the disease, it seems as infectious as the <term>small-pox</term>. Dr. Heberden <note>William Heberden (1710–1801) was a prominent English physician; he is credited with providing the first clear clinical description of chickenpox in 1767</note> wetted a thread in the most developed <note>original: "concocted"</note> pus-like fluid of the <term>chicken-pox</term> that he could find; and, after making a slight incision, the thread was kept against the arm of a person who had formerly had the disease. The little wound healed up immediately and showed no signs of any infection. From the great similarity between the two diseases, it is probable that some persons have been inoculated with the <term>chicken-pox</term> instead of the <term>small-pox</term>, and that the resulting illness has been mistaken for the <term>small-pox</term> by hasty or inexperienced observers.

It is a promising sign in cases of *<term>palsy</term>* <note>original: "palsy"; paralysis or loss of motor function</note> when the patient feels a slight degree of painful itching in the affected parts; and, if a fever should arise, it is very likely to cure the <term>palsy</term>. When the sense of feeling remains, there is much more room to hope for a cure than when feeling is gone along with the power of motion. But when we observe the flesh to waste away and the skin to appear withered and dry, we may look upon the disease as incurable. *<term>Convulsions</term>* occurring alongside a <term>palsy</term> are a fatal sign.

When *<term>fainting</term>* happens at the beginning of any acute disease, it is not a good omen; but when it takes place during the increase or at the height of the disease, the danger is somewhat less. In general, when <term>fainting</term> comes on without any evident cause, it is to be dreaded. In violent *<term>hemorrhages</term>* <note>original: "hæmorrhages"</note>, however, it is favorable, as the bleeding vessels gain time to contract and recover themselves, which may allow the patient to escape death. When persons of a full habit <note>original: "full habit"; a plethoric or robust physique, thought to have an excess of blood</note> *faint* through an excess of passion, they ought to be bled without delay and should drink vinegar or lemon juice diluted with water. After the bowels are emptied by an <term>enema</term> <note>original: "clyster"</note>, they should take a <term>pain-relieving drink</term> <note>original: "paregoric draught"; typically a medicine containing opium used to soothe pain or diarrhea</note> and go to bed.

*Prognostics from <term>convulsions</term>.* Except in some few cases, convulsive disorders are always to be dreaded, though less so in young people than in those who are advanced in life. Those which attack girls under the age of <term>puberty</term> will generally cease upon the first appearance of their <term>menstrual periods</term> <note>original: "menses"</note>; boys likewise have a chance of being relieved as they grow older. But in grown adults, unless the cause is very evident, a cure is hardly to be expected, especially after the disease has lasted a long time. The treatment is much the same as that for <term>epilepsy</term>.
