<page-num>221</page-num>

*<term>Epilepsy</term>* <note>original: "epilepsy"; a neurological disorder marked by sudden recurrent episodes of sensory disturbance, loss of consciousness, or convulsions</note> is frequently preceded by a headache, exhaustion, some disturbance of the senses, restless sleep, unusual dread, dimness of sight, a ringing in the ears, heart palpitations, and coldness of the joints. In some patients, there is a sensation of <term>formication</term> <note>original: "formication"; a sensation that resembles small insects crawling on or under the skin</note>, or a cold breeze, etc., ascending from the lower extremities toward the head. If the <term>epilepsy</term> begins before puberty, there is some hope of it disappearing at that time. However, it is a bad sign when it attacks a person around their twenty-first year, and even worse if the fits grow more frequent; in those cases, the physical functions are often destroyed, as well as those of the mind, and the patient becomes dull and foolish. Sometimes it will end in melancholy or madness, and sometimes in a fatal <term>apoplexy</term> <note>original: "apoplexy"; a stroke</note> or <term>palsy</term> <note>original: "palsy"; paralysis</note>. It has sometimes been observed, however, that <term>epilepsies</term> have been cured by the appearance of <term>skin diseases</term>, such as the itch <note>scabies</note>, <term>smallpox</term>, <term>measles</term>, etc. Therefore, if any of these appear, it may be considered a favorable <term>prognostic</term> <note>a medical forecast of the likely outcome of a disease</note>.

*Signs of <term>diabetes</term>.*—<term>Diabetes</term> first shows itself by a dryness of the mouth and thirst, white frothy saliva, and urine in a somewhat larger quantity than usual. A heat begins to be felt in the bowels, which at first is slightly sharp and gradually increases. Thirst continues to grow by degrees, and the patient slowly loses the power of holding their urine for any length of time. The most singular phenomenon in this disease is that the urine seems to be entirely or mostly stripped of its animal nature, and to be heavily filled with a <term>sugary salt</term>, scarcely distinguishable from that obtained from the sugar-cane. This discovery was first made by Dr. Dobson of Liverpool <note>Dr. Matthew Dobson (1732–1784) was the first to prove that the sweetness of a diabetic's urine was caused by sugar</note>, who conducted experiments on the urine of a person suffering from diabetes; the patient discharged 28 pints of urine every day, while taking in only 12 to 14 pounds of solid and liquid food during the same time. When a person notices any of the mentioned symptoms (particularly the quantity and insipidity <note>original: "insipidity"; lack of flavor. Bristol water <note>Mineral water from the Hotwells spring in Bristol, which was a fashionable and widely prescribed treatment for diabetes in the 18th century</note> is considered a specific remedy for this disorder.

The wound becomes swollen, hard, and raised, accompanied by a peculiar pricking sensation in the area. Pains shoot from the wound toward the throat; sometimes it is surrounded by bruised <note>original: "livid"</note> or red streaks and appears to be in a state of inflammation, though frequently there is nothing unusual to be observed about it. The patient becomes depressed <note>original: "melancholy"</note>, seeks solitude, and feels sickness in the stomach. Sometimes the characteristic symptom of the disease, the dread of water <note>original: "hydrophobia"</note>, comes on all at once. We have an instance of one who, having taken an emetic <note>original: "vomit"</note> of <term>ipecacuanha</term> <note>a root used to induce vomiting</note> for the nausea he felt in his stomach, was seized with the dread of water while he was drinking the warm water required for the medicine. Sometimes the disease begins like a common sore throat; as the soreness increases daily, the symptoms of the dread of water show themselves as a convulsive spasm of the muscles of the throat <note>original: "fauces"; the opening at the back of the mouth</note>. In others, the mind seems to be primarily affected, and they have a real dread of water or any liquid before they even try whether they can swallow it or not.

Dr. James, in his *Treatise on Canine Madness*, mentions a boy sent out to fill two bottles with water who was so terrified by the noise of the liquid running into them that he fled into the house crying out that he was bewitched. He also mentions the case of a farmer who, going to draw some ale from a cask, was terrified to such a degree by the sound of it running into the vessel that he ran out in great haste with the spigot still in his hand. But, in whatever manner this symptom appears, it is certain that the most painful sensations accompany every attempt to swallow liquids. Indeed, the mere sight of water, of a looking-glass, or of anything clear or transparent <note>original: "pellucid"</note> will cause the utmost uneasiness or even throw the patient into convulsions.

Regarding the state of the mind itself in this disease, it does not appear that the patients lose their reason. Some have, by sheer force of resolution, conquered the dread of water, though they could never conquer the convulsive motions caused by the contact of liquids. Yet even this resolution has been of no use; for as the convulsions and other symptoms increase, they almost always destroy the unhappy patients. However, in this distemper, the symptoms are so various that they cannot all be listed, for we seldom read of two cases of the dread of water that do not differ remarkably from one another. When a person is bitten, the <term>prognosis</term> <note>a forecast of the likely outcome of a disease</note> regarding the ensuing disease is very uncertain. Not everyone who is bitten falls ill; indeed, Dr. Vaughan relates that, out of thirty people bitten by a mad dog, only one was seized with the dread of water. During the interval between the bite and the time the disease appears, there are no symptoms by which we can certainly judge whether it will manifest or not.

**Scurvy.** The first indication of a tendency toward scurvy <term>scorbutic diathesis</term> is generally a change of color in the face, from a natural and healthy look to a pale and bloated complexion, accompanied by listlessness and a dislike for any sort of exercise. Soon after, the gums become itchy and swollen, and they tend to bleed at the slightest touch. The breath becomes offensive, and as the gums swell more and more each day, they turn a bruised purple <note>original: "livid"</note> and eventually become extremely overgrown and rotten <note>original: "fungous and putrid"</note>. This is because they are continually in contact with the external air, which in every case encourages the decay of substances inclined to rot, and is indeed absolutely necessary for the production of actual rottenness. The symptoms of scurvy, like those of every other disease, vary somewhat in different people according to their specific constitution, and they do not always progress in the same regular order for every patient. 

But what is very remarkable about this disease is that, despite the various and immense burdens of distress the patients suffer, there is no nausea at the stomach, the appetite remains, and the senses remain sharp almost until the very end. When lying at rest, patients make no complaints and feel little distress or pain; but the moment they attempt to rise or move, their breathing becomes difficult, with a kind of tightness or catching and great oppression; sometimes they have even been known to fall into a fainting spell <note>original: "syncope"</note>. This catching of the breath upon movement, along with the loss of strength, low spirits, and decaying gums, are considered the essential or distinguishing symptoms of the disease.

**The jaundice** first shows itself by listlessness and a lack of appetite; the patient becomes dull, oppressed, and generally constipated <note>original: "costive"</note>. After these symptoms have lasted only a very short time, a yellow color begins to spread over the white part of the eye <note>original: "tunica albuginea"</note> and the fingernails. The urine becomes dark and high-colored, with a yellowish sediment capable of staining linen yellow, while the stools are whitish or gray. 

In some patients, there is a most violent pain in the upper middle part of the abdomen <note>original: "epigastric region"</note>, which increases considerably after meals. In some cases, the disease degenerates into an incurable edema <note>original: "dropsy"</note>; indeed, there have been many instances of people who died of this fluid retention after the jaundice itself had been totally removed. The appearance of mild diarrhea, accompanied by stools containing bile, together with the ending of pain, are signs that the disease is being cured. We should not, however, always conclude that because the disease is not accompanied by sharp pain, it is therefore incurable; for frequently the passage of a stone <note>original: "concretion"</note> through the bile ducts is accompanied only by a sensation of slight discomfort. If the disease goes away, its return must be prevented by a course of strengthening <term>tonic</term> medicines, particularly cinchona bark <note>original: "Peruvian bark"</note> and medicines that prevent decay <term>antiseptics</term>. But we can by no means be certain that the jaundice will not return,

*Stone in the bladder.* The signs of a stone in the bladder are: pain, especially about the sphincter <note>the ring of muscle that closes the bladder</note>; bloody urine resulting from riding a horse or being jolted in a carriage; a sense of weight in the perineum <note>the area between the anus and the genitals</note>; an itchiness of the head of the penis <note>original: "glans penis"</note>; slimy sediment in the urine; and frequent stoppages while urinating. A distressing urge to evacuate the bowels <term>tenesmus</term> also occurs while the urine is being discharged.

*Imaginary vision of objects which do not exist.* This often takes place when the body is diseased, and then the patient is said to be delirious. Sometimes, however, in these cases it does not amount to full delirium, but the person imagines he sees gnats or other insects flying before his eyes. Sometimes everything he looks at seems to have black spots in it, which is a very dangerous sign. Sometimes sparks of fire also appear before his eyes; these appearances are not to be disregarded, as they frequently precede a stroke <term>apoplexy</term> or an epileptic seizure. On the other hand, it is feared that little benefit can be gained from paying attention to this warning sign <term>prognostic</term>, as the fits usually follow so suddenly.

### ANGINA PECTORIS.
<note>Latin: "Strangling of the chest"</note>

Dr. Heberden <note>Dr. William Heberden (1710–1801), who first described the condition in 1768</note> was the first who described this disease, though it is extremely dangerous and, by his account, not very rare. It seizes those who are subject to it when they are walking—and particularly when they walk soon after eating—with a most disagreeable and painful sensation in the breast which seems to threaten immediate destruction. However, the moment they stand still, all the uneasiness vanishes. In all other respects, patients at the beginning of this disorder are well and have no shortness of breath; in this way, angina pectoris is totally different from other chest ailments. After it has continued for some months, the fits will not cease immediately upon standing still; it will begin to occur not only when the patients are walking, but even when they are lying down, forcing them to get out of their beds every night for many months together. In one or two very stubborn <note>original: "inveterate"</note> cases, it has been brought on by the motion of a horse or carriage, and even by swallowing, coughing, going to the bathroom, speaking, or by any mental distress. The persons affected were all men, almost all of whom were above fifty years of age, and most of them had short necks.

...and a tendency to be fat. Something like it, however, was observed in one woman who was paralyzed <term>paralytic</term>; and one or two young men complained of it in a slight degree. Other practitioners have observed it in very young persons. When an attack <note>original: "fit"</note> of this sort is triggered by walking, its duration is very short, as it goes off almost immediately upon stopping. If it occurs in the night, it will last an hour or two. Dr. Heberden met with one patient in whom it once continued for several days; during all that time, the patient seemed to be in imminent danger of death. Most of those attacked with the distemper died suddenly, though this rule was not without exceptions; Dr. Heberden observed one who passed away after a lingering illness of a different nature. The breastbone <note>original: "os sterni"</note> is usually pointed to as the seat of this malady; it seems as if the pain is under the lower part of that bone, and at other times under the middle or upper part, but it always leans more to the left side. In many cases, there is also a pain around the middle of the left arm, which appears to be located in the biceps muscle.

The appearance of Dr. Heberden's paper in the *Medical Transactions* <note>a prestigious medical journal of the time</note> very soon raised the attention of the medical profession <note>original: "the faculty"</note> and produced other observations from physicians of eminence; namely, Dr. Fothergill, Dr. Wall of Worcester, Dr. Haygarth of Chester, and Dr. Percival of Manchester. It also induced an unknown sufferer to write Dr. Heberden a very sensible letter, describing his feelings in the most natural manner. Unfortunately, three weeks after the date of this anonymous letter <note>original: "epistle"</note>, he died suddenly, just as the writer himself had feared. 

The youngest subject that Dr. Fothergill ever saw afflicted with this disorder was about thirty years of age, and this person was cured. The method that succeeded with him was a course of pills composed of a gum resin mass <term>gum-pill</term>, soap, and mercury sulfide <note>original: "native cinnabar"; a mineral once used in medicine but now known to be toxic</note>, taken with a light iron-based bitter tonic <term>chalybeate bitter</term>. This was continued for some months, after which he went to the spa at Bath for several successive seasons and regained his usual health. He was ordered to be very sparing in his diet, to keep his bowels open, and to use moderate exercise on horseback, but not to take long or fatiguing walks. 

The only symptom mentioned in this patient was a tightness <note>original: "stricture"</note> around the chest, which came on if he was walking uphill, walking a little faster than ordinary, or if he was riding a very brisk trot; moderate exercise of any kind did not affect him. This uneasy sensation always obliged him to stop, as he felt himself threatened with immediate death if he had continued to go forward. According to Dr. Fothergill's observation, it is the sharp, constricting pain across the chest that particularly marks this singular disease. It is prone to happen upon a certain degree of muscular motion or whatever agitates the nervous system. In such cases as fell under the inspection of Dr. Fothergill, he very seldom met with one that was not attended with an irregular and skipping <term>intermitting</term> pulse—and this occurred not only during the flare-ups <term>exacerbations</term>...

# AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES. 227

...but it often happened when the patient was free from pain and at rest. However, Dr. Heberden observes that the pulse is, at least sometimes, not disturbed; he mentions having once had an opportunity to confirm this by feeling the pulse during an attack <term>paroxysm</term>. No doubt these variations, along with many other minor details, will occur in this disease just as they do in every other, because of the diversity of the human body. If the symptoms that generally predominate and define the disease are present, they will always justify us in naming the condition. Thus, when we find a constricting pain across the chest accompanied by a sense of strangling or suffocation—and even more so if this pain strikes across the breast into one or both arms—we should not hesitate to diagnose the case as *angina pectoris*.

Regarding the nature of this disease, it appears to be purely spasmodic <term>caused by muscle spasms</term>. This opinion will readily occur to anyone who considers: how suddenly it comes and goes; the long intervals of perfect health; the relief provided by wine and spirituous cordials; the influence of strong emotions <note>original: "passionate affections of the mind"</note> over it; the relief that comes from changing the posture of the head and shoulders or from remaining perfectly still; how many years it can continue without otherwise harming health; and how well it tolerates the motion of a horse or carriage (a circumstance that often distinguishes spasmodic pains from those caused by ulcers). Finally, it mostly occurs after a full meal and, in certain patients, at night just after their first sleep. This is the same time when the nightmare <term>incubus</term> <note>often referring to sleep apnea or heavy pressure on the chest during sleep</note>, convulsive asthma, and other ailments—rightly attributed to disordered nerves—are particularly likely to return or worsen. 

Taking all these circumstances together, there can be little doubt that this condition is spasmodic. However, even if this is admitted, it may not be so easy to determine which specific muscles are affected. The violent sense of strangling or choking shows that circulation through the lungs is interrupted during the peak of the attack. This, along with the peculiar constricting pain under the breastbone <term>sternum</term>—which, according to Dr. Heberden’s observation, always leans toward the left side—and that most distressing and alarming sensation which threatens immediate death if it continues, might lead us to conclude that the heart itself is the muscle affected. The only objection to this idea (which would be insurmountable if it were always observed) is that the pulse is not always interrupted during the attack. The findings from two dissections support the opinion that the spasm affects the heart. In one subject, the left ventricle (and we may assume the right one as well, though it is not mentioned) was found as empty of blood as if it had been washed. In another, the tissue of the heart appeared whitish, not unlike a ligament <note>a tough, fibrous tissue</note>—likely caused, in both cases, by the force

# A KEY TO MEDICINE <note>original: "PHYSIC"</note>

...of the spasm squeezing the blood out from the vessels and cavities. If we accept this hypothesis, we must conclude that the spasm can only occur to a mild degree as long as the patient survives the attack <term>paroxysm</term>. An affliction of this sort in this part of the body, if it were of any significant duration or violence, would inevitably prove fatal. Accordingly, as far as could be traced, the people known to suffer from this disease have generally died suddenly.

Dissections <note>post-mortem examinations</note> also show that, whatever the true location of the spasm may be, it is not necessary for the heart or its immediate appendages to be in a diseased <note>original: "morbid"</note> state for an attack to occur. In three out of the six autopsies that have been made public so far, these parts were found to be healthy. Upon opening the body of the gentleman who wrote the letter to Dr. Heberden, "upon the most careful examination, no obvious cause of his death could be discovered; the heart, in particular, with its vessels and valves, were all found in a natural condition." In the case communicated by Dr. Percival to the publishers of the *Edinburgh Medical Commentaries*, "the heart and descending aorta <note>original: "aorta descendens"</note> were found in a healthy state." And in Dr. Haygarth’s patient, upon opening the chest <note>original: "thorax"</note>, the lungs, the membrane around the heart <note>original: "pericardium"</note>, and the heart itself appeared perfectly healthy. This is not even mentioning Dr. Fothergill’s patient (R. M.), in whose body the only diseased appearance near the heart was a small white spot near the tip <note>original: "apex"</note>. So, the cause—whatever its nature might have been—was either too far away or of too subtle a nature to be seen by the anatomist. 

However, there was one circumstance in two of the subjects that is worth remembering, which shows that the constitution <term>crasis</term> <note>original: "crasis"; the healthy mixture or temperature of the blood</note> of their blood while they were living must have been greatly damaged: specifically, the blood did not clot <note>original: "coagulating"</note>, but remained at a cream-like consistency, without any separation into the liquid part and the clotted part <term>serum and crassamentum</term>.

From everything published so far, it does not appear that any significant progress has been made toward an actual cure for this unusual spasm. The very sensible and attentive Dr. Heberden (to whom the public is highly indebted for first making this disorder known) confesses that bloodletting, induced vomiting, and other evacuations do not seem to do any good. Wine and cordials taken at bedtime will sometimes prevent or weaken the fits, but nothing does this as effectively as **opiates**. In short, he recommends the medicines usually called "nervous" or "cordial"—those that relieve and quiet convulsive motions and strengthen the fading spark of life. 

Dr. Wall mentions one patient, out of the twelve or thirteen he had seen, who applied to him early in the disease and was considerably relieved by the use of <term>antimonial medicines</term> <note>remedies containing the metal antimony</note> joined with <term>fetid gums</term> <note>strong-smelling resins like asafoetida, used to treat "hysterical" or nervous symptoms</note>. This patient was still living at the time the doctor wrote his paper (November 1772) and was moving about with tolerable ease. Two others were taken by other disorders; all the rest died suddenly. ...to prevent the disorder from gaining ground and to alleviate present distress. Accordingly, he prescribes a diet that is most likely to prevent irritability. These were the only means that occurred to English physicians for opposing this formidable disease.

## NARROWING <note>original: 'STRAITNESS'</note> OF THE ESOPHAGUS.

This condition <note>original: 'distemper'</note> has been described only by Dr. Munckley <note>Dr. Nicholas Munckley (1715–1770), an English physician known for his early observations on esophageal strictures.</note>, who considers it one of the most distressing diseases of the human body. Its beginning is generally so slight that it is scarcely worth noticing; patients perceive only a small obstacle when swallowing solid food. They usually continue in this state for many months. During this time, all liquid foods—and even solids when cut small and swallowed slowly—are consumed without much difficulty. 

By degrees the evil increases, and the passage through the esophagus becomes so narrow that not even the smallest solid can pass through it. Instead, after being held for some time at the part where the obstacle has formed, the food is vomited back up with a very peculiar hollow noise and the appearance of a convulsion. The site of this malady is sometimes near the top of the esophagus, and at other times farther down, nearer the upper opening <note>original: 'superior orifice'</note> of the stomach. 

In this latter case, the part of the digestive tube above the obstruction is frequently so stretched <note>original: 'dilated'</note> by the food trapped within it that it can hold a large quantity. The kind of vomiting by which the food is returned through the mouth comes on sooner or later after the attempt to swallow, depending on how near or remote the affected part is. In the final stage of this disease, not even liquids can be swallowed or pass into the stomach, and the patient literally starves to death. Upon the autopsy <note>original: 'dissection'</note> of those who have died in this manner, the esophagus is found to be considerably thickened. In some, the diseased part is so contracted within that it will scarcely allow a common medical probe to pass; in others, the walls adhere together in such a...

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE MEANS OF PRESERVING HEALTH.

### I. Rules for the Management of those in Weak Health <note>original: "VALETUDINARIANS"</note>.

That part of the medical system which lays down rules for the preservation of health and the prevention of diseases, termed *Hygiene* <note>original: "Hygeine"</note>, is not to be strictly understood as if it applied only to people who enjoy perfect health and have no fear of disease—for such people seldom desire or attend to medical advice. Instead, it should be considered as relating to those in weak health <term>valetudinarians</term>, or to those who, though not actually sick, may have sufficient reason to fear they will soon become so. Therefore, these rules must be applied to correct disease-prone tendencies <term>morbific dispositions</term> and to avoid the various things known to be the underlying or potential causes of diseases. 

From the way the various temperaments <note>The "four temperaments" (Sanguine, Choleric, Melancholic, and Phlegmatic) were a traditional medical theory used to describe a person's physical and mental constitution based on bodily fluids or "humors."</note> are usually mentioned by medical writers, it would seem as if they meant that every individual constitution must belong to one of the four. However, this is far from being practical, since the vast majority of people have constitutions so unclearly defined that it is hard to say to which of the temperaments they belong.

### A KEY TO PHYSIC.

When we actually meet with particular persons who clearly have either: 1. Too much strength and rigidity of the body's fibers, along with too much sensitivity; 2. Too little strength, and yet too much sensitivity; 3. Too much strength, but little sensitivity; or, 4. Little sensitivity joined to weakness—we should view such persons as being more or less in a state of fragile health <term>original: "valetudinary state"</term>. These disease-causing <term>original: "morbific"</term> tendencies must be watched closely, lest these individuals fall into the specific diseases associated with their different temperaments.

People of the first-mentioned temperament are liable to suffer from continuous fevers, especially those of an inflammatory nature. Their plan for preserving health should consist of temperate living regarding both diet and exercise. They should carefully avoid immoderate drinking and be remarkably cautious that none of the body’s natural discharges are blocked. People of this physical habit bear medical "evacuations" well, especially bleeding <note>Bloodletting was a common treatment to reduce "excess" blood in people with strong, inflammatory constitutions.</note>. However, they ought not to lose blood except when it is truly necessary to reduce the total amount; too much of this treatment would likely weaken the constitution until it matches the second-mentioned temperament, where strength is lacking but sensitivity is excessive.

Persons of the second temperament are remarkably prone to suffer from painful and spasmodic diseases and are easily upset. Women with this delicate constitution are very disposed to "hysterical" complaints <note>In the 1700s, "hysterical" referred to a wide range of nervous and physical symptoms thought to be unique to women.</note>. The goal here should be to strengthen the body's tissues <note>original: "solids"</note> through moderate exercise, cold bathing, *Peruvian bark* <note>original: "cinchona bark," used to treat fevers and as a general tonic</note>, and *iron-rich waters* <note>original: "chalybeate-waters"</note>. Constant and particular attention should be paid to the state of the digestive organs to prevent them from being overloaded with any kind of digestive waste <note>original: "saburra"</note> which might produce gas <note>original: "flatus"</note> or irritate the sensitive membranes of the stomach and intestines. Such a disorder would soon spread to the entire nervous system. Persons of this constitution should never take any harsh laxatives <note>original: "drastic purges"</note> or strong medicines that induce vomiting <note>original: "emetics"</note>; nor should they be bled except in cases of urgent necessity. A principal part of managing these extremely irritable constitutions consists of avoiding all sudden changes of any sort—especially regarding diet and clothing—and in keeping the mind as calm as possible. This explains the great benefits such people receive from using medicinal spring waters at their source; they benefit from the freedom from care and serious business that usually defines places designed for the recovery of the sickly.

The third-mentioned temperament, where there is an excess of strength and but little sensitivity, does not seem remarkably prone to any distressing or dangerous type of disease. Therefore, it can hardly be supposed that persons so circumstanced— <note>The text ends mid-word; "circumstanced" implies the person's situation or physical condition.</note>

These arise from a lack of absorbent power in the vessels and from a general sluggishness of the circulation. This is done by reducing food intake, increasing natural discharges, exercising more, and sleeping less.

### II. Rules for those who enjoy perfect Health.

### On CARBON DIOXIDE <note>original: "Fixed Air"</note> as a MEDICINE.

The antiseptic <note>germ-killing or rot-preventing</note> qualities of "fixed air"—or as it is now more generally called, aerial or carbonic acid gas <note>modern: carbon dioxide</note>—have led to its introduction as a medicine for "putrid" (infectious or decaying) disorders and various other ailments. Dr. Percival notes that, although it is fatal if inhaled <note>original: "inspired"</note> in a very large quantity, it can be breathed in smaller amounts without danger or discomfort. This conclusion is confirmed at the town of Bath, where the waters breathe out large amounts of this mineral gas, and the bathers inhale it without harm. At Buxton also, where the bath is located in an enclosed vault, any harmful effects from such vapors <note>original: "effluvia"</note> would certainly be noticed if they were toxic.

Encouraged by these and other considerations, he administered carbon dioxide in more than thirty cases of pulmonary tuberculosis <term>phthisis pulmonalis</term> by directing his patients to inhale the vapors of a bubbling <note>original: "effervescing"</note> mixture of chalk and vinegar through the spout of a coffee pot. In several instances, the persistent fever <term>hectic fever</term> was considerably reduced, and the coughed-up phlegm <note>original: "matter expectorated"</note> became less foul-smelling and more regular in consistency <note>original: "better digested"</note>. However, he was not fortunate enough to achieve a total cure in any single case, even though the use of this gas was combined with appropriate internal medicines. 

But Dr. Withering was more successful. One tuberculosis patient under his care recovered completely through this treatment; another's condition was greatly improved; and a third, whose case was truly desperate, seemed to be kept alive by it for more than two months. It should be noted that carbon dioxide can only be used with any hope of success in the later stages of pulmonary tuberculosis, when the patient is coughing up pus. Furthermore, after the rupture and drainage of a lung abscess <term>vomica</term>, this remedy promises to be a powerful source of relief <note>original: "palliative"</note>. ### ON MEDICAL ELECTRICITY.

The application of this subtle fluid <note>In the 18th century, electricity was thought to be a literal fluid that flowed through bodies.</note> to medicinal purposes was considered soon after the discovery of the electric shock; and, after various shifts in its reputation, its medical virtues now seem to be fairly well established. Mr. Cavallo, who has published the latest and best treatise on Medical Electricity, entirely disapproves of giving violent shocks. He finds it most effective to expose the patient to the *electrical aura*—a gentle stream of air discharged from an iron or wooden point. Or, if shocks are given, they should be very slight, and not exceed twelve or fourteen at a time. In this way, he recommends it as effective in a great number of disorders. The patient may be electrified for three to ten minutes; but, if sparks are drawn, they should not exceed the number of shocks mentioned above.

Rheumatic disorders, even those of long standing, are relieved and sometimes quite cured simply by drawing the electric fluid from the affected part with a wooden point, or by drawing sparks through flannel. The operation should be continued for about four or five minutes, repeating it once or twice every day.

The gout, extraordinary as it may appear, has certainly been cured by means of electricity in various instances. The pain has generally been lessened, and sometimes the disease has been removed so well that it did not return again. In those cases, the electric fluid was directed by means of a wooden point, although sometimes, when the pain was too great, a metal point alone was used.

Deafness—except when it is caused by the physical destruction <note>original: "obliteration"</note> or improper shape of the internal parts—is either entirely or partly cured by drawing sparks from the ear with a glass-tube director, or by drawing the fluid with a wooden point. Sometimes it is appropriate to send exceedingly small shocks (for instance, of one-thirteenth of an inch) from one ear to the other. It has been constantly observed that, whenever the ear is electrified, the discharge of earwax is considerably promoted.

The toothache, caused by cold, rheumatism, or inflammation, is generally relieved by drawing the electric fluid with a point directly from the tooth, and also externally from the face. But when the body of the tooth is affected <note>meaning the internal structure is decayed</note>, electrification is of no use; it seldom or never relieves the disorder, and sometimes increases the pain to a prodigious degree.

Inflammations of every sort are generally relieved by a very gentle electrification <note>original: "electrization"</note>. In inflammations of the eyes, directing the electric fluid <note>In the 18th century, electricity was thought to be a physical fluid that could be directed toward or drawn away from the body.</note> by means of a wooden point is often very beneficial; the pain is quickly reduced, and the inflammation is generally cleared away in a few days. In these cases, the patient's eye must be kept open, and care should be taken not to bring the wooden point too near it to avoid causing a spark. Sometimes it is sufficient to direct the fluid with a metal point, though excessive irritation should always be avoided. It is not necessary to continue this operation for three or four minutes without stopping. Instead, after directing the fluid for about half a minute, the patient should be allowed a short rest to wipe away their tears, which generally flow very heavily. Then, the operation may be continued again for another half-minute, repeating this four or five times every day. 

The condition <term>gutta serena</term> <note>original: "gutta serena"; a historical term for a type of blindness where the eye looks healthy but the patient cannot see, often corresponding to modern amaurosis or optic nerve damage.</note> has sometimes been cured by electrification; but it must be admitted that it has proven ineffective in many such cases, even when administered for a long time and with great care. However, it has never been known to make anyone’s condition worse. The best method for using electricity in such cases is first to draw the electric fluid with a wooden point for a short time, and then to send about half a dozen small shocks—about one-twentieth of an inch long—from the back and lower part of the head to the forehead, just above the eye. 

A remarkable disease of the eye was perfectly cured by electrification some time ago: it was a cloudiness <note>original: "opacity"</note> of the vitreous humor of the eyes. Furthermore, all cases of <term>fistula lacrymalis</term> <note>original: "fistula lacrymalis"; a blockage or infection of the tear duct that causes a persistent, often pussy discharge.</note> that Mr. Cavallo <note>Tiberius Cavallo (1749–1809) was an influential physicist who wrote extensively on the medical uses of electricity.</note> has known to be treated by skilled people for a sufficient time have been entirely cured. The method generally used involves drawing the fluid with a wooden point and taking very small sparks from the affected part. The operation may be continued for about three or four minutes every day. It is remarkable that in those cases, after curing the tear duct blockage, no other disease was caused by stopping the discharge, such as blindness or inflammation.

Paralysis <note>original: "Palsies"</note> is seldom perfectly cured by means of electricity, especially when the condition is long-standing; however, patients are generally relieved to a certain degree. The method of electrifying in these cases is to draw the fluid with a wooden point and to draw sparks through flannel, or through the patient's usual clothing if it is not too thick. The operation may be continued for about five minutes per day.

Ulcers, or open sores of every kind, even chronic ones, are generally inclined to heal through electrification. The general effects are a reduction in inflammation and, at first, an increase in the discharge of healthy pus <note>original: "properly-formed matter"; historical doctors believed "laudable pus" was a sign that a wound was healing correctly.</note>. This discharge gradually decreases as the edges of the sore shrink until it is fully cured. In these cases, the gentlest electrification must be used to avoid excessive irritation, which is generally harmful. To draw or direct the fluid with

Skin rashes <note>original: "cutaneous eruptions"</note> have been successfully treated with electrification. However, in these cases, it must be observed that if the wooden point is kept too near the skin—enough to cause any considerable irritation—the rash will be made to spread further. In this kind of disease, the immediate and general effect of the wooden point is to cause a warmth around the electrified part, which is always a sign that the electrification is being correctly administered.

The application of electricity has perfectly cured various cases of St. Vitus’s dance <note>A historical term for Sydenham’s chorea, a disorder characterized by rapid, uncoordinated jerking movements.</note>, or the disease which is commonly called by that name. It is the opinion of some very learned physicians that the real disease called St. Vitus’s dance, which was more frequent in the past than it is today, is different from the one that now goes by that name. In treating this disease, shocks of about one-tenth of an inch may be sent through the body in various directions, and sparks may also be drawn from the patient. However, if this treatment proves very disagreeable to the patient, then the shocks must be reduced or even omitted; instead, other more gentle applications must be substituted.

Scrofulous tumors <note>original: "Scrophulous"; referring to scrofula, a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck.</note>, when they are just beginning, are generally cured by drawing the electric fluid from the part with a wooden or metal point. This is one of those diseases in which the action of electricity particularly requires the aid of other medicines to effect a cure more easily. This is because scrofulous conditions commonly accompany a very weak constitution <note>original: "laxity of the habit"</note> and a general cachexia <note>original: "cachexy"; a state of physical wasting and malnutrition associated with chronic disease.</note>, which must be countered by proper remedies.

It is remarkable that this patient was so relieved by drawing the fluid from the area with a metal point that the excruciating pains she had suffered for many years almost entirely disappeared. However, when the electric fluid was drawn using a wooden point, the pains actually increased.

Abscesses, when they are just beginning—and in general whenever there is any tendency for pus to form—are dispersed by electrification. The application of electricity has often been found beneficial for dropsy <note>A historical term for edema, or swelling caused by excess fluid in body tissues.</note> when it is just beginning, or rather in the tendency toward dropsy; however, it has never been of any use in advanced cases. Swellings in general that do not contain any pus <note>original: "matter"</note> are frequently cured by drawing out the electric fluid with a wooden point. The operation should be continued for three or four minutes every day. It is very remarkable that in some cases of "white swellings" <note>A historical term for chronic, pale swellings of the joints, often associated with tuberculosis of the bone or joint.</note> completely cured by means of electricity, the bones and cartilages remained somewhat disfigured.

The most effective and certain method has been drawing sparks through flannel or clothing for about ten minutes or a quarter of an hour. The patients may be electrified either during the time of the fever fit or shortly before the time it is expected to begin.

...readily cured by means of electricity, even when the disease is of long standing, and after the most powerful medicines used for it have proved ineffectual. The cases of this sort in which electrification <note>original: "electrization"</note> has proved useless are so few, and the successful ones so numerous, that the application of electricity for this disease may be justly considered as an efficacious and certain remedy. 

Great care and knowledge are required in order to distinguish the arrest of menstruation <note>original: "menses"</note> from a state of pregnancy. In the former, the application of electricity, as we observed above, is very beneficial; whereas, in the latter, it may be attended with very disagreeable effects. It is therefore a matter of great importance to ascertain the real cause of the condition before electricity is applied in these cases. Pregnant women may be electrified for other diseases, but always by using very gentle means and directing the electric fluid through parts of the body distant from those used for reproduction <note>original: "subservient to generation"</note>. 

In the actual suppression of menstruation, small shocks—about one-twentieth of an inch in length—may be sent through the pelvis. Sparks may be taken through the clothes from the areas adjacent to the seat of the disease. Additionally, the electric fluid may be transmitted by applying the metallic or wooden ends of two directors <note>Handheld tools used to guide the electric current to specific parts of the body.</note> to the hips, in contact with the clothes; some of the clothing may be removed if it is too thick. These various applications of electricity should be regulated according to the constitution of the patient. The number of shocks may be about twelve or fourteen. The other applications may be continued for two or three minutes, repeating the operation every day. However, both strong shocks and any application of electricity stronger than the patient can comfortably bear should be avoided; for these means sometimes cause a discharge greater than intended, which is not easily cured. In cases of uterine hemorrhages, there is no evidence that the application of electricity was ever beneficial. Perhaps a very gentle electrification, such as keeping the patient insulated and connected with the prime conductor <note>The main component of an electrical machine that collects and holds the electric charge.</note> while the machine is in action, may be of some benefit.

In respect to unnatural discharges and fluxes in general, it may be observed that some discharges are quite unnatural or external in origin, such as the lacrimal fistula <note>original: "fistula lacrymalis"; an abnormal opening or tear in the skin near the eye caused by a blocked tear duct.</note> and some types of venereal disease. Others are only increased versions of natural discharges, such as menstruation <note>original: "menses"</note>, perspiration, and so on. Now, the power of electricity in general has been found more beneficial for the first type than for the second type of discharges, which are mostly increased by it.

In venereal disease <note>A historical term for sexually transmitted infections, primarily syphilis and gonorrhea.</note>, electrification has generally been forbidden, as it has commonly increased the pains and other symptoms rather than diminishing them. Indeed, considering that any sort of stimulus has been found hurtful to persons afflicted with that disorder, it is no wonder that electricity has produced some bad effects, especially in the manner it was administered some time ago—namely, by giving strong shocks.

...only can direct), and watch it very carefully until I discover the saline particles beginning to gather and look white, or of some other color, at the extremities of the edges. Then—having adjusted the microscope beforehand for its reception, equipped with the fourth lens <note>original: "glass"</note>, which is the most suitable <note>original: "fittest"</note> for most of those experiments—I place it under my eye and bring it exactly to the focus of the magnifier. After running over the whole drop, I fix my attention on that side where I observe any increase or pushing forward of crystalline matter from the circumference towards the center. 

This motion is extremely slow at the beginning, unless the drop has been overheated, but quickens as the water evaporates. In many kinds, towards the conclusion, it produces configurations with an inconceivable swiftness. These are composed of an infinity of parts which are adjusted to each other with an elegance, regularity, and order beyond what the most exact pencil in the world, guided by a ruler and compasses, could ever equal, or even the most luxuriant imagination could fancy. 

When this action once begins, the eye cannot be taken off, even for a moment, without losing something worth observation; for the figures alter every instant until the whole process is over. In many sorts, after all seems at an end, new forms arise that are entirely different from any other kind; these separate from the first and continue to act after the first has finished. In some subjects, three or four different sorts are observable, with few or none of them being simple and homogeneous <term>homogeneous: consisting of parts all of the same kind</term>. 

When the configurations are fully formed and all the water has evaporated, most kinds of them are soon destroyed again by moisture or the action of the air upon them; their points and angles lose their sharpness, become uneven and defaced, and moulder away, as it were. However, a few are permanent, and, being enclosed between glasses, may be preserved for many months or even years as entertaining objects for the microscope. 

It often happens that a drop of saline solution can hardly be spread on the slip of glass because of the glass's smoothness; it instead breaks into little globules, as it would do if the surface were greasy. This was very troublesome until I found a way of preventing it by rubbing the broken drop with my finger over the glass so as to leave the surface smeared with it. On this smeared place, when dry, another drop of the solution may be spread very easily in whatever form one pleases. 

It also sometimes happens that when a heated drop is placed properly for examination, the observer finds he can distinguish nothing. This is due to saline steams that, rising from the drop, cover and obscure the objective lens <note>original: "object-glass"</note>; therefore, it must immediately be wiped away with a soft cloth or leather. In all examinations of saline solutions by the microscope, even those made in the daytime, I always employ the light of a candle and advise every observer to do the same. Because the configurations are exceedingly transparent, they are rendered much more distinguishable...

**Figure 1** shows the microscopic crystals of nitre <note>original: "nitre"; an archaic term for potassium nitrate, commonly known as saltpeter.</note> or saltpeter. Throughout the process, there seems to be a violent agitation in the fluid, and most commonly, toward the end, a few octahedrons (composed of eight triangular planes, or two four-sided pyramids joined base to base) appear.

This salt grows slowly and therefore requires patience. At last, the true crystals usually begin to appear in the middle of the drop, forming beautiful branches.

### 4. Alum

The microscopic crystals of this salt <note>original: "Alum"; a chemical compound, specifically potassium aluminum sulfate, used historically in medicine, dyeing, and tanning.</note> appear more or less perfect depending on the strength of the solution and the amount of heat used in the experiment. A solution of alum, no matter how saturated with the salt, will not be found very strong after sitting for some days, because in that time many crystals will have already formed in it. This separation often leaves the remaining liquid too weak for the experiment; however, by holding the small glass bottle over or near a fire, the crystals will dissolve again. After it has stood for about half an hour, it may then be used. 

When a drop is put on the glass and properly heated, it usually shows a dark cloud at first, which appears to move near the edge. This cloud runs quite swiftly to both the right and left until it is either stopped by the obstruction of regular crystals or else proceeds both ways at once until it has surrounded the whole drop. Then, the two ends rush together and join into one (a, a). This cloudy part, which seems to be violently moving while it runs around the edge, appears on close examination to consist of salts forming long and very slender lines. These lines are much finer than the smallest hair and cross each other at right angles. As they move along, rows of solid crystals are produced from their inner edges. These are composed of many slanted, flat sides (b, b), all of which tend toward the shapes of the regular crystals to be described—

Before the center of the drop begins to shoot, several exceedingly minute bodies may be discernible at the bottom of the fluid. These rise to the top after a little while and soon take on a distinct shape, as seen at (5). Their growth is very quick and, for some time, fairly equal. The other branches enlarge very little after this, as all the attraction seems to be concentrated in the one that first began to lengthen. As more branches are pushed out from this one, and they in turn push out others, the whole appears as seen at (8). It is not uncommon to see some crystals in the middle of the drop where, instead of the straight stems described above, a kind of zig-zag is formed with spicules like those in the other figures (7).

7. **Salt of lead**, or *sugar of lead* <note>original: "saccharum saturni"; an archaic name for lead(II) acetate, a sweet-tasting but highly toxic chemical once used in various industrial and medicinal applications.</note>. A little of this salt dissolved in hot water immediately makes it look milky. After letting it stand for fifteen minutes to settle, it is ready to be examined under a microscope. If a drop of it is then placed on a glass slide and held over a fire to excite the particles, a fairly even and regular border of a clear, transparent film or gluey substance (*aaaa*) will be seen forming around the edge. If the heat is too sudden or intense, this film runs over the entire surface of the drop and hardens on the glass so firmly that it is very difficult to remove. However, if moderate warmth is used—and not for too long—this border only moves a little way into the drop. It forms a kind of radiating pattern (*bbbb*) made of fine lines, or rather bundles of lines, starting from the center toward the inner edge of the border and spreading out at nearly equal distances in every direction toward the outside. Afterward, a radiation toward the inside is produced from the same centers. This is composed of parallelograms <note>original: "parallelograms"; four-sided shapes with opposite sides parallel.</note> of different lengths and widths. From one, and sometimes both, of their angles, very slender shoots are often seen; these are perhaps the best possible representations of a mathematical line <note>In historical geometry, a "mathematical line" was defined as having length but no thickness; the author is marveling at how thin these crystals appear.</note>. The ends of the parallelograms are usually cut off at right angles, but they are sometimes seen at an oblique angle (*cccc*). Centers with similar radiating lines—and some of the gluey matter as their base—are sometimes formed in the drop entirely separate from the edges. In these, it is very common to find secondary lines branching off from the primary ones, and others from those through many stages, creating a very beautiful figure (D).

16. **Salt of hartshorn** <note>original: "Salt of hartshorn"; an aqueous solution of ammonia, historically derived from the horns of deer (harts).</note>. These have a dividing line running through their whole length from end to end, from which other short lines emerge at small intervals, opposite one another; all of these point with the same degree of slant <note>original: "obliquity"</note> toward the base (*cc*). Among these enlarged figures, a few continue to sprout forward, tapering toward a point; however, before they form a point, they swell again and begin, as it were, afresh. ### Of ANIMAL MAGNETISM.

ANIMAL MAGNETISM is a sympathetic connection <note>original: "sympathy"</note> that exists between a magnet and the "insensible perspiration" (the invisible vapors or sweat) of the human body. Through this connection, an ether <term>ether: a hypothetical, weightless fluid once believed to fill all space and transmit forces like light and heat</term>—or a universal flow of particles <note>original: "effluvia"</note>—is made to pass back and forth through the pores of the skin <note>original: "cuticle"</note> in the same way that electrical fluid passes through objects. It is by this process that many medical cures are performed.

The system began in 1774 with a German philosopher named Father Hehl, who strongly recommended the use of magnets in medicine. Franz Mesmer, a physician from the same country, became the primary founder of the system by adopting Hehl’s principles. Mesmer had already made a name for himself with a *Dissertation on the Influence of the Stars upon the Human Body*, which he publicly defended as a thesis at the University of Vienna. He later toured Germany, advertising everywhere the great cures he performed through animal magnetism, and arrived in Paris at the beginning of 1778.

In Paris, he was first supported by the author of the *Dictionary of the Wonders of Nature* <note>original: "Dictionnaire des Merveilles de la Nature"</note>. A large number of Mesmer's cures were published in that work, and Mesmer himself received high praise for his honesty and logical reasoning. The physician soon gathered a following of patients. In April 1778, he retreated to Creteil <note>a village near Paris</note>, returning a short time later with his patients perfectly cured. 

His success was now so great, and the number of patients increased so rapidly, that the doctor was soon forced to take on students to help with his treatments. These students were just as successful as Mesmer himself. Their profits were so immense that one of them, a man named M. Deslon, earned more than £100,000 <note>an enormous fortune in the late 1700s</note>. In 1779, Mesmer published a me-

<keywords>Camphor, Manna, microscopy, Animal Magnetism, Franz Mesmer, Father Hehl, M. Deslon, Paris, medical history, ether</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the study of Animal Magnetism, following the previous page's initial definition of the "universal flow of particles." It begins in the middle of a sentence discussing Franz Mesmer's early publications.</meta>

[me]moir on the subject of Animal Magnetism, promising afterwards a complete work upon the same, which should make as great a revolution in philosophy as it had already done in medicine.

The new system gained ground daily; and soon became so fashionable, that the jealousy of the medical faculty <note>original: "the faculty"; referring to the established medical profession</note> was thoroughly awakened, and a formal request concerning it was made to the French government. In consequence of this, a committee was appointed to inquire into the matter, consisting partly of physicians and partly of members of the Royal Academy of Sciences, with Dr. Benjamin Franklin at their head. Mesmer himself refused to have any communication with the committee: but his most celebrated pupil, Deslon, was less scrupulous, and explained the principles of his art in the following manner:

1. Animal magnetism is a universal fluid, constituting an absolute plenum <term>plenum: a space entirely filled with matter, as opposed to a vacuum</term> in nature, and is the medium of all mutual influence between the celestial bodies <note>original: "celestial bodies"; stars and planets</note> and between the earth and animal bodies.

2. It is the most subtle <note>original: "subtile"</note> fluid in nature; capable of a flow and ebb <note>original: "flux and reflux"</note>, and of receiving, propagating, and continuing all kinds of motion.

3. The animal body is subjected to the influences of this fluid by means of the nerves, which are immediately affected by it.

4. The human body has poles and other properties analogous to the magnet.

5. The action and power <note>original: "virtue"</note> of animal magnetism may be communicated from one body to another, whether animate or inanimate.

6. It operates at a great distance without the intervention of any other body.

7. It is increased and reflected by mirrors; communicated, propagated, and increased by sound; and may be accumulated, concentrated, and transported.

8. Notwithstanding the universality of this fluid, all animal bodies are not equally affected by it; on the other hand, there are some, though but few in number, whose very presence destroys all the effects of animal magnetism.

9. By means of this fluid, nervous disorders are cured immediately, and others indirectly <note>original: "mediately"</note>; and its powers, in short, extend to the universal cure and preservation of mankind.

From this theory, Monsieur Deslon engaged: 1. To prove to the commissioners that such a thing as animal magnetism existed; 2. To prove its utility in the cure of diseases; and to communicate to them all that he knew upon the subject. The commissioners accordingly attended the room where the patients underwent the magnetical operations. The apparatus consisted of a circular platform made of oak, raised about a foot and a half from the ground. At the top of it were a number of holes, in which were iron rods with movable joints for the purpose of applying them to any part of the body. The patients were placed in a circle around it, each touching an iron rod, which he could apply to any part of his body at pleasure; they were joined to one another by a cord passing round their bodies, the design being to increase the effect through communication. ### Of ANIMAL MAGNETISM.

ANIMAL MAGNETISM <note>Now known as Mesmerism, this was a late 18th-century theory that suggested an invisible natural force possessed by all living things could be used to heal</note> is a sympathy which exists between the magnet and the insensible perspiration of the human body. Through this connection, an ether, or universal effluvia <note>original: "effluvia"; an invisible discharge of particles or vapors</note>, is made to pass and repass through the pores of the skin <note>original: "cuticle"</note> in the same manner as electrical fluid passes through bodies, and by which many cures are performed.

The system originated in 1774 from a German philosopher named Father Hehl, who strongly recommended the use of the magnet in medicine. Mr. Mesmer, a physician of the same country, became the direct founder of the system by adopting Hehl’s principles. He had already distinguished himself by a *Dissertation on the Influence of the Stars upon the Human Body*, which he publicly defended in a thesis before the University of Vienna. He afterwards made a tour through Germany, publishing everywhere the great cures he performed by means of animal magnetism, and arrived at Paris in the beginning of the year 1778. 

Here he was first patronized by the author of the *Dictionary of the Wonders of Nature* <note>original: "Dictionnaire des Merveilles de la Nature"</note>, in which work a great number of his cures were published; Mesmer himself also received ample testimony regarding his candor and solid reasoning. Our physician soon collected some patients, and in the month of April 1778, he retired to Créteil, from which he returned in a short time with them perfectly cured. His success was now great, and patients increased so rapidly that the doctor was soon obliged to take in pupils to assist him in his operations. These pupils succeeded just as well as Mesmer himself, and so great was their profit <note>original: "emolument"</note> that one of them, named Mr. Deslon, earned upwards of £100,000 sterling <note>An enormous fortune in the 1700s, equivalent to millions of dollars today</note>. In 1779 Mesmer published a memoir on the subject...

memoir <note>original: "moir"; the first syllable was on the previous page</note> on the subject of Animal Magnetism, promising a complete work on the same later, which he claimed would create as great a revolution in philosophy as it had already done in medicine.

The new system gained ground daily and soon became so fashionable that the jealousy of the medical faculty was thoroughly awakened, and an application concerning it was made to the French government. Consequently, a committee was appointed to inquire into the matter, consisting partly of physicians and partly of members of the Royal Academy of Sciences, with Dr. Benjamin Franklin at their head. Mesmer himself refused to have any communication with the committee; but his most celebrated pupil, Deslon, was less hesitant <note>original: "scrupulous"</note> and explained the principles of his art in the following manner:

1. Animal magnetism is a universal fluid, constituting an absolute plenum <note>original: "plenum"; a space completely filled with matter, as opposed to a vacuum</note> in nature, and is the medium of all mutual influence between the celestial bodies and between the earth and animal bodies.
2. It is the most subtle fluid in nature; capable of a flux and reflux <note>original: "flux and reflux"; a flowing and ebbing, like the tide</note>, and of receiving, spreading, and continuing all kinds of motion.
3. The animal body is subjected to the influences of this fluid by means of the nerves, which are immediately affected by it.
4. The human body has poles and other properties analogous to the magnet.
5. The action and power <note>original: "virtue"</note> of animal magnetism may be communicated from one body to another, whether animate or inanimate.
6. It operates at a great distance without the intervention of any other body.
7. It is increased and reflected by mirrors; communicated, spread, and increased by sound; and may be accumulated, concentrated, and transported.
8. Notwithstanding the universality of this fluid, all animal bodies are not equally affected by it; on the other hand, there are some—though but few in number—whose presence destroys all the effects of animal magnetism.
9. By means of this fluid, nervous disorders are cured immediately and others indirectly <note>original: "mediately"</note>; its benefits, in short, extend to the universal cure and preservation of mankind.

From this theory, Mr. Deslon pledged: 1. To prove to the commissioners that such a thing as animal magnetism existed; 2. To prove its utility in the cure of diseases; and to communicate to them all that he knew upon the subject. The commissioners accordingly attended the room where the patients underwent the magnetic operations. The apparatus consisted of a circular platform made of oak, raised about a foot and a half from the ground. At the top of it were a number of holes containing iron rods with movable joints for the purpose of applying them to any part of the body. The patients were placed in a circle around it, each touching an iron rod which he could apply to any part of the body at will; they were joined to one another by a cord passing around their bodies, the design being to increase the effect by communication. “**On Crises.** A crisis is an effort of nature against a disorder, attempting to clear away the obstacles in the circulation and restore harmony or balance to all parts of the body. Few diseases can be cured without a crisis, especially those caused by obstructions and similar issues. There are two types of crises. The natural one, attributed to nature alone, gets rid of whatever is harming her through increased movement, resulting in vomiting, bowel movements <note>original: "motion"</note>, perspiration, and so on. These are the most beneficial <note>original: "salutary"</note>, as nature acts quietly and without violence. She expels the obstacles that block circulation by gently moving the molecules that form those blockages until they are released through perspiration and other means. 

The forced crisis is sometimes beneficial for obstructions, or for gas <note>original: "windy"</note> and digestive <note>original: "bilious"</note> complaints. These occur when nature is unable to expel what is harming her on her own. The use of Animal Electricity and Magnetism <note>Mesmerism</note> activates the whole body. To affect a person standing behind you, face a mirror and magnetize their reflection using a conductor. The reflection <note>original: "re-action"</note> of the fluid will produce a crisis.

# **OF SOMNAMBULISM.**

Somnambulism <note>sleepwalking or a trance state</note> is a state between sleeping and waking, sharing characteristics of both; the patient is a somnambulist when he can do the same things as if he were awake. These natural somnambulists, who get up at night and do many wonderful things, are well-documented <note>original: "demonstrated"</note>. They are diseased and may be cured by treatment. Magnetic somnambulists are those for whom art has found a means of absorbing or suspending some of their external senses for a while. The patient eats and drinks, goes up and down, plays the harpsichord, and does many things you desire of him, provided he is willing. The first I saw was at the Marquis de Puységur’s <note>Armand-Marie-Jacques de Chastenet, Marquis de Puységur (1751–1825), a student of Mesmer who discovered "artificial somnambulism," or the mesmeric trance</note> in the year 1784; all those who had claimed to do it in this country before were impostors. For all this, we are indebted to Dr. Mesmer <note>Franz Mesmer (1734–1815), the German physician who theorized "animal magnetism"</note>.

Whenever any person has a real somnambulist—which is very easy to achieve with care—they possess a treasure. We call them *malades médecins* <note>French: sick physicians</note>. These beings see in the dark and move through an external atmosphere, just like a glow-worm; they also have an internal atmosphere, which they use to perceive objects, whether present or distant, visible or invisible. I have had several who described to me what they could perceive. They differ in many respects according to their constitution. One must not always depend upon what they say, as they sometimes vary. You may make them move in any direction by your will alone; or, by moving your conductor <note>a metallic rod or wand used to direct "magnetic fluid"</note> any way upon the floor, they will follow its directions. You may make them play any instrument they know how to play; they will read, write, and work; they will do all this better than if they were awake. Being deprived of their other faculties, these specific ones become stronger. No physician can diagnose the disease of a person better than a real somnambulist. They seldom fail to identify the diseases of unknown persons and prescribe for them. In the future, when the science is better established, I shall publish a full account of the theory of somnambulism.

Some will accuse me of saying too much; but those who know me personally will never accuse me of relating anything that I cannot demonstrate. Those who repeat these marvelous stories harm themselves and the science in the eyes of truly learned men. These stories, like traditions handed down from generation to generation that become improbable over time, lose their former luster. I would advise my pupils to try those experiments I have shown them first, and try the others afterward.

**ON SLEEPWALKING.** <note>original: SOMNAMBULISM. In the context of Mesmerism, this refers to a trance state induced by "animal magnetism" rather than ordinary sleepwalking.</note> Sleepwalking is a state between sleeping and waking, sharing qualities of both; a patient is a sleepwalker <note>original: somnambule</note> when he can perform the same actions as if he were awake. These natural sleepwalkers, who get up at night and do many wonderful things, are well-documented. They are suffering from a condition and may be cured by treatment. 

The "magnetic sleepwalkers" are those for whom science <note>original: art</note> has found a means of absorbing or suspending some of their external senses for a time; the patient then eats and drinks, moves about, plays the harpsichord, and does many things you request of him, provided he is willing. The first case I saw was at the Marquis de Puységur’s in the year 1784; all those who had claimed to do this in this country before then were impostors. For all this knowledge, we are indebted to Dr. Mesmer <note>Franz Mesmer (1734–1815), the doctor who proposed the theory of "animal magnetism," later called Mesmerism.</note>. Whenever someone has a real sleepwalker—which is very easy to achieve with care—they possess a treasure. We call them **sick physicians** <note>original: malades medecins; patients who, while in a trance, were believed to be able to diagnose their own and others' illnesses.</note>. These beings see in the dark and move through an external atmosphere, just like a glow-worm; they have, besides, an internal atmosphere which they use to perceive objects, whether present or distant, visible or invisible. 

I have had several patients who described to me what they could perceive. They differ in many respects according to their physical constitution. One must not always depend on what they say, as they vary sometimes. You may make them move in any direction by your will alone; or, by moving your conductor <note>A metal rod or "wand" used to direct the supposed magnetic fluid.</note> any way upon the floor, they will follow its directions. You may make them play on any instrument they know; they will read, write, and work. They will do all of this better than if they were awake. Being deprived of their other faculties, these specific abilities become stronger. No doctor can diagnose a person's disease better than a real sleepwalker. They seldom fail to tell unknown persons their diseases and prescribe for them. In the future, when the science is better established, I shall publish a full account of the theory of sleepwalking.

Some will accuse me of having said too much; but those who know me personally will never accuse me of reporting anything which I cannot prove. Those who repeat these marvelous stories without evidence only hurt themselves and the reputation of the science in the eyes of truly learned men. Those stories—like legends handed down from generation to generation that become improbable over time—lose their former brilliance. I would advise my pupils to try those experiments I have shown them first, and try the others afterward.

### Arguments to Prove that Animal Magnetism is the Cause of Sympathy in Humans, other Animals, Plants, and so on.

The constant flow and return <note>original: flux and reflux</note> of the vital principles and bodily fluids <note>original: corporeal humours</note> in humans—without which both motion and life are stopped—produce those effects of sympathy and antipathy which are actually natural rather than miraculous. The atmospheric particles surrounding each individual receive the proper attraction and repulsion from the universal fluid. In the various crossings of these individual atmospheres, some emanations between two beings are more attractive, while others are more repulsive. Likewise, when one body possesses more fluid than another, it will repel; the body with less will make an effort to restore itself into equilibrium or sympathy with the other body. Robin Abraham Benhannes <note>Likely a reference to a contemporary or historical authority cited in Mesmeric or occult texts</note> says that iron or ferruginous particles are everywhere—not only in the mineral world, but in our blood and bones;

Just as a magnet attracts iron particles, everything is naturally subject to magnetism through the power of attraction or sympathy.

I could provide many examples to prove the sympathetic affection that exists between people of the same family, beliefs, or social groups, or anything else that binds them harmoniously together. However, since everyone has experienced this, I will say no more about it.

The "magnetic fluid" often causes contractions in other parts of the body when a muscle is wounded, which in turn produces various movements in other organs. Whether these parts have a secret connection <note>original: affinity</note> or not is still debated, but I believe they do. These movements have surprised many doctors who have studied this field, especially Barthez <note>Paul Joseph Barthez (1734–1806), a famous French physician who founded the Vitalist school of medicine.</note>, who explained them as a subtle motion he called the *vital fluid*. He might just as well have called it "animal electricity" or "magnetism."

### On ANTIPATHY.

We do not all resemble the Trojan shepherd <note>Paris, the prince of Troy in Greek mythology, who was tasked with judging which goddess—Hera, Athena, or Aphrodite—was the most beautiful by awarding her a golden apple.</note> who awarded the apple to the most beautiful. It is not always the most handsome woman who wins our love; our internal emotions are involuntary reactions that happen regardless of beauty and are the precursors to love. Similarly, when two personal atmospheres are in balance—meaning their physical emissions <note>original: corpuscular emanations</note> are compatible with each other—it produces sympathy or attraction. But when these atmospheres conflict, it produces antipathy or repulsion.

Differences in temperament, religious arguments, and politics often cause deep-seated hatred. How else can we explain the sudden dislike we feel for certain things or people, if not through the unpleasant impressions sent to our nerves, and then to our brains, by the energy <note>original: emission</note> coming from those people or objects? This can only be called antipathy.

Through antipathy, many people can detect the illnesses of others; they feel the same pain within themselves, often on the opposite side of their own body. If I place a sick person in contact with someone in a state of mesmeric trance <note>original: somnambulism; in the context of animal magnetism, this refers to a deep, sleep-like state where the patient was thought to possess heightened perception.</note>, the person in the trance instantly feels the same pain—though only as long as they are touching. This might be called "sympathy," but because they are suffering to some degree during that time, it is more accurately called antipathy. It is well known that many people have a natural aversion to various animals, and so on.

Animals are affected in different ways according to their species by corpuscular emissions <note>original: corpuscular emissions; in 18th-century science, these were thought to be tiny particles or "effluvia" released by bodies that could influence others at a distance.</note>, but these effects are nearly identical when they flow from members of the same species. Like the phoenix, nature only dies to be reborn and returns brighter from its own ashes. 

Without believing (as the ancients did) that a musical string made from a wolf's intestines and another from a sheep's cannot harmonize, or that if two drums were made from their skins, the sound of the wolf-skin drum would silence the other, it is clear that antipathy between certain species is an instinctive tool given to them to find prey or avoid enemies.
