### Of ATTRACTION and REPULSION, otherwise called SYMPATHY and ANTIPATHY, in PLANTS.

Plants, like humans, have their own processes of transpiration and emission produced by the pressure of a magnetic fluid that penetrates them. They carry this life-giving <note>original: "vivifying"</note> fluid in all their fibers and also have their own private spheres of attraction and repulsion. This explains the inclination some vegetables seem to have to grow closer to each other, to flourish, and to die together; conversely, it explains the hatred observed between others and the efforts they seemingly make to repel each other.

The vine seems to thrive near the elm, the olive tree with the aloe tree, the plane tree <note>original: "plantain"; in this context, likely the oriental plane tree rather than the common weed or the fruit.</note> with the fig tree, the agaric <note>A type of fungus or mushroom.</note> with the cedar <note>original: "cedrus"</note>, asparagus with pennyroyal, and the cocoa tree grows vigorously under the shade of the ebony tree. Resinous trees are favorable to the *semla* <note>original: "semla"; an obscure reference, possibly referring to a starch-bearing plant or a transcription error for a specific balsam.</note>, and the cotyledon <note>A genus of succulent plants.</note> and the fir tree are favorable to different species of wolfsbane <note>original: "aconitum"</note> and nightshade <note>original: "solanum"</note>. By a similar sympathy, the poppy beautifies the harvest, the water-lily likes the crowfoot <note>original: "ranunculus"</note>, and rue likes the water-lily. The lily grows beautifully near the rose and near garlic, where it appears more brilliant and smells more fragrant, even though the smell of the garlic is so offensive. However, the rose is unfavorable to onions, basil <note>original: "basilicum"</note> withers near rice, and cabbages die away near the sowbread <note>original: "cyclamen"</note> and wild marjoram <note>original: "origanum"</note>. The oak does not like the olive, vines dislike laurel and hemlock, and hemlock dies away near vines. ### Concerning Indisposition and Disease.

It has been observed that human life is a measure of universal motion. In its origin, this motion becomes <term>tonical</term> <note>original: "tonical"; referring to "tone," the healthy state of tension and vigor in the body's tissues</note> when applied to matter, which is destined to form the organs and <term>viscera</term> <note>viscera: the internal organs of the body, especially those in the abdomen and chest</note>, and afterward to maintain and regulate their functions. Human life begins in motion and ends in rest. The complete ending of this tonic motion is death. Just as in all of nature motion is the source of every combination—while rest is the source of matter—so, in humans, the principle of life becomes the cause of death.

Every unfolding and formation of an organized body depends on the various and successive relationships between motion and rest. Once their balance is determined, the number of possible relationships between the one and the other must also be fixed. The distance between two set points may be considered as representing the duration of life; one of these points is motion, and the other is rest. The continuous progression of the various proportions between the two constitutes the progress and revolution of life. Proceeding thus from motion toward rest, we arrive at the point of their equilibrium; after that point, we begin to die by degrees.

That progression of various modifications between motion and rest may have an exact proportion, or that proportion may be disturbed. If a person runs through that progression without the proportion being disturbed, they live in a state of good health and arrive at their end without illness. On the contrary, as soon as the proportions are troubled, disease begins. Illness is nothing more than a disturbance in the progression of motion and life, which may be considered as existing either in the solid parts of the body or in the fluids. If it exists in the solids, it disturbs the harmony of the properties of the organic bodies by diminishing one and increasing the other. If it exists in the fluids, it disturbs their local and internal motion.

A deviation from motion in the solids, by altering their properties, disturbs the functions of the internal organs and the various processes that ought to take place. A deviation from the internal motions of the <term>humours</term> <note>humours: according to older medical theories, the four primary fluids of the body (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) that determined health and temperament</note> causes them to degenerate. A deviation from local motions produces obstruction or weakness, fever or irritation.

The slowing or stopping of motion produces obstructions or weakness; the acceleration of motion produces fever or irritability. The perfection of the solids or organs consists in the harmony of all their properties and functions. The result of these organic functions is the quality of the fluids, along with their internal and local motion. To be able to restore the general harmony of the body, we must restore the functions of the organs; because, once their functions are re-established, they correct everything that can be fixed and separate everything that cannot be restored.

# A KEY TO MEDICINE,

The effort that nature or the **viscera** <term>viscera: the internal organs of the body, such as the heart, lungs, and intestines</term> exert upon the **humors** <term>humors: according to ancient and early modern medicine, the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determined health and temperament</term> is called a *crisis* or *paroxysm*. No disease can be cured without such a crisis. In every crisis, we distinguish three states: agitation, processing (digestion), and removal (evacuation). Since disease is a departure from harmony, that deviation or tendency may be more or less significant and produce various noticeable effects, which are called *symptoms*. If those effects are produced by the natural course of the disease, they are called *symptomatic sensations*; if, on the contrary, they are the result of nature’s efforts to fight the cause of illness, they are called *critical symptoms*. It is of the greatest importance to distinguish between them in medical practice, so that a doctor can prevent and stop the former while encouraging the latter.

It follows from what has been said that all causes of disease disturb and alter, to some degree, the balance between matter and motion, the proportion of the internal organs, and the balance between fluids and solids. Consequently, through their various applications, they produce a weakening or a disturbance in the properties of matter. To remedy the effects of this weakening and disturbance, and to destroy or stop them, the restoration of these properties must be provoked. This means that in animal bodies, "irritability" or <term>animal electricity</term> <note>animal electricity: a historical concept, often associated with Luigi Galvani, suggesting that a form of electricity was the vital force of life within tissues</note> must be increased through different stimuli. There are two methods of doing this: 
1. To lessen the obstacles preventing health.
2. To increase the restorative action of nature through a constant, subtle, gentle, and harmonious application of magnetic currents.

A body that is in harmony is hardly sensitive to the effects of animal electricity and magnetism. This is because applying a uniform and general action cannot alter proportions that are already exact and in balance with that harmony. If, on the contrary, a body is not in harmony—that is to say, if its proportions are disturbed—the habit of experiencing that "dissonance" (disharmony) prevents it from being as sensitive. It only becomes sensitive through the application of animal electricity and magnetism because that treatment highlights the underlying state of disharmony. Based on these principles, it is easy to understand why sick people, as they draw near to recovery, gradually become insensitive to animal electricity and magnetism. A complete lack of sensitivity to its power signifies a perfect cure.

It follows from these same principles that the application of animal electricity and magnetism must often increase pain at first. This happens because its action causes the *symptomatic sensations* to diminish or cease; meanwhile, as nature’s efforts against the causes of disease are increased, it is absolutely necessary for the *critical symptoms* to increase in the same proportion.

By carefully observing these various effects, we are able to perfectly distinguish the symptoms. The unfolding of these symptoms occurs in the reverse order of how the disease was first formed. It may be compared to a ball of twine, which must be unwound in the exact opposite order in which it was originally wound up.

It was not my intention to discuss this treatise at such great length in my current work. Yet, our understanding may, to some extent, unravel the mysteries of nature through logical inquiry and speculation. These insights captivate our senses, increase our admiration, and awaken in us a reverent awe of the future and a grateful awareness of the goodness and mercy of Him who gave us life.

For this blessing and this command occurred *before* the formation of Eve, as anyone who reads the Scriptures must know.

In this dual capacity, therefore, Adam received the blessing of God when He said to him,
> "Be fruitful and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowls of the air," etc.

The six days of creation were now completed, and on the seventh day God rested from all His work. Having formed Adam and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, he became a *living soul*. ## AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES.

To this era <note>original: "æra"</note>, which gave birth to our many misfortunes, we must look for 그 source of relief <note>original: "alleviation"</note> and cure which the forgiving hand of Providence has graciously provided for those who will seek them; *for out of the ground the Lord has caused medicine to grow; and he who is wise will not despise them; for with such he heals men and takes away their pains.* <note>Ecclesiasticus 38:4, 7</note>

Since man became subject to the natural elements by his fall, he receives the makeup of his body from them. We owe the disorders of the body to the violence and impurity of the elements; we rightly blame the diseases of the soul on the temptations and charms of the devil. Meanwhile, through the powers of the mind and the light of the gospel, we may still avoid the poison of sin and become members of that eternal kingdom, which is the sure reward of the good and virtuous.

The imperfections and diseases of the body, therefore, beginning with Adam, are consequently passed down to his descendants. These may be divided into *hereditary* and *accidental* categories. Hereditary complaints stem from a certain defect in physical strength <note>original: "animal powers"</note> or an imperfect state of the circulatory system <note>original: "sanguiferous system"</note> at the time of conception <note>original: "copulation"</note>. Accidental maladies consist of all those illnesses caused by the unbalanced <note>original: "discordant"</note> or decaying <note>original: "putrid"</note> state of the elements—not only while the child is in the womb but from its birth until the final hour of its life. It should be noted here that the increase or decrease of both hereditary and accidental diseases depends almost entirely on the purity or impurity of the blood. For if the blood is pure in both the male and female at the time of conception <note>original: "impregnation"</note>, the fetus <note>original: "fœtus"</note> will naturally be strong and healthy. Likewise, if care is taken after birth <note>original: "parturition"</note> and throughout life to keep the blood in an untainted and lively <note>original: "elastic"</note> state, we will not only avoid the common effects of excessive cold, heat, and moisture, but also that dreadful series of intense <note>original: "acute"</note> diseases caused by decay and infection. Or, should they happen to attack us, the effect will be slight and temporary. This is a fact that should surely remain in the minds of those who value the blessing of health or wish to live a long, active, and pleasant life. This is, therefore, a topic of such great importance that I will now show how hereditary complaints are passed on during the act of conception—how they are increased and nurtured in the womb—how accidental diseases develop—and how both of these enemies to human health and happiness may be prevented or overcome.

At the upper end of this canal, the uterus (or womb) is located. It is shaped like a pyramid, with its tip <note>original: "apex"</note> toward the vagina. Its greatest length in virgins is no more than two or three inches, and its width is scarcely one; its internal cavity must therefore be very small. After what has been said, it may appear pointless to pursue any further disproof of the idea that male semen travels through the Fallopian tubes or through the mouth of the womb. I shall now ask: by what law of nature, or by what physical effort, is the male semen to be guided through this cone-shaped and twisted canal? Can the semen possess any active force to push itself through the stiff openings of this organ and overcome the natural closing <note>original: "collapse"</note> of the tubes? The stimulating power of the semen must soon be lost in a vessel which it does not have the power to expand; and we cannot suppose it is capable of acting in a direction completely opposite to the acknowledged function of the tubes. It must be by involuntary muscle movement <note>original: "irritability"</note> that the egg <note>original: "ovum"</note> is carried into the womb <note>original: "uterus"</note> from the ovaries; and we know of no vessels in any part of the body whose action is double and contrary. This system, therefore, is highly improbable.

The [fallopian] tubes, it is said, are remarkably swollen <note>original: "distended"</note> during intercourse <note>original: "coition"</note> by the blood rushing into the numerous vessels that run between their layers. By this means, they become erect, and their fringed ends <note>original: "fimbriated terminations"</note> are applied to the ovaries <note>original: "ovaria"</note>. It is also solemnly claimed that dissections of pregnant <note>original: "gravid"</note> women and the comparative anatomy of animals <note>original: "brutes"</note> support this opinion. If it were not for the serious respect this anatomical observation has long received, surely nobody would bother pointing out its absurdity. Even if we allow that this swelling <note>original: "turgidity"</note>, with all its accompanying circumstances, really happens in a *living person*, how could it possibly exist in a corpse limp with death? This is especially true in a human body used for dissection, where death must have occurred a significant time before.

But this swelling, though it may sometimes happen (and even then, to a much lesser degree than alleged), does not always occur. And when it does take place, it seems to be a companion and promoter of sexual pleasure <note>original: "libidinous gratification"</note> rather than a primary and essential factor in conception. For many women, the embraces of a man are extremely, if not completely, indifferent; for some, they are even absolutely disagreeable; yet these women are still fertile <note>original: "prolific"</note>.

There is no difficulty in suggesting a very sufficient and natural reason why the female parts directly involved in intercourse <note>original: "the venereal congress"</note> should become swollen with incoming blood and sometimes become tightened <note>original: "constricted"</note>. Nature, though she generally seems opposed to excessive lust, sometimes permits it; and these are the means she seems to have provided for increasing it. Besides, it is appropriate that the animal instinct which drives the reproduction of the species should not be denied its satisfaction—no matter how animalistic <note>original: "brutal"</note> these sensations and ideas may seem to a refined <note>original: "purified"</note> philosopher.

These biological functions, then—however they may contribute to the mutual sensitivity of the sexes during the pleasure of animal passion—appear to have no real influence on the process of reproduction <note>original: "generation"</note> after intercourse has ended. In fact, we have reason to believe that their action or influence does not extend beyond the vagina (except as part of the rest of the genital system) even during intercourse itself. If a rush of blood to these parts always caused these effects, what physical stress <note>original: "violence"</note> would the ovaries be exposed to through repeated intercourse and every return of the menstrual cycle?

During the menstrual flow, a very significant swelling <note>original: "distension"</note> must surely take place throughout most, if not all, of the genital system. Does every sexual act <note>original: "venereal act"</note> affect the ovaries <note>original: "ovaria"</note> and thereby produce more fetuses, or cause a waste of eggs <note>original: "ova"</note>? And are the organs themselves not incapacitated or weakened in their energy by such repeated exertion? We have every reason, then, to conclude that the tension and tightening of the female organs—caused by the rush of blood during intercourse—if they matter at all, are intended solely to promote physical pleasure. They have no direct influence on the actual movement of the semen through the previously described paths to the ovaries.

Overall, it is certainly not uncertain <note>original: "no ways equivocal"</note> that semen cannot, in any way, be applied to the ovaries by the fimbriae <note>the finger-like projections at the end of the fallopian tubes</note>. It cannot ascend or move through the twists and turns of the fallopian tubes; it cannot spread apart and cross the compressed uterus; and it cannot even force a passage through the rigid barrier of the cervix <note>original: "cervix uteri"</note>. The likelihood that a "seminal vapor" <note>original: "*aura seminalis*"; a historical theory that a gas or spirit from the semen, rather than the fluid itself, caused conception</note> moves through these same paths is disproven by these same arguments. Furthermore, the fanciful opinions based on the presence of microscopic organisms <note>original: "animalcules"; an early term for sperm</note> in the semen—as well as the idea of "organic bodies" provided by the fluids of both sexes that supposedly unite in the uterus—must suffer the same fate, as far as this alleged opening is concerned. 

It may, however, seem strange that a doctrine so ancient and so universally believed should be so easily overthrown; this may give the thoughtful reader a poor impression of the current state of medical literature. He may indeed wonder why, while every other science has become rational and respectable through the efforts of those who study them, medicine alone has been able to resist a thousand years of hard work. Although it has been taken out of the hands of untrained caretakers <note>original: "nurses"</note> and the profession has become dignified and profitable, it can hardly be said today to offer a single unquestionable fact. In the volumes of physiology compiled by the most learned physicians and drawn from the most scholarly sources, would an unbiased philosopher find the dogmas of medicine consistent with nature or with common sense?

But since semen, in one way or another, contains that animating principle vital for reproduction <note>original: "generation"</note>, and since the ovaries undeniably produce something from which a living creature develops, it becomes demonstrably clear that the influence of the male seed must be powerfully combined with the female and directed to the ovaries before this can happen. We have already seen how this *cannot* happen; let us now try to point out a logical way in which it might be achieved. For this purpose, we must return to the vagina (or canal of the uterus), as it is the primary female organ that actually contributes to reproduction, and without its full and complete use, conception <note>original: "impregnation"</note> cannot take place. It therefore requires a very detailed and careful investigation.

## AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES.

The vagina is elastic and somewhat membranous, composed of muscular fibers, blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics <note>vessels that carry lymph, a fluid containing white blood cells</note>. It begins from beneath, at the labia minora <note>original: "nymphae"</note>, and, rising at an angle for about five inches, it ends at the uterus. Its capacity differs greatly in different individuals, and even in the same individual at different stages of life. A very respectable anatomist finishes his description of it by saying, it is "adaptable to the male organ in all its dimensions" <note>original: *membro virili secundum omnes dimensiones accommodabilis*</note>. Its inner membrane, though very uneven, is delicately smooth and, due to its nervous texture, exquisitely sensitive; the outer membrane is more spongy and muscular; and the entire body of the canal is very plentifully supplied with blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics. We know little more of the lymphatics of these parts than that they are proportionally more numerous here than in any other part of the body. Those which originate in the exterior parts of the female genital system pass through the inguinal glands <note>lymph nodes in the groin</note>, while the deep-seated ones take a much more direct course to their place of union with the lacteals <note>lymphatic vessels that absorb fats</note>. We shall be more specific about these when we present our observations in favor of the theory that a very powerful absorption occurs within the vagina.

The entrance into the canal of the uterus from the outside is guarded by the labia minora <note>original: "nymphae"</note>, which form a raised area on each side. These are so uniquely constructed and arranged that we must think poorly of any physiologist who could suppose they were merely secondary parts intended to serve the urethra. Indeed, as Nature frequently achieves more than one goal through a single structure, we shall not pretend to limit the secondary or inferior functions which the labia minora may serve. however, we see much reason to believe they were created to assist powerfully in preventing the speedy escape of the male semen, thereby exposing it longer to the action of the absorbent system. A multitude of circumstances support this belief, and it is not weakened by the claim that these ridges do not constitute a perfectly regular and complete valve. 

Immediately within this barrier, a structure based on the same principles as the labia minora—but more elegant and powerful—begins. It continues over the surface of the vagina, gradually growing finer until it disappears into smoothness near the upper end of the canal. This structure consists of the *rugae* <note>folds or ridges</note> of the vagina, so accurately drawn and described by Albrecht von Haller <note>a famous 18th-century Swiss anatomist and physiologist</note> and others. These have been dismissed by some anatomists, who describe them as useful only for increasing sexual pleasure or allowing for expansion during intercourse <note>original: "coition"</note> and childbirth <note>original: "parturition"</note>. It is a mean and disgraceful reflection on the important order and operations of Nature to suppose that these *rugae*—which are not randomly arranged, but are regulated with as much precision and uniformity as any other part of the genital system—were created for such simple reasons. I say it is worthless <note>original: "nugatory"</note> and presumptuous to assert that this intricate, extensive, and beautiful arrangement has been so minutely crafted for no other purpose but merely to

During pregnancy, however, the uterine system is not always able to use up the excess supply of blood <note>original: "surcharge of blood"</note>, and thus cannot offset the body’s periodic effort to menstruate. Let us now move a little closer to our subject. It is beyond doubt that, regardless of how semen acts upon the female, it does not act instantly, despite the general assertions of many authors. However productive sexual intercourse <note>original: "coition"</note> may be, the fertilized product of the ovaries <note>original: "ovaria"</note> is not immediately released <note>original: "disengaged"</note>. We dare not confirm this fact from observations made on human subjects, because such observations have never been attempted, nor could they ever be with the smallest probability of success. However, the dissection of animals <note>original: "brutes"</note> by the most eminent anatomists, performed with a direct view to clarifying this fact, confirms it as far as such evidence can be admitted.

In the dissection of small animals by De Graaff <note>Reinier de Graaff (1641–1673) was a Dutch physician and anatomist who discovered the follicles in the ovary where eggs develop.</note>, he found no discernible alteration in the uterus during the first forty hours after sexual intercourse, but a gradual change was perceivable in the ovaries. What he supposed to be the ripened origin of the future animal—at the end of that time—lost its transparency and became opaque and reddish <note>original: "ruddy"</note>. After that time, the fimbriae <note>The finger-like projections at the end of the fallopian tubes.</note> were found closely applied to the ovaries; the cavities from which the eggs <note>original: "ova"</note> had been squeezed <note>original: "expressed"</note> were discernible; and about the third day, the eggs were discovered in the uterus. In large animals, and in those whose period of uterine gestation was longer, it was found that the progress we have been describing was proportionally slower.

The same experiments have been made by different anatomists, perhaps with very different goals; and though they have not always been managed with the same judgment and skill, yet all of them more or less confirm the idea that there is a very considerable lapse of time intervening between productive copulation and the expulsion of the egg <note>original: "ovum"</note> from the ovaries. But if this is the case with animals that soon arrive at puberty, and which—unlike human creatures—do not copulate perfectly before puberty, whose lives are short, and whose progress in equal periods of time is more rapid than that in man; then, by parity of reason, it must happen that in women the period between impregnation and the expulsion of the fertilized product of the ovaries must be considerably greater than what has been observed to take place in these animals.

If all this is true, how are we to suppose Nature is employed during this interval? We believe it is during this period that the entire female constitution is working under the fertilizing <note>original: "fecundating"</note> influence of the seminal fluid, which is taken into the blood by the absorbents <note>The lymphatic or absorbent vessels.</note>. Meanwhile, the ovaries are largely participating in this, and their product is ripening by means of the general stimulating process. The same process which matures <note>original: "maturates"</note> the egg also tends to facilitate its release. The ovaries, as well as their product, are at this time enlarged, and other changes subject to the examination of our senses are induced. It is no proof against the reality of this general alteration in the circulatory system, and the subsequent revolution in the ovaries, that the whole process is accomplished with very little visible disturbance, either local or universal. In cases involving a significant physical alteration in the blood, the same quietness and lack of obvious symptoms often prevail. We know of no operation in the human body—whether intended for the ordinary purposes of life and health or for the removal of disease—that does not, to a greater or lesser degree, involve the machinery of the entire system. A single mouthful of food, while it is prepared, purified, and applied to its ultimate purposes, is subjected to the action of all the known parts of the body (and without doubt to all those parts whose properties we are still unfamiliar with). A draught of cold water spreads its influence almost instantaneously from one extremity to the other. The slightest wound disturbs even the most remote parts and is followed, quite often, by the most unhappy effects. Can we suppose that the most essential process of the human body—reproducing itself—is accomplished in some obscure corner, with infinitely less ceremony and importance than a bit of spit is cast into the wind? The obvious physical means of reproduction are already considered lowly enough; we do not need to use our ingenuity to degrade them further.

It is during this interval, between successful sexual intercourse <note>original: "coition"</note> and the release of the egg <note>original: "ovum"</note> from the ovaries <note>original: "ovaria"</note>, that family resemblance, inherited diseases, and similar traits are passed on and acquired. Instead of the influence that a mother's imagination is supposed to have over the form of her child, might we not suspect that the male's seminal fluid—working during this interval alongside the female's influence on the egg—produces a likeness based on the influence of the male and female "tinctures" <term>In 18th-century medicine, "tinctures" referred to the vital or spiritual qualities of bodily fluids believed to carry life force.</term> in their combined principles? It is only during this period that the father's diseases can be passed to the child. If we do not acknowledge this window of time and the general action of the seminal fluid, we cannot see how they could be transmitted, whereas the mother's diseases can be passed on then or at a much later period, given how the child is nourished while in the uterus and at the breast.

One might argue against this early and effective acquisition of resemblance by pointing out that the fetus <note>original: "foetus"</note> does not even develop the division of its largest limbs until long after it has left the ovaries. However, we are confident that since the fetus takes its entire form and all other properties from the active, subtle nature of these blended tinctures, there is no reason why it should not possess this hereditary potential just as much as its other traits. If resemblance depended on the woman’s imagination, how does it happen that the children of those whose "loose" behavior makes the father's identity uncertain—and whose affections end the moment their lust is satisfied—are just as frequently recognizable by their likeness to their fathers as children born into more fortunate circumstances? 

If physical features are not established during this period, and if the imagination is not actually useless in this regard, how was the "six-fingered family" mentioned by Maupertuis <note>Pierre Louis Maupertuis (1698–1759) was a French philosopher and scientist who made early contributions to the study of genetics and heredity.</note> continued? When a woman from that family married a man who had only the usual number of fingers, the appearance of that deformity in her children became unpredictable or stopped entirely. We must assume her imagination was active—whether she was alarmed by the fear of continuing a deformed race or driven by the vanity of passing on such a remarkable trait—yet the outcome did not follow her thoughts. # A KEY TO PHYSIC,

...suppose that the most important function of the human body—its own reproduction—is to be accomplished in a hidden corner, and with infinitely less ceremony and importance than spitting into the wind? The visible means of reproduction are already sufficiently looked down upon; we do not need to use our creativity to degrade them further.

It is during this interval, between successful conception <note>original: "productive coition"</note> and the release of the egg <note>original: "ovum"</note> from the ovaries <note>original: "ovaria"</note>, that resemblance, hereditary diseases, and similar traits are passed on and acquired. Rather than the influence that a mother's imagination is often thought to have over the form of the child, could we not suspect that the seminal fluid <note>original: "feminal fluid"—likely a printer's error for "seminal," or referring to the male's seed in the generation process</note> of the male, working during this time with the influence of the female upon the egg, triggers a resemblance based on the influence of the male and female qualities <note>original: "tinctures"</note> in their joined biological principles? 

It is during this period only that the diseases of the father can be passed to the child. If we do not acknowledge this window of time and the general role of the male's fluid, we cannot see how paternal diseases could be communicated; in contrast, the mother's diseases may be passed then or at a much later period, considering how the child is nourished while it is in the womb <note>original: "uterus"</note> and at the breast. 

One might argue against this early and effective acquisition of resemblance by pointing out that the fetus <note>original: "foetus"</note> does not even develop the distinct divisions of its largest limbs until long after the egg has left the ovaries. However, we are confident that since the fetus takes its entire form and other properties from the active power <note>original: "subtilty"</note> of these blended essences, there is no reason why it should not possess this hereditary blueprint <note>original: "faculty"</note> just as much as its other traits. 

If resemblance depended upon the imagination of the woman, how is it that the children of those whose loose behavior makes the father's identity uncertain—and whose feelings end the moment their lust is satisfied—are just as often recognizable by their likeness to the father as children born in more stable circumstances? If physical features are not established during this early period, and if imagination is not actually the cause, how was the six-fingered family mentioned by Maupertuis <note>Pierre Louis Maupertuis (1698–1759), a French scientist who performed early studies on the inheritance of extra fingers (polydactyly).</note> able to continue that trait? When a woman from that family married a man with the normal number of fingers, the recurrence of the family deformity became unpredictable or stopped. We must assume her imagination would not have been inactive or diminished, whether she was alarmed by the fear of continuing a deformed race or driven by the vanity of passing on such a remarkable physical trait. 

If a pregnant woman's imagination were as powerful as many have tried to claim, a mother who was unfaithful in her heart (even if not in her actions) would always betray her wandering affections through the child's appearance. Even a virtuous woman might accidentally reveal that she had looked with as much interest at a handsome stranger as she had looked at the aquiline nose <note>A curved nose like an eagle's beak, then considered a prominent and noble feature.</note> or other striking features of her husband.

# A KEY TO PHYSIC,

From these observations, it seems reasonable to infer that although climate, lifestyle, occupation, or imitation cannot significantly change the physical form or features of a living animal, these circumstances can affect a lineage over many generations. By causing a change in the overall biological makeup of both the male and female, these factors can eventually cause a change in their offspring.

Based on what has been discussed, it seems rational to conclude that during sexual intercourse <note>original: "coition"</note>, the reproductive fluid <note>original: "prolific fluid"</note> is not carried directly through the Fallopian tubes or pushed through the opening of the uterus to the ovaries <note>original: "ovaria"</note>. Instead, it is taken up by the absorbent vessels and carried into the circulatory system <note>original: "sanguiferous system"</note>, where every active principle that can affect the human body is also transported. After circulating through the blood, it is pushed through the corresponding vessels into the ovaries by its own natural drive and the additional stimulus it receives from the mother. If it finds one or more eggs <note>original: "ova"</note> in a state ripe for fertilization <note>original: "impregnation"</note>, conception occurs accordingly. One or more eggs are fertilized, depending on how many mature eggs are in the ovaries. However, if none of the eggs are mature enough, or if they happen to be damaged by harmful bodily fluids <note>original: "offending humours"</note>, weakness, or disease, then fertilization fails. This is just like what happens to a rotten <note>original: "addled"</note> egg or a damaged grain of corn planted in the earth.

On the other hand, if the male organ lacks vigor, or if the semen is lacking in quantity, consistency, or potency, it fails to stimulate the female fluid and is unable to bring about fertilization. Therefore, for sexual intercourse to result in offspring, the male must undoubtedly convey a complex biological extract <note>original: "elaborate tincture"</note> to the female. This extract contains the essence of his entire system, both mental and physical. In this act, the greatest energies and powers of the mind, body, and soul are closely connected, and all contribute their specific influence to the "seed." Every father must be aware of this when he considers the action of the heart (the seat of life), the brain (the seat of the soul), and the total powers of the body—all concentrated and driven, as it were, through the reproductive system. I believe that anyone who carefully weighs these arguments will not doubt that this fluid contains the active principles of both the *body and the soul*. I take it as confirmed by the evidence of the Bible <note>original: "Scripture"</note> that it conveys the direct image of the parent. We are told in the Bible that one absolute and unmistakable form was given to man, created in the direct image of God <note>original: "Deity"</note>. Thus, man was organized and commanded to pass on to future generations that divine image or "signature" which God had graciously stamped upon him. # A KEY TO MEDICINE <note>original: "PHYSIC"</note>

In the third month, the human form can be clearly identified; all the parts of the face can be distinguished; the shape of the body is clearly marked out; the hips and the abdomen are raised, and the hands and feet are plainly visible. The upper limbs <note>original: "extremities"</note> are observed to grow faster than the lower ones; and the separation of the fingers may be seen before that of the toes. The veins of the placenta are now filled, and are seen to connect with the umbilical cord <note>original: "tube"</note>. This stage of pregnancy <note>original: "gestation"</note> is accurately shown in Illustration No. 4 of the attached engraving.

In the fourth month, the fetus seems to be complete in all its parts and is about four inches in size. The fingers and toes, which were at first joined together <note>original: "coalesced"</note>, are now separated from each other, and the intestines appear in all their coils and twists like little threads. The veins of the placenta begin to be filled with blood, and the umbilical cord is considerably enlarged, as may be seen in the fifth figure of the attached plate.

In the fifth month, the bodily structure being perfected in all its parts and a complete circulation of the blood established, the mother <term>quickens</term> <note>Quickening refers to the first moment a pregnant woman feels the fetus move.</note>. The fetus now takes on a more upright posture, which matches the shape of the uterus. Its head is found more elevated, its lower limbs are more extended, and its knees are drawn upwards with its arms resting upon them. It now measures from seven to eight inches in length and is described in the first figure of the second attached plate.

Towards the end of the sixth month, the fetus begins to change its position in the womb and will frequently be found to lean either to the right or to the left side of the mother. It will by this time have increased to nine or ten inches; its usual posture after quickening may be seen in the second figure of the second attached plate.

In the seventh month, the child acquires strength and firmness, as may be shown by those painful kicks <note>original: "throws"</note> and twitchings which its mother feels from time to time; it has now increased to eleven or twelve inches.

In the eighth month, it generally measures from fourteen to sixteen inches; and in the ninth month, or towards the end of its full term, it has increased from eighteen to twenty-two inches or more. At this time the head, by becoming relatively heavier than the other parts, is gradually pushed downward; falling into the birth canal, it brings on what is termed the pains of <term>parturition</term> <note>The medical term for the process of giving birth.</note>, or natural labor. For the exact position of the child in the womb during these last three months, as well as the previous ones, see the corresponding figures in the two attached engravings, all of which were accurately drawn from actual fetuses removed from the wombs of different women.

# AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES.

The nourishment of the <term>fetus</term> <note>original: "fœtus"</note> during all this time is derived from the <term>placenta</term>, which is originally formed out of that part of the <term>egg</term> <note>original: "ovum"</note> which is closest to the <term>top of the womb</term> <note>original: "fundus uteri"</note>. The remaining part of the egg is covered by a membrane called the *<term>spongy chorion</term>*; within which is another called the *<term>true chorion</term>*, which includes a third, termed the *<term>amnion</term>* <note>original: "amnios"</note>. This contains a liquid, or watery fluid, in which the fetus floats until the time of its birth. Before the child acquires a distinct and regular form, it is called an *<term>embryo</term>*; but from the time all its parts become visible, it takes and retains the name of *<term>fetus</term>* until its birth. 

During the progress of impregnation, the <term>uterus</term> <note>the womb</note> undergoes <note>original: "suffers"</note> considerable changes. Although it enlarges as the egg increases, it is never actually full in relation to its contents; for, in early <term>pregnancy</term> <note>original: "gestation"</note>, these are confined to the top of the womb only. Even though the capacity of the womb increases, it is not mechanically stretched, because the thickness of its sides does not diminish. There is a proportional increase in the quantity of fluids, and therefore nearly the same thickness remains as before impregnation. 

The <term>pregnant womb</term> <note>original: "gravid uterus"</note> is of different sizes in different women and must vary according to the size of the fetus and the <term>membranes</term> <note>original: "involucra"</note> surrounding it. Its position will also vary according to the increase of its contents and the posture of the body. For the first two or three months, the cavity of the top of the womb is triangular, as it was before impregnation; but, as the uterus stretches, it gradually acquires a more rounded form. In general, the uterus never rises directly upward, but inclines slightly at an angle, most commonly to the right side. However, its position is never so slanted <note>original: "oblique"</note> as to be the sole cause of either preventing or slowing delivery. 

Its increase in size does not seem to arise merely from being stretched, but depends on the same biological growth as the extension of the skin on a growing child. This is proven by some recent instances of <term>ectopic pregnancies</term> <note>original: "extra-uterine fœtuses"</note>, where the uterus was nearly the same size as if the egg had been contained within its cavity—despite being empty—due to the additional nourishment being transmitted to the organ. The internal surface, which is generally quite smooth except where the placenta attaches <note>original: "adheres"</note>, is lined with a delicate growth <note>original: "efflorescence"</note> from the uterus. After delivery, this appears as if torn and is shed with the <term>post-birth discharge</term> <note>original: "cleansings"</note>. This is the *<term>deciduous membrane</term>* <note>original: "membrana decidua"</note> described by Dr. Hunter <note>William Hunter (1718–1783), a famous Scottish anatomist and physician.</note>. He describes it as a <term>thin layer</term> <note>original: "lamella"</note> from the inner surface of the uterus; however, <term>Signor Scarpa</term> <note>Antonio Scarpa (1752–1832), an Italian anatomist and contemporary of Hunter.</note>, with more probability, considers it to be composed of a <term>thickened, clot-forming fluid</term> <note>original: "inspissated coagulable lymph"</note>.

Though the uterus is gradually stretched from the moment of conception, which causes considerable changes, it is very difficult to judge a pregnancy from physical appearances in the early months. For the first three months, the <term>mouth of the womb</term> <note>original: "os tincæ," literally "tench's mouth," referring to the cervix</note> feels smooth and even, and its opening is as small as it is in a virgin state. When any difference can be perceived, around the fourth or fifth month, from the lowering of the top of the womb...

Through the pelvis, the bump or projecting part of the <term>mouth of the womb</term> <note>original: "os tincæ," literally "tench's mouth," referring to the cervix</note> will seem larger, longer, and more expanded; but, after this period, it shortens, particularly at its front and sides, and its opening or "lips" begin to separate, so that its cone-like appearance is destroyed. The <term>neck of the womb</term> <note>original: "cervix"</note>, which in the early months is nearly shut, now begins to stretch and to be expanded toward the <term>mouth of the womb</term>. During the whole term of <term>pregnancy</term> <note>original: "utero-gestation"</note>, the mouth of the uterus is strongly sealed with a thick, ropy mucus, which lines it and the <term>neck</term>, and begins to be discharged as labor approaches. In the last week, when the <term>neck of the womb</term> <note>original: "cervix uteri"</note> is completely stretched, the uterine opening begins to form an oval tube instead of a narrow slit, or it assumes the appearance of a ring on a large globe. Often at this time—especially in women with sagging abdomens—it disappears entirely, moving out of the reach of a finger during a physical examination. Therefore, the <term>opening of the womb</term> <note>original: "os uteri"</note> is not aligned with the central axis of the uterus, as has generally been supposed.

About the fourth month, or between the fourth and fifth, the <term>top of the womb</term> <note>original: "fundus uteri"</note> begins to rise above the pubic bone or the brim of the pelvis, and its <term>neck</term> is stretched by nearly one-third. In the fifth month, the belly swells like a ball and the skin becomes tight; the <term>top of the womb</term> is about halfway between the pubic bone and the navel, and the neck is half-stretched. After the sixth month, the greatest part of the <term>neck of the womb</term> dilates until it forms almost a single cavity with the <term>top of the womb</term>. In the seventh month, the <term>top of the womb</term> advances as far as the <term>navel</term> <note>original: "umbilicus"</note>. In the eighth, it reaches midway between the navel and the <term>pit of the stomach</term> <note>original: "scrobiculus cordis"</note>; and in the ninth, it reaches the <term>pit of the stomach</term> itself. By then, the neck is entirely stretched and, along with the <term>mouth of the womb</term>, becomes the thinnest and weakest part of the uterus. Thus, at full term, the uterus occupies all the navel and <term>lower abdominal</term> <note>original: "hypogastric"</note> regions. Its shape is almost pear-shaped—that is, more rounded above than below—and it has a constriction on that part which is surrounded by the brim of the pelvis. The secondary parts of the uterus change very little during pregnancy, except for the <term>broad ligaments</term> <note>original: "ligamenta lata"</note>, which get narrower as the uterus enlarges and are almost entirely flattened out by full term.

The various diseases affecting the uterine system, and other ailments of the <term>internal abdominal organs</term> <note>original: "abdominal viscera"</note> in weak and sickly women, will frequently trigger the symptoms and take on the appearance of real pregnancy. Complaints arising from a simple lack of menstruation are sometimes mistaken for "breeding." When a tumor also forms in the region of the uterus and gradually becomes more and more bulky, the symptoms it causes are so distinct and the resemblance to pregnancy so very striking that the misinformed patient is often deceived, and even the experienced physician can be fooled.

# AND THE OCCULT SCIENCES.

Hard (scirrhous), polyp-like, or fleshy (sarcomatous) tumors in or around the uterus or pelvis; <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "dropsy," an old term for edema or an abnormal buildup of fluid</note> or <term>gas</term> <note>original: "ventosity"</note> of the uterus or tubes; fatty tumors (steatoma) or fluid in the ovaries; and abdominal (ventral) pregnancy are the common causes of such deceptive appearances. In many of these cases, the menstrual periods disappear; nausea, retching, and other symptoms of pregnancy follow; gas in the bowels will be mistaken for the movement of the child; and, in the advanced stages of the disease, the pressure of the swelling affects the adjacent organs. Swelling and hardness of the breasts occur, and sometimes a sticky or watery fluid drips from the nipple. These circumstances strongly convince the woman of her pregnancy, until time, or the often-dreadful consequences that follow, finally convince her of her fatal mistake.

Other kinds of <term>false pregnancy</term> <note>original: "spurious gravidity"</note>, which are less hazardous in nature than any of the previous ones, are commonly known by the names *false conceptions* and *moles*. The former of these is nothing more than the dissolution of the fetus in the early months. The placenta is afterwards retained in the womb and—due to the addition of blood clots (coagula) or as a result of disease—is expelled in a hardened or enlarged state. When it remains longer and comes out in the form of a fleshy or hard mass without any cavity in the center, it is distinguished by the name <term>mole</term> <note>original: "mole," a term used here to describe various types of abnormal uterine masses, including what modern medicine might call a hydatidiform mole</note>. Simple blood clots, retained in the uterus after delivery or after immoderate bleeding at any period of life and squeezed by the pressure of the uterus into a fibrous or compact form, constitute another species of mole that occurs more frequently than any of the others. These, though they may take on the appearance of pregnancy, are generally expelled spontaneously and are seldom followed by dangerous consequences. But, when two or more eggs (ova) descend into the uterus and attach themselves so near one another that they adhere in whole or in part—forming only one body with shared membranes and water—this body will form a confused, irregular mass, which is called a <term>monster</term> <note>original: "monster," an archaic medical term for a fetus with significant congenital abnormalities or fused twins</note>. Thus, a "monster" may either be missing its organic parts or be supplied with an extra set of parts derived from another egg. This results from a defect or accident in nature, which is entirely beyond the power of medicine to fix or prevent.

It would seem, however, from a proper contemplation of the facts mentioned above, from the frame and structure of women, and from the ultimate end and purpose of their biology, that almost every malady resulting from a state of pregnancy (except the last one mentioned) may be largely prevented or removed. The natural <term>temperature</term> <note>In historical medicine, "temperature" referred to the balance of "humors" or vital heat</note> of women differs to a very considerable degree from that of men, because their blood and juices are intended for an opposite and distinct purpose. It is for this reason that obstructions of the menstrual periods, their excess, or the failure of the office intended for them, constitute those specific maladies which we term *Diseases of Women*.

Life and health are established by their proper mixture in the constitution or the circulating mass of the blood; on the contrary, disease and death are produced by their discordant, defective, or overpowering influence.

The treatment and future health of young ladies deserve very close and serious attention. The evident distinction between the male and female in their structure and purpose, in their bodily strength and vigor, and in their reproductive fluids, demands the utmost attention from the women themselves and the tenderest care from the physician. 

Nor can we too often or too earnestly caution parents and guardians against the evils of that absurd, though fashionable, style of raising young ladies by confining them almost entirely to their rooms, keeping them on a poor, low diet, and using artificial means to make them thin and delicate. This occurs more in women than in the females of other species—even though they have the same organs—because of the upright posture of humans. In women, the vagina and other canals are positioned vertically (perpendicular to the ground), so the pressure of the blood is directed toward their openings. In animals (referred to here as "brutes"), these parts are parallel to the ground, so the pressure is placed entirely on the sides of those vessels. 

The author believes this discharge happens in this part of the body rather than any other because the structure of the vessels encourages it. The arteries are very numerous, and the veins are winding and curvy, which makes them more likely to slow down the force of the blood. Consequently, in a <term>plethoric</term> <note>original: "plethoric," referring to a condition of having an excessive fullness of blood or bodily fluids</note> case, this leads to the bursting of the ends of the vessels. This lasts until enough has been discharged to ease the vessels of their overload. To this, he adds the consideration of the soft, spongy texture of the <term>uterus</term>, and the vast number of veins and arteries with which it is filled. 

Therefore, once a healthy young woman has finished growing, she begins to produce more nourishment than is needed to support her body. Since she is no longer growing larger, this extra nourishment must fill the blood vessels—especially those of the uterus and breasts, as they are the least compressed. These vessels will expand more than others. When the small lateral vessels empty their <term>humor</term> <note>original: "humour," referring to bodily fluids</note> into the cavity of the uterus, it becomes filled and stretched. This causes pain, heat, and heaviness to be felt around the lower back and pelvic area (<term>pubes</term>). 

At the same time, the vessels of the uterus will expand so much that they release blood into the uterine cavity; its opening will be lubricated and loosened, and blood will flow out. As the quantity of blood decreases, the pressure on the vessels lessens, and they will contract more tightly to hold the blood in again, allowing only the thicker part of the <term>serum</term> <note>the clear, watery part of the blood</note> to pass until, eventually, only the usual fluid is released. Again, more fluids are prepared and easily stored in the vessels that have already been expanded; this is why the <term>menses</term> <note>the monthly menstrual period</note> come and go at different intervals for different people.

This hypothesis is thoughtfully opposed by Dr. Drake, who argues that there is no such "plenitude" (excessive fullness), or at least that it is not necessary for menstruation. He argues that if the periods were caused by such an accumulation of blood (<term>plethora</term>), the symptoms would appear gradually. The heaviness, stiffness, and lack of energy—which are the necessary symptoms of having too much blood—would be felt long before the periods were completed. Women would begin to feel heavy and unwell shortly after their last discharge ended, and the symptoms would increase daily. 

However, this contradicts all experience. Many women who have regular and easy cycles have no warning at all; their only way to avoid a socially embarrassing accident ("indecent surprise") is by keeping track of the time. Some women who have lost track of time have been caught off guard in ways that would not happen if a body full of excess blood were giving them physical warnings. According to the hypothesis of excess blood, the last hour contributed no more than the first; and consequently, the alteration should not be greater in the one than in the other, setting aside the actual start of the discharge.

There are others who subscribe to the doctrine of fermentation, and maintain that the evacuation in those parts is an effect of a bubbling or boiling of the blood (<term>effervescence</term> <note>original: "effervescence or ebullition," terms used in early medicine to describe a chemical-like reaction or "boiling" in the blood</note>). The first two suppose a "ferment" unique to women, which produces this flow and affects that part of the body only, or at least principally. *Dr. Graaf*, who is less specific in his notion, only supposes a reaction in the blood raised by some ferment, without explaining how it acts or what it is. The sudden swelling (<term>turgescence</term>) of the blood led them all to think that it arose from something previously external to the blood. This led them to seek an imaginary ferment in the organs most affected; however, no anatomical inquiry could ever reveal such a substance, find any container for it, or logically prove its existence. Again, the heat that frequently accompanies this swelling led them to think the case was more than just a <term>plethora</term> <note>original: "plethora," a condition of having too much blood in the body</note>, and that there was some extraordinary internal motion occurring at that time.

*Dr. Drake* contends that it is not only necessary for there to be a ferment, but a receptacle for this ferment as well. He concludes—from the suddenness and violence of the symptoms—that a great quantity must be conveyed into the blood in a short time. Consequently, it must have been already gathered in some container where its action was restrained while it was stored. He claims to identify the place of both, making the gallbladder the container and the bile the ferment. He thinks this liquid is well adapted to raise a fermentation in the blood when discharged into it in quantity. As it is contained in a receptacle that does not allow for a continual flow, it may be reserved there until, at a certain period of time, the bladder becomes swollen and full. Then, through the pressure of the surrounding internal organs (<term>viscera</term>), it releases the gall. This fluid, by way of the <term>lacteals</term> <note>original: "lacteals," vessels that carry milky fluid from the intestines to the bloodstream</note> working its way into the blood, may raise that reaction which causes the opening of the uterine arteries. These are the age of fourteen or fifteen, when the menses begin to flow, and the age of forty or fifty, when they subside. At their commencement, we generally find that difficulties and subsequent diseases arise from a *deficiency* of flow; whereas, according to the previous doctrine of excess blood, they would then *always* flow with the greatest freedom. At the period when they should cease, they are prone to come in such abundance as to bring on heavy bleeding (<term>flooding</term>), which not only endangers but too frequently destroys life—a fatal consequence that could not possibly happen if the arguments above were true.

### OF FEMININE, OR LUNAR, DISEASES.

Experience, as well as the demonstrations given in my *Treatise on the Occult Sciences*, indisputably proves that the reproductive (<term>vegetative or procreative</term>) faculties of women are universally governed by the phases (<term>lunations</term>) of the moon. The first appearance of the menstrual flow (<term>catamenia</term> <note>original: "catamenia," a medical term for menstruation derived from the Greek word for "monthly"</note>), if it is natural, invariably comes with the new or full moon, or sometimes—though very seldom—at the beginning of her first or last quarters. This natural process is rightly considered a sure sign of the ability to conceive and of reaching complete puberty. Whenever this season arrives, whether early or late, the constitution of every female undergoes a considerable change. The greatest care and attention are then necessary, since the future health and happiness of every woman depends, in a great measure, upon her conduct at this period. It is the duty of mothers, and of those who are entrusted with the education of girls, to instruct them early in how to care for and manage themselves at this critical moment. # A KEY TO PHYSIC.

...approaches as a gradual accumulation necessarily requires. If we consider what violent symptoms come on in an hour, we shall be extremely puzzled to find the mighty increase <note>original: "accession"</note> of matter, which should, in an hour or a day's time, make such great alterations. According to the hypothesis of accumulation, the last hour contributed no more than the first; and consequently, the alteration should not be greater in the one than in the other, setting aside the actual eruption of blood.

There are others who support the doctrine of fermentation, and maintain that the evacuation in those parts is an effect of an effervescence or bubbling <note>original: "ebullition," a term from early chemistry describing a boiling or bubbling state</note> of the blood. This opinion has been maintained by Dr. Charleton, Bale, De Graaf, and Drake. The first two of these suppose a ferment peculiar to women, which produces this flux and affects that part only, or at least principally. Dr. De Graaf, being less specific in his notion, only supposes a bubbling of the blood raised by some ferment, without explaining how it acts or what it is. The sudden swelling <note>original: "turgescence"</note> of the blood caused them all to think that it arose from something previously external to the blood. This led them to look to the organs principally affected to find an imaginary ferment—which no anatomical inquiry could ever show, nor any reasoning necessarily prove, nor any storage place be found for. Again, the heat that frequently accompanies this swelling led them to think the case was more than just a surplus of blood <note>original: "plethora," a medical condition thought to be caused by an excess of bodily fluids</note>, and that there was some extraordinary internal motion occurring at that time.

Dr. Drake contends that it is not only necessary for there to be a ferment, but a receptacle for this ferment as well. Concluding from the suddenness and violence of the symptoms that a great quantity must be conveyed into the blood in a short time, he argues it must have been ready and gathered in some container where its action was restrained while lodged there. He pretends to identify the place of both, claiming the gall-bladder is the receptacle and the bile is the ferment. He thinks this liquid is well-adapted to raise a fermentation in the blood when discharged into it in large quantities. As it is contained in a receptacle that does not allow for a continual flow, it may be reserved there until, in a certain period of time, the bladder becomes swollen and full. Then, through the pressure of the overlying internal organs <note>original: "incumbent viscera"</note>, it emits the gall. This gall, by way of the lacteals <note>vessels that carry fats and lymph from the digestive tract</note> insinuating itself into the blood, may raise that bubbling which causes the opening of the uterine arteries. To confirm this, he alleges that persons of a bilious constitution <note>having a temperament dominated by "yellow bile," often associated with being irritable or fiery</note> have their periods either more plentifully or more frequently than others; and that diseases clearly caused by bile are attended with symptoms resembling those of women struggling with difficult menstruation. 

However, if this argument were admitted, men would have periods as well as women. To this he answers that men do not abound in bile as much as women, as the pores of men are more open and carry off more of the watery <note>original: "serous"</note> part of the blood, which is the vehicle...

### CONCERNING THE WHITE DISCHARGE <note>original Latin: *fluor albus*; commonly known as "the whites"</note>.

The **white discharge** <note>original: *fluor albus*</note>, female weakness, or "the whites," as it is commonly called, is a disease of the womb and its neighboring parts. It involves the discharge of a pale, greenish, or yellow fluid, accompanied by a loss of strength, pain in the lower back <note>original: "loins"</note>, poor digestion, and a pale, sickly appearance. The quantity, color, and thickness <note>original: "consistence"</note> of the discharge mostly depend on how long the disease has lasted, the patient’s general health <note>original: "habit of body"</note>, and the cause of the illness. Weakly women with poor muscle tone <note>original: "lax solids"</note> who have had many children and have long suffered from poor health are the most susceptible to this unpleasant disease. Unfortunately, they often suffer more severely than others, as a delicate physical frame often goes hand-in-hand with the most sensitive feelings. In Holland, this condition is very frequent and is almost unique to that place because of the damp environment. The surrounding air is so saturated with moisture that it relaxes the body and stops perspiration, forcing the excess fluid onto the bowels or the womb; in the first case, this produces **diarrhea** <note>original Latin: *diarrhœa*, literally "a flowing through"</note>, and in the second, it produces the white discharge or female weakness. The discharge often comes from the vessels that facilitate menstruation. In delicate patients where those vessels are weak and stay open too long, the white discharge sometimes begins immediately after the menstrual period ends and disappears gradually as the vessels close. A fresh infection, called gonorrhea <note>original: "gonorrhœa"</note>, is malignant and inflammatory; the whites <note>original Latin: "fluor albus"</note> most commonly arise from relaxation and bodily weakness. In gonorrhea, the discharge chiefly proceeds from the parts near the urinary passage and continues while the menstrual periods <note>original: "menses"</note> flow; but in the whites, it is supplied from the cavity of the womb and its passage, and then the menstrual periods are seldom regular. 

In gonorrhea, an itching, inflammation, and heat during urination are the forerunners of the discharge; the opening <note>original: "orifice"</note> of the urinary passage is prominent, and the patient is affected with a frequent urge to urinate. 

In the whites, pains in the lower back <note>original: "loins"</note> and loss of strength accompany the discharge; and, if any inflammation or heat of urine follows, it happens to a lesser degree and only after the discharge has continued for a long time—at which point the discharge becomes sharp and irritating <note>original: "acrimonious"</note> and chafes <note>original: "excoriates"</note> the surrounding parts.

# OF BARRENNESS, OR INFERTILITY.

### DISCOMFORTS ACCOMPANYING PREGNANCY.

Though pregnancy is not a disease, but rather a natural change in the animal economy <term>animal economy: the system of physical and biological processes that maintain a living body</term> which every female is designed to undergo, it is nonetheless attended by a variety of complaints that require great attention. In a small village in Somersetshire, in the year 1759, a girl was born with the hair on her head in two remarkably distinct colors. ### THE STATE OF WOMEN DURING MENOPAUSE <note>original: "Turn of Life"</note>.

The most critical and dangerous time of a woman's life is when her menstruation <note>original: "menses"</note> ceases to flow, which usually happens between forty and fifty years of age. The great change that this produces—caused by such a large flow being returned into the body's system <note>original: "habit"</note> without previous preparation—is the sole cause of its danger. Every woman must be more or less aware when this period arrives and should conduct herself accordingly. When the menstruation is about to stop, it appears for the most part irregularly, both in timing and amount—once every fortnight, or every three, five, or six weeks. Sometimes it is very light, and other times it occurs in excessive quantities. Due only to a lack of necessary care and attention during the time that the menstruation shows these signs of its departure, many and various complaints follow. Among these are cold chills followed by violent flushing of the face and heat in the hands and feet <note>original: "extremities"</note>; restless nights, troublesome dreams, and unstable moods; inflammation of the bowels; spasms; stiffness in the limbs, swollen ankles, and sore, painful, inflamed legs; hemorrhoids <note>original: "the piles"</note>, and other symptoms of an overabundance of blood <note>original: "plenitude"</note>.

But all of this might easily be prevented by following a proper routine <note>original: "regimen"</note> and taking these Tinctures as the occasion may require. Whenever a woman has reason to suspect her menstruation is about to leave her, let her lose four, five, or six ounces of blood <note>note: bloodletting was a standard medical practice of the 1700s to reduce "excess" fluids</note>, as her physical condition <note>original: "habit of body"</note> will allow. Then, let her make a herbal tea <note>original: "decoction"</note> by taking one pound of gentian roots and half a pound each of senna and orange peels. Pour a gallon of hot water upon them, and after it has stood for twenty-four hours, pour off the liquid for use. 

She should take twenty to forty drops of the *Lunar Tincture* in a small glass <note>original: "gill-glass"; about 4 ounces</note> full of the herbal tea mentioned above, every night and morning for ten days. Then, let her continue taking it every morning for ten days more, and afterward once every two or three days—or more often if the discharge is of a bad color and smell—until the condition is corrected. This course must be followed every spring and autumn <note>original: "fall"</note> for a month or six weeks in a row by all women who find their menstruation comes irregularly or too lightly, until it entirely ceases. 

After it has ceased, the patient should put herself under a course of the *Solar Tincture* for a month or six weeks, taking one spoonful in a wine glass of warm water every night and morning for a week. Then, let it be taken only once a day in cold water for the remainder of the time. If she occasionally takes two tablespoons of the *Solar Tincture* diluted in a large glass <note>original: "tumbler"</note> of warm water as a drink after dinner or supper, instead of wine or brandy and water, it will be very beneficial in establishing a healthy state of the blood and carrying off the sticky fluids <note>original: "viscid humours"</note> generally produced by the menstrual flow <note>original: "flux"</note> returning into the system.

### OF MASCULINE, OR SOLAR, DISEASES.

Solar diseases are all those that arise from a hot and dry cause, and have their origin in the blood and lymph. Just as the rays flowing from the sun are the fountain of life and heat for the great world—the universal system of nature—so the blood flowing from the heart is the fountain of life and heat for the little world: the universal system of the *microcosm* <note>from the Greek for "little world," this was the traditional belief that the human body is a miniature reflection of the entire universe</note>, or the human body. 

And again, just as the stream of rays from the sun regulates the seasons and produces the variety of climates, so the stream of blood in a person's body (as it is affected by the sun) regulates and diversifies the form and figure of the entire human race. Just as seasons and climates are subject to the external elements—which are still governed by the superior influence of the sun—they are rendered either mild, healthful, and productive, or turbulent, pestilential, and barren. In the same way, the entire circulating mass of blood is affected by changes in climates and seasons, and by all the variations and agitations of the surrounding atmosphere. Because of this, diseases are induced in the blood; these are either mild, burning, or acute, in proportion to how much the <term>sanguiferous fluid</term> <note>the blood-carrying fluid, or the blood itself</note> becomes distempered and impaired by the action of the surrounding atmosphere. Thus we perceive the sun's influence on the human frame and discover that the origin of disease is in the blood. For animal life can only be sustained, and the body preserved in health and vigor, as long as this vital stream is kept in proper circulation, pure and uncontaminated.

From the express words of scripture—Leviticus 17:11, 14 and Deuteronomy 12:23—we are justified in concluding that "*in the BLOOD is the LIFE*"; and there is no doubt that the living principle of the blood constitutes the life of the body. This was the opinion of the celebrated <note>William Harvey (1578–1657), the physician who first described the systemic circulation of blood</note> Hervey, as well as many of the ancient philosophers and physicians; the late <note>John Hunter (1728–1793), a pioneering Scottish surgeon and anatomist famous for his work on blood and inflammation</note> Mr. John Hunter declared himself to be of the same way of thinking. 

We find that the blood unites living parts, in some circumstances, as certainly as the fresh sap of a branch from one tree unites it with that of another. If either of these fluids were considered to be foreign or dead matter, they would act as irritants <note>original: "stimuli"</note>, and no union would take place in the animal or vegetable kingdoms. Mr. Hunter established this argument by the following experiment: Having removed the testicle from a living rooster, he inserted it into the abdomen of a living hen. Many weeks later, when injecting fluid into the liver of the hen, he found the fluid entered the testicle of the rooster as well, which had come in contact with the liver and stuck to it. In the nature of things, there is not a more intimate connection between life and a solid part than between life and a liquid. For, although we are more accustomed to connect life with the former than the latter, yet the only real difference

The only difference which can be shown between a solid and a fluid is that the particles of the one are less movable among themselves than those of the other. Besides, we often see the same body fluid in one case and solid in another. The blood will also become vascular <note>filled with blood vessels</note> like other living parts. Mr. Hunter <note>John Hunter (1728–1793), a pioneering Scottish surgeon and anatomist who argued that blood was "alive"</note> affirms that, after amputations, the <term>coagula</term> <note>blood clots</note> in the ends of arteries form vessels and may be injected by injecting these arteries. He had a preparation by which he could demonstrate vessels rising from the center of what had been only a clot of blood and opening into a stream of circulating blood. 

If blood is taken from the arm in the most intense cold which the human body can bear, it raises the thermometer to the same height as blood taken in the most sultry heat. This is a strong proof of the blood's being alive; for living bodies alone have the power of resisting great degrees of both heat and cold, and of maintaining in almost every situation, while in health, that temperature which we distinguish by the name of <term>animal heat</term> <note>internal body temperature</note>. 

Blood is likewise capable of being acted upon by a stimulus; for it coagulates from exposure as certainly as the cavities of the abdomen and thorax <note>the chest</note> inflame from the same cause. The more it is alive—that is, the more the animal is in health—the sooner it coagulates on exposure. The more it has lost of its <term>living principle</term> <note>the vital force believed to animate living matter</note>, as in the case of violent inflammations, the less it is sensible to the stimulus produced by being exposed, and it coagulates later. 

We may likewise observe that the blood preserves life in different parts of the body. When the nerves going to a part are tied or cut, the part becomes paralytic and loses all power of motion, but it does not mortify <note>decay or die</note>. If the artery is cut, the part dies, and mortification ensues. What keeps it alive in the first case? Nothing but the living principle, which alone can keep it alive; and this phenomenon is inexplicable on any other supposition than that life is contained in the blood. 

Another argument is drawn by Mr. Hunter from a case of a fractured <term>os humeri</term> <note>original: "os humeri"; the humerus, or upper arm bone</note>.
