As the bones had not united, Mr. Hunter injected the arm after death. He found that the cavity between the ends of the bones was filled up with blood which had coagulated. This blood had become vascular, or full of vessels. In some places, it was very much so. 

He does not maintain that all coagulated blood becomes vascular, and indeed the reason is obvious: for it is often thrown out and coagulated in parts where its becoming vascular could serve no purpose in the system—as, for example, in the cavities of <term>aneurismal sacs</term> <note>original: "aneurismal sacs"; the bulging walls of a weakened artery, known today as aneurysms</note>. For this reason, they say, it is plain we must suppose the nervous system, and not the blood, to properly contain the life of the animal, and consequently to be the principal vital organ. 

The supporters of this argument deny that the vital fluid is secreted from the blood by the brain. They say that any fluid secreted from the blood must be watery, inelastic, and inactive, whereas the nervous fluid is full of vigor, elastic, and volatile in the highest degree. They argue that the great necessity for the circulation of blood through all parts of the body—despite the presence of the nervous fluid in those same parts—is because a degree of tension is necessary to be given to the fibers to prepare them for the influx of the nervous fluid. This tension, they believe, is received from the filling of the blood vessels, which are dispersed everywhere along with the nerves.

To follow this opinion through every argument would prove tedious and unnecessary, as the following short observations will decide the matter absolutely against the patrons of the nervous system. In the first place, if we can prove the life of the human body to have been communicated from a fluid to the nervous system, the argument by analogy will be very strongly in favor of the supposition that this remains the case. 

Now, it is most evident that this was once the case. I have shown that the human body—as well as the body of every other living creature—in its first state is a **gelatinous mass** <note>original: "gelatinous mass"; here referring to the early embryonic state before organs are defined</note> without muscles, nerves, or blood vessels. Nevertheless, this jelly-like matter even at that time contained the nervous fluid. There can be no doubt of this because the nerves are formed out of it and derive their original power from it. Furthermore, it is remarkable that the brain is observed to be the part of the animal that is formed first. We can give no further account of this gelatinous or procreative fluid than that it is the nutritious matter from which the whole body appears to be formed. At the original formation of man and other animals, therefore, this nutritious matter was made the **substratum** <note>the foundation or base layer</note> of the whole body—consisting of muscles, nerves, blood vessels, and so on. Nay, more: it was the immediate **efficient cause** <note>the primary agent or force that produces an effect</note> of the nervous power itself. Again, in the formation of the embryo,

Consequently, as soon as the blood became the only nutritious juice of the body, the nervous fluid took up its residence there. From the blood, it diffused itself along the nerves, where it was regulated exactly according to the model originally formed in the embryo. 

Perhaps it may be said that the vital power, once it has taken possession of the human or any other body, requires no addition or supply, but remains there in the same quantity from first to last. If we suppose the nervous power to be immaterial, this would indeed be the case, and there would be an end to reasoning on the subject. However, if we call this power a volatile and elastic fluid, it is plain that there will be more need for replenishment for such a power than for any other fluid in the body, as its volatility and elasticity will encourage it to escape in great quantities through every pore of the body. 

It may perhaps be objected that it is absurd to suppose the blood is capable of organizing matter in such a way as to direct its own motions. Yet, we have positive proof of even this in the case of the **electric fluid** <note>original: "electric fluid"; an 18th-century term for electricity, which was then thought to be a type of weightless fluid.</note>. For if any quantity of this matter tends to go from one place to another where it meets with difficulty—through the air, for instance—it will throw small conducting substances before it in order to facilitate its progress. Also, if a number of small and light conducting substances are laid between two metallic bodies so as to form a circle, for example, a shock of electricity will destroy that circle. It will place the small conducting substances nearer to a straight line between the two metals, as if the fluid knew there was a shorter passage and resolved to take it if it should have occasion to return. 

Lastly, it is universally allowed that the brain is a **secretory organ** <note>A gland or organ that produces and releases a specific substance.</note>, made up of an infinite number of small glands which have no other **excretories** <note>Channels or ducts for discharge.</note> than the **medullary fibers** <term>medullary fibers</term> <note>Nerve fibers located in the white matter of the brain.</note> and nerves. As a considerable quantity of blood is carried to the brain and the minute arteries end in these small glands, it follows that the nervous fluid must come from the blood. Now, there is no gland in the human or any other body that will not discharge the fluid it is appointed to secrete in a very considerable quantity if its duct is cut. Upon the cutting of a nerve, therefore, the fluid secreted by the brain ought to be discharged; yet, no such discharge is visible. Man, however, is not left without defense against so many and such great dangers. The human body possesses a most wonderful power by which it preserves itself from diseases, wards off many, and very quickly cures some that have already begun, while others are more slowly brought to a successful conclusion by the same means. This power, called the self-ruling power <note>original: *autocrateia*</note> or the healing power of nature <note>original: *vis medicatrix naturæ*</note>, is well known to both physicians and philosophers, who most justly celebrate it; for this alone is sufficient for curing many diseases and is helpful in all. In fact, even the best medicines work only by stimulating and properly directing this expulsive force. Through this force, waste fluids <note>original: "excrementitious humours"</note> from food and blood are expelled through the proper channels of evacuation and the excretory ducts—chiefly by means of **insensible perspiration**. By this power, the harmful fluids in the blood and bodily juices are constantly being released. But although physicians rightly place confidence in this power, and though it generally cures minor diseases, we should not think that more serious conditions should be left to the unassisted efforts of nature. Physicians must therefore avoid a two-fold error: either dismissing the healing power of nature too much when it could achieve a complete cure if left alone, or placing too much confidence in these natural efforts, leaving them unsupported until the severity of infection or disease undermines the constitution and destroys everything in its path.

The primary and constant means by which foul and harmful fluids in the blood and juices are continually carried away is undoubtedly through the pores and vessels of perspiration. It is essential for good health to keep these open, which is the principal purpose for which medicines are used. When this evacuation is abundant and visible to the eye, as in sweat, the perspiration is called **sensible**; but where it is so light <note>original: "volatile"</note> that the senses do not notice it, as is the case in the body's normal state, it is called **insensible perspiration**. 

The vessels through which perspiration occurs lie slanted <note>original: "obliquely"</note> open under the small scales <note>original: *squamæ*</note> of the cuticle, or outer layer of skin <note>original: "scarf-skin"</note>. Sanctorius <note>Santorio Santorio (1561–1636) was a Venetian physician who famously weighed himself, his food, and his waste for decades to study metabolism.</note> discovered in Italy—observing middle-aged people with moderate diets and easy lifestyles—that the matter "insensibly perspired" (evaporated through the skin and lungs) accounted for five-eighths of the food consumed. This left only three-eighths for bodily nutrition and for waste from the nose, ears, intestines, bladder, and other organs.

The same author demonstrates that as much waste is released through insensible perspiration in a single day as is evacuated by stool in fourteen days. Specifically, in the course of a night, about sixteen ounces are typically discharged as urine, four ounces by stool, and over forty ounces by insensible perspiration. He also observes that if a person consumes eight pounds of food and drink in a day, five pounds of it are released through insensible perspiration. He adds a timeline: within five hours of eating, about one pound is perspired; from the fifth to the twelfth hour, about three pounds; and from the twelfth to the sixteenth hour, barely half a pound. Monsieur Dodart <note>Denis Dodart (1634–1707) was a French physician known for his long-term metabolic studies similar to those of Sanctorius.</note>, based on experiments conducted over thirty-three consecutive years, proves that we perspire much more in youth than in old age. In some people, perspiration is so abundant that they produce very little solid waste, even though they eat heartily.

The benefits of insensible perspiration are so vital that animal life could not be sustained without it. The general cause of perspiration is the circulation and heat of the blood, which allows the body to cast off harmful substances. The great subtlety, consistency, and abundance of this perspiration—and its increase after sleep—are primary signs of perfect health and the main way to maintain it. Conversely, any deviation from these is the first certain sign of approaching illness.

Perspiration is carried out, maintained, and increased by the internal organs <note>original: "viscera"</note>, blood vessels, and tissues; by movement or exercise up to the point where visible sweat first appears; by the moderate practice of sexual activity <note>original: "venery"</note>; and by seven or eight hours of sleep while the body is well-covered but not weighed down by heavy bedding. Other factors include a cheerful mood; light, fermented, yet solid food (not fatty); and pure, rather than heavy, air. The opposites of these factors—as well as an increase in other bodily evacuations—diminish, prevent, or corrupt perspiration. 

From this, we see the cause and effect of this perspiration: its role in keeping body parts soft and flexible and in replacing lost fluids, but primarily in keeping the nerve endings <note>original: "nervous papillæ"</note> moist, fresh, and alert, so they can be stimulated by objects and transmit those sensations. This is why a blockage of normal perspiration leads to so many ailments, particularly fevers, agues <note>fever and chills, often associated with malaria</note>, and respiratory discharges <note>original: "rheums"</note>. Too much perspiration causes weakness and fainting, while too little (or none at all) causes the capillary vessels to dry up, wither, and fail. This also leads the larger waste-clearing organs <note>original: "emunctories"</note> to become blocked, which disturbs circulation and causes sharp, irritating fluids <note>original: "humours"</note> to be retained; and hence

Cold prevents perspiration by constricting the pores of the skin and thickening the liquids circulating in the cutaneous glands <note>the glands of the skin</note>. Heat, on the contrary, increases it, both by opening the excretory ducts of the glands and by increasing the fluidity and speed of the humours <note>original: "humours"; the traditional medical theory of the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that were thought to determine health and temperament</note>. To determine the state and condition of perspiration—which is necessary for judging the health of the body—Sanctorius invented a weighing-chair. With this, he examined the quantity and degree of perspiration under various bodily conditions, different air temperatures, and in the intervals between eating, drinking, and sleeping.

Some of the more extraordinary phenomena observed in this study are: that for some time after eating, perspiration is at its lowest; that it is greatest between the fifth and twelfth hour after meals; and that riding on horseback, in a coach, or on a ship, as well as brisk motion on ice, promote perspiration surprisingly. Above all, however, a brisk friction <note>vigorous rubbing</note> of the skin promotes it. It was also noted that perspiration is naturally much lower in women than in men. 

Perspiration is also influenced by the passions of the mind. For instance, anger and joy increase both perspiration and urine, while fear and sadness lessen them. Anger causes a strong motion in the membranes of the heart and quickens its contraction and dilation. This, in turn, speeds up the contraction and dilation of the blood vessels and secreting <note>original: "fecerning"; an archaic term for the process of secreting or separating fluids</note> ducts, consequently increasing the discharge of perspiration and urine. This increase is more or less in proportion to the strength and duration of the passion. Joy affects these discharges in the same way as anger. In the passions of fear and sorrow, perspiration and urine are lessened by the depression of the soul's activity under those states. The proportion of perspiration to urine is increased by all exercises that increase the movement of the blood and warm the skin.

We have an account of a person who, by passing many nights in astronomical observations <note>original: "speculations"</note>, had his perspiration so obstructed by the cold and damp air of Holland that a shirt he had worn for five or six weeks was as clean as if it had been worn for only one day. The consequence of this was that he developed subcutaneous waters <note>edema or dropsy; fluid trapped under the skin</note>, though he was eventually cured. 

The garments best calculated to encourage and promote insensible perspiration, to keep the mouths of the tiny vessels open, and to guard the body from the too sudden and violent effects of cold, are those made of flannel. For this reason, flannel shirts and waistcoats—or even a square piece of flannel worn over the breast or the pit of the stomach, particularly in the winter months—produce beneficial effects for weakly and debilitated constitutions, and act as a valuable preventative for the healthy and robust. ### BITE OF A MAD DOG, OR ANY VENOMOUS REPTILE.

The fatal disease resulting from the bite of a mad dog is *hydrophobia* <note>original: "Hydrophobia"; from the Greek words for "water" and "fear"</note>, or "dread of water." This symptom first suggested the practice of dipping patients in the sea as a cure. It is very remarkable that these patients have not only a dread of water, but of everything bright or transparent. Soon after this condition takes hold, the mind becomes impaired; this shows that the poison is carried through the blood to the nervous fluid, and from there to the brain. Dr. James, in his *Treatise on Canine Madness*, mentions a boy sent out to fill two bottles with water who was so terrified by the noise of the liquid running into them that he fled into the house crying out that he was bewitched. He also mentions the case of a farmer who, going to draw some ale from a cask, was terrified to such a degree at its running into the vessel that he ran out in great haste with the spigot still in his hand. 

But in whatever manner this symptom comes on, it is certain that the most painful sensations accompany every attempt to swallow liquids. Indeed, the bare sight of water, of a looking glass, or of anything clear or translucent <note>original: "pellucid"</note> will cause the utmost uneasiness, or even throw the patient into convulsions. In this disease there seems to be an extreme sensitivity and irritability of the nervous system. The eyes cannot bear the light or the sight of anything white; the least touch or motion offends them, and they need to be kept as quiet and in as dark a place as possible. Some complain of the coldness of the air, frequently when it is really warm. Others complain of violent heat and have a great desire for cold air, which yet never fails to increase the symptoms. In all cases, there is a great flow of saliva into the mouth; this is exceedingly troublesome to the patients, as it has the same effect upon their throat <note>original: "fauces"; the opening at the back of the mouth</note> that other liquids [have.]

The head feels heavy and the ears tingle; the urine is clear <note>original: "limpid"</note>. At last they grow weary; the fits become less violent and cease toward the end. The pulse becomes weak, irregular, and not very quick; they sweat, and finally the whole body becomes cold. They settle themselves quietly as if to go to sleep, and so they die. A general observation was that the lint and dressings of the wounds, even when dry, were always black, even when the pus appeared healthy in color and appearance. In one of Dr. Wolf’s patients who recovered, the blood smelled intolerably foul as it was drawn from a vein; and one of Mr. Vaughan’s patients complained of an unbearable, foul <note>original: "foetid"</note> smell coming from the wounded part, though nobody but himself could perceive it. But this does not always happen; for Mr. Vaughan mentions the case of a patient in whom, "when he had apparently ceased to breathe, the cynic spasm <note>original: "spasmus cynicus"; a convulsive distortion of the facial muscles, often resembling a forced, grimacing grin</note> was observable, with an odd convulsive motion in the muscles of the face. It was also remarkable that, in the last hours of his life, this patient stopped calling for drink—which had been his constant request—but was perpetually asking for something to eat."

Hydrophobia <note>literally "fear of water," a primary symptom of rabies</note> seems to be a symptom peculiar to the human race; for the rabid <note>original: "mad"</note> animals which spread the infection do not seem to have any dread of water. Despite this, dipping <note>the practice of forcibly submerging a person or animal in water, often the sea, as a supposed cure</note> is the common remedy for the treatment of both dogs and men. Regarding the symptoms of madness in dogs, they are very ambiguous <note>original: "equivocal"</note>. Those symptoms specifically listed by some authors are only what might be expected in dogs that are overheated or agitated by being violently pursued and struck. 

One symptom, if it could be relied upon, would settle the matter: namely, that all other dogs avoid and run away from one that is rabid. Even large dogs will not attack even the smallest dog infected with this disease. Based on this assumption, some point out a method for discovering whether a dog that has been killed was really rabid or not: by rubbing a piece of meat along the inside of its mouth and then offering it to a healthy dog. If the healthy dog eats it, it is a sign the first dog was not rabid; but if the healthy dog rejects it with a kind of howling noise, it is certain that the first one was. Dr. James <note>Dr. Robert James (1703–1776), an English physician famous for his medical dictionary and "fever powders"</note> tells us that among dogs, the disease is infectious just by staying in the same place. He claims that after a kennel has been once infected, any dogs placed in it will be in danger of going mad for a considerable time afterward. A remedy for this, he says, is to keep geese in the kennel for some time. He rejects as false the opinion that dogs stop barking when they go mad, though he admits that there is a very significant change in their bark, which becomes hoarse and hollow.

Regarding the immediate cause among mankind, there is not the least doubt that hydrophobia is caused by the saliva of the rabid animal mixing with the blood. It does not appear that this can take effect through the outer skin <note>original: "cuticula"</note>; but when the skin is broken, the smallest quantity of saliva is sufficient to spread the disease. A slight scratch from the teeth of a rabid animal has been found just as deadly <note>original: "pernicious"</note> as a large wound. It is also certain that the infection has been spread by the bites of dogs, cats, wolves, foxes, weasels, pigs, and even roosters and hens when they are in a state of madness. However, it does not appear that the disease is transmissible from one person suffering from hydrophobia to another, whether by a bite or any other means.

## OF THE
# PRINCIPLES
### OF
# LIFE AND DEATH.

Life denotes the animated state of nature; and in human beings <note>OCR error: "inhuman beings"</note>, it exists as long as a union of the soul and body lasts. With us, therefore, life continues until such a separation has really taken place. This separation can no more be said to have happened during the peak <note>original: "paroxism"</note> of a fit, or from a blow which for a time deprives us of sensation, or in the *early* period of an unnatural or sudden death, than it can be said to happen during the time we are asleep. It is the lack of proper skill at such times that too often causes death to occur when life still absolutely exists in the blood and might, with a little care, have been preserved. Death is, therefore, the act of separation of the soul from the body; in this sense, it stands opposed to life, which consists in their union. An animal body, through the actions inseparable from life, undergoes a continual change and experiences its decay <note>original: "dissolution"</note> by degrees. Its smallest fibers become rigid; its minuter vessels...

...vessels grow into solid fibers that are no longer permeable <note>original: "pervious"</note> to fluids; its larger vessels grow hard and narrow, and everything becomes contracted, closed, and bound up. At length, through the course of these changes, death becomes inevitable as the necessary consequence of life. But it is rare indeed that life is prolonged this far, or that death occurs merely from the natural decay and impairment of old age. Accidental diseases, and our own neglect of preserving our health, usually cut the work short.

The signs of death are often very uncertain. If we consult what Winslow or Bruhier <note>Jacques-Bénigne Winslow (1669–1760) and Jean-Jacques Bruhier d'Ablaincourt (1685–1756) were famous physicians who wrote extensively on the uncertainty of the signs of death and the dangers of premature burial.</note> have said on this subject, we shall be convinced that the boundary <note>original: "shade"</note> between life and death is so nearly invisible that even all the powers of medical art can scarcely determine where the one ends and the other begins. The color of the face, the warmth of the body, and the flexibility of the joints are but uncertain signs of life still remaining. On the contrary, a pale complexion, a cold body, stiffness in the limbs, the stopping of all motion, and the total lack of feeling in the body parts are only uncertain marks that death has begun. In the same manner, regarding the pulse and breathing, these movements are so often suppressed that it is impossible to perceive them.

By bringing a mirror near to the mouth of the person supposed to be dead, people often expect to find whether he breathes or not. But this is a very uncertain experiment: the glass is frequently clouded <note>original: "sullied"</note> by the moisture <note>original: "vapour"</note> of the dead man's body; and often the person is still alive even though the glass is not tarnished at all. There are many instances of persons who have endured all of these and afterwards recovered without any outside assistance, to the astonishment of those watching. 

This surely ought to be a warning against hasty burials, especially in cases of sudden death. It is shocking to reflect that some hundreds of valuable members of society are annually torn from their grieving families by some accidental sudden cause and hurried thoughtlessly to the grave, even though the principles of life in them were capable of being revived! In the biological system <note>original: "animal œconomy"</note>, "*the BLOOD is the LIFE*"; (Leviticus 17:11, 14; Deuteronomy 12:23); therefore, if its circulation is suspended or destroyed, death follows. For this reason, whenever any accident has happened by which sudden death appears to have occurred—whether by blows, seizures <note>original: "fits"</note>, falls, suffocation, strangulation, drowning, apoplexy <note>a stroke</note>, convulsion fits, thunder and lightning, assassination, duelling, or similar events—let the unfortunate person be carried into a warm house and laid by the fire, or put into a warm bed. There, as the blood warms and expands <note>original: "rarefying"</note>, it will press in every direction. Resisted by the valves, it will swell to fill the limp <note>original: "flaccid"</note> right auricle <note>one of the upper chambers</note> of the heart, which had become empty and still from the shock. This stimulation of the heart's fibers will put them back into motion. The right auricle, being thus filled and stimulated into contraction, fills the ventricle; the ventricle, being irritated by this, likewise contracts and empties itself into the pulmonary artery. The moment this is done, the circulation begins again where it left off. The lungs, being filled by the oxygen <note>original: "dephlogisticated air," a term used by 18th-century chemists before "oxygen" became the standard name</note> contained in the medicine, begin to act, and life is restored—provided the organs and fluids are in a fit state for it, which they undoubtedly are much more often than is imagined. 

Nor is this stimulating action of the Tincture upon the heart at all surprising; for every medical man knows, or ought to know, that the heart, even when taken out of the body, will beat again and try to perform its functions if it is pricked with a pin or has warm water thrown upon it, even if it had been motionless for some time before. No person, therefore, should be considered dead until the energy of the blood is so far gone that it can never again be stirred to fill and stimulate the contraction of the venous sinus <note>original: "sinus venosus"</note> and the auricle of the heart.

## OF THE CRISIS, OR CRITICAL TURN, OF A DISEASE.

The crisis of a disease is nothing other than the struggle between nature and the illness <note>original: "infirmity"</note> to see which of them shall prevail. If nature overcomes the malignancy of the disease at the time of the crisis, it is a sure sign it will be cured; but if the sickness prevails, it is then a dangerous <note>original: "pernicious"</note> crisis and shows sudden changes for the worse. Every sudden and vehement movement of the disease may be called a crisis; therefore critical, decisive <note>original: "decretory"</note>, and fatal <note>original: "dismal"</note> days are all one and the same thing. They signify nothing more than a certain and more sure judgment of the illness afflicting the patient—either becoming more powerful or less intense—at those times when the true crisis happens. Therefore, a crisis is to be calculated from that moment of time when the disease first attacked <note>original: "invaded"</note> the patient. On this ground, I shall make some observations to prove the truth of what I have now to deliver, and of what I have before so often proved: that I cannot but marvel at the wonderful providence of God, who disposes all things by number, weight, and measure. He prescribes to the whole system of nature so unchangeable <note>original: "immutable"</note> a law that it would be as easy for the Heaven and the Earth to return to their original chaos as to break and violate <note>original: "infringe"</note> that unchangeable law, unless the divine will and pleasure alters it miraculously.

We distinguish <note>original: "discriminate"</note> two sorts of diseases: acute and chronic. Of acute diseases, some are simple acute, others *peracute* (that is, very acute), and others again are *perper-acute*, or exceedingly acute. Those that are simple acute are finished in eight, ten, eleven, fourteen, twenty, or twenty-one days. They are ended in the time the Moon travels through <note>original: "traceth"</note> the twelve celestial signs of the zodiac, which is twenty-seven days and eight hours.

Those acute diseases which undergo changes are very fickle; for sometimes they increase, and sometimes they subside <note>original: "are remitted"</note>, according to whether the Moon meets with the beams of either beneficial <note>original: "benefice"</note> or harmful <note>original: "baneful"</note> planets. Sometimes they change from acute diseases into chronic; thus, a continued fever may change into a hectic fever <note>a fever associated with wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note>, or an intermittent fever into a continual fever; and these diseases end within forty days.

Very acute diseases are those that end in five, six, seven, or eight days; among which is the disease called *peripneumonia* <note>original: "inflammation of the lungs"</note>. Exceedingly acute diseases are those that end in three or four days at farthest, such as pestilences, apoplexies, etc.

Chronic diseases follow the motion of the Sun, and it is about ninety days before the first crisis begins to appear; for in that time the Sun comes to the proper quartile <term>an astrological aspect where a planet is 90 degrees from its starting position, often marking a period of tension or change</term> of the place he was in at the decumbiture <term>the moment a patient first takes to their bed due to illness</term>, as appears in hectic fevers, dropsies, and the like. This cycle continues through all twelve signs of the zodiac, and over again if the disease has not ended by then, as will clearly appear in the following Table. <header>AND OCCULT SCIENCE.</header>

With respect to moderate or slight diseases, Hippocrates asserted, in the first place, that contraries (or opposites) are the remedies for each other. He explains this maxim with an aphorism, in which he says that evacuations <note>The process of emptying or clearing the body of fluids.</note> cure those illnesses <note>original: "distempers"</note> which come from repletion <note>original: "repletion"; a state of being overfull, often from excess food or fluids.</note>, and repletion cures those that are caused by evacuation. Similarly, heat is destroyed by cold, and cold by heat, and so on.

In the second place, he asserted that medicine <note>original: "physic"</note> is the addition of what is wanting and the subtraction or reduction of what is superfluous. This axiom is explained by the fact that there are some juices or humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health.</note> which, in particular cases, ought to be drained <note>original: "evacuated"</note>, driven out of the body, or dried up; while others ought to be restored to the body or produced there again. 

As to the method for this addition or reduction, he gives this general caution: you ought to be careful not to fill up or empty the body all at once, too quickly, or too much. It is equally dangerous to heat or cool the body suddenly; in fact, you ought not to do it at all, for anything that runs to an excess is an enemy to nature.

In the fourth place, Hippocrates allowed that we ought sometimes to dilate (open) and sometimes to lock up (close) the passages. We should open the passages by which the humors are naturally discharged when they are not sufficiently open or when they are blocked. On the contrary, we should close or narrow the passages that are too relaxed when the juices passing through them should not be doing so, or when they pass in too great a quantity. 

He adds that we ought sometimes to smooth and sometimes to make rough; sometimes to harden and sometimes to soften; sometimes to make more fine or supple; and sometimes to thicken. We must sometimes rouse the body and at other times stupefy it or take away sensation—all in relation to the solid parts of the body or to the humors. 

He also gives this further lesson: we ought to pay attention to the course the humors take—where they come from and where they go. Consequently, when they go where they should not, we should make them turn around or carry them another way, almost like redirecting the course of a river. On other occasions, we should endeavor, if possible, to recall the humors or make them return back again, drawing upward those that have a tendency to go downward, and drawing downward those that tend upward. We ought also to carry off, by convenient ways, whatever is necessary to be removed, and not let the humors once emptied <note>original: "evacuated"</note> enter back into the vessels. 

Hippocrates also gives the following instruction: when we do anything according to reason, even if the success does not match our expectations, we ought not to change our method of acting too easily or too hastily, as long as the reasons for it remain sound. But, as this maxim might sometimes prove deceptive, he gives the following as a correction to it:

> "We ought," he says, "to mind with a great deal of attention what gives ease and what creates pain; what is easily supported and what cannot be endured."

## CULPEPER’S BRITISH HERBAL.

---

Having given a detailed <note>original: "minute"</note> description of the plants and herbs contained in Culpeper’s British Herbal, along with their medical properties and effects, I shall proceed to an investigation of some foreign trees, plants, and herbs that are now in general use among us. First, we will look at the:

### PERUVIAN or JESUIT’S BARK.

**PERUVIAN BARK** <note>original: "CORTEX PERUVIANUS"</note>, also called *quinquina*, *kinkinna*, *quina-quina*, Fathers' powder <note>original: "pulvis patrum"; a name given because Jesuit priests introduced it to Europe in the 1600s</note>, and popularly known as Jesuit’s bark, is the bark of a tree growing in the West Indies. It is called by the Spaniards *palo de calenturas*, meaning <note>original: "q. d." or "quasi dictum"</note> fever-wood, because of its extraordinary power in removing all kinds of intermittent <note>original: "intermitting"</note> fevers and agues <note>term: Ague was a common name for malaria or any fever characterized by shivering and sweating.</note>. The Indians commonly call it the *fuddling-tree* because of its property of intoxicating fish when either its wood or bark is beaten and soaked in the water where they are. 

The tree that yields this noble remedy <note>original: "specific"</note> is only found in Peru, in the province of San Francisco de Quito (or Quinto), near the city of Loja <note>original: "Loxa"</note>; though some say it is also found in Potosí, and Father Labat claims it is in the island of Guadeloupe <note>original: "Guadeloupa"</note>. While on the tree, the bark is streaked, appearing a whitish-yellow on the outside and a pale tan-color within.

The Spaniards distinguish four sorts of this precious bark: the *reddish bark* <note>original: "cascarilla colorada"</note>; the *yellowish* <note>original: "amarylla"</note>; the *curling* <note>original: "crespilla"</note>; and the *whitish* <note>original: "blanca"</note>. The red and yellow varieties are considered the best; the curling is the pro-

produce of the same sort of tree, only growing in a colder climate, which impairs the quality of the bark and renders it whitish on the outside and cinnamon-colored within, making it unfit for medicinal use. As for the *blanca* <note>original: "white bark"</note>, it is procured from another species of the tree that has a much larger trunk, leaves of a lighter green color, and bark made of a very thick, spongy substance that is whitish on the outside. It is also so tough that it requires the force of an axe to slice it from the tree. When first cut down, it is as bitter as the best sort and has the same power <note>original: "virtue"</note> in the cure of intermittent fevers; however, when dry and kept for any length of time, it grows insipid and becomes useless. In reality, both sorts are found to have much surer and quicker effects when fresh <note>original: "green"</note> than when dry, so that the Europeans only receive the second-rate benefits. What is worse, the inferior sort is very plentiful, while the good sort is very scarce and hard to find; for this reason, large quantities of the worst sort are usually mixed with the little bit of fine bark sent yearly to Panama for transport to Europe.

The *amarylla* <note>original: "yellowish"</note>, or "small bark," which curls up like sticks of cinnamon and is much esteemed in England—as it is supposed to be taken from the branches of the tree and therefore more effective in curing fevers—is actually only the bark of the younger trees, which curls in this manner because it is very thin. The bark of the branches is never gathered, as it would not compensate for the expense of cutting it. The season for cutting the bark is in August, the only settled dry time in the country. After a tree has been stripped of its bark, it requires eighteen or twenty years for good bark to grow back. Mr. Arrot, a Scottish surgeon who had gathered the bark in the place where it grows, is of the opinion that the gathering of the better sort of bark will soon come to an end, or at least be very much reduced. This is partly because of its distance from any inhabited place and the density <note>original: "impenetrability"</note> of the woods where it grows, and partly because of the lack of indigenous people <note>original: "Indians"</note> to cut it, whose population <note>original: "race"</note>, through the cruelties of the Spaniards, is likely to become totally extinct.

The most accurate account we have ever received of the tree which produces the *quinquina*, or true Peruvian bark, is from Monsieur de la Condamine <note>Charles Marie de La Condamine (1701–1774), a French explorer and scientist</note> who, while traveling through parts of America, chose the route of Loja <note>original: "Loxa"</note>, where the finest bark is gathered and where the greatest number of the trees is found. Taking instructions from Monsieur de Jussieu <note>Joseph de Jussieu (1704–1779), a French botanist</note>, he informed himself concerning it. The *quinquina* tree never grows in the plains; it is a constant inhabitant of the mountains and is easily known from the trees among which it stands by its erect growth and its height when it is of a significant age, as it always carries its head above the rest, as well as by its size. These trees are never found in clumps or clusters together, but always separate or single among other kinds. It is very rare, however, to find any large ones at this time on the mountain where the bark is gathered, as the great demand for it has made

<meta>This page continues the botanical description of the Peruvian bark tree (Cinchona), specifically detailing the harvesting process, the dangers of improper drying, and a precise anatomical description of its leaves, flowers, and seeds.</meta>

<header>CULPEPER's BRITISH HERBAL.</header>

This led the harvesters to bark all the trees, causing them all to perish; for old trees never recover from being stripped of their bark, though young ones frequently do. The bark is now gathered at all times, provided the weather is dry. When the bark is taken off, it is laid in the sun until it is perfectly dry. Neglecting this step and packing the bark while it is still moist has often caused it to become moldy and spoiled. Merchants once attributed this to harvesting at the wrong time of the moon, when it was actually entirely due to the bark being put into the transport skins while too wet.

The leaves of the <term>quinquina-tree</term> <note>the Cinchona tree, native to the Andes and the source of quinine</note> grow on <term>pedicels</term> <note>original: "pedicles"; the small stalks that support individual leaves</note> about half an inch long. They are very smooth and glossy, and of a beautiful green, though somewhat paler on the underside than the top. They are perfectly smooth at the edges and have an oblong shape, pointed at the tip and rounded at the part where they join the stalk. They are between two and a half to three inches in length, and an inch and a half to two inches in breadth. The middle rib of the leaf is rounded on the upper side and is usually reddish, especially near the <term>pedicel</term>; the entire leaf often turns red when it is fully mature. All the small branches toward the top of the tree end in one or more clusters of flowers which, before they open, resemble the shape and color of common lavender. When these open, they change their color. Each stalk that supports one of these clusters grows from the <term>axil</term> <note>original: "ala"; the angle between the upper side of a leaf and the stem</note> of a leaf and divides into many small branches. Each branch ends in a <term>calyx</term> <note>original: "cup"; the green, leaf-like base of a flower</note> divided into five parts, which supports a flower resembling that of a <term>hyacinth</term>. It is composed of a tube three-quarters of an inch long, which is divided at the end into five, and sometimes six, <term>lobes</term> <note>original: "segments"</note>. These are a beautiful deep red on the inside and are <term>serrated</term> <note>notched like the teeth of a saw</note> around the edges in a very elegant manner. From the bottom of the flower's tube grows a white <term>pistil</term> <note>the female reproductive part of the flower</note> topped by a long green head; this rises above the level of the flower's <term>lobes</term> and is surrounded by five <term>stamens</term> <note>original: "stamina"; the male reproductive parts</note> which support <term>anthers</term> <note>original: "apices"; the pollen-bearing tips of the stamens</note> of a pale yellow color. These remain hidden within the flowers. The tube is a dull red and is covered with a kind of whitish down. After the flower has fallen, the <term>calyx</term> swells in the middle into the shape of an olive, which gradually grows into a fruit divided into two <term>cells</term> <note>internal chambers</note>. As it dries, it becomes shorter and the whole fruit becomes rounder than its natural state.

...produce of the same sort of tree, only growing in a colder climate, which impairs the quality of the bark, rendering it whitish on the outside and cinnamon-colored within, and unfit for medicinal use. As for the *blanca* <note>Spanish for "white"</note> bark, it is procured from another species of the tree with a much larger trunk, leaves of a lighter green, and bark with a very thick, spongy substance that is whitish on the outside. It is so tough that it requires the force of an ax to slice it from the tree. When first cut down, it is as bitter as the best variety and has the same power to cure <term>intermittent fevers</term> <note>original: "intermitting fevers"; fevers that stop and start at intervals, most notably malaria</note>; but when dry and kept for any length of time, it becomes tasteless and useless. In reality, both sorts are found to have much surer and quicker effects when green than when dry, so that Europeans only receive the second-rate benefits. What is worse, the inferior sort is very plentiful, while the good sort is very scarce and difficult to obtain. For this reason, large quantities of the worst sort are usually mixed with the little bit of fine bark sent yearly to Panama for export to Europe.

The *amarylla* <note>Spanish for "yellow"</note>, or small bark, which curls up like sticks of cinnamon and is highly esteemed in England, is supposed to be taken from the branches of the tree and therefore thought to be more effective in curing fevers. However, it is actually only the bark of younger trees, which is very thin and curls in this manner. The bark of the branches is never gathered, as it would not be worth the cost of the labor. The season for cutting the bark is in August, the only reliably dry time in that country. After a tree has been stripped of its bark, it takes eighteen or twenty years for a good layer of bark to grow back. Mr. Arrot, a Scottish surgeon who gathered the bark in its native region, is of the opinion that the collection of the better sort of bark will soon come to an end, or at least be very much reduced. This is partly because of its distance from any inhabited place and the density of the woods where it grows, and partly because of the lack of indigenous people to cut it, whose population—due to the cruelties of the Spaniards—is likely to become totally extinct.

The most accurate account we have ever received of the tree that produces the *quinquina* <note>the Cinchona tree, the source of quinine</note>, or true Peruvian bark, is from Monsieur de la Condamine. While traveling through parts of America, he chose the route of Loxa <note>modern Loja, Ecuador</note>, where the finest bark is gathered and where the greatest number of the trees are found. Following the instructions of Monsieur de Jussieu <note>Bernard de Jussieu, a famous French botanist</note>, he informed himself about the plant. The *quinquina* tree never grows in the plains; it is a constant inhabitant of the mountains. It is easily recognized among the surrounding trees by its erect growth and its height when it is of a significant age, as it always carries its canopy above the rest, and also by its size. These trees are never found in clumps or clusters together but always grow separately or singly among other kinds. However, it is very rare to find any large ones at this time on the mountain where the bark is gathered, as the great demand for it has...

The bark is now gathered at all times, provided the weather is dry. When the bark is taken off, it is laid in the sun until it is perfectly dry. Neglecting this step and packing the bark while it is still damp has often caused it to become moldy and spoil; the merchants have attributed this to harvesting it during the wrong phase of the moon, when it was actually entirely due to its being put into the skins <note>Bark was often transported in animal hides or "serons"</note> while too moist.

The leaves of the <term>quinquina-tree</term> <note>original: "quinquina-tree"; the Cinchona tree, from which quinine is derived</note> stand on <term>pedicels</term> <note>original: "pedicles"; the small stalks that attach a leaf or flower to the main stem</note> about half an inch long. The middle rib of the leaf is rounded on the upper side and is usually of a reddish color, especially toward the <term>pedicel</term>. The whole leaf often becomes red when it is perfectly mature. All the small branches toward the top of the tree end in one or more clusters of flowers, which, before they are open, resemble the shape and color of common lavender. When these open, they change their color; each stalk that supports one of these clusters arises from the <term>axil</term> <note>original: "ala"; the angle between the upper side of a leaf and the stem</note> of one of the leaves and divides into many small branches. Each of these ends in a cup divided into five parts, which supports a flower resembling that of the hyacinth. It is composed of a tube three-quarters of an inch long, which at the end is divided into five, and sometimes six, segments. These are a beautiful deep red inside and are serrated <note>toothed like a saw</note> around the edges in a very elegant manner. From the bottom of the tube of the flower there arises a white pistil, topped by a long green head; this rises above the level of the flower's segments and is surrounded by five <term>stamens</term> <note>original: "stamina"</note>, which support <term>anthers</term> <note>original: "apices"; the pollen-bearing part of the stamen</note> of a pale yellow color. Acad. Scienc. Par. 1738"; Memoirs of the Academy of Sciences, Paris, 1738</note>. By this description, it appears that those who first introduced the tree to us were very ignorant of its nature and characteristics, as they called it a species of *sebesten* <note>original: "sebesten"; a name for the fruit of the Cordia tree, which is unrelated to the Cinchona tree</note>.

The use of this febrifuge <note>original: "febrifuge"; a medicine used to reduce fever</note> seems to have been known by the indigenous people for a very long time, probably as early as 1500. Their method of taking it was to pound the bark and let it infuse in water, then drink the resulting infusion. Their hatred for their conquerors, the Spaniards, led them to keep it a secret from them for a long time. Even when the remedy became known among the residents of Loxa <note>modern-day Loja, Ecuador</note>, it remained a secret to the rest of the world. Its great value was never generally known until the year 1653. 

At that time, the wife of the viceroy of Peru, the Countess of Chinchon, had been ill for a long time with an intermittent fever that would not respond to any known remedies. The *corregidor* <note>original: "corregidor"; a Spanish magistrate or local administrative official</note> of Loxa sent a quantity of the quinquina bark to the viceroy, assuring him that it would cure the lady even though all other means had failed. Because of this, the magistrate was summoned to Lima, and after he administered the medicine to many other people with safety and success, the lady finally took it and was cured. 

Immediately after her recovery, she sent for a large quantity of the bark, had it ground into powder, and distributed it herself to those who needed it. This is how it earned the name "the Countess's powder." However, the lady soon grew tired of this duty and placed the Jesuits in charge of it. As they continued to provide it to the sick with the same success, it was then called "the Jesuits' powder." 

These reverend fathers soon found a way to send a quantity of it to Cardinal Lugo, who distributed it with equal success in Rome. After him, the apothecary at the college gave it for free to the poor with the same good effects, under the name of the "Jesuits' powder" or "the Cardinal’s powder." Later, the upper classes were made to pay for the medicine with its equivalent weight in silver to cover the costs of its importation, while the poor still received it for free. Louis XIV, who was then the Dauphin <note>original: "dauphin"; the title for the heir apparent to the French throne</note> of France, was cured by it of a fever that had not responded to other medicines. 

When the Count and Countess of Chinchon returned to Spain, their physician, Juan de Vega, who brought a great quantity of it back with him, sold it at a high price. Soon after this, large quantities were sent over on the galleons. However, the high demand from Europe caused the residents of Loxa to adulterate <note>original: "adulterate"; to make something poorer in quality by adding another substance</note> it with other barks, which nearly caused the medicine to lose its well-deserved reputation. Quinquina trees are currently found across the entire chain of mountains adjoining Cajanuma and in many other parts of the Americas.

...the reason for their ignorance about how to prepare and prescribe it, which caused it to fall out of use until around the year 1679. At that time, Mr. Talbot, an English medical practitioner, brought it back into fashion because of the great number of cures he performed at the court and in the city of Paris with this powder, prepared in his specific way. The secret of his method was made public soon after through the generosity of King Louis XIV, who rewarded Talbot for the discovery with 5,000 crowns. The preparation involves about two ounces of the *cortex* <note>original: "cortex"; Latin for "bark"</note> in powder form, infused in a sand-heat <note>a method of heating a vessel evenly by placing it in a container of hot sand</note> with about a quart of red wine. After this infusion, the wine must be poured off, and two or three ounces should be given every three or four hours between *paroxysms* <note>original: "paroxysms"; the periodic fits or recurring attacks of a fever</note> until the desired effect is achieved.

Quinquina <note>the bark from which quinine is derived, used to treat malaria</note> is sold either as bark or as a powder. Those who buy it in bark form must choose pieces that are very dry and compact—those that have never been dampened and which break cleanly and smoothly. It should be brittle between the teeth, easily ground into powder, and produce a powder of a pale cinnamon color. It has a musty kind of smell, yet enough of an aromatic quality that it is not unpleasant. The inferior types, when broken, appear woody, and they separate into fibers when chewed. The "female" bark is considerably thicker, whiter on the outside, redder on the inside, and has a weaker smell and taste than the former; it is much inferior in medicinal strength. The small, fine, "quilled" <note>bark that has dried into small, straw-like tubes</note> barks, which are <term>shagreened</term> <note>having a rough or granular texture like untanned leather</note> on the outside and reddish on the inside with a bitter, musty taste, are the most highly valued. The powder must be well-sifted, and care should be taken to buy it from trustworthy people, as it is very easy to <term>sophisticate</term> <note>to adulterate, fake, or mix with inferior substances</note> it, and it is difficult to detect the fraud. 

The red bark, recently brought into high reputation by the experiments of the clever Dr. Saunders <note>William Saunders (1743–1817), a prominent Scottish physician who wrote a famous treatise on the superior efficacy of red cinchona bark</note>, possesses the virtues of the common bark in a much higher degree. A quantity of it was introduced to London as part of the cargo of a Spanish ship from Lima, which was captured by an English frigate in 1779 and carried into Lisbon. Whether this is the bark of the trunk of full-grown trees, the branches, or young trees yielding the pale bark—or whether the trees are of different species—has not yet been accurately determined. In the province of Santa Fe, two kinds of *cinchona* have been lately discovered: one of which is the red bark of Peru, and the other is one of the white species.

The bark acts as a bitter, an <term>absorbent</term>, and an <term>astringent</term> (or <term>styptic</term> <note>a substance that stops bleeding or shrinks body tissues</note>). Regarding its bitterness, Monsieur Reneaulme <note>Michel-Louis Reneaulme de la Garanne (1675–1739), a French physician and botanist</note> observes that it becomes fit to soften sour, sharp juices; for "a sour and a bitter make a sweet." Furthermore, as an absorbent, it dulls the sharp points of acids and prevents them from acting; consequently, it preserves the fluidity of the body's juices, which acids would otherwise cause to clot. As a styptic, it must have earthy parts to absorb <term>serosities</term> <note>excess watery fluids or thin secretions in the body</note>, by which the parts that were previously dampened and relaxed will contract. By this means, the bark increases the "spring" and tension of the body's fibers. As a bitter, it warms the body and aids perspiration by warming and increasing...

The reason for their ignorance regarding how to prepare and prescribe it caused it to fall out of use until about the year 1679. At that time, Mr. Talbot, an English medical practitioner, brought it into popularity again due to the great number of cures achieved around the court and city of Paris with this powder, prepared according to his method. The secret of his preparation was soon after made public by the generosity of Louis XIV, who rewarded Talbot for the discovery with 5,000 crowns. The preparation consists of about two ounces of the *cortex* <note>original: "cortex"; the Latin word for bark, specifically referring here to Cinchona or Peruvian bark</note> in powder form, steeped in a sand-heat <note>original: "sand-heat"; a method of heating a container by placing it in hot sand to ensure an even, controlled temperature</note> with about a quart of red wine. After steeping, the wine must be poured off, and two or three ounces given every three or four hours between the paroxysms <note>original: "paroxysms"; the periodic fits or attacks of a fever</note> until the desired result is achieved.

The quinquina is sold either as bark or as powder. Those who buy it as bark must choose specimens that are very dry and compact. Bark that has never been dampened, breaks cleanly and smoothly, is easily crumbled between the teeth, is easily powdered, and yields a powder of a pale cinnamon color is best. It has a musty kind of smell, yet enough of an aroma that it is not disagreeable. The inferior kinds appear woody when broken and separate into fibers when chewed. The "female" bark is considerably thicker, whiter on the outside, redder on the inside, and weaker in smell and taste than the former, and is much inferior in medicinal value. The small, fine, "quilled" <note>bark that has dried and curled into small tubes or scrolls</note> barks, which are rough-textured on the outside and reddish within, with a bitter, musty taste, are the most highly valued. The powder must be well-sifted, and care must be taken to buy it from trusted persons, as it is very easy to sophisticate <note>original: "sophisticate"; to adulterate or cheapen a medicine by adding inferior or fake ingredients</note> it, and difficult to detect the fraud.

The **red bark**, lately brought into reputation by the experiments of the ingenious Dr. Saunders, possesses the virtues of the common bark in a much higher degree. A quantity of it was introduced to London as part of the cargo of a Spanish ship from Lima, which was captured by an English frigate in 1779 and carried into Lisbon. In the province of Santa-Fe, two kinds of *cinchona* have lately been discovered: one is the red bark of Peru, and the other is a white species.

The *cortex* is a bitter, absorbent, and astringent, or styptic <note>a substance that shrinks tissues and can stop bleeding</note>. From its bitterness, M. Again, as an absorbent, it blunts the sharp edges of acids and prevents their action; consequently, it preserves the fluidity of the bodily juices, which acids would otherwise cause to clot. As a styptic, it must contain earthy parts to absorb serosities <note>original: "serosities"; thin, watery fluids in the body</note>, which allows parts that were previously moistened and relaxed to contract themselves. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Peruvian bark (quinquina/cortex), moving from its history to its physiological effects and the specific protocols for administering it to treat fevers and other ailments.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>

-> APPENDIX TO <-

the fluidity of the bodily fluids <note>original: "juices"; refers to the "humors" or fluids of the body</note>. Its primary action is the strengthening of the solid parts of the body. Its medical uses are determined based on these properties. Its chief use is in curing agues <note>original: "agues"; a period of fever and chills, often associated with malaria</note> and intermittent fevers; for this purpose, it is applied to patients of all ages and most constitutions. It produces this effect better than any other medicine intended for the same purpose, in a ratio of 365 to 1. 

It is common to give a gentle emetic <note>original: "emetic"; a substance that induces vomiting</note> of ipecacuanha before administering the bark. By preparing the digestive tract in this way, the bark is not only more successful but also is not as likely to cause those discomforts—namely, swelling in the belly and nausea—which often arise when such preparation is neglected. The bark must never be administered during the paroxysm <note>original: "paroxysm"; the fit or period of highest intensity of a fever</note> of an ague or intermittent fever. Instead, it should be given in such a quantity, at times between the fits, as to prevent the return of the fever. 

Giving the bark during continuous fevers is considered dangerous; care must be taken that a temporary reduction of a continuous fever is not mistaken for an intermission <note>original: "intermission"; a period where the fever breaks or stops temporarily before returning at a regular time</note>, which happens at specific or stated times. The bark is given in several ways: as a powder, or in the form of an electuary <note>original: "electuary"; a medicinal paste made of powder mixed with honey or syrup</note>, extract, bolus <note>original: "bolus"; a large, soft pill</note>, infusion, tincture, and so on. When the stomach can tolerate it, the preparation in a very fine powder is the most useful and pleasant.

If the bark acts as a laxative <note>original: "take downward"</note>, then Venice treacle <note>original: "Venice treacle"; an ancient, complex compound of many ingredients, including opium, used as a universal medicine</note>, diascordium <note>original: "diascordium"; a sedative medicine made from dried herbs and opium</note>, conserve of roses, terra Japonica <note>original: "terra Japonica"; also known as catechu, an astringent plant extract</note>, doses of laudanum, and similar medicines must be added to the preparations. When there happens to be an interruption of the menstrual cycle <note>original: "obstruction of the menses"</note> from taking the bark, or to prevent this, it is advisable to add black hellebore, æthiops mineral <note>original: "æthiops mineral"; a black powder made of mercury and sulfur</note>, cinnabar <note>original: "cinnabar"; mercury sulfide</note>, etc., to its preparations. 

The bark is often used for young children with agues by means of a clyster <note>original: "clyster"; an enema</note>; it is also applied to the wrists and the soles of the feet, worked up into a stiff paste with turpentine and Venice treacle, which usually works. Dr. Helvetius, physician to the King of France, wrote a book over twenty years ago entirely on the subject of curing agues by giving the bark as an enema. He claims that this is safer and no less certain than taking the bark by mouth. Dr. Cockburn, in his *Treatise of Sea Diseases*, asserts the contrary: he argues that taking the bark internally is just as safe, and much more certain and quick. He also notes that we know how to remedy all the inconveniences the bark may occasion. Dr. Sydenham, and after him Mr. Rencaume and others, have successfully prescribed the bark for melancholic and hysteric conditions, commonly called the "vapours" <note>original: "vapours"; an 18th-century term for depression, anxiety, or nervous disorders</note>.

The virtues of this medicine are well known at this time, but the large size of the doses in the common forms of powder, or infusion in wine or water, are great disadvantages. Furthermore, our common methods of giving it as an extract or resin are unreliable and have their own drawbacks. ...one-third of the usual dose, by means of its dry extract; twenty-four grains of which, it is asserted, contain the entire effectiveness of a dram <note>original: "dram"; a unit of weight equal to 60 grains or 1/8th of an ounce</note> of the finest bark in powder. Hence it appears very evident that when we take the bark in its raw form <note>original: "in substance"</note>, only about a third part of what we are forced to swallow is of any use to us; and that same portion is all we can expect from the virtues of any decoction <note>original: "decoction"; a medicine made by boiling plant material in a liquid</note> or infusion of it. *Memoirs of the Academy of Sciences, Paris, 1758.*

Wine—which is a liquid partly watery, partly salty, and partly spirituous <note>original: "spirituous"; containing alcohol</note>—is a solvent <term>menstruum</term> much more suitable for extracting the virtues of the bark than mere water, as it is much better able to dissolve the juices or sap that have been condensed and thickened <note>original: "inspissated"</note> in the bark of the tree. For this reason, a strong infusion of bark in this solvent remains clear and keeps the resin suspended even when cold. In this respect, it differs from an infusion in boiling water; when the water infusion cools, the resin settles to the bottom <note>original: "precipitates itself"</note>. Thus, it is heat alone which can suspend the resin in a watery infusion of the bark; in a wine-based one, the spirituous and flammable part of the liquor does the same thing. 

As the resin of the bark (which there is great reason to believe possesses all the virtues of that medicine) is entirely separated from watery infusions when they are cold, it has been said there can be very little dependence placed on the common clear infusions made with water. The remaining taste in these water-based infusions is only a faint bitterness, which arises from the gummy and salty parts of the dried juices of the bark. The entire solid substance <note>original: "whole concrete"</note>, which alone possesses the virtue of the medicine, is of the nature of those bodies properly called *gum resins*, which are only very imperfectly soluble in water, and for which wine is the proper solvent. 

It has been found that cold water, acting more gradually than boiling water, extracts both the gummy and resinous principles of the bark. Infusions made by soaking <note>original: "macerating"</note> one ounce of bark in fine powder in eight or twelve ounces of water, without heat, for twenty-four (or even twelve) hours, have been successfully administered in doses of the clear liquid of two or three ounces. It is a common opinion that bark in its raw, powdered form is more effective than any preparation of it. *Lewis, Materia Medica.*

Peruvian bark has been found very effective in preventing colds. The method in which it was used, in a case mentioned in the *Philosophical Transactions*, was (after due preparation by bloodletting or purging <note>standard medical practices of the era used to balance the body's internal fluids</note>) to take two ounces of it every spring and fall. By this method, a habit of catching colds and the resulting sore throat was cured. *Philosophical Transactions, No. 478. p. 3.*

The antiseptic power of the bark has been abundantly demonstrated, and we have many accounts of its great effects in the cure of gangrenes and tissue death <note>original: "mortifications"</note>. See *Medical Essays of Edinburgh, vol. iii. art. 5.* We also have several accounts of the good effects of this medicine in treating ulcers and smallpox, and also in scrofulous <term>scrofulous</term> <note>referring to scrofula, a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck</note> complaints.

...the fluidity of the bodily fluids <note>original: "juices"</note>. Its primary operation is that of strengthening the solid tissues of the body. Its medical uses are determined based on these properties. Its chief use is in curing agues <note>original: "agues"; periodic fevers with shivering fits, often associated with malaria</note> and intermittent fevers, for which purpose it is applied to patients of all ages and most constitutions. It produces this effect better than any other medicine intended for the same purpose, in the ratio of 365 to 1. It is common to give a gentle emetic of ipecacuanha <note>a plant root used to induce vomiting to clear the stomach</note> before the administration <note>original: "exhibition"</note> of the bark. By thus preparing the digestive passages, the bark is not only more successful but is also not as likely to cause those ailments—namely, swelling in the belly, nausea, etc.—which often arise when such preparation is neglected. The bark must never be administered during the peak <note>original: "paroxysm"</note> of an ague or intermittent fever; instead, it should be given in such a quantity at times between the fever fits as to prevent a return of the attack. Administering the bark during continual fevers is considered dangerous, and care must be taken that the temporary easing <note>original: "remission"</note> of a continual fever is not mistaken for a true break <note>original: "intermission"</note> in the fever, which happens at particular or stated times. The bark is given several ways: namely, in powder, in the form of an electuary <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note>, extract, bolus <note>a large medicinal pill</note>, infusion, tincture, etc. When the stomach can tolerate it, the preparation in very fine powder is the most useful and agreeable.

If the bark causes diarrhea <note>original: "take downward"</note>, Venice treacle <note>original: "Venice treacle"; a famous ancient multi-ingredient compound used as a cure-all and sedative</note>, diascordium <note>an herbal electuary used to treat pain and diarrhea</note>, conserve of roses, catechu <note>original: "terra Japonica"; an astringent plant extract</note>, doses of laudanum <note>tincture of opium</note>, etc., must be added to the preparations. When there happens to be an obstruction of menstruation <note>original: "menses"</note> from the administration of the bark—or to prevent it—it is advisable to add to its preparations black hellebore, ethiops mineral <note>a mixture of mercury and sulfur</note>, cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note>, etc. The bark is often used for young children suffering from agues by way of an enema <term>clyster</term>; it is also applied to the wrists and soles of the feet, worked up into a stiff mass with turpentine, Venice treacle, etc., which usually serves the purpose. For this reason, a strong infusion of bark in wine remains clear and keeps the resin suspended even when cold. # APPENDIX TO

<page-num>8</page-num>

In cases of this kind, the bark probably releases a quantity of subtle vapor, or fixed air <note>carbon dioxide</note>, through fermentation. This is sufficient to neutralize <note>original: "saturate"</note> the irritating <note>original: "acrimonious"</note> matter. Even when putrefaction has progressed further, larger doses of this medicine will release more of the antiseptic vapor; when this reaches the blood, it will restore its proper thickness <note>original: "consistence"</note> and correct its sharpness. *Macbride’s Essays*, 3rd edition, page 140, etc. The bark has also been used, alongside other medicines, to cure periodic headaches, as well as hysterical, hypochondriacal, dizzy <note>original: "vertiginous"</note>, and epileptic complaints. It is also a very useful medicine for a weak stomach, uterine discharge <note>original: "fluxes"</note>, and various chronic diseases caused by a looseness or weakness <note>original: "laxity and debility"</note> of the body's tissues <note>original: "fibres"</note>.

Medical writers have recorded many instances of jaundice, dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, asthma, and the entire range of nervous disorders being brought on in a surprisingly short time after an improper <note>original: "injudicious"</note> administration of the bark. Among others, those interested may consult the *Medical Essays and Observations of Edinburgh*, volume 4, article 24. It has been discovered that Peruvian bark is effective in curing gangrene <note>original: "mortifications"</note> caused by internal factors. The history of this discovery is as follows: In 1715, Mr. *Rushworth*, a surgeon in Northampton, gave it to a patient suffering from gangrene. After seeing further proof of its benefits in this disease, he shared his discovery in 1731. Mr. *Amyand* soon tested it in similar cases and found it successful in seven instances. Mr. *John Douglas* confirmed this with the case history of one of his patients, which he published in 1732; soon after, Mr. *Shipton* reported his success with this medicine to the Royal Society. Mr. *Rushworth* and Mr. *Amyand* confirmed its use for gangrene caused by internal illness; however, Rushworth believed it was not suitable for all such cases, particularly when the patient’s fever was constant rather than intermittent. Mr. *Douglas* seemed to think it would succeed in all cases of gangrene. All three of these gentlemen gave a dose of half a dram <note>about 1.8 grams</note> every four hours. Mr. *Shipton* increased the dose to two scruples <note>about 2.6 grams</note> and administered it while the fever continued. He proposed that it be tested on eating sores <note>original: "nomæ"</note>, spreading ulcers <note>original: "phagædenæ"</note>, skin eruptions <note>original: "herpes"</note>, or other difficult-to-heal <note>original: "chironion"</note> ulcers.

Some call the gentian root the "European Cinchona" <note>original: "quinquina"</note> because it is effective against fevers that come and go <note>original: "intermitting fevers"</note>. The sea-side beech of Jamaica (known as *Cinchona Caribaea* by *Linnaeus*) is a species of the "Jesuit’s bark" produced in Jamaica and the Caribbean islands. Its properties have been accurately described by Dr. *Wright*, who found it very effective in treating the dangerous "remittent" fevers <note>fevers that fluctuate but do not disappear</note> of the West Indies. It has lately been administered in London for intermittent fevers, where it has performed a cure as completely as the Peruvian bark. *Philosophical Transactions*, volume 67, 504. *Medical Commentaries*, volume 5, page 398, part 2.

## BREAD-FRUIT TREE. ARTOCARPUS.

THIS tree is called *artocarpus* (from the Greek *artos*, meaning "bread," and *karpos*, meaning "fruit" <note>original: αρτος, bread, and καρπος, fruit</note>). It is a genus of the <term>monandria</term> <note>plants with flowers having only one stamen</note> order, belonging to the <term>monoecia</term> <note>plants where male and female flowers are separate but found on the same plant</note> class of plants. It has a cylindrical <term>amentum</term> <note>a catkin, or a spike of small, petal-less flowers</note> which thickens gradually and is covered with flowers; the male and female flowers are found in different catkins. In the male flower, the <term>calyx</term> <note>the green outer protective layer of a flower</note> has two valves, and the <term>corolla</term> <note>the petals of a flower</note> is missing. In the female flower, there is neither a calyx nor a corolla; the <term>stylus</term> <note>the stalk of the female organ that receives pollen</note> is single, and the <term>drupe</term> <note>a fleshy fruit with a central pit or many-celled center</note> contains many cells.

Though this tree has been mentioned by many voyagers—particularly by William Dampier, Georg Eberhard Rumphius, and Lord Anson—very little notice seems to have been taken of it until the return of Captain Wallis from the South Seas, and since that time by others who have visited Tahiti <note>original: Otaheite</note> and some other countries in the East Indies. Captain Dampier relates that in Guam, one of the Mariana <note>original: Ladrone</note> Islands, "there is a certain fruit called the bread-fruit, growing on a tree as large as our large apple trees, with dark leaves. The fruit is round and grows on the boughs like apples, about the size of a good penny loaf; when ripe, it turns yellow, soft, and sweet. However, the natives take it while it is green and bake it in an oven until the rind is black; they then scrape this off and eat the inside, which is soft and white, like the inside of freshly baked bread. It has neither seed nor stone, but if it is kept for more than twenty-four hours, it becomes harsh. As this fruit is in season eight months of the year, the natives eat no other sort of bread during that time. They told us that all the Mariana Islands had plenty of it. I never heard of it in any other place."

Rumphius, after describing the tree, observes that "the fruit is shaped like a heart and grows to the size of a child's head. Its surface or rind is thick, green, and covered everywhere with bumps of a four-sided or six-sided <note>original: quadragonal or hexagonal</note> shape, like cut diamonds but without points. The flatter and smoother these bumps are, the fewer seeds are contained in the fruit, and the greater the quantity of pith, which is of a stickier <note>original: glutinous</note> nature. The internal part of the rind, or peel, consists of a fleshy substance full of twisted fibers which look like fine wool; these adhere to and, in some measure, form the fruit. The fleshy part of this fruit becomes softer toward the middle, where there is a small cavity formed without any nuts or seeds—except in one species, which has only a small number. This sort is not good unless it is baked or prepared in some other way. However, if the outward rind is removed and the fibrous flesh is dried and afterward boiled with meat, as we do cabbage, it then has the taste of artichoke bottoms. The inhabitants of Ambon <note>original: Amboyna</note> cook it in coconut water; but they prefer it roasted on coals until the outer part or peel is burnt. They afterward cut it into pieces and eat it with coconut milk."

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics of the bread-fruit tree (Artocarpus) and details its discovery and culinary uses as recorded by 17th and 18th-century explorers in the South Pacific and East Indies.</summary>
