### APPENDIX TO

Some people make fritters of it or fry it in oil; and others, such as the Sumatrans <note>original: Sumatrians</note>, dry the internal soft part and keep it to use instead of bread with other food. It provides a great deal of nourishment and is very satisfying, and therefore appropriate for hard-working people. Being of a gentle astringent <term>astringent</term> <note>a substance that causes the contraction of body tissues</note> quality, it is good for persons with a laxative habit of body.

"It is more nourishing boiled in our manner with fat meat than roasted on coals. The milky juice which drips <note>original: distils</note> from the trunk, when boiled with coconut oil, makes a very strong bird-lime <term>bird-lime</term> <note>a sticky substance used for trapping birds</note>. This tree is to be found on the eastern parts of Sumatra, and in the Malay language, it is called *soccus* and *soccus capas* <note>original: *soccus*; likely a transcription of the Malay name *Sukun*</note>. It grows likewise about the town of Bantam in Java, and in Ballega <note>possibly Bangkalan or Madura</note> and Madura, and is known there by the name of *soccus*."

In Anson's voyage, we are informed "that the *rima* <note>a Spanish or Tagalog name for the bread-fruit</note>, or bread-fruit tree, is common in all the Mariana Islands <note>original: Ladrone islands</note> and some of the Philippines. It is somewhat larger than our apple tree and bears a broad, dark-colored leaf with five notches <note>original: indentures</note> on each side. The fruit hangs on boughs like apples and is the size of a penny loaf <note>a small loaf of bread sold for a penny, weighing about 12 ounces</note>, with a thick, tough rind which turns yellow when fully ripe. The natives gather it before it is quite ripe and bake it until the crust is quite black; then they scrape <note>original: rasp</note> it, and there remains a nice loaf with a tender yellow crust. The crumb of it is soft and sweet as a newly baked roll; it is without any seeds or stones. This fruit the inhabitants enjoy for about seven months, during which they never eat any other kind of bread. But they are obliged to bake it every day; for when it grows a little stale, it becomes harsh and husky, somewhat like the potato bread made in the West of England. There is, however, a remedy for this: cutting the loaf into slices when it is fresh and drying it in the sun, by which it is changed into the pleasantest rusk <term>rusk</term> <note>a hard, dry, twice-baked bread</note> that can be eaten."

Captain Cook, in his voyage, observes that this fruit not only serves as a substitute for bread among the inhabitants of Tahiti <note>original: Otaheite</note> and the neighboring islands but also, prepared in various ways, composes the principal part of their food. It grows on a tree that is about the size of a medium-sized oak; its leaves are frequently a foot and a half long, of an oblong shape, deeply lobed <note>original: sinuated</note> like those of the fig tree, which they resemble in color and texture, and in the secretion of a milky juice upon being broken. The fruit is about the size and shape of a newborn child's head. The surface is net-like <note>original: reticulated</note>, not much unlike a truffle; it is covered with a thin skin and has a core about as big as the handle of a small knife. The edible part lies between the skin and the core; it is as white as snow and somewhat of the consistency of new bread. It must be roasted before it is eaten, being first divided into three or four parts; its taste is mild <note>original: insipid</note>, with a slight sweetness somewhat resembling that of the

This fruit is also cooked in a kind of oven, which renders it soft and somewhat like a boiled potato; not quite as starchy <term>farinaceous</term> <note>original: farinaceous; having a floury or starchy texture</note> as a good potato, but more so than those of an average sort. From the bread-fruit, they also make three dishes by adding either water or the milk of the coconut to it, then beating it into a paste with a stone pestle, and afterwards mixing it with ripe plantains, bananas, or the sour paste which they call *mahie*.

The *mahie*, which is likewise used as a substitute <term>succedaneum</term> <note>original: succedaneum; a substitute, especially for medicine or food</note> for ripe bread-fruit before the season begins, is made as follows: the fruit of the bread-fruit tree is gathered just before it is perfectly ripe; and, being laid in heaps, it is closely covered with leaves. In this state, it undergoes a fermentation and becomes disagreeably sweet. The core is then taken out whole, which is done by gently pulling out the stalk, and the rest of the fruit is thrown into a hole dug for that purpose (generally inside the houses) and neatly lined at the bottom and sides with grass. The whole is then covered with leaves, and heavy stones are laid upon them; in this state, it undergoes a second fermentation and becomes sour, after which it will not change for many months. It is taken out of the hole as it is needed for use; and, being made into balls, it is wrapped in leaves and baked. After it is cooked, it will keep for five or six weeks. It is eaten both cold and hot; and the natives seldom make a meal without it, though to Europeans the taste is as disagreeable as that of a pickled olive generally is the first time it is eaten. The fruit itself is in season eight months of the year, and the *mahie* supplies the inhabitants during the other four.

To procure this principal article of their food (the bread-fruit) costs these happy people no trouble or labor except climbing up a tree. The tree which produces it does not indeed grow wild <note>original: spontaneously</note>; but, if a man plants ten of them in his lifetime—which he may do in about an hour—he will as completely fulfill his duty to his own and future generations as the native of our less temperate climate can do by plowing in the cold of winter and reaping in the summer's heat as often as these seasons return; even if, after he has procured bread for his present household, he should convert a surplus into money and save it for his children.

There are two species of *Artocarpus* <note>original: *Artocarpus*; from the Greek *artos* (bread) and *karpos* (fruit)</note>, namely <note>original: viz.</note> the *incisus* <note>original: *incisus*; Latin for "cut" or "gashed"</note>, with gashed leaves; and the *integrifolia* <note>original: *integrifolia*; Latin for "entire leaf"</note>, with whole leaves. There is also said to be another distinction: between that which bears fruit with stones or seeds, and that in which the fruit has none. The reproductive parts of the tree which bears the fruit without stones are defective. The catkin <term>amentum</term> <note>original: amentum; a cylindrical flower cluster</note>, which contains the male parts, never expands. The styles <term>styli</term> <note>original: styli; the part of the female organ of a flower</note>, or female part of the fruit, are likewise deficient. From this, it follows that there can be no stones or seeds, and therefore that this tree can be propagated only by suckers or layers; although it is abundantly evident that it must originally have

### CASHEW-NUT TREE. ANACARDIUM.

*Anacardium*, the cashew-nut tree, is a genus of the **single-pistil** <note>original: monogynia</note> order, belonging to the **ten-stamen** <note>original: decandria</note> class of plants; and in the natural method ranking under the twelfth order, **pot-herbs** <note>original: holoraceæ</note>. The characters are: The flower cup <note>original: calyx</note> is divided into five parts, the divisions being egg-shaped <note>original: ovate</note> and shedding <note>original: deciduous</note>; the blossom <note>original: corolla</note> consists of five reflected petals, twice the length of the flower cup; the stamens <note>original: stamina</note> consist of ten hair-like <note>original: capillary</note> filaments shorter than the flower cup, one of them sterile <note>original: castrated; meaning it does not produce pollen</note>; the pollen-tips <note>original: antheræ</note> are small and roundish. The pistil has a roundish ovary <note>original: germen</note>; the style <note>original: stylus</note> is awl-shaped <note>original: subulated</note>, bent inward <note>original: inflected</note>, and the length of the blossom; the stigma is slanted <note>original: oblique</note>. There is no seed vessel <note>original: pericarpium</note>; the base <note>original: receptaculum</note> is very large and fleshy. The seed is a large kidney-shaped nut, placed above the base.

Of this, only one species is as yet known to botanists: the *Anacardium occidentale*. It grows naturally in the West Indies and reaches a height of 20 feet in its native regions, but cannot be preserved in Britain without the greatest difficulty. The fruit of this tree is as large as an orange and is full of an acid juice, which is frequently used in making punch. At the tip <note>original: apex</note> of this fruit grows a nut, the size and shape of a hare's kidney, but much larger at the end nearest the fruit than at the other. The shell is very hard; and the kernel, which is sweet and pleasant, is covered with a thin film. Between this film and the shell is lodged a thick, blackish, flammable liquor of such a burning <note>original: caustic</note> nature in the fresh nuts that, if the lips happen to touch it, blisters will immediately follow. The kernels are eaten raw, roasted, or pickled. 

The caustic liquor just mentioned is esteemed as an excellent cosmetic by the young ladies of the West Indies, but they must certainly suffer a great deal of pain in its application; and, as fond as our British females are of a beautiful face, it is highly probable they would never submit to be flayed alive to obtain one. When any of the former think themselves too much tanned by the scorching rays of the sun, they gently scrape off the thin outside of the nut and then rub their faces all over with it. Consequently, the person’s skin cannot appear normal in less than a fortnight, by which time the new skin looks as fair as that of a newborn child. Enslaved people in Brazil cure themselves effectively of stomach disorders by eating the yellow fruit of this tree. The juice, being acidic, cuts through the thick, tough humours <note>original: "humours" — in historical medicine, these were the bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament</note> which obstructed the free circulation of the blood, and thus removes the complaint. This cure, however, is not always voluntary; for their masters, the Portuguese, deny them any other sustenance and release them into the woods where cashew nuts grow in great abundance, leaving them the choice to perish by famine or sustain themselves with this fruit. The milky juice of this tree will stain linen a good, permanent black that cannot be washed out.

This plant is easily raised from the nuts, which should each be planted in a separate pot filled with light, sandy earth and plunged into a good hot-bed of tanner's bark <note>A gardening technique using fermenting bark to produce heat for growing tropical plants</note>. They must also be kept from moisture until the plants emerge, otherwise the nuts are prone to rotting. If the nuts are fresh, the plants will come up in about a month; and in two more months, they will be four or five inches high with large leaves. Because of this quick progress, many people have been deceived into imagining the plants would continue such rapid growth; however, with all the care that can be taken, they never exceed a height of two and a half feet, and for the most part reach scarcely half that. The native people eat the nuts lightly roasted, dipped in water or wine, and sprinkled with salt as an aphrodisiac <note>original: "provocative to venery"</note>, for which they are found to be a most remarkable stimulant. The juice will stop diarrhea and cure diabetes, and the oil is used by painters to give their colors a lasting black and to preserve wood from rotting.

## CANELLA ALBA, or WHITE CINNAMON.

The *Canella alba* <note>Latin: "White Cinnamon"</note> is a genus of the *monogynia* order <note>Plants with one pistil</note>, belonging to the *dodecandria* class <note>Plants with twelve to nineteen stamens</note> of plants, and in the natural method ranking under the twelfth order, *holoracem*. The calyx is three-lobed; the petals are five; the antherae (pollen-bearing parts) are sixteen, growing to a bladder-shaped nectary <note>original: "urceolated nectarium"</note>; and the fruit is a three-chambered <note>original: "trilocular"</note> berry with two seeds. There is but one species, the *alba*, which usually grows about twenty feet high and eight or ten inches in thickness in the dense woods of most of the Bahama Islands. The leaves are narrow at the stalk, growing wider at their ends, which are broad and rounded, having only a middle rib; they are very smooth and of a light, shining green. In May and June the flowers, which are five-petaled <note>original: "pentapetalous"</note>, come forth in clusters at the ends of the branches. They are red and very fragrant, and are succeeded by round berries the size of large peas, which are green and, when ripe...

In the berry, these seeds are encased in a slimy coating <note>original: "mucilage"</note>. The bark is the White Cinnamon <note>original: "canella alba"</note> found in pharmacies. It is brought to us rolled into long quills <note>hollow tubes of dried bark</note>, thicker than cinnamon, and both the outside and inside are whitish, inclining slightly toward yellow. Infusions of it in water are yellowish and smell of the spice, but they are more bitter than aromatic. Tinctures made with pure alcohol <note>original: "rectified spirit"</note> have the warmth of the bark but little of its smell. Diluted alcohol <note>original: "proof-spirit"</note> dissolves the aromatic as well as the bitter qualities of the bark and is therefore the best solvent <note>original: "menstruum"</note>.

White Cinnamon is the inner bark, separated from the thin, rough outer layer and dried in the shade. Pharmacies distinguish between two types of this bark, differing from each other in the length and thickness of the quills; however, they are both from the same tree, with the thicker pieces being taken from the trunk and the thinner ones from the branches. This bark is a warm, pungent aromatic, though not the most pleasant kind; nor are any of its preparations particularly palatable.

White Cinnamon <note>original: "Canella alba"</note> is often employed where a warm stimulant for the stomach is necessary and to mask the taste of other ingredients. Currently, however, it is little used in compositions by the Royal College of Physicians of London; the only standard <note>original: "officinal"</note> formula in which it is used is the **aloetic powder** <note>original: "pulvis aloeticus" — a laxative preparation</note>. But in the Edinburgh College, it is an ingredient in the **bitter tincture** <note>original: "tinctura amara"</note>, **bitter wine** <note>original: "vinum amarum"</note>, **rhubarb wine** <note>original: "vinum rhei"</note>, and so on. It is useful for covering the taste of other substances. This bark has been confused with what is called "Winter’s Bark," which belongs to a very different tree.

### COFFEE-TREE. COFFEA.

The coffee-tree is supposed to be a native of Happy Arabia <note>original: "Arabia Felix" — the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula, primarily modern-day Yemen</note>. It seldom rises more than sixteen or eighteen feet in height; the main stem grows upright and is covered with a light-brown bark. The branches grow horizontally and in opposite pairs, crossing each other at every joint, so that every side of the tree is fully covered by them, forming a pyramid shape. The leaves also grow in opposite pairs; when fully grown, they are about four or five inches long and two inches broad in the middle, tapering toward each end. The edges are wavy, and the surface is a bright green. The flowers grow in clusters at the base of the leaves, sitting close to the branches; they are tubular and spread open at the top, where they are divided into five parts. They are pure white and have a very pleasant scent but last only a short time. The fruit, which is the only useful part, resembles a cherry.

It grows in clusters and is arranged along the branches under the axillae <term>axillae</term> (the upper angle where a leaf joins a stem) of the leaves, of the same green as the laurel, but somewhat longer. When it reaches a deep red color, it is gathered for the mill in order to be manufactured into those coffee beans now so generally known. The mill is composed of two wooden rollers, furnished with iron plates eighteen inches long and ten or twelve in diameter. These moveable rollers are made to approach a third which is fixed, and which they call the "chops." Above the rollers is a hopper, in which they put the coffee, from where it falls between the rollers and the chops; there it is stripped of its outer skin and divided into two parts, as may be seen by the forms of it after it has undergone this operation, being flat on one side and round on the other. 

From this machine, it falls into a brass sieve where the skin drops between the wires, while the fruit slides over them into baskets placed ready to receive it. It is then thrown into a vessel full of water, where it soaks for one night, and is afterwards thoroughly washed. When the whole is finished and well dried, it is put into another machine called the peeling-mill. This is a wooden grinder, turned vertically upon its treadle by a mule or a horse. In passing over the coffee, it takes off the parchment <term>parchment</term> (the tough, thin inner skin of the coffee cherry), which is nothing but a thin skin that detaches itself from the berry as it grows dry. 

The parchment being removed, it is taken out of this mill to be put into another, which is called the winnowing-mill. This machine is provided with four pieces of tin fixed upon an axle, which is turned by a slave with considerable force; the wind that is made by the motion of these plates clears the coffee of all the pellicles <term>pellicles</term> (thin husks or skins) that are mixed with it. It is afterwards put upon a table, where the broken berries and any filth that may remain among them are separated by Negroes <note>This refers to the enslaved labor force used in colonial coffee production during the 18th century.</note>; after which the coffee is fit for sale. 

The coffee tree is cultivated in Arabia, Persia, the East Indies, the Isle of Bourbon <note>modern-day Réunion</note>, and several parts of America. It is also raised in botanic gardens in many parts of Europe. Prince Eugene's <note>Prince Eugene of Savoy (1663–1736), a famous military commander and collector whose gardens at Belvedere in Vienna were renowned.</note> garden at Vienna produced more coffee than was sufficient for his own consumption. It delights particularly in hills and mountains, where its root is almost always dry, and its head frequently watered with gentle showers. It prefers a western aspect and ploughed ground without any appearance of grass. 

The plants should be placed at eight feet distance from each other, and in holes twelve or fifteen inches deep. If left to themselves, they would rise to the height of sixteen or eighteen feet, as already observed; but they are generally limited to five feet for the convenience of gathering their fruit with greater ease. Thus dwarfed, they extend their branches so that they cover the whole spot around them. They begin to yield fruit the third year but are not in full bearing until the fifth. Along with the same infirmities that most other trees are subject to, these are likewise in danger of being destroyed by a worm or by the scorching rays of the sun. ...generally a gravelly or chalky bottom. In the latter, it languishes for some time and then dies. In the former, its roots—which rarely fail to strike between stones—obtain nourishment and keep the tree alive and fruitful for thirty years. This is nearly the natural lifespan for coffee plants. By the end of this period, the owner not only finds himself without trees but also finds his land so depleted that it is unfit for any kind of farming. Unless he is situated where he can clear a patch of virgin land <term>virgin land</term> (land that has never been farmed or cultivated) to compensate for the area totally exhausted by the coffee trees, his loss is irreparable.

The coffee produced in Arabia is found to so greatly excel that raised in the American plantations or elsewhere that the cultivation of the tree is now rarely practiced in any of the British colonies. Large plantations of this kind were formerly established in some of them, and it was proposed to Parliament that they should provide proper encouragement for cultivating this commodity there, to enable the planters to undersell those importing from Arabia. Accordingly, there was a reduction in the duty <term>duty</term> (a tax on imported or exported goods) payable on all coffee imported from our colonies in America, which at that time was supposed to be sufficient encouragement for this trade. However, the inferiority of American coffee compared to Arabian coffee has almost ruined the project. 

The late Mr. Miller <note>original: Philip Miller (1691–1771), an influential Scottish botanist and author of "The Gardeners Dictionary"</note> proposed some improvements in the method of cultivation. According to him, the trees are planted in soil that is too moist, and the berries are gathered too soon. He says they should be permitted to remain on the trees until their skins are shriveled and they fall when the trees are shaken. This will indeed greatly diminish their weight, but the value of the product will thereby be increased to more than double that of coffee gathered earlier. In Arabia, they always shake the berries off the trees, spreading cloths to catch them, and taking only those that fall easily each time. 

Another cause of poor quality may be the method of drying the berries. He observes that they are very likely to absorb moisture or the flavor of anything placed near them. For example, a bottle of rum placed in a closet where a tightly sealed canister of coffee berries stood on a shelf at a considerable distance so tainted the berries in just a few days that they became very unpleasant. The same thing happened when a bottle of spirit of wine <term>spirit of wine</term> (highly concentrated alcohol or ethanol) stood in the same closet with coffee and tea; both were spoiled by it within a few days. Some years ago, a coffee ship from India had a few bags of pepper put on board; the flavor was absorbed by the coffee, and the entire cargo was spoiled. 

For these reasons, Mr. Miller directs that coffee berries should never be transported in ships loaded with rum, nor laid out to dry in houses where sugar is boiled or rum is distilled. When they are fully ripe, they should be shaken off only when the trees are perfectly dry and then spread upon cloths in the sun. They should be brought under cover every evening to prevent dew or rain from falling on them. When perfectly dry, they should...

The coffee tree, as we have already observed, is sometimes cultivated in European gardens, but for this, it requires the help of a <term>stove</term> (a heated greenhouse or hothouse). It makes a fine appearance at all seasons of the year, being an evergreen, but especially when in flower and when the berries are red—which is generally in the winter—allowing them to remain in that state for a long time. It is grown from the berries, but they must be planted immediately after being gathered from the tree because they lose their ability to germinate <note>original: "vegetative quality"</note> in a very short time. When they have been sent abroad, those that have been in transit for even a fortnight have consistently failed to grow. Therefore, if these trees are desired, the young plants themselves must be sent if they are coming from any distance. The fresh berries may be planted in small pots and placed into a hotbed of <term>tanners' bark</term> (shredded oak bark used to provide steady heat through fermentation). If the bed is at a proper temperature, the young plants will appear in a month or five weeks' time, and in six weeks more, they will be ready for transplanting into separate pots. During summer, they must be frequently watered, but not too abundantly; otherwise, the roots will be prone to rotting. 

The first sign of the plants being unhealthy is their leaves secreting a sticky juice <note>original: "sweating out a clammy juice"; this likely refers to honeydew produced by pests like scale or aphids</note>. After this, they become infested with insects that cannot be destroyed until the plants have recovered their health. Thus, at the first appearance of these insects, the trees should be moved into fresh soil, and every possible care should be taken to restore them. The ailments affecting them generally result either from their having been put into pots that are too large or from the soil around them being too heavy <note>original: "stiff"</note> or over-watered. The most suitable soil for them is that of a kitchen garden, which is naturally loose and not prone to becoming compacted <note>original: "subject to bind"</note>, especially if it has been consistently well worked and fertilized.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of coffee, moving from cultivation methods to a historical account of how the drink and the plant spread from the Middle East to Europe and the Americas.</meta>

The origin of coffee as a common drink is not well known. Some attribute it to the prior of a monastery who, after being informed by a goatherd that his goats would wake and caper all night after browsing on the coffee tree, became curious to test its properties <note>original: "virtue"</note>. Accordingly, he first tried it on his monks to prevent them from sleeping during morning prayers <note>original: "matins"</note>. Others, citing Sehehabeddin, credit the discovery of coffee to the Persians. It was learned from them in the 15th century by Gemaleddin, the mufti <note>A mufti is a Muslim legal expert empowered to give rulings on religious law.</note> of Aden, a city near the mouth of the Red Sea. Having tried its benefits himself, Gemaleddin found that it cleared the mind <note>original: "dissipated the fumes which oppressed the head"</note>, inspired joy, acted as a laxative <note>original: "opened the bowels"</note>, and prevented sleep without causing discomfort. He first recommended it to his dervishes <note>Members of a Muslim religious order known for their devotional practices.</note>, with whom he used to spend the night in prayer. 

Their example made coffee popular in Aden; legal scholars drank it for study, craftsmen to work, and travelers to walk through the night. In short, everyone in Aden drank coffee. From there, it passed to Mecca, where it was adopted first by the devout and then by the rest of the people. From Arabia Felix <note>original: "Arabia Felix"; Latin for "Happy Arabia," an ancient name for the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula.</note>, it passed to Cairo. In 1511, Kahie Beg prohibited it, believing that it caused intoxication and inclined people toward forbidden things. However, Sultan Causou immediately lifted the prohibition, and coffee spread from Egypt to Syria and Constantinople. The traveler Thevenot was the first to bring it to France. In 1652, a Greek servant named Pasqua—brought to England by Mr. Daniel Edwards, a Turkey merchant <note>A merchant who traded with the Ottoman Empire.</note>, to prepare his coffee—set up the first profession as a coffee seller <note>original: "coffee-man"</note> and introduced the drink to this island.

In the year 1714, the magistrates of Amsterdam, wishing to pay a compliment to Louis XIV, King of France, presented him with a fine specimen of this rare tree. It was carefully and skillfully packed for transport by water and protected from the weather by an ingenious glass-covered container <note>original: "curious machine covered with glass"</note>. The plant was about five feet high, an inch in diameter at the stem, and was in full foliage with both green and ripe fruit. It was viewed on the river with great interest and curiosity by several members of the Academy of Sciences. It was afterwards taken to the royal garden at Marly under the care of Monsieur de Jussieu, the King’s professor of botany. The year before, de Jussieu had written a report <note>original: "memoir"</note>, printed in the *History of the Academy of Sciences of Paris* in 1713, describing the characteristics of this genus. This report included a fine illustration <note>original: "elegant figure"</note> of the tree, taken from a smaller plant he had received that year from Monsieur Pancras, the mayor <note>original: "burgomaster"</note> of Amsterdam and director of the botanical garden there.

In 1718, the Dutch colony at Surinam began to plant coffee for the first time. In 1722, Monsieur de la Motte Aigron, the governor of Cayenne, while on business in Surinam, used a clever trick <note>original: "artifice"</note> to smuggle a plant from there. By the year 1725, that plant had produced many thousands of offspring.

# CULPEPER’S BRITISH HERBAL.

In 1727, the French, perceiving that this acquisition might be of great advantage in their colonies, conveyed to Martinique <note>original: "Martinico"</note> some of the plants; from there, it most probably spread to the neighboring islands. By the year 1732, it was cultivated in Jamaica, and an act was passed to encourage its growth on that island. Thus was laid the foundation of a most extensive and beneficial trade for the European settlements in the West Indies.

The preparation of coffee consists in roasting, or giving it a precise degree of parching <note>original: "torrefaction"</note>, on an earthen or metallic plate until it has acquired a brownish hue equally deep on all sides. It is then ground in a mill, using only as much as serves the current occasion. A proper quantity of water is next boiled, and the ground coffee is put into it. After it has just boiled, it is taken from the fire, and—the liquid <note>original: "decoction"</note> having stood a while to settle and clear—they pour it into dishes. The ordinary method of roasting coffee among us involves a tin cylindrical box full of holes, through the middle of which runs a spit. Under this is a semicircular hearth containing a large charcoal fire. With the help of a mechanical jack, the spit turns quickly and so roasts the berry, which is occasionally taken up to be shaken. When the oil rises and the berry has grown to a dark-brown color, it is emptied into two containers <note>original: "receivers"</note> made with large hoops whose bottoms are iron plates. There the coffee is shaken and left until almost cold; if it looks bright and oily, it is a sign it is well done.

Very different accounts have been given regarding the medicinal qualities of this berry. To determine its real effects on the human body, Dr. Percival has conducted several experiments, the results of which he gives in the following words:

> "From these observations we may infer that coffee is slightly astringent <note>A substance that tends to shrink or constrict body tissues.</note> and antiseptic; that it moderates the fermentation of food during digestion <note>original: "alimentary fermentation"</note>, and is a powerful sedative <note>While we now recognize coffee as a stimulant, 18th-century physicians often categorized its effects on the nerves or stomach differently.</note>. Its action on the nervous system probably depends on the oil it contains, which receives its flavor and is rendered mildly burnt-smelling <note>original: "empyreumatic"</note> by the process of roasting. Neumann <note>Caspar Neumann (1683–1737), a famous German chemist.</note> obtained by distillation from one pound of coffee: five ounces, five drams, and a half of water; six ounces and half a dram of thick, foul-smelling oil; and four ounces and two drams of a useless residue <note>original: "caput mortuum"; Latin for "dead head," a term used by early chemists for the inert solid remains left after distillation.</note>. And it is well known that rye, roasted <note>original: "torrefied"</note> with a few almonds (which furnish the necessary proportion of oil), is now frequently employed as a substitute for these berries.

> "The medicinal qualities of coffee seem to be derived from the pleasant roasting which it produces in the stomach, and from the sedative powers it exerts on the vital force <note>original: "vis vitæ"; Latin for "force of life," the energy believed to animate the body.</note>. Hence, it assists digestion and relieves headaches; it is taken in large quantities, with particular appropriateness, by the Turks and Arabians because it counteracts the narcotic effects of opium, to the use of which those nations are much addicted."

"In people with delicate constitutions <note>original: "habits"</note>, coffee often causes insomnia <note>original: "watchfulness"</note>, tremors, and many of those complaints labeled as 'nervous.' "The following interesting and important observation is taken from a letter I received from Sir John Pringle <note>A Scottish physician and a founder of modern military medicine</note> in April 1773: 'While reading your section on coffee, I remembered a quality I had noticed in that drink which confirms what you said about its sedative properties. It is the best treatment for relieving the attacks of recurrent asthma that I have seen. The coffee should be the best Mocha <note>original: "Mocco"</note>, freshly roasted <note>original: "burnt"</note>, and made very strong immediately after grinding. I have usually ordered an ounce for one cup <note>original: "dish"</note>, which is to be repeated fresh after an interval of fifteen to thirty minutes; I instruct that it be taken without milk or sugar. This medicine is mentioned generally by Dr. William Musgrave in his treatise *On Irregular Gout* <note>original: "De Arthritide anomala"</note>; but I first heard of it from a physician here who, having once practiced in Lichfield, had been informed by the elderly residents there that Sir John Floyer <note>An English physician (1649–1734) famous for his work on asthma</note>, during the final years of his life, stayed free from—or at least lived comfortably with—his asthma by using very strong coffee. It seems he made this discovery after the publication of his book on that disease.' Since receiving that letter, I have frequently prescribed coffee for asthma with great success.

### CITRUS, OR FORBIDDEN-FRUIT TREE.

The forbidden-fruit tree <note>In the 18th century, this name was often applied to a variety of pomelo or an early ancestor of the modern grapefruit</note> closely resembles the common orange tree in its trunk, leaves, and flowers; however, the ripe fruit is larger and longer than the biggest orange. It has a taste somewhat like a shaddock <note>A large, thick-skinned citrus fruit (Citrus maxima) from which the grapefruit descended</note>, but its delicious flavor far exceeds that of the shaddock as well as the best orange. These are elegant evergreens, growing in this country to a height of about five to ten feet. They form full, handsome heads, densely adorned with beautiful large leaves all year round, and they produce an abundance of sweet flowers in spring and early summer. Even in this climate, these flowers are often followed by a large amount of fruit that sometimes reaches reasonable ripeness. Although all varieties were originally grown from seeds, the only certain way to maintain specific varieties is by budding or inarching <term>a grafting technique where a branch of one plant is joined to another while both are still attached to their own roots</term> them onto stocks grown from seed to a suitable size. Since young trees are imported in abundance from abroad, this method is rarely used in this country. However, those who are interested may do it for curiosity in the following way: early in the spring, obtain some seeds <note>original: "kernels"</note>, which can be found in plenty from rotten or properly ripened fruit. In March, plant seeds in pots of rich, light earth half an inch deep, and place them in a hot-bed <note>A bed of decaying manure or bark covered with soil, used to provide warmth for seeds.</note> under frames and glass. Manure or tan <note>original: "tan"; crushed oak bark used in tanning which generates heat as it decomposes</note> may be used, but the latter is preferable, as it allows for air and frequent sprinkling of water. In two or three weeks, the plants will emerge; and, in six or eight weeks more, they will have grown four or five inches or more in height. You must now give them more air and water. About the middle of June, harden them by exposure to the open air, where they should remain until October. Then, move them into the green-house to stand until the spring. In March or April, plant them individually in small pots, being careful to shake them out of the seed-pots <note>OCR original: "feed-pots"</note> with their roots intact. They must be watered immediately after planting, and the watering must be repeated occasionally. After this, they are to be treated as woody exotics of the green-house; in a year or two, the largest of those intended for stocks <note>The base plant onto which a bud or graft is attached.</note> will be ready for budding.

The operation for budding is performed in the month of August and is done in the common way; however, the buds must be taken from trees of a good variety that bear fruit well. As soon as the operation is finished, the pots with their plants must be placed in the green-house or in a glass case. Alternatively, where there is the convenience of a spare bark-pit <note>A pit filled with tanning bark used to provide gentle, sustained heat for plants.</note> where the heat is almost exhausted, the pots may be placed there for two or three weeks. In either case, however, the air must be admitted freely by opening the front glasses; you should also provide a slight shade of mats during the middle of hot, sunny days and supply them with water every two or three days during this kind of weather. In three or four weeks, the buds will have united with the stock; at that point, it will be proper to loosen the bandages so that they have room to swell. The buds, however, will all remain dormant until the next spring. They may also be propagated by <term>inarching</term> <note>A method of grafting where two living plants are joined together while both remain on their own roots until the graft takes.</note>, which is done in the common way; but the method of budding is found to produce much handsomer trees and is therefore preferred.

But the cheapest and most rapid method of obtaining a collection of these kinds of trees is to use those imported from *Spain*, *Italy*, and *Portugal*. These arrive in chests without any earth on their roots, having had their roots and heads trimmed slightly. They are commonly from one inch to two or three inches in diameter at the stem, and from two to five feet in height. With the assistance of a bark-bed, they readily take root and grow freely, forming as good a tree in two years as could be raised here by inarching or budding in fifteen or twenty years. They are sold in the *Italian* warehouses <note>Specialty shops in London that imported Mediterranean goods such as oils, fruits, and citrus trees.</note> in *London*. Their price is from three shillings to a guinea each, depending on their size; and they are generally advertised as soon as they arrive, which is early in the spring—and the sooner they are bought, the better. In choosing these trees, it must be observed that they are commonly budded at such a height on the stem as to form heads from about two to five feet high; and as they are frequently furnished with two buds, one on each side of the stem,

They are often heavily laden with blossoms; when these are very thick, it is proper to thin them slightly, removing the smallest. It should also be noted that, as the trees continue blooming and setting their fruit for three months, once a full crop of fruit is set, it is beneficial to the trees and the fruit to pick off the excess blossoms as they are produced, though some people allow them to remain for their appearance.

### GARCINIA, OR MANGOSTEEN.

The *Garcinia* is a genus of the single-pistil <note>original: "monogynia"; the botanical order of plants having only one style or pistil.</note> order, belonging to the twelve-stamen <note>original: "dodecandria"; a class of plants with twelve to nineteen stamens.</note> class of plants; and in the natural method, it ranks under the 18th order, the two-horned plants <note>original: "bicornes"; a botanical order referring to the horn-like shape of the anthers.</note>. The calyx <note>The outer protective part of a flower.</note> is four-leaved <note>original: "tetraphyllous"</note> and positioned below the ovary; there are four petals; the berries are eight-seeded <note>original: "octospermous"</note> and crowned with a shield-like stigma <note>The part of the plant that receives pollen.</note>. There is but one species, the mangosteen <note>original: "mangostana"</note>.

## **G A R C I N I A, OR M A N G O S T A N.**

The *Garcinia* is a genus of the <note>original: "monogynia order"</note> "one-style" order, belonging to the <note>original: "dodecandria class"</note> class of plants (those having twelve to nineteen stamens). In the natural botanical method, it ranks under the 18th order, <note>original: "bicornes"</note> "two-horned." The <note>original: "calyx is tetraphyllous inferior"</note> outer flower casing has four leaves and is positioned below the fruit; there are four petals; the berries <note>original: "octospermous"</note> contain eight seeds and are crowned with a shield-like <term>stigma</term> <note>the part of the plant that receives pollen</note>. There is but one species, the *Mangostana* (Mangosteen).

...mangosteen <note>original: "gostana"</note>, a tree of great elegance, and producing the most pleasant fruit of any yet known.

This tree has been very accurately described by Dr. Garcin, in honor of whom—as its most accurate describer—Linnaeus gave it the name *Garcinia* in the 35th volume of the *Philosophical Transactions* <note>The Philosophical Transactions was the world's first purely scientific journal, published by the Royal Society.</note>. It grows, he informs us, to above seventeen or eighteen feet high, “with a straight, tapering stem like a fir,” having a regular tuft in the form of an oblong cone, composed of many branches and twigs, spreading out equally on all sides without leaving any gaps. Its leaves, he observes, are oblong, pointed at both ends, entire, smooth, of a shining green on the upper side, and an olive color on the back. Its flower is composed of four petals, almost round or a little pointed; their color resembles that of a rose, only deeper and less lively. 

The calyx <term>calyx</term> <note>The outer protective layer of a flower bud, usually green and leaf-like.</note> of this flower is made of one piece, expanded, and cut into four lobes. The two upper lobes are somewhat larger than the lower ones; they are greenish on the outside and a fine deep red within. The red of the upper lobes is more lively than that of the lower ones. This calyx encloses all the parts of the flower; it is supported by a pedicel <note>original: "pedicle"; the stalk of an individual flower.</note> which is green and constantly grows from the end of a twig above the last pair of leaves. 

The fruit is round, the size of a small orange, from an inch and a half to two inches in diameter. The body of this fruit is a capsule of one cavity, composed of a thick rind somewhat like that of a pomegranate, but softer, thicker, and fuller of juice. Its thickness is commonly a quarter of an inch. Its outer color is a dark brownish-purple, mixed with a little gray and dark green. The inside of the peel is a rose color, and its juice is purple. Finally, this skin has a styptic <term>styptic</term> <note>A substance that contracts organic tissue or stops bleeding; here referring to a dry, puckering taste.</note> or astringent taste, like that of a pomegranate, but it does not stick to the fruit it contains. 

The inside of this fruit is a furrowed globe, divided into segments much like those of an orange, but unequal in size, which do not stick to each other. The number of these segments is always equal to the number of the rays on the top that covers the fruit. The fewer segments there are, the larger they are. Often, in the same fruit, some segments are twice as large as those next to them. These segments are white, slightly transparent, fleshy, membranous, and full of juice like cherries or raspberries, with a taste like strawberries and grapes combined. Each segment encloses a seed the shape and size of an almond stripped of its shell, having a bulge on one of its sides. These seeds are covered with two small skins, the outermost of which serves as a base for the filaments and membranes that make up the pulp. The substance of these seeds is very similar to that of chestnuts in terms of their consistency, color, and astringent quality.

According to Captain Cook, in his *Voyage Round the World* (vol. iii, p. 737), the *Garcinia mangostana* of Linnaeus is unique to the East Indies. It is about the size of a crab-apple and of a deep red-wine color. On the top of it is the figure of five or six small triangles joined in a circle, and at the bottom are several hollow green leaves, which are the remains of the blossom. When they are to be eaten, the skin—or rather the thick rind—must be taken off. Under this are found six or seven white kernels placed in a circular order; the pulp with which these are surrounded is the fruit, and nothing can be more delicious. It is a happy mixture of tart and sweet which is no less wholesome than pleasant. Like the sweet orange, it is allowed in any quantity to those who are suffering from a fever, whether of the putrid or inflammatory kind.

According to Captain Cook, in his *Voyage round the World*, volume 3, page 737, the *Garcinia mangostana* of Linnaeus is peculiar to the East Indies. It is about the size of a crab apple and of a deep red-wine color. On the top of it is the figure of five or six small triangles joined in a circle; and at the bottom are several hollow green leaves, which are remains of the blossom. When they are to be eaten, the skin, or rather the rind, must be taken off; under which are found six or seven white kernels, placed in a circular order. The pulp with which these are enveloped is the fruit, and nothing can be more delicious. It is a happy mixture of the tart and the sweet, which is no less wholesome than pleasant. Like the sweet orange, it is allowed in any quantity to those who are afflicted with a fever, whether of the putrid or inflammatory kind.

### MANCHINEEL-TREE. *HIPPOMANE.*

This is a genus of the <note>original: "adelphia order"</note> adelphia order (plants with stamens joined in bundles), belonging to the <note>original: "monœcia class"</note> monoecia class (plants with separate male and female flowers on the same individual); and in the natural method ranking under the 38th order, <note>original: "tricoccæ"</note> tricoccae (plants with three-lobed fruits). The male has an <note>original: "amentum"</note> amentum (catkin) and a <note>original: "bifid perianthium"</note> two-part floral envelope, without any <term>corolla</term> (petals); the female <note>original: "perianthium"</note> floral envelope is <note>original: "trifid"</note> divided into three parts; there is no <term>corolla</term>. The <term>stigma</term> (the part of the flower that receives pollen) is <note>original: "tripartite"</note> divided into three; and the fruit is a plum or <note>original: "capsule tricoccus"</note> three-celled capsule.

*Species.* 1. The manchineel with oval, saw-edged leaves is a native of all the West Indian islands. It has a smooth brownish bark; the trunk divides upwards into ma-

...many branches, garnished with oblong leaves about three inches long. The flowers come out in short spikes at the end of the branches, but they do not make a great appearance, and are followed by fruit of the same shape and size as a golden pippin <note>A variety of apple.</note>. The tree grows to the size of a large oak. 2. The *biglandulosa*, with oblong bay-leaves, is a native of South America; it grows to as large a size as the first species, from which it differs mostly in the shape of its leaves. 3. The *spinosa*, with holly-leaves, is a native of Campeachy <note>modern: Campeche, Mexico</note>, and seldom rises above twenty feet high; the leaves greatly resemble those of the common holly and are set with sharp prickles at the end of each indentation. They are a bright green and remain all year.

*Culture.* These plants, being natives of very warm climates, cannot be preserved in this country without a stove <note>A "stove" was a historical term for a heated greenhouse or hothouse.</note>; nor can they by any means be made to grow above five or six feet high even with that assistance. They are propagated by seeds, but must have very little moisture, or they will certainly be killed by it.

*Properties.* These trees have a very poisonous quality, abounding with an acrid milky juice of a highly caustic nature. Strangers are often tempted to eat the fruit of the first species; the consequences of which are an inflammation of the mouth and throat, and pains in the stomach, etc., which are very dangerous unless remedies are speedily applied. The wood is much esteemed for making cabinets, bookcases, etc., being very durable, taking a fine polish, and not being liable to become worm-eaten. However, as the trees abound with the milky caustic juice already mentioned, fires are made around their trunks to burn out this juice; otherwise, those who fell the trees would be in danger of losing their sight if the juice flew into their eyes. This juice raises blisters on the skin wherever it falls, turns linen black, and makes it fall apart in holes. It is also dangerous to work the wood after it is sawn; for, if any of the sawdust happens to get into the eyes of the workmen, it causes inflammation and the loss of sight for some time. To prevent this, they generally cover their faces with fine lawn <note>A very thin, lightweight fabric made of linen or cotton.</note> while working the wood. It is with the juice of this tree that the Indians used to poison their arrows.

### MARSH-MALLOW OF SURINAM. *ALTHÆA.*

THIS plant is called at Surinam *okkerum*, and is an elegant species of the marsh-mallow, so well known to botanists. It grows about six feet high and bears double flowers, some of which are yellow and white, and others red. If the fruit is cut, a milky liquor drops out, which is clammy and takes the form of threads. They boil this and make a drink of it in America, which is famous for treating internal bruises and most diseases of the stomach and bowels.

Besides this, there are three other species of the marsh-mallow, which I shall describe here. 1. The *vulgaris*, or common marsh-mallow, is a native of Britain, and has

It has a perennial root and an annual stalk that dies back every autumn. The stalks grow upright to a height of four or five feet. These are decorated with leaves that are hoary <note>covered with fine, white hairs</note>, soft to the touch, and arranged alternately on the branches. The flowers emerge from the leaf axils <note>original: "under the wings of the leaves"</note>, similar to those of the mallow, and are a purplish white.

2. The *hirsuta* <note>original: "hirsuta," Latin for hairy</note>, or hairy marsh-mallow, is native to Spain and Portugal. It is a low-growing plant whose branches trail along the ground unless they are supported by stakes. The leaves and stalks are covered with stiff hairs. The flowers appear like those of the common variety but are smaller and have purplish centers <note>original: "bottoms"</note>.

3. The *cannabina* <note>original: "cannabina," referring to its hemp-like appearance</note>, or shrubby marsh-mallow, is native to Hungary and Istria. It has a woody stem that grows to a height of four or five feet and produces many side branches. The flowers bloom in the same way as the other species but are a deeper red color. This variety rarely flowers in its first year unless the summer is warm. However, if the plants survive the winter, they will flower early the following summer and produce healthy seeds.

*Culture.* Although the *vulgaris* <note>original: "vulgaris," Latin for common</note> is found naturally in salt marshes, it will thrive when transplanted into any soil or location; however, it will always grow larger in moist soil than in dry soil. It may be propagated either by dividing the roots in autumn when the stalks die back, or by sowing the seeds in the spring. If the seeds of the second species (*hirsuta*) are sown in April, the plants will flower in July and produce ripe seeds in September. They should be sown in the spot where they are intended to stay, as the roots grow deep into the ground; unless the plants are moved while very young, they rarely survive transplantation. The seeds of the *cannabina* should also be sown where they are to remain for the same reason. They require a sheltered location and dry soil; otherwise, they will not survive the winter. In fact, they rarely live longer than two years in this country, despite all possible care.

*Medicinal Uses.* The *vulgaris* (common marsh-mallow) is the only species used in medicine. The entire plant, especially the root, is rich in a mild mucilage <note>a thick, gluey substance produced by plants</note>. It has the general properties of an emollient <note>a substance that soothes or softens the skin or internal membranes</note> medicine. It is useful for treating "thin, acrimonious juices" <note>referring to an imbalance of bodily fluids or irritants</note> and instances where the natural lining of the intestines has been worn away. It is primarily recommended for severe "defluxions" <note>original: "defluxions," a discharge of fluid, such as mucus from the lungs</note> of the lungs, hoarseness, and dysentery. It is also used for kidney <note>original: "nephritic"</note> and bladder stone <note>original: "calculous"</note> complaints. This is not, as some have believed, because the medicine has any special power to dissolve or expel stones <note>original: "calculus"</note>, but because it lubricates and relaxes the vessels, allowing for a freer and easier passage. The root is sometimes used externally to soften and "mature" <note>bring to a head</note> hard tumors. When chewed, it is said to provide relief for children during difficult teething <note>original: "dentition"</note>.

This root gave its name to an "officinal" <note>a medicine kept in stock at an apothecary or drugstore</note> syrup, decoction <note>a concentrated liquor resulting from boiling a medicinal substance</note>, and ointment. It was also an ingredient in the compound powder of gum tragacanth and the oil and plaster of mucilages. However, of all these formulas <note>original: "formulæ"</note>, only the syrup is still in use.

## MANDRAKE (*ATROPA*)

The fruit of this plant has been highly recommended for treating infertility. Its fresh root is a powerful laxative; the dose is between ten and twenty grains when taken as a solid, and between half a drachm and a full drachm when taken as an infusion <note>original: "infusion"; a liquid extract made by soaking the plant in water</note>. It has been found helpful for "hysteric complaints" <note>original: "hysteric complaints"; a historical term for a wide range of physical and emotional symptoms once attributed to the uterus</note>, but it must be used with great caution. Otherwise, it will cause convulsions and many other dangerous symptoms. It also possesses sedative <note>original: "narcotic"</note> qualities. At present, only the fresh leaves are occasionally used in pain-relieving <note>original: "anodyne"</note> and skin-softening <note>original: "emollient"</note> poultices <note>original: "cataplasms"</note> and warm medicinal washes <note>original: "fomentations"</note>. It used to be an ingredient in one of the old standard ointments <note>original: "officinal unguents"</note>, but both that ointment and the plant itself are now rejected from our official medical guides <note>original: "pharmacopoeias"</note>. However, it still holds a place in foreign medical guides and may perhaps deserve further study.

Naturalists tell strange stories about this plant; but setting aside its power to induce sleep <note>original: "soporiferous virtue"</note>, modern botanists will hardly vouch for any of them. They even doubt the human shape usually attributed to its roots, especially since the discovery of the tricks used by quacks <note>original: "charlatans"</note> who carve the roots into that shape to deceive gullible people. The illustration provided in the accompanying plate, however, was drawn from a genuine root.

In the Bible, Moses informs us (Genesis 30:14) that Reuben, the son of Leah, was in the field and happened to find mandrakes, which he brought home to his mother. Rachel wanted them and obtained them from Leah on the condition that Leah should sleep with Jacob the following night. The Hebrew term <term>dudaim</term>, used here by Moses, is one of those words that even modern Jews do not fully understand. Some translate it as "violets," others as "lilies" or "jasmine." Junius calls it "agreeable flowers"; Codurquus identifies it as a "truffle" or "mushroom"; and Calmet claims it is the "citron." Those who support the translation as "mandrakes" argue that Rachel, being barren and having a great desire to conceive, wanted Leah’s mandrakes because of their supposed fertility-enhancing properties. The ancients gave mandrakes the name "apples of love," and gave Venus the title *Mandragoritis* <note>original: "Mandragoritis"; meaning "She of the Mandrake"</note>. Furthermore, the Emperor Julian, in his letter to Calixenes, says that he drinks the juice of mandrakes to excite sexual desire <note>original: "amorous inclinations"</note>.

## MIMOSA, OR SENSITIVE PLANT

This is a genus of the *polygamia* order <note>plants with male, female, and hermaphrodite flowers on the same or different plants</note>, belonging to the *monœcia* class of plants; in the natural method, it ranks under the thirty-third order, *lomentaceæ* <note>plants bearing legumes or pods</note>. The hermaphrodite calyx <note>the outer protective cover of the flower</note> is five-toothed <note>original: "quinquedentate"</note>; the corolla <note>the petals</note> is five-cleft <note>original: "quinquefid"</note>; there are five or more stamens <note>original: "stamina"</note>, one pistil, and a pod <note>original: "legume" </note>. The male calyx is five-toothed; the corolla is five-cleft, with five, ten, or more stamens. The name <term>mimosa</term> signifies "mimic."

...and [the name] is given to this genus on account of the sensitivity of the leaves, which, by their motion, mimic or imitate, as it were, the motion of animals. To this genus Linnaeus joins many of the *acacias*; and it comprises near 60 different species, all natives of warm climates. Of the sorts cultivated here in our greenhouses <note>original: "stoves"; heated rooms used for tropical plants</note>, etc., some are of the shrub and tree kind, and two or three are herbaceous perennials and annuals. 

The sensitive kinds are exceedingly curious plants because of the very singular circumstance of their leaves receding rapidly from the touch and running up close together. In some sorts, the leaf-stalks <note>original: "footstalks"</note> and everything else are affected, so as instantly to fall downward as if fastened by hinges; these last are called "humble sensitives." They all have winged leaves, each wing consisting of many small leaflets <note>original: "pinnæ"</note>. 

In the *System of Vegetables* <note>original: "Systema Vegetabilium," a work by Linnaeus</note>, this genus—including the *mimosas*, properly so called, and the *acacias*—is divided into several sections, distinguished by the shape, position, and arrangement of the leaves, such as: simple, simply-winged <note>original: "simply-pinnated"</note>, twin-paired <note>original: "bigeminous"</note> and triple-paired <note>original: "tergeminous"</note>, paired and winged <note>original: "conjugate and pinnated"</note>, or doubly winged. The following are the most remarkable:

*Species, with their properties.* 

1. **The *sensitiva***, or common sensitive humble plant, rises with a shrub-like, prickly stem, branching six or eight feet high and armed with crooked spines. It has paired winged leaves with twin lobes or wings—the inner ones being the smallest—with each leaf on a long leaf-stalk. At the sides and ends of the branches, it produces many purple flowers in roundish heads, followed by broad, flat, jointed pods in radiating clusters. This is something of the "humble sensitive" kind; the leaves, leaf-stalks, and all recede from the touch, though not with such ease as in some of the following sorts.

2. **The *pudica***, or "bashful" <note>original: "pudica"; Latin for bashful or modest</note> humble plant, rises with a shrub-like, drooping <note>original: "delinated"; likely a transcription error for "declinate," meaning bent downward</note>, prickly stem, branching two or three feet around and armed with hairy spines. It has winged, finger-like <note>original: "digitated"</note> leaves, each leaf being made of five or more long leaflets attached by their base to a long leaf-stalk and spread out above like the fingers of a hand. At the sides and ends of the branches are roundish heads of greenish-white flowers, followed by small, jointed, prickly pods. This is truly of the "humble sensitive" kind; for at the slightest touch, the leaves instantly recede, contract, close, and—together with the leaf-stalk—quickly drop downward, as if ashamed at the approach of the hand.

3. **The *pernambucana***, or Pernambuco slothful mimosa, has shrub-like, trailing <note>original: "procumbent"</note>, thornless <note>original: "unarmed"</note> stems, branching two or three feet around. It has doubly winged leaves of three or four pairs of short-winged leaflets, and at the leaf-axils <note>original: "axillas"; the angle between the leaf and the stem</note> it has drooping spikes of flowers with five stamens <note>original: "pentandrous"</note>, the lower ones being sterile <note>original: "castrated"</note>. This species recedes very slowly from the touch, only contracting its leaflets a little when touched sharply; hence the name "slothful mimosa."

4. **The *asperata*** <note>original: "apperata"</note>, or Panama sensitive plant. Of this curious species, which has been well described by Dr. Browne (but not illustrated), there is a good illustration in the *Remains* <note>original: "Reliquiæ"; likely referring to the *Reliquiæ Houstounianæ*, a botanical work</note>...

It grows in moist places and by the sides of rivulets in the parishes of St. James and Hanover, Jamaica. It is only sensitive in the leaflets, but it moves quickly.

6. **The *viva***, or lively mimosa (also known as the smallest sensitive weed), has many creeping roots and spreads itself so as to cover large spots of ground. These are followed by little, short, hairy pods containing smooth, shining seeds. This is the most sensitive of all the mimosas, the *pudica* not excepted. By running a stick over the plant, a person may write his name, and it will remain visible for ten minutes <note>referring to the way the leaves collapse along the path of the stick</note>.

At the leaf pits, it bears globular heads of purple flowers, followed by four-valved <note>original: "quadrivalvular"</note> pods. This is of the "humble" sensitive kind, with both the leaves and the leaf-stalks <note>original: "footstalks"</note> recoiling from the touch.

9. **The *cornigera***, or horned Mexican mimosa, commonly called the great horned acacia, has a shrubby, upright, irregular <note>original: "deformed"</note> stem that branches out unevenly. It is protected by very large, white, horn-like spines that grow in pairs and are joined <note>original: "connated"</note> at the base. 10. **The *farnesiana***, or fragrant acacia, grows in woodlands and waste lands across most of Jamaica, reaching a height of twenty-five to thirty feet with a proportional thickness. The bark of the trunk is brown and scaly, and the branches grow alternately. It is adorned with bright green, twice-feathered leaves and fragrant yellow globe-shaped flowers that emerge from the leaf pits <term>axillæ: the angle between the upper side of a leaf and the stem</term>. The pods are about three inches long and half an inch broad; they are light brown, smooth, flattened, and contain five or six smooth, flat seeds. Formerly, the flowers of this tree were used as an ingredient in the "Treacle of Andromachus" <note>original: "theriaca andromachi," a famous ancient medical compound used as a universal antidote</note> found in old medical guides <note>original: "dispensatories"</note>. The tree is sometimes planted as a hedge or fence around enclosures, and the timber, though small, is useful for farming and local construction <note>original: "rural economy"</note>.

11. **The *arborea***, or wild tamarind tree, is common in all the woodlands of Jamaica, especially near established settlements. It grows to a significant height and is quite thick. The timber is excellent and serves many purposes in farming and local industry. It is the color of cedar, quite hard, and takes a high polish. The leaves are numerous, and the flowers are white and globe-shaped. The pods are about a foot long and a beautiful scarlet color; when they are ripe, they open and twist. The seeds then appear; they are oblong, smooth, shiny black, and quite soft. Overall, the combination of leaves, flowers, and pods gives this tree a unique and beautiful appearance. In Britain, this plant is raised in hothouses, but it seems that with a little effort it could be grown in the open air. A tree of considerable size once grew in the garden of the late Dr. William Pitcairn <note>Dr. William Pitcairn (1711–1791) was a Scottish physician and botanist who established a famous botanical garden in Islington</note> at Islington, near London.

12. **The *latifolia***, shag-bark, or white wild tamarind. This excellent timber tree is very common in Jamaica and grows to a moderate height and thickness. The trunk is rough and scaly. The leaves are numerous, diamond-shaped <note>original: "rhomboidal"</note>, and have a yellowish tint. The flower spikes grow from the leaf pits <note>original: "axillæ"</note> and are yellow in color. The seed vessels are flat, jointed, and twisted. The seeds are the size of a vetch <note>a type of legume or pea</note>, white, and finely streaked with blue. There is a variety of this tree that some botanists call *M. serpentina* <note>Mimosa serpentina</note>. The main difference is in the leaves, which are smaller and a shiny dark green.

13. **The lebeck, or ebony tree.** This tree is a native of the East Indies but is grown from seeds in Jamaica and St. Vincent's. 14, 15. **The *cinerea* <note>original: "cinerea," Latin for "ash-colored"</note> and *pinnata* <note>original: "pinnata," Latin for "feather-leaved"</note>, cashew bushes.** These species are common around Kingston and Spanish Town, Jamaica, and grow with slender trunks to about twenty feet. Dr. Roxburgh of Madras, among many useful discoveries, has found the lac insect <note>An insect that produces a resinous secretion used to make shellac</note> on this specimen of mimosa. The plant is a variety of the *cinerea* and appears rather to be the *M. pinnata* <note>original: "M. pinnata," the Mimosa pinnata</note> described by Linnaeus. It is hoped that in a short time the useful insect just mentioned may be transported from Asia to the West Indies, where this gum, or rather wax, may also be produced.

16. **The *scandens* <note>original: "scandens," Latin for "climbing"</note>, cocoons, or masootoo wyth** (The "climbing giant-pod" <note>original: "Gigalobium scandens"</note>, Browne's Jamaica, page 302; the "greatest perennial bean" <note>original: "Phaseolus maximus perennis"</note>, Sloane’s Catalogue, page 68; the "Perein Kaku-valli," *Hortus Malabaricus*, volume 8, tables 32, 3, 4). This species of mimosa is common in all the upland valleys and woodlands on the north side of Jamaica. It climbs up the tallest trees and spreads itself in every direction by means of its tendrils <term>cirrhi: slender, curling organs of a plant used for climbing</term> or claspers, forming a complete arbor and covering the space of an acre from a single root. This habit has a harmful effect on the trees or bushes it shades. Because light, air, and rain (which are necessary for all plants) are shut out, the leaves drop off, the tree gradually rots, and the limbs fall down under the weight of this parasite.

The roots of this plant grow close to the surface <note>original: "superficially"</note> under the ground or grass. The trunk is seldom thicker than a man's thigh and sends off many branches with numerous thin green leaves; each leaf ends in a tendril or clasper that helps it fasten to trees or bushes. The flower spikes grow from the axils <term>axillæ: the angle between the upper side of a leaf and the stem</term>; they are slender, and the individual flowers <note>original: "florets"</note> on them are small and numerous. The pod is perhaps the largest and longest of any in the world, sometimes reaching eight or nine feet in length and five inches in width. It is jointed and contains ten or fifteen seeds. These seeds are brown, shiny, flattened, and very hard; they are called **cocoons**. These are the same seeds mentioned in the *Philosophical Transactions*, number 222, page 298, by Sir Hans Sloane, as being washed ashore on the Hebrides and Orkneys. This happens in the following way: the seeds or beans fall into the rivers and are carried to the sea. The trade winds carry them westward until they enter the Gulf Stream, which forces them northward along the coast of America and the Bahama Islands. Because the winds blow frequently and strongly from America, these seeds are then driven eastward toward...

9. The *cornigera* <note>original: "cornigera," Latin for "horned"</note>, or horned Mexican mimosa, commonly called the great horned acacia, has a shrubby, upright, twisted <note>original: "deformed"</note> stem, branching irregularly, and is armed with very large, white, horn-like spines in pairs, joined <note>original: "connated"</note> at the base; it has doubly-feathered <note>original: "bipinnated"</note> leaves spaced thinly and flowers growing in spikes. This species is valued as a curiosity for the oddity of its large spines, which resemble the horns of animals and are often variously wreathed, twisted, and contorted.

10. The *farnesiana* <note>original: "farnesiana," the sweet acacia</note>, or fragrant acacia, grows in woodlands and waste lands in most parts of Jamaica, rising to twenty-five or thirty feet with a corresponding thickness. The bark of the trunk is brown and scaly, and the branches are alternate. It is adorned with doubly-feathered <note>original: "bipinnated"</note> leaves of a bright green color and yellow globular flowers growing from the leaf-axils <note>original: "axillæ," the angle where the leaf meets the stem</note> that have a fragrant smell. The pods are about three inches long and half an inch broad; they are light brown, smooth, compressed, and contain five or six smooth, flat seeds. Formerly, the flowers of this tree were used as an ingredient in the "Theriac of Andromachus" <note>original: "theriaca andromachi," a famous ancient medicinal "cure-all" compound</note> mentioned in old pharmaceutical books <note>original: "dispensatories"</note>. The tree is sometimes planted as a hedge or fence around enclosures, and the timber, though small, is useful in rural farming <note>original: "economy"</note>.

11. The *arborea* <note>original: "arborea," Latin for "tree-like"</note>, or wild tamarind tree, is common in all the woodlands, especially near where settlements have been made in Jamaica. It rises to a considerable height and is proportionally thick. The timber is excellent and serves many purposes in rural farming; it is the color of cedar, quite hard, and takes a good polish. The leaves are numerous, and the flowers are globular and white. The pods are about a foot long and a fine scarlet color; when they are ripe, they open and become twisted. The seeds then appear; they are oblong, smooth, shining black, and quite soft. Overall, from the leaves, flowers, and pods, this tree exhibits a singular and beautiful contrast. In Britain, this plant is raised in hothouses, but it appears that with a little effort it may be grown in the open air. A good-sized tree of this sort grew in the garden of the late Dr. William Pitcairn at Islington, near London.

12. The *latifolia* <note>original: "latifolia," Latin for "broad-leaved"</note>, shag-bark, or white wild tamarind. This excellent timber tree is very common in Jamaica and rises to a moderate height and good thickness. The trunk is rough and scaly; the leaves are numerous, diamond-shaped <note>original: "rhomboidal"</note>, and have a yellowish tint. The flower spikes grow from the leaf-axils <note>original: "axillæ"</note> and are yellow in color. The seed vessels are flat, jointed, and twisted. The seeds are the size of a vetch <note>A type of pea-like legume</note>, white, and finely streaked with blue. Of this tree, there is a variety which some botanists call *M. serpentina* <note>original: "M. serpentina," or snakelike Mimosa</note>. The chief difference is in the leaves, which are smaller and a shining dark green.

17. The catechu tree, according to Mr. Ker, grows only to twelve feet in height and to one foot in diameter. It is covered with a thick, rough, brown bark, and toward the top it divides into many close-knit branches. The leaves are doubly winged <term>original: bipinnated; a compound leaf where the leaflets are themselves divided</term> and are placed alternately upon the younger branches. The primary leaflets <term>original: partial pinnæ</term> are nearly two inches long and commonly consist of fifteen to thirty pairs, with small glands inserted between them. Each wing is usually furnished with about forty pairs of small leaflets <term>original: pinnulæ; or linear lobes</term> covered with short hairs. The spines are short, curved backward <note>original: "recurved"</note>, and placed in pairs at the base of each leaf. The flowers are both bisexual <note>original: "hermaphrodite"</note> and male, and they grow in dense spikes that emerge from the leaf joints <term>original: axillæ; the angle between the leaf and the stem</term> and are four or five inches long. The calyx <note>the outer protective layer of a flower</note> is tube-shaped, hairy, and divides at the edge into five oval, pointed segments. The corolla <note>the inner circle of petals</note> is made of a single petal <term>original: monopetalous</term>, whitish, and of the same form as the calyx but twice its length. The filaments <note>the stalks of the stamens</note> are numerous and hair-like, double the length of the petals, attached at the base of the ovary <term>original: germen</term>, and topped with roundish pollen-heads <term>original: antheræ</term>. The ovary is oval and supports a slender style <note>the stalk connecting the ovary to the stigma</note> which is the same length as the filaments and ends in a simple stigma <note>the part of the flower that receives pollen</note>. The fruit, or pod, is lance-shaped, brown, smooth, and flattened, with a wavy <note>original: "undulated"</note> thin edge; it contains six or eight roundish, flattened seeds which produce a sickening <note>original: "nauseous"</note> odor when chewed. From this tree, which grows abundantly in the mountainous parts of India <note>original: Hindostan</note> and flowers in June, is produced the medicinal drug long known in Europe by the name *terra japonica* <note>original Latin: "Japanese earth," an astringent resin extract</note>.

18. The *Nilotica* <note>original: "Nilotica," referring to the Nile</note>, or true Egyptian acacia, grows to a greater height than the previous species. The bark of the trunk is smooth and gray, while the bark of the branches usually has a purplish tint. The leaves are doubly winged <note>original: "bipinnated"</note> and placed alternately. The primary leaflets <note>original: "partial pinnæ"</note> are opposite each other, featuring a small gland between the outermost pair and many pairs of narrow, oval-shaped smaller leaflets <note>original: "pinnulæ"</note>. The spines are long, white, and spreading, growing from each side of the leaf base. The flowers are both bisexual <note>original: "hermaphrodite"</note> and male; they take a spherical shape and grow four or five together upon slender flower stalks <term>original: peduncles</term> which emerge from the leaf joints <note>original: "axillæ"</note>. The calyx is small, bell-shaped, and divided at the opening into five tiny teeth. The corolla consists of five narrow, yellowish segments. The filaments are numerous and hair-like, and are furnished with roundish yellow pollen-heads <note>original: "antheræ"</note>. The ovary <note>original: "germen"</note> is cone-shaped and supports a slender style topped with a simple stigma. The fruit is a long pod resembling that of the lupin <note>a type of legume</note> and contains many flat brown seeds. It is a native of Arabia and Egypt and flowers in July.
