Although the *Mimosa nilotica* <note>the Egyptian acacia</note> grows in great abundance over the vast extent of Africa, gum arabic is produced chiefly by those trees situated near the equatorial regions. We are told that in Lower Egypt, the sun's heat is never intense enough for this purpose. The gum seeps out <term>original: exudes</term> in a liquid state from the bark of the trunk and branches of the tree, in a similar way to the gum often produced on cherry trees and similar plants in this country; by exposure to the air, it soon becomes solid and hard. 

In Senegal, the gum begins to flow when the tree first opens its flowers and continues during the rainy season until the month of December, when it is collected for the first time. Another collection of the gum is made in March from cuts made in the bark; it is said that the extreme dryness of the air at that time makes these incisions necessary. Gum arabic is now usually imported into England from Barbary <note>a historical term for the coastal regions of North Africa</note>. It is no longer packed in skins, as was the practice in Egypt and Arabia, but in large casks or barrels <term>original: hogsheads</term>. 

The common appearance of this gum is well known, and the various shapes it takes seem to depend on various accidental circumstances during its seeping <note>original: "transudation"</note> and hardening <note>original: "concretion"</note>. Gum arabic of a pale yellowish color is the most highly valued. On the contrary, those pieces which are large, rough, roundish, and of a brownish or reddish hue are found to be less pure; these are said to be produced from a different species of Mimosa (*Mimosa senegal*). However, Arabian and Egyptian gum is commonly mixed with pieces of this kind, similar to the gum that comes from the coast of Africa near the Senegal River.

Gum arabic cannot be dissolved by alcohol <note>original: "spirit"</note> or oil, but in twice its quantity of water, it dissolves into a mucus-like <note>original: "mucilaginous"</note> fluid with the consistency of a thick syrup. In this state, it serves many useful purposes by allowing oily, resinous, and fatty <note>original: "pinguious"</note> substances to be mixed with water. The sticky <note>original: "glutinous"</note> quality of gum arabic causes it to be preferred over most other gums as a soothing treatment <term>original: demulcent; a substance that forms a soothing film over a mucous membrane</term> for coughs, hoarseness, and other respiratory illnesses <note>original: "catarrhal affections"</note>. It is used to dull <note>original: "obtund"</note> irritating, sharp fluids <note>original: "acrimonious humours"</note> and to replace lost mucus. It has been very generally employed in cases of burning during urination <note>original: "ardor urinæ"</note> and painful, restricted urination <term>original: stranguary; a condition where urination is slow and painful</term>. However, it is the opinion of Dr. Cullen that "even this soothing liquid, as an internal treatment, can be of no service beyond the digestive tract <note>original: "alimentary canal"</note>."

19. The *Senegal* <note>the Gum Senegal tree</note> is a native of Guinea and was introduced to Jamaica some time ago. Dr. Wright tells us he saw both this and the *Nilotica* species—both about the size of a cherry tree—growing at Dr. Paterson's in the parish of Hanover, Jamaica. The flowers are globe-shaped and fragrant. The pods are brown and about the size of a goose quill. When the tree is cut, it seeps gum arabic, though in smaller quantities and less transparent than the version sold in shops, which is obtained from the *Nilotica* described above. There are over forty other species listed in the *System of Plants* <note>original: "Systema Vegetabilium", a major botanical work by Carl Linnaeus</note>.

In the attached illustration <note>original: "Plate"</note> is shown an undescribed species of unusual size, mentioned by Mr. Paterson in his travels among the Khoikhoi <note>original: "Hottentots," a historical term for the Khoisan people of Southern Africa</note>, though it was not described in detail. Like several other species of mimosa, it produces a gum which the local people consider a particularly delicate food. The leaves and the tips of the lower branches seem to be the primary food <term>original: aliment</term> of the giraffe <note>original: "camelopardalis"</note>. Due to the spread of its boughs and the smoothness of its trunk, the tree provides a sufficient defense for a species of social <note>original: "gregarious"</note> bird against snakes and other reptiles that would otherwise destroy its eggs. Mr. Bruce <note>James Bruce (1730–1794), a Scottish explorer who sought the source of the Blue Nile</note> describes two plants that seem to belong to this genus: one named *ergett el dimmo*, and the other *ergett el krone*. The former, in our author's opinion, should be named *Mimosa sanguinea*. Its name in the Ethiopian <note>original: "Abyssinian"</note> language means "the bloody ergett," a name derived, he suggests, from the fact that it is partly made of beautiful pink filaments. When the blossoms are fully open, the upper part consists of yellow curled filaments, and the lower part of pink filaments of a similar shape. In its unripe state, the part that later becomes pink is green and made of small nodules <note>original: "tubercles"</note> that are larger and more spaced out than those that produce the yellow filaments; the latter are smaller and more tightly packed. The leaves are bipinnate <term>original: double-pinnated; having leaflets that are themselves divided into smaller leaflets</term>.

The name of the other species, in the Ethiopian language, means "the horned ergett," which our author believes is named for the shape of its seed pods. The flower closely resembles that of the *acacia vera* in size and shape, except that it is attached to the branch by a strong, woody stalk of considerable length. This stalk grows from the base of the branch that bears the leaves and is protected by its lower part as if in a case. The branches are all covered with short, strong, and sharp thorns, with their points curved backward toward the root. The pods are covered with a prickly kind of hair that rubs off easily on the fingers and sticks to them, causing a very unpleasant sensation. They have thirteen sections; in each section are three hard, round, and shiny seeds of a dark brown color. Both of these shrubs close their leaves at the start of the heavy rains in the wet season and never fully open them again until the dry season returns.

## MYRISTICA, OR NUTMEG-TREE.

The *myristica*, or nutmeg tree, is a genus of plant belonging to the class *dioecia* <note>original: "dioecia"; plants with male and female flowers on separate individuals</note> and the order *syngenesia* <note>original: "syngenesia"; plants with stamens fused together by their anthers</note> in the *New Genera of Plants* <note>original: "New Genera Plantarum"</note> by Linnaeus, as edited by Schreber. It also belongs to the natural order *Lauri* <note>the laurel family</note> in his fourth class, the Monocotyledons <note>original: "Monocotylidones"; plants that have a single embryonic leaf</note>. The male calyx <term>the outer protective part of a flower</term> is single-leafed <note>original: "monophyllous"</note>, strong, and divided into three oval-shaped segments <note>original: "lacinii"</note>. In the middle of the base <note>original: "receptacle"</note> rises a column the same height as the calyx, to the upper part of which the

Anthers <note>original: "antheræ"</note> are attached. They vary in number from three to twelve or thirteen. The female calyx <note>the outer protective layer of a flower</note> and corolla <note>the petals of a flower</note> are the same as in the male, but located on a distinct tree. The ovary <note>original: "germen"</note> is oval-shaped; the style is short, with a bifid <note>split into two parts</note> stigma; the segments <note>original: "lacinii"</note> of which are oval and spreading. The fruit is of the type called a **drupe** <note>original: "drupa"; a fleshy fruit with a single shell or stone, like a peach</note>. It is fleshy, roundish, sometimes having a single chamber <note>original: "unilocular"</note>, sometimes having two valves <note>original: "bivalved"</note>, and it bursts at the side when ripe. The seed is enveloped with a fleshy and fatty membranous substance, which divides into filaments; (this, in one of the species, is the mace found in shops). The seed, or nutmeg, is round or oval-shaped, has a single chamber, and contains a small kernel, patterned on the surface by fibers running in the form of a screw.

### Species
There are five species of this genus according to some authors; but, since some of these are only varieties, they may be reduced to three, namely:

1. **Myristica fatua**, or wild nutmeg: This grows in Tobago and rises to the height of an apple tree; it has oblong, lance-shaped, downy leaves, and hairy fruit. The nutmeg of this tree is aromatic, but when taken internally it is narcotic, causing temporary drunkenness, delirium, and madness.

2. **Myristica sebifera**, (*Virola Sebifera*, Aublet, page 904. table 345.) A tree frequent in Guiana, rising to forty or even sixty feet high. Upon wounding the trunk, a thick, sharp, red juice runs out. Aublet says nothing of these nutmegs being aromatic; he only observes that a yellow fat is obtained from them, which serves many economic and medical purposes, and that the natives make candles from it.

3. **The Myristica moschata**, or common nutmeg, reaches a height of thirty feet, producing numerous branches which rise together in tiers. It is covered with bark that is a reddish-brown on the trunk, but the young branches are a bright green color. The leaves are nearly elliptical, pointed, wavy at the edges, and veined obliquely; they are bright green on the upper side and whitish on the under side, standing alternately upon stalks. The flowers are small and hang upon slender stalks <note>original: "peduncles"</note> coming from the axils <note>original: "axillæ"; the angle between the leaf and the stem</note> of the leaves. Both male and female flowers grow on separate trees. Mr. Schwartz, who has carefully examined this as well as the first two species preserved in spirits, places them among the **monadelphia** <note>a botanical classification where stamens are fused into a single bundle</note>.

The nutmeg has been supposed to be the *Comacum* <note>a fragrant fruit mentioned in ancient texts</note> of Theophrastus, but there seems to be little foundation for this opinion; nor can it with much probability be thought to be the *Chrysobalanus* <note>literally "Golden Acorn"</note> of Galen. Our first knowledge of it was evidently derived from the Arabians; Avicenna called it *jiausiban*, or *jausiband*, which signifies "nut of Banda" <note>original: "nut of bands"; likely referring to the Banda Islands where nutmeg originated</note>. Rumphius both illustrated and described this tree; but the illustration given by him is so imperfect, and the description so confused, that Linnæus, who gave it the generic name *myristica*, was unable to assign its proper characteristics. Sonnerat's account of the *muscadier* <note>French: nutmeg tree</note> is even more erroneous; and the younger Linnæus

# APPENDIX TO

[Linnaeus] was unfortunately misled by this author, placing the *myristica* <note>nutmeg</note> in the class *polyandria* <note>a botanical group of plants characterized by having many stamens</note> and describing the corolla <note>the petals of a flower</note> as consisting of five petals. Thunberg, who examined the flower of the nutmeg, places it in the class *monoecia* <note>plants that have separate male and female flowers on the same individual</note>. According to his description, the male flower has only one filament <note>the stalk of a stamen</note> surrounded at the upper part by the anthers <note>the pollen-bearing part of the flower</note>. Since the filaments are short and slender and the anthers are united, this mistake could easily happen. 

Monsieur De La Marck informs us that he received several branches of the *myristica*, containing both flowers and fruit, from the Isle of France <note>modern-day Mauritius</note>. A nutmeg tree was introduced there by Monsieur Poivre in 1770; it is now very large and continually produces flowers and fruit. From these branches, which were sent by Monsieur Céré (the director of the King's garden on that island), Monsieur De La Marck has been able to describe and illustrate this and other species of the *myristica* with reasonable accuracy. This is shown in the attached plate, which is explained below:

**Figure a.** A sprig with its reproductive organs. The drupe <note>a fleshy fruit with a single stone, like a peach</note> is shown at its natural size, bursting open.
**Figure b.** The full-grown fruit cut lengthwise.
**Figure c.** Another section of the same fruit.
**Figure d.** The nutmeg enveloped within its covering, the mace.
**Figure e.** The fatty membrane, or mace, spread out.
**Figure f.** The nutmeg at its natural size.
**Figure g.** The nutmeg with one end of its external skin <note>original: "tegument"</note> removed.
**Figure h.** The nutmeg with its outer skin entirely removed.
**Figure i.** A cross-section <note>original: "transverse section"</note> of the nutmeg.

The seeds or kernels, known as nutmegs, are well known because they have long been used for both cooking and medicine. When distilled with water, they yield a large amount of essential oil that smells like the spice itself. After distillation, an-insipid, fatty <note>original: "sebaceous"</note> substance is found floating on the water. If the liquid from boiling <note>original: "decoction"</note> is evaporated until thick <note>original: "inspissated"</note>, it produces an extract with an oily, slightly bitter taste and very little astringency <note>a dry, puckering mouthfeel</note>. Pure alcohol <note>original: "rectified spirit"</note> extracts the full medicinal essence of nutmegs through soaking <note>original: "infusion"</note> and loses very little of it during distillation; therefore, an alcohol-based extract possesses the flavor of the spice to a high degree.

When heated, nutmegs yield a significant amount of clear yellow oil when pressed; this oil hardens into a fatty consistency as it cools. In shops, we find three types of oily substances called "oil of mace," though they are actually squeezed from the nutmeg. The best kind is brought from the East Indies in stone jars; it has a thick consistency, the color of mace, and a pleasant, fragrant smell. The second sort is paler and of much lower quality; it comes from Holland in solid, usually flat, square masses. The third sort is the worst of all and is commonly called "common oil of mace." It is an artificial mixture of tallow <note>original: "sevum"</note>, palm oil, and similar fats, flavored with a small amount of genuine nutmeg oil.

**Method of gathering and preparing Nutmeg.** When the fruit is ripe, the natives climb the trees and gather it by pulling the branches toward them with long hooks. Some people are employed in opening them immediately and in taking off the green shell or first rind, which is laid together in a heap in the woods where, in time, it putrefies <note>rots or decays</note>. As soon as the putrefaction has taken place, there springs up a kind of mushroom called *musk boletes* <note>original: *boleti moschatuni*; mushrooms that grow on decaying plant matter</note>, which are blackish in color and much valued by the natives, who consider them delicate eating. When the nuts are stripped of their first rind, they are carried home, and the mace is carefully taken off with a small knife. The mace, which is a beautiful red but afterward assumes a darkish or reddish color, is laid to dry in the sun for the space of a day and then removed to a place less exposed to the sun's rays, where it remains for eight days so that it may soften a little. They afterward moisten it with seawater to prevent it from drying too much or from losing its oil. They are careful, however, not to use too much water, lest it should become putrid and be devoured by worms. Finally, it is put into small bags and squeezed very tightly. Mace must not be confused with *macer* <note>original: *macer*; an ancient medicinal bark mentioned by classical authors, often confused with nutmeg mace in early modern botany</note>.

The nuts, which are still covered with their woody <term>ligneous</term> shell, are exposed to the sun for three days and afterward dried before a fire until they make a sound when shaken. They then beat them with small sticks in order to remove their shell, which flies off in pieces. These nuts are divided into three groups: the first contains the largest and most beautiful, which are destined to be brought to Europe; the second contains those reserved for the use of the inhabitants; and the third contains the smallest, which are irregular or unripe. These are burned, and part of the rest is used for extracting oil by pressure. A pound of them commonly yields three ounces of oil, which has the consistency of tallow <note>hard animal fat</note> and has entirely the taste of nutmeg. Both the nut and mace, when distilled, provide an essential, transparent, and volatile <note>easily evaporated</note> oil of an excellent flavor. The nutmegs which have been thus selected would soon rot if they were not watered, or rather pickled, with lime-water made from burnt <term>calcined</term> shellfish, which they dilute with saltwater until it reaches the consistency of a fluid pulp. Into this mixture they dip the nutmegs, contained in small baskets, two or three times until they are completely covered with the liquid. They are afterward laid in a heap where they heat up and lose their excess moisture by evaporation. When they have "sweated" sufficiently, they are then properly prepared and fit for a sea voyage.

In the Island of Banda <note>an island group in Indonesia, historically the only source of nutmeg</note>, the fruit of the nutmeg tree is preserved whole in the following manner: When it is almost ripe, but before it opens, it is boiled in water and pierced with a needle. They next lay it in water to soak for ten days until it has lost its sour and sharp taste. They then boil it gently in a syrup of sugar, to which—if they wish it to be hard—a little lime is added. This operation is repeat—

...soaked for eight days, and each time the syrup is renewed. The fruit, when thus preserved, is put for the last time into a pretty thick syrup and is kept in earthen pots closely shut. These nuts are likewise pickled with brine or with vinegar; and when they intend to eat them, they first steep them in fresh water and afterwards boil them in syrup of sugar, etc.

*Uses.* Nutmegs preserved entire are presented as desserts, and the inhabitants of India sometimes eat them when they drink tea. Some of them use nothing but the pulp; others likewise chew the mace; but they generally throw away the kernel, which is really the nutmeg. Many who perform sea-voyages to the north chew this fruit every morning. The medicinal qualities of nutmeg are supposed to be aromatic, anodyne <note>pain-relieving</note>, stomachic <note>beneficial to the stomach</note>, and restringent <note>astringent or binding</note>; and with a view to the last-mentioned effects, it has been much used in diarrheas and dysenteries. To many people, the aromatic flavor of nutmeg is very agreeable; they, however, should be cautious not to use it in large quantities, as it is apt to affect the head and even to manifest a hypnotic <note>sleep-inducing</note> power in such a degree as to prove extremely dangerous. *Bontius* speaks of this as a frequent occurrence in India, and Dr. *Cullen* relates a remarkable instance of this soporific <note>sleep-inducing</note> effect of the nutmeg which fell under his own observation, and hence concludes that in apoplectic <note>relating to strokes</note> and paralytic <note>relating to paralysis</note> cases, this spice may be very improper. 

He observes that a person by mistake took two drams <note>about 7 grams or two teaspoons</note> or a little more of powdered nutmeg: he felt it warm in his stomach without any uneasiness, but in about an hour after he had taken it, he was seized with a drowsiness which gradually increased to a complete stupor and insensibility; and not long after, he was found fallen from his chair, lying on the floor of his chamber in the state mentioned. Being laid in bed, he fell asleep; but, awaking a little from time to time, he was quite delirious; and he thus continued alternately sleeping and delirious for several hours. By degrees, however, both these symptoms diminished, so that in about six hours from the time of taking the nutmeg, he was pretty well recovered from both. Although he still complained of a headache <note>original: head-ach</note> and some drowsiness, he slept naturally and quietly the following night, and the next day was quite in his ordinary health. 

The officinal <note>standard pharmacological</note> preparations of nutmeg are a spirit and essential oil, and the nutmeg in substance roasted to render it more astringent. Both the spice itself and its essential oil enter several compositions, such as the aromatic confection <note>original: confectio aromatica</note>, compound spirit of ammonia <note>original: spiritus ammoniae com.</note>, etc. Mace possesses qualities similar to those of the nutmeg but is less astringent, and its oil is supposed to be more volatile and acrid.

*Remarks on the Trade of Nutmegs.* Nutmeg trees grow in several islands in the eastern ocean. The wood-pigeon of the *Moluccas* is unintentionally a great planter of these trees and disseminates them in places where a nation, powerful by its commerce <note>likely referring to the Dutch East India Company, which maintained a strict monopoly on the spice trade</note>, thinks it for its interest that they should be rooted out and destroyed.

<meta>This page continues the history and commerce of spices, specifically detailing the Dutch East India Company’s monopoly on nutmeg, cloves, and cinnamon during the 18th century.</meta>

### CULPEPER'S BRITISH HERBAL.

The Dutch, with their tireless patience in overcoming the greatest obstacles, long claimed for themselves the entire harvest of nutmegs, as well as those of cloves and cinnamon. These grew in the islands of Ternate, Ceylon, etc., and the Dutch controlled them either by right of conquest or by paying subsidies <note>financial grants</note> to the islanders, who found these payments much more profitable than the former harvest of their trees. It is nevertheless true that they persuaded or forced the inhabitants of the Moluccas <note>the "Spice Islands" of Indonesia</note> to cut down and uproot all the clove trees, which they then preserved only on the islands of Amboyna and Ternate, which are largely under Dutch control. We know for certain that the Dutch pay 18,000 rixdollars <note>a silver coin used in Europe and its colonies</note> annually to the King of Ternate as a tribute or gift to compensate him for the loss of his clove trees in the other Molucca islands. Furthermore, they are bound by treaty to buy all the cloves brought by the natives of Amboyna to their warehouses at a price of three and three-quarter pence per pound. They have likewise succeeded in destroying cinnamon trees everywhere except on the island of Ceylon. The same is true for white pepper, and so on, so that the trade for all of Europe and a great part of Asia in these commodities passed through Dutch hands for a long time.

The Dutch held massive and very valuable warehouses <note>original: "magazines"</note> of these precious aromatic spices both in India and Europe. They actually kept sixteen years' worth of stock on hand, and never supplied their neighbors with the most recent harvest, but always with the oldest crop; for example, in 1760, they sold what had been stored in 1744. It is commonly said that when the Dutch have too large a quantity of cloves, nutmegs, and other spices in their warehouses, they throw them into the sea; however, the reality is that they dispose of their excess spices by burning them. On June 10, 1760, M. Beaumare <note>likely a contemporary traveler or merchant</note> saw a fire in Amsterdam near the admiralty where the fuel was valued at 8,000,000 livres <note>a former French currency</note>, and just as much was to be burned the following day. The feet of the spectators were bathed in the essential oils flowing from these substances, but no person was allowed to gather any of it, much less take any of the spices from the fire. Some years earlier, on a similar occasion and in the same place, a poor man who had picked up some nutmegs that rolled out of the fire was, as M. Beaumare was informed, arrested and condemned to immediate execution. 

We will only add that despite the protectiveness <note>original: "jealousy"</note> of the Dutch and the great pains they take to keep the sale of cloves entirely to themselves, they have never been able to prevent their own officers in several parts of India from stealing and selling considerable quantities of them. M. de Jaucourt <note>Louis de Jaucourt, a famous contributor to the French *Encyclopédie*</note> informs us that, in order to defraud the company, these officers sell the spices to the ships of other nations they meet at sea. They then dampen the remaining stock with water so that the weight remains the same number of quintals <note>a unit of weight, roughly 100 pounds</note> as their original cargo. The quantity sold can amount to ten quintals out of every hundred before the clerks at the warehouses in Batavia <note>modern-day Jakarta</note>, where the spices are received, even notice the theft.

We are informed by Mr. Romé de Lisle, who lately arrived from India, that the English obtain a great deal of cinnamon, pepper, and cloves from the island of Sumatra. The primary trading center <note>original: "staple"</note> for this commodity, which greatly offends the Dutch, is located at the trading post <note>original: "factory"</note> of Bencoolen <note>modern-day Bengkulu, Indonesia</note>. We have likewise seen a specimen of fairly good cinnamon grown at Martinique <note>original: "Martinico"</note>. The French, to prevent the export of gold and silver coin <note>original: "specie"</note> to pay for these aromatic and exotic products, have attempted to introduce the cultivation of them into some of their own colonies. A great many plants of the clove and nutmeg tree have been obtained and planted in the Isle of France <note>modern-day Mauritius</note>, the Island of Bourbon <note>modern-day Réunion</note>, and also at Cayenne <note>in French Guiana</note>, where they appear very promising.

### FLOWERING PAVONIS.

THIS plant <note>now known as *Caesalpinia pulcherrima* or the Peacock Flower</note> grows nine feet in height and bears most beautiful yellow flowers. The seed, when steeped in water and given as a strong medicinal tea <note>original: "decoction"</note> to a woman in labor, greatly assists the delivery. For this reason, those Indian slaves who have considered themselves cruelly used by their masters in the plantations take great pains to obtain this tree for the purpose of inducing abortion, which they know it never fails to achieve. Those enslaved people <note>original: "negroes"</note> who are brought from Guinea and Angola were the first discovered making use of this plant; while they ate it or drank a tea made from its leaves or seeds, they neither conceived nor gave birth to children. When challenged about this <note>original: "remonstrated with"</note>, they said they would sooner die than bring children into slavery, who, as they grew up, would have to undergo the same heavy labor <note>original: "yoke"</note> and suffer all the cruelties inflicted on their unfortunate parents. Tournefort calls this tree *poinciana flore pulcherrimo* <note>Latin: "Poinciana with the most beautiful flower"</note>. It grows in all warm climates and is found in many parts of America.

### PIMENTO, or JAMAICA PEPPER TREE.

THE Jamaica pepper tree is a species of the myrtle, a genus of the *monogynia* <note>plants with a single pistil</note> order, belonging to the *icosandria* <note>plants with twenty or more stamens</note> class of plants; in the natural method, it ranks under the 19th order, *hesperideæ* <note>a Linnaean classification for myrtle-like plants</note>. The calyx <note>the outer protective part of a flower</note> is five-cleft <note>original: "quinquefid"</note> and positioned above the fruit; there are five petals; the berry contains two or three seeds <note>original: "dispermous or trispermous"</note>. There are fourteen species, of which the most remarkable are:

1. The ***communis***, or common myrtle tree, which rises with a shrubby, upright, firm stem, branching extensively all around into a dense, full head. It grows eight or ten feet high and is very closely covered with oval, spear-shaped <note>original: "oval-lanceolate"</note>, entire leaves, mostly arranged in opposite pairs. These are from half an inch to an inch and a half long and one inch broad, sitting on short stalks. It produces numerous small, pale flowers from the axils <note>original: "axillas"; the angle between the leaf and the stem</note>, appearing singly on each stalk and having two-leaved coverings <note>original: "diphyllous involucrums"</note>; each flower is followed by a small, oval, dark-purple berry.

### CULPEPER'S BRITISH HERBAL

The most significant varieties are:

*   **Broad-leaved Roman myrtle**, with oval, shining, green leaves, an inch and a half long and one inch wide; it is remarkably productive of flowers <note>original: "floriferous"</note>.
*   **Gold-striped broad-leaved Roman myrtle**.
*   **Broad-leaved Dutch myrtle**, with spear-shaped, sharp-pointed, dark-green leaves, an inch long and about three-quarters of an inch wide.
*   **Double-flowered Dutch myrtle**.
*   **Broad-leaved Jews' myrtle**, having leaves placed in threes at each joint. Because of this particular growth pattern, this species is held in universal high regard among the Jewish community for their religious ceremonies, particularly in decorating their tabernacles <note>This refers to the Jewish festival of Sukkot, where myrtle (hadass) is one of the "Four Species" used in ritual observances.</note>. Many gardeners around London cultivate it with great care to sell to these people, who are often obliged to purchase it at the rate of sixpence or a shilling for a small branch. The true kind, having the leaves exactly in threes, is very scarce and is a curiosity; but by care in its propagation—taking only the perfectly three-leaved <note>original: "ternate-leaved"</note> shoots for cuttings—it may be increased quickly enough. It is worth the attention of the curious, and particularly those who raise myrtles for the London markets.
*   **Orange-leaved Spanish myrtle**, with oval, spear-shaped leaves, an inch and a half long or more and an inch wide. They grow in clusters around the branches and resemble the shape and color of orange-tree leaves.
*   **Gold-striped leaved orange myrtle**.
*   **Common upright Italian myrtle**, with its branches and leaves growing more erect; the leaves are oval, lance-shaped, sharp-pointed, and nearly an inch long and half an inch wide.
*   **Silver-striped upright Italian myrtle**.
*   **White-berried upright Italian myrtle**.
*   **Portugal acute-leaved myrtle**, with spear-shaped, oval, sharp-pointed leaves about an inch long.
*   **Box-leaved myrtle**, with weak branches and small, oval, blunt <note>original: "obtuse"</note>, bright green <note>original: "lucid-green"</note>, closely-placed leaves.
*   **Striped box-leaved myrtle**.
*   **Rosemary-leaved myrtle** has <note>original: "hath"</note> erect branches and small, narrow, lance-shaped, sharp-pointed, shining green, and very fragrant leaves.
*   **Silver-striped rosemary-leaved myrtle**.
*   **Thyme-leaved myrtle**, with very small, closely-placed leaves.
*   **Nutmeg-myrtle**, with erect branches and leaves; the leaves are oval, sharp-pointed, and finely scented like a nutmeg.
*   **Broad-leaved nutmeg-myrtle**.
*   **Silver-striped leaved nutmeg-myrtle**.
*   **Crested <note>original: "Cristated"</note> or cock's-comb myrtle**, frequently called **bird's-nest myrtle**, has narrow sharp-pointed leaves that are crested at intervals.

All of these are beautiful evergreen shrubs of exceeding fragrance. They are foreign plants <note>original: "exotics"</note> originally from the southern parts of Europe, Asia, and Africa; consequently, in this country, they require the shelter of a greenhouse in winter. All of them—though rather of the small-leaved kind—have foliage that is closely placed and remains all year, and they are very productive of flowers <note>original: "floriferous"</note> in summer. When there is a collection of the different sorts, they afford an agreeable source of variety with each other. They therefore deserve universal esteem as primary greenhouse plants, especially as they are all so easily raised from cuttings and are of such easy culture that they can be grown in every garden where there is any sort of greenhouse, or

The most important varieties are: Broad-leaved Roman myrtle, with oval, shining, green leaves, an inch and a half long and one inch wide; it is remarkably free-flowering <note>original: "floriferous"</note>. Gold-striped broad-leaved Roman myrtle. Broad-leaved Dutch myrtle, with lance-shaped <note>original: "spear-shaped"</note>, sharp-pointed, dark-green leaves, an inch long and about three-quarters of an inch wide. Double-flowered Dutch myrtle. 

Broad-leaved Jews myrtle has leaves placed in threes at each joint. Because of this particular feature, this species is highly valued by the Jewish community for use in their religious ceremonies, particularly in decorating their tabernacles <note>referring to the festival of Sukkot</note>. Many gardeners around London cultivate it with particular care to sell to them; these customers are often obliged to purchase a small branch for the price of sixpence or a shilling. The true variety, having leaves exactly in threes, is very scarce and is considered a curiosity. However, by being careful during propagation—taking only the shoots with three leaves per node <note>original: "perfectly ternate-leaved shoots"</note> for cuttings—it may be increased quickly enough. It is well worth the attention of the curious gardener, particularly those who grow myrtles for the London markets. 

Orange-leaved Spanish myrtle has oval, lance-shaped leaves, an inch and a half long or more and an inch wide, which grow in clusters around the branches and resemble the shape and color of orange-tree leaves. Gold-striped leaved orange myrtle. Common upright Italian myrtle has branches and leaves that grow more vertically; the leaves are oval and lance-shaped, sharp-pointed, and nearly an inch long and half an inch wide. Silver-striped upright Italian myrtle. White-berried upright Italian myrtle. Portugal acute-leaved myrtle has lance-shaped, oval, sharp-pointed leaves about an inch long. Box-leaved myrtle has weak branches and small, oval, blunt <note>original: "obtuse"</note>, shining green, closely-set leaves. Striped box-leaved myrtle. 

Rosemary-leaved myrtle has upright branches and small, narrow, lance-shaped, sharp-pointed, shining green, very fragrant leaves. Silver-striped rosemary-leaved myrtle. Thyme-leaved myrtle has very small, closely-set leaves. Nutmeg-myrtle has upright branches and leaves; the leaves are oval, sharp-pointed, and finely scented like a nutmeg. Broad-leaved nutmeg-myrtle. Silver-striped leaved nutmeg-myrtle. Crested <note>original: "Cristated"</note> or cock's-comb myrtle, frequently called bird's-nest myrtle, has narrow sharp-pointed leaves that are crested at intervals. 

These are all beautiful evergreen shrubs of exceeding fragrance. They were originally exotic plants from the southern parts of Europe, Asia, and Africa; consequently, in this country, they require the shelter of a greenhouse in winter. All of these, though mostly of the small-leaved kind, have dense foliage that remains all year and flowers abundantly in summer. When a collection of the different sorts is kept, they provide an agreeable variety to one another. They therefore claim universal esteem as primary greenhouse plants, especially as they are all so easily raised from cuttings and are of such easy culture that they are attainable in every garden where there is any sort of greenhouse, or

2. The pimenta, *pimento*, Jamaica pepper, or allspice tree grows over thirty feet tall and two feet in circumference. The branches near the top are heavily divided and densely covered with leaves, which remain green year-round, giving the tree a beautiful appearance. The bark is very smooth on the outside and grey in color. The leaves vary in size and shape but are generally about four inches long, veined, pointed, elliptical, and a deep, shining green. The flowers grow in clusters or panicles <note>original: "panicles," branched flower clusters</note> on divided stalks that usually grow at the ends of the branches. The calyx <note>the outer protective part of a flower bud</note> is divided into four rounded segments. There are also four petals: small, white, oval-shaped, and curved backward <note>original: "reflex"</note>, positioned opposite the segments of the calyx. The filaments <note>the stalks of the stamens</note> are numerous, longer than the petals, spreading, and greenish-white, rising from the calyx and the upper part of the ovary <note>original: "germen"</note>. The anthers <note>original: "antheræ," the pollen-bearing part of the flower</note> are rounded and pale yellow. The style is smooth, simple, and upright; the stigma <note>the part of the flower that receives pollen</note> is blunt. The ovary develops into a round, juicy berry containing two flat, kidney-shaped seeds. 

This tree is native to Central America <note>original: "New Spain"</note> and the West Indian islands. It grows in great abundance in Jamaica, flowering in June, July, and August. Every part of the tree, including the flowers, gives off a fragrant, aromatic scent. When ripe, the berries are dark purple and filled with a sweet pulp that birds eat greedily. By passing the seeds through their digestive tracts <note>original: "muting the seeds"</note>, the birds spread these trees throughout the woods. It is believed that this process causes the seeds to ferment slightly, making them more likely to grow than seeds gathered directly from the tree.

The *pimento* is a beautiful, fragrant evergreen and provides a lovely display in the hothouse <note>original: "stove," a heated greenhouse</note> throughout the year. It was first introduced and grown in this country by Mr. Philip Miller in 1739. Regarding their flowering period, all varieties of the common myrtle <note>original: *myrtus communis*</note> bloom here in July and August, and most are very heavy-flowering <note>original: "floriferous"</note>. The broad-leaved Roman variety, in particular, is often covered in flowers, which on some types are followed by berries that ripen in winter. The pimento also flowers in the hothouse with great beauty and vigor. The flowers of most varieties are small but numerous, each formed of five oval petals and many stamens <note>original: "stamina"</note>. ### Properties and Uses
The leaves and flowers of the common upright myrtle have an astringent <note>tightening or contracting</note> quality and are used for cleansing the skin, stabilizing teeth when loosened by scurvy, and strengthening body fibers. A distilled water is drawn from the flowers and young tops that is detersive <note>cleansing</note>, astringent, and cosmetic, often used in gargles. A decoction <note>a liquid made by boiling</note> of the flowers and leaves is applied in fomentations <note>warm medicinal compresses</note>. The berries have a binding, cleansing quality; the chemical oil obtained from them is excellent for the hair and is used in pomades and most other external beauty products for the face and skin. As an internal medicine, these berries have little to no value.

In the *Portable Dictionary of Natural History* <note>original: "Dictionnaire portatif d' Histoire Naturelle"</note>, a story is told which, if true, demonstrates the strongly astringent quality of myrtle.

> "Myrtle," he says, "is also the base of a pomade called *The Countess's Pomade* <note>original: "Pommade de la Comtesse"</note>, which is well known due to an extraordinary historical event. One of those fashionable young men who loiter around the dressing tables <note>original: "toilets"</note> of beautiful women happened one day to be left alone in that 'storehouse of the graces.' With eager curiosity, he examined the perfumes, the smelling bottles, the scented powders, the essences, and the cosmetics. To give his lips a brighter red color and more flexibility, and to remove some unsightly spots, he lightly spread the 'fatal' pomade with a careless finger. He then looked at himself in the mirror and admired his own beauty. When the lady entered, he wished to speak, but his lips had contracted so tightly that he could only stammer. The lady looked at him with astonishment; at length, glancing at her dressing table, she discovered the open jar and realized the cause of his mistake. She enjoyed a hearty laugh at the expense of her admirer, whose confusion revealed his indiscretion."

Pimento berries are mostly imported into Britain from Jamaica, which is why they are called *Jamaica pepper*. They are also called *all-spice* because their taste and aroma are thought to resemble a mixture of many different spices. It is one of the primary products of Jamaica, where "pimento-walks" <note>large plantations</note> are established on a large scale, some covering several acres of ground. When the berries reach full size but before they begin to ripen, they are picked from the branches and laid out in the sun for several days until they are sufficiently dried. This process must be handled with great care; on the first and second days of exposure, the berries must be turned very often and always protected from rain and evening dew. After this process is finished—which is determined by the color and the rattling of the seeds inside the berries—they are packed into bags or hogsheads <note>large wooden barrels</note> for the market. Pimento, which was at first brought over for culinary <note>original: "dietetic"</note> uses, has been long employed in apothecary shops as a substitute <note>original: "succedaneum"</note> for the more costly aromatic spices from the East. It is moderately warm and has an agreeable flavor, somewhat resembling a mixture of cloves, cinnamon, and nutmegs. When distilled with water, it yields an elegant essential oil that is so heavy <note>original: "ponderous"</note> that it sinks in water; it is moderately sharp <term>pungent</term> in taste, and in smell and flavor it approaches oil of cloves, or rather a mixture of cloves and nutmegs. Through soaking <term>maceration</term> or gentle heating <term>digestion</term> in rectified spirit <note>highly concentrated alcohol</note>, it imparts the full extent of its virtues. In the process of distillation, it gives over very little of its essence to this solvent <term>menstruum</term>; nearly all of its active matter remains concentrated in the thickened <term>inspissated</term> extract. 

Pimento can scarcely be considered a primary medicine. However, it is a pleasant aromatic, and for this reason, it is frequently used with different drugs that require such a pleasing addition <note>original: "grateful adjunct"</note>. Both the *Pharmacopoeias* <note>official books containing lists of medicinal drugs and their preparations</note> provide directions for making water-based and alcohol-based distillations from these berries, and the Edinburgh College of Physicians also provides orders for the *essential oil of Jamaica pepper* <note>original: "oleum esstentiale piperis Jamaicensis"</note>.

## P L A N T A I N - T R E E. *MUSA*.

The plantain tree is a genus of the single-style <note>original: "monogynia"</note> order, belonging to the six-stamen <note>original: "hexandria"</note> class of plants; in the natural method, it ranks under the eighth order, *scitamineae* <note>a group of ginger-like plants</note>. 

The outer part <term>calyx</term> of the male hermaphrodite flower is a sheath <note>original: "spatha"</note>; the petals <term>corolla</term> consist of two parts <note>original: "dipetalous"</note>; one petal is upright and five-toothed <note>original: "quinquedentate"</note>; the other is nectar-producing <note>original: "nectariferous"</note>, hollow <term>concave</term>, and shorter. There are six stalks <term>filaments</term>, five of which are fully formed <note>original: "perfect"</note>; there is one style; the ovary <term>germen</term> is positioned below the flower <term>inferior</term> and does not produce fruit <term>abortive</term>. The female hermaphrodite has the same outer parts, petals, stalks, and pistil as the male, but with only one stalk <term>filament</term> being fully formed; the berry is oblong and has three angles at the bottom. The most remarkable species are: 
1. The *Musa paradisaica*, or Jamaica plantain.
2. The *Musa sapientum*, or banana tree. (See the Plate).

The first sort is cultivated in all the islands of the West Indies, where the fruit serves the native people as bread; some of the white settlers also prefer it to most other foods, especially to yams and cassava <note>original: "cassada"</note> bread. The plant rises with a soft, fleshy stem <note>original: "stalk"</note> fifteen or twenty feet high. The lower part of the stem is often as thick as a man’s thigh, diminishing gradually toward the top where the leaves come out on every side. These leaves are often eight feet long and from two to three feet broad, with a strong, fleshy central vein <term>mid-rib</term> and a great number of crosswise <term>transverse</term> veins running from the central vein to the edges. The leaves are thin and tender, so that when they are exposed to the open air, they are generally torn by the wind; because they are so large, the wind has great power against them. These leaves emerge from the center of the stem and are rolled up when they first appear; but when they have grown above the stems, they expand and turn backward. When the plant is grown to its full height, the spikes of flowers will appear in the centre, which is often near four feet in length and nods on one side. The flowers come out in bunches; those in the lower part of the spike are the largest, while the others diminish in size as they go upward. Each of the bunches is covered with a **spathe** <term>a large, leaf-like sheath that covers a flower cluster</term> or sheath of a fine purple color, which drops off when the flowers open. The upper part of the spike is made up of male or barren flowers, which are not followed by fruit but fall off with their covers. 

The fruit, or plantain, is about a foot long and an inch and a half or two inches in diameter. It is at first green, but when ripe, it is a pale-yellow color. The skin is tough, and within is a soft pulp of a luscious, sweet flavor. The spikes of the fruit are often so large that they weigh over forty pounds. The fruit of this variety is generally cut before it is ripe. The green skin is pulled off, and the heart is roasted in a clear fire for a few minutes and frequently turned; it is then scraped and served as bread. Boiled plantains are not as palatable. 

This tree is cultivated on a very extensive scale in Jamaica; without its fruit, Dr. Wright <note>William Wright (1735–1819) was a Scottish physician and botanist who documented the plants of Jamaica</note> says the island would scarcely be habitable, as no other type of food could supply its place. Even flour or bread itself would be less agreeable and less able to support the laborious enslaved workers <note>original: "laborious negro"</note>, so as to enable them to do their business or to keep in health. Plantains also fatten horses, cattle, swine, dogs, fowls, and other domestic animals. The leaves, being smooth and soft, are employed as dressings after the application of blisters <note>medicinal plasters used to irritate the skin and "draw out" ailments</note>. The water from the soft trunk is astringent <term>a substance that shrinks or constricts body tissues</term> and is employed by some to check diarrhea. Every other part of the tree is useful in different parts of rural economy <note>original: "œconomy"; the management of farm resources and household production</note>. The leaves are used for napkins and tablecloths and are also food for hogs.

The second sort <note>likely referring to the banana</note> differs from the first by having its stalks marked with dark purple stripes and spots. The fruit is shorter, straighter, and rounder; the pulp is softer and has a more luscious taste. It is never eaten green; but, when ripe, it is very agreeable, either eaten raw or fried in slices as fritters, and is relished by all ranks of people in the West Indies. Both the plants mentioned above were carried to the West Indies from the Canary Islands, where, it is believed, they had been brought from Guinea <note>a region on the west coast of Africa</note>, where they grow naturally. They are also cultivated in Egypt and in most other hot countries, where they grow to perfection in about ten months from their first planting to the ripening of their fruit. When their stalks are cut down, several **suckers** <term>shoots springing from the base or roots of a plant</term> will come up from the root, which will produce fruit in six or eight months. By cutting down the stalks at different times, there is a constant succession of fruit all year round.

## PLANTAIN-TREE. MUSA.

The plantain tree is a genus of the "single-style" <term>Monogynia: plants with flowers having only one pistil or female organ</term> order, belonging to the "six-stamen" <term>Hexandria: a Linnaean class of plants with six stamens</term> class of plants. In the natural system, it is ranked under the eighth order, the ginger-like plants <note>original: *scitamineæ*</note>. The flower-cup <note>original: *calyx*</note> of the male hermaphrodite flower is a sheath <note>original: *spatha*</note>; the petals <note>original: *corolla*</note> consist of two parts: one petal is upright and has five teeth, and the other is a shorter, concave, nectar-producing part. There are six filaments (the stalks of the male organs), five of which are fertile; there is one style (the female organ's stalk); and the base of the flower <note>original: *germen*</note> is positioned below the petals and fails to produce fruit. The female hermaphrodite flower has the cup, petals, stalks, and pistil of the male, but with only one fertile filament; the berry is long and has three angles at the bottom. The most notable species are: 1. The *Musa paradisaica*, or Jamaica plantain; 2. The *Musa sapientum*, or banana tree. See the Plate.

The first variety is cultivated in all the islands of the West Indies, where the fruit serves as bread for the indigenous people; some of the white people also prefer it to most other things, especially to yams and cassava <note>original: "cassada"</note> bread. The plant grows with a soft stalk to a height of fifteen or twenty feet. The lower part of the stalk is often as thick as a man's thigh, tapering gradually to the top where the leaves sprout from every side. These leaves are often eight feet long and two to three feet wide, with a sturdy, fleshy central rib and a great number of veins running across from the rib to the edges. The leaves are thin and delicate, so that where they are exposed to the open air, they are generally torn by the wind; because they are so large, the wind has great power against them. These leaves emerge from the center of the stalk and are rolled up when they first appear; but when they have grown above the stalks, they unfold and curve backward. [...plants. This growth can] be seen by the naked eye; and, if a fine line is drawn level with the top of the leaf, in an hour’s time the leaf will be nearly an inch above it. When the plant is grown to its full height, the flower spikes will appear in the center, which is often nearly four feet in length and leans to one side. The flowers come out in bunches; those in the lower part of the spike are the largest, while the others decrease in size as they go up. Each bunch is covered with a spathe <term>spathe: a large bract or leaf-like sheath enclosing a flower cluster</term> or sheath of a fine purple color, which drops off when the flowers open. The upper part of the spike is made up of male or sterile <note>original: "barren"</note> flowers, which do not produce fruit but fall off with their covers. The fruit, or plantain, is about a foot long and an inch and a half to two inches in diameter. It is green at first, but when ripe, it is a pale yellow color. The skin is tough, and inside is a soft pulp with a lusciously sweet flavor. The spikes of fruit are often so large that they weigh more than 40 pounds. The fruit of this variety is generally cut before it is ripe. The green skin is pulled off, and the heart is roasted in a clear fire for a few minutes and frequently turned; it is then scraped and served as bread. Boiled plantains are not as tasty. This tree is cultivated on a very extensive scale in Jamaica; Dr. Wright <note>Dr. William Wright (1735–1819) was a Scottish physician and botanist who lived in Jamaica and wrote extensively on its flora.</note> says the island would scarcely be habitable without its fruit, as no other food source could take its place. Even flour or bread itself would be less pleasant and less able to support the hard-working laborers <note>original: "laborious negro"</note>, helping them to do their work or stay in health. Plantains also fatten horses, cattle, pigs, dogs, chickens, and other domestic animals. The leaves, being smooth and soft, are used as dressings after blisters. The liquid from the soft trunk is astringent <term>astringent: a substance that causes the contraction of body tissues, often used to stop bleeding or secretions</term> and is used by some to treat diarrhea. Every other part of the tree is useful in various aspects of rural economy <note>original: "œconomy"</note>. The leaves are used for napkins and tablecloths and as food for hogs.

The second variety differs from the first because its stalks are marked with dark purple stripes and spots. The fruit is shorter, straighter, and rounder; the pulp is softer and has a sweeter taste. It is never eaten green; but when ripe, it is very pleasant, whether eaten raw or fried in slices as fritters, and is enjoyed by all classes of people in the West Indies. Both of these plants were carried to the West Indies from the Canary Islands, where it is believed they had been brought from Guinea, where they grow naturally. They are also cultivated in Egypt and in most other hot countries, where they grow to perfection in about ten months from the first planting to the ripening of their fruit. When their stalks are cut down, several suckers will grow up from the root, which will produce fruit in six or eight months. Thus, by cutting down the stalks at different times, there is a constant supply of fruit all year round.

<header>APPENDIX TO</header>

Pimento, which was at first brought over for dietary uses, has been long employed in apothecary shops as a substitute <note>original: "succedaneum"</note> for more costly Eastern spices. It is moderately warm and has an agreeable flavor, somewhat resembling a mixture of cloves, cinnamon, and nutmegs. When distilled with water, it yields a fine essential oil that is so heavy <note>original: "ponderous"</note> it sinks in the water; it is moderately sharp in taste, while its smell and flavor are close to oil of cloves, or rather a mixture of cloves and nutmegs. Through soaking or heating <note>original: "maceration or digestion"</note>, it transfers all its virtues to purified alcohol <note>original: "rectified spirit"</note>. In the process of distillation, it gives over very little to this solvent <note>original: "menstruum"</note>, as nearly all its active matter remains concentrated in the thickened <note>original: "inspissated"</note> extract. Pimento can scarcely be considered a medicine on its own; however, it is a pleasant aromatic, and for this reason, it is frequently used with different drugs that require such a pleasing addition. Both the official drug manuals <note>original: "Pharmacopœias"</note> provide directions for making water-based and alcohol-based distillations from these berries, and the Edinburgh College also includes the essential oil of Jamaican pepper <note>original: "oleum essentiale piperis Jamaicensis"</note>.

### P L A N T A I N - T R E E. *Musa.*

The plantain tree is a genus of the "one pistil" <note>original: "monogynia"</note> order, belonging to the "six stamens" <note>original: "hexandria"</note> class of plants; in the natural classification method, it ranks under the eighth order, ginger-like plants <note>original: "scitamineæ"</note>. The calyx <term>calyx: the protective outer layer of a flower</term> of the male hermaphrodite is a spathe, or sheath; the corolla <term>corolla: the petals of a flower</term> has two petals. One petal is upright and five-toothed <note>original: "quinquedentate"</note>; the other is nectar-producing, hollow, and shorter. There are six filaments <term>filament: the stalk of a stamen that supports the pollen-producing anther</term>, five of which are perfect; there is one style and an inferior, undeveloped ovary <note>original: "germen"</note>. The female hermaphrodite has the calyx, petals, filaments, and pistil of the male, but with only one perfect filament; the berry is oblong and three-angled below. The most remarkable species are: 1. The *Musa paradisaica*, or Jamaica plantain; 2. The *Musa sapientum*, or banana tree. See the Plate.

The first variety is cultivated in all the islands of the West Indies, where the fruit serves the Indians as bread; some of the white people also prefer it to most other things, especially to yams and cassava <note>original: "cassada"</note> bread. The plant rises with a soft stalk fifteen or twenty feet high; the lower part of the stalk is often as large as a man's thigh, diminishing gradually to the top where the leaves come out on every side. These are often eight feet long and from two to three feet broad, with a strong fleshy mid-rib and a great number of transverse veins running from the mid-rib to the borders. The leaves are thin and tender, so that where they are exposed to the open air, they are generally torn by the wind; because they are so large, the wind has great power against them. These leaves emerge from the center of the stalk and are rolled up at their first appearance; but when they have grown above the stalks, they expand and turn backward. In Europe, some of these plants are preserved in the gardens of enthusiastic collectors <note>original: "curious persons"</note> who have greenhouses <note>original: "hot-houses"; a heated building for growing tropical plants.</note> large enough to house them. In many of these, the plants have ripened their fruit quite well. However, because they grow very tall and their leaves are large, they require more room in the greenhouse <note>original: "stove"</note> than most people are willing to allow them. They are propagated by suckers, which sprout from the roots of plants that have already fruited; often, even younger plants will grow suckers if their growth is stunted.

The fruit of the banana tree is four or five inches long, about the size and shape of a medium-sized cucumber, and has a strong, pleasant flavor. The leaves are two yards long and a foot wide in the middle. They join to the top of the tree trunk and frequently hold a great quantity of water in their hollows, which flows out if a small cut is made into the tree where the leaves meet. Bananas grow in large bunches that weigh twelve pounds or more. The trunk of the tree is so porous that it does not deserve to be called wood. The tree is a perennial only through its roots, as the rest of the plant dies back to the ground every autumn.

When the natives of the West Indies—according to Labat <note>Jean-Baptiste Labat (1663–1738), a French clergyman and travel writer who documented life in the Caribbean.</note>—prepare for a voyage, they make a supply of banana paste. This serves as both food and drink when needed. To make it, they take ripe bananas and, after squeezing them through a fine sieve, form the solid fruit into small loaves. These are dried in the sun or in hot ashes after being wrapped in the leaves of the Indian flowering reed <note>Likely *Canna indica*.</note>. When they want to use this paste, they dissolve it in water, which is done very easily. The resulting thick liquid has a pleasant, slightly acidic taste that makes it both refreshing and nourishing. The banana is highly valued, and even revered, by the natives of Madeira, who call it the "forbidden fruit." They consider it an almost unpardonable <note>original: "inexpiable"</note> crime to cut it with a knife. This is because, when cut open, they claim the fruit shows a likeness of our Savior’s crucifixion; to cut the fruit with a knife is, in their view, to wound his sacred image.

Some authors have imagined that the banana tree was the one whose leaves Adam and Eve <note>original: "our first parents"</note> used to make coverings <note>original: "aprons"</note> for themselves in Paradise. The sacred text, indeed, calls the leaves used for that purpose *fig leaves*. In a beautiful but mistaken description, the poet Milton affirmed that the "bearded" or Bengal fig <note>The Banyan tree (*Ficus benghalensis*), known for its aerial roots that look like beards.</note> was the tree mentioned. However, ancient authors often referred to the banana fruit as a "fig." Furthermore, because of their great size and strength, banana leaves were much more suitable for a covering than those of the Bengal fig, which are rarely more than six or eight inches long and three inches wide. On the other hand, banana leaves—being three, four, or five feet long and wide in proportion—would surely have been chosen over all others, especially since they could be easily...

Some have supposed that the Abyssinian plant **ensete** is a species of *musa* <note>original: "muſa"; the botanical genus that includes bananas and plantains.</note>. It is said to be native to the province of Narea <note>An ancient kingdom in what is now southwest Ethiopia.</note>, where it grows in the large marshes and swamps common to that province. This is due to the many rivers that begin in that country and have only a slight slope toward the ocean. This plant, as well as the coffee tree, is said to have been unknown in Abyssinia <note>Modern-day Ethiopia.</note> before the arrival of the Galla <note>The Oromo people, a large ethnic group in Ethiopia.</note>, who brought both plants with them. It grows perfectly near Gondar, but the main plantations are in parts of Maisha and Gouth, west of the Nile, where it is almost the only food for the Galla people who live there. Maisha is almost entirely flat, so rainwater sits still and prevents the sowing of grain. If it were not for the ensete, therefore, the Galla would have almost no vegetable food. Mr. Bruce <note>James Bruce (1730–1794), a Scottish explorer who spent years in Ethiopia and wrote "Travels to Discover the Source of the Nile."</note> thinks that the ensete may have been cultivated in some of the gardens of Egypt near Rosetta, but that it was not native to that country. He strongly disagrees with the opinion that this plant is a species of *musa*.

"It is true," he says, "that the leaf of the banana resembles that of the ensete. It bears figs and has a growth coming from its trunk that ends in a cone shape, differing from the ensete mainly in size and the number of its parts. However, the figs of the banana are the size and shape of a cucumber, and this is the part that is eaten. This 'fig' is sweet, though mealy, and has a very pleasant taste. It is thought to have no seeds, though in fact, there are four small black seeds in every fig. But the figs of the ensete are not edible. They are made of a soft, tender substance that is watery and tasteless; in color and texture, they resemble a rotten apricot. They are conical in form and slightly crooked at the lower end, being about an inch and a half long and an inch wide at their thickest point. Inside these is a large stone half an inch long, shaped like a bean or a cashew nut and dark brown in color. This stone contains a small seed, which rarely hardens into fruit and usually consists only of skin. 

The long stalk that bears the figs of the ensete grows from the center of the plant—or rather, it is the body or solid part of the plant itself. On this stalk, where it begins to bend, there are several loose leaves. Then the fig grows directly on the body of the plant without any individual stem. After this, the top of the stalk is crowded with small leaves, in the middle of which the flower ends in the shape of an artichoke. In contrast, in the banana, the artichoke-shaped flower grows at the end of the shoot or stalk that comes from the middle of the plant, and the upper part of that same stalk bears the rows of figs. The leaves of the ensete are a web of lengthwise fibers packed closely together; the leaves grow from the bottom without stems, whereas the banana is shaped like a tree and has been mistaken for one. One half of it is divided into a stem, and the other is a head formed with..."

The hippopotamus is generally thought to represent a Nile flood that has been so abundant as to be destructive. ### TURKEY RHUBARB (*RHEUM*)

Rhubarb is a genus belonging to the ninth class and third order of the Linnaean system <note>original: "enneandria trigynia class"; a historical method of classifying plants by the number of their male and female reproductive parts</note>. Its characteristics are as follows: the flower has no calyx <note>original: "empalement"</note>; it has one petal, which is narrow at the base and closed; the edge is divided into six parts, which are blunt and alternating in size; it has nine hair-like stamens <note>original: "stamina"</note> inserted into the petal of the same length, ending in oblong, blunt anthers <note>original: "summits"</note>. It has a short three-sided ovary <note>original: "germen"</note> with almost no style, crowned by three feathered stigmas that are bent backward. The ovary later becomes a large three-sided seed with sharp, membrane-like <note>original: "membranaceous"</note> edges. The botanist Philip Miller identifies four species, and Carl Linnaeus identifies five. True rhubarb is now sown in many gardens, and it may eventually succeed so well here that we can grow enough of this valuable drug to satisfy our own needs.

The rhubarb with hairy leaves and equal stalks has generally been considered the true rhubarb plant. It was grown from seeds sent from Russia—as those of the true rhubarb—to Bernard de Jussieu in Paris, Isaac Rand at the Chelsea Physic Garden, and Linnaeus at Uppsala. It is native to China and Siberia and has been grown in some of our own gardens, where it is found to grow vigorously in the open ground. Some have derived its name from *Rha*, the river we call the Volga, and *barbarum*, as if to say <note>original: "q. d." or quasi dictum</note> "the root found by the barbarians on the river Volga." 

However, it is necessary to note that in 1763, Dr. Hope received rhubarb seeds from Russia, which Dr. Mounsey assured him were the seeds of the true rhubarb. Having sown them in the open ground at Edinburgh, they produced a different species, specifically the *Rheum palmatum* of Linnaeus, which has leaves deeply cut into pointed sections. He observed that the root of this plant, though harvested while too young and at an improper season (July), perfectly matched the best foreign rhubarb in color, smell, taste, and its quality as a laxative <note>original: "purgative quality"</note>. See his botanical description and drawing of the plant in the *Philosophical Transactions* <note>original: "Phil. Trans."</note>, volume 55, article 32. Perhaps, says Dr. Lewis, the roots of both species may be of the same quality and used interchangeably <note>original: "promiscuously"</note>. 

The *rhaponticum* <note>False Rhubarb or Siberian Rhubarb</note> is a different species from either of these. Mr. Bell informs us in his *Travels* that the best rhubarb grows in that part of Eastern Tartary called Mongolia <note>original: "Mongallia"</note>, which serves as a boundary between Russia and China. This plant, he says, does not run and spread itself like dock weeds, but grows in tufts at various distances, as if the seeds had been dropped intentionally. Since the Mongols <note>original: "Mongalls"</note> do not think it worth cultivating, the marmots—which burrow under the shade of its spreading leaves and likely feed on its leaves and roots—contribute to its growth. They do this partly through the manure their dung provides, and mainly by digging up and loosening the earth, into which

# APPENDIX TO

...the ripe seeds, blown by the wind, fall and immediately take root. After digging and gathering the rhubarb, the Mongols <note>original: "Mongalls"</note> cut the large roots into small pieces to make them dry more quickly. They scoop a hole in the middle of every piece and draw a cord through it to hang them in a convenient place; however, by this practice, they destroy some of the best parts of the root.

All rhubarb plants, Miller <note>Philip Miller (1691–1771), an influential English botanist and gardener</note> says, are propagated by seeds. These should be sown in autumn soon after they are ripe, so the plants will come up the following spring; whereas, if they are sown in the spring, they will not sprout until the next year. The plants should remain where the seeds are sown. When they appear in the spring, the ground should be hoed to remove weeds, and the plants should be thinned—like carrots and parsnips—leaving them six or eight inches apart at the first hoeing, and at least a foot and a half apart at the second. After this, the plants require no further care except for weeding. In autumn, the leaves decay and the ground should be cleaned; it should also be hoed and cleaned in the spring when the plants put out new leaves. In the second year after they sprout, the strongest will produce flowers and seeds, and most will flower by the third year. The roots will last many years without decaying, and it is said that the old roots of the true rhubarb are much better than the young ones. They thrive in a rich soil that is neither too dry nor too moist, and where the soil is deep enough for their roots to grow downward; in such land, their leaves will be very large and their roots will grow to a great size.

Two types of rhubarb roots are found in shops. The first is imported from Turkey and Russia in roundish pieces with the bark removed and a hole through the middle. Externally, they are a yellow color; internally, they are variegated with lively reddish streaks. The other type, which is less valued, comes directly from the East Indies in longish pieces that are harder, heavier, and more compact than the first kind. The first sort is prone to growing moldy or worm-eaten unless kept very dry, while the second is less subject to these problems. It is said that some of the more industrious tradesmen <note>original: "artists"; here meaning practitioners or merchants</note> fill the worm-holes with certain mixtures and color the outside of damaged pieces with powder from finer rhubarbs or even cheaper materials. The signs of good rhubarb are: a lively color when cut; being firm and solid without being stony or hard; being easily powdered <note>original: "pulverable"</note> and appearing as a fine, bright yellow when ground; turning saliva a deep saffron tint when chewed; and not feeling slimy or mucilaginous in the mouth. Its taste is mildly acrid <note>original: "subacrid"</note>, bitter, and somewhat astringent <note>original: "styptic"</note>; the smell is lightly aromatic.

Rhubarb is a mild laxative <note>original: "cathartic"</note> and is commonly considered one of the safest and most harmless substances of this class. Besides its purgative <term>purgative: a substance used to encourage or cause bowel movements</term> quality, it has a...

# CULPEPER'S BRITISH HERBAL

...[The first is] a mild astringent one, which can be detected by taste and by the way it turns an inky black color when mixed with iron-based <note>original: "chalybeate"</note> solutions. Because of this, it is found to strengthen the tone of the stomach and intestines, leaving the bowels firm <note>original: "costive"</note>. It is one of the most useful purgatives for diarrhea, dysentery, and all disorders resulting from a weakness or looseness of the body's tissues <note>original: "fibres"</note>. It is frequently given for this digestive and strengthening quality rather than for producing any significant bowel movements. It tints the urine a deep yellow color. 

Rhubarb in its raw powder form purges more effectively than any preparation made from it; the dose is from a scruple to a dram <note>A scruple is approximately 1.3 grams; a dram is approximately 3.9 grams.</note>. By roasting it with gentle heat until it becomes easily crumbled <note>original: "friable"</note>, its laxative power is decreased, and its astringency is thought to be increased. 

The purgative quality of rhubarb is extracted more perfectly by water than by pure alcohol <note>original: "rectified spirit"</note>. The root remaining after being soaked in water is almost, if not entirely, inactive; however, after being repeatedly soaked in alcohol, it still remains considerably purgative. When the rhubarb has given up everything that alcohol can extract, it still imparts a deep color and purgative properties to water. A dram of the extract formed by thickening <note>original: "inspissating"</note> a water-based infusion is no more effective than a scruple of the raw powdered root. However, half a dram of the extract made from an alcohol-based tincture proves to be a moderate purgative, though it is hardly more effective than an equal amount of the powder. The alcohol-based extract dissolves almost entirely in water; therefore, the tincture (like the alcohol-based infusions of most other vegetables) does not turn milky when mixed with watery liquids. Of the water-based extract, scarcely more than one-fourth dissolves in pure alcohol, and the part that does not dissolve is more purgative than the part that does. From this, it appears that rhubarb contains much more gummy or mucilaginous matter than resinous matter, and its purgative quality seems to reside chiefly in a combination of gummy and saline material.

Tinctures of this root are prepared in pharmacies using standard-strength alcohol <note>original: "proof spirit"</note> and Mountain wine <note>A sweet dessert wine from Malaga, Spain.</note>, in the proportion of one ounce of rhubarb to one pint of the solvent <term>menstruum</term>. These preparations are used chiefly as mild laxative tonics for stomach weakness, indigestion, diarrhea, cramping <note>original: "colicky"</note>, and other similar complaints. They are commonly flavored with a little cardamom seed and saffron—specifically, two drams of the former and one of the latter for the amount of root mentioned above. In this way, the wine-based and spirit-based <note>original: "vinosa & spirituosa"</note> tinctures of rhubarb are formed. 

For some purposes, a tincture called "sweet tincture of rhubarb" <note>original: "tinctura rhei dulcis"</note> is prepared from rhubarb and cardamom seeds with alcohol, with two ounces of white rock candy dissolved in the strained liquid. For other purposes, instead of sweets and aromatics, gentian and snake-root are added—at a ratio of a dram and a half of the former and a dram of the latter—along with a scruple of cochineal <note>A red dye made from crushed insects, used here as a coloring agent.</note> as a coloring ingredient.
