### APPENDIX TO

The ripe seeds, blown by the wind, fall and immediately take root. After digging and gathering the rhubarb, the Mongols <note>original: "Mongalls"</note> cut the large roots into small pieces to make them dry more readily. In the middle of every piece, they scoop a hole through which a cord is drawn to hang <note>original: "suspend"</note> them in a convenient place; by this practice, they destroy some of the best part of the root.

All rhubarb plants, says Miller <note>Philip Miller (1691–1771) was a celebrated English botanist and head gardener at the Chelsea Physic Garden.</note>, are propagated by seeds, which should be sown in autumn soon after they are ripe; the plants will then come up the following spring. However, if they are sown in the spring, they will not come up until the next year. The plants should remain where the seeds are sown. When they appear in the spring, the ground should be hoed to cut up the weeds, and the plants should be thinned, like carrots and parsnips, leaving them six or eight inches apart at the first hoeing, and at least a foot and a half apart at the second hoeing. After this, the plants require no other care except keeping them free from weeds. In autumn, the leaves decay, at which time the ground should be cleared; it should also be hoed and cleaned in the spring when the plants put out their new leaves. In the second year after they come up, the strongest will produce flowers and seeds; by the third year, most of them will flower. The roots will last for many years without decaying; it is said that the old roots of the true rhubarb are much better than the young ones. They thrive in a rich soil that is neither too dry nor too moist, and where there is enough depth for their roots to grow downward. In such land, their leaves will be very large and their roots will grow to a great size.

Two types of rhubarb roots are found in shops. The first is imported from Turkey and Russia in rounded pieces, with the bark removed and a hole through the middle of each. Externally, they are yellow; internally, they are variegated with vivid reddish streaks. The other type, which is less valued, comes directly from the East Indies in longish pieces that are harder, heavier, and more compact than the first kind. The first type is likely to grow moldy and worm-eaten unless kept very dry; the second is less prone to these issues. Some of the more industrious merchants <note>original: "artists"; here referring to those skilled in deceptive trade practices</note> are said to fill the worm-holes with certain mixtures and to color the outside of the damaged pieces with powder from finer rhubarb, or sometimes even cheaper materials. The signs of high-quality rhubarb are a vivid color when cut, being firm and solid (but not stony or hard), being easy to grind into a fine, bright yellow powder, and turning the saliva a deep saffron color when chewed without feeling slimy or gummy in the mouth. Its taste is slightly acid <note>original: "suacbrid," likely an OCR error for "sub-acid"</note>, somewhat bitter, and slightly astringent <note>original: "styptic"</note>; the smell is lightly aromatic.

# CULPEPER'S BRITISH HERBAL 51

It has a mild astringent quality, which can be identified by its taste and by the way it turns an inky black when mixed with iron-based <note>original: "chalybeate"</note> solutions. Consequently, it is known to strengthen the tone of the stomach and intestines, to make the bowels slightly constipated <note>original: "costive"</note>, and to be one of the most useful laxatives for treating diarrhea, dysentery, and all disorders caused by a weakness or looseness of the bodily tissues <note>original: "laxity of the fibres"</note>. It is frequently given for this stomach-strengthening and restorative <note>original: "corroborating"</note> virtue, rather than for the purpose of producing any significant bowel movements. It stains the urine a bright yellow color. 

Rhubarb in its raw form <note>original: "in substance"</note> purges more effectively than any prepared version; the dose is from one scruple to one dram <note>A scruple is about 1.3 grams; a dram is about 3.9 grams in the old apothecaries' system.</note>. By roasting it with gentle heat until it is easily crumbled, its laxative <note>original: "cathartic"</note> power is reduced, and its astringent property is believed to increase. The laxative properties of rhubarb are extracted more perfectly by water than by pure alcohol <note>original: "rectified spirit"</note>. The root remaining after being treated with water is almost, if not entirely, inactive; however, after repeated soaking <note>original: "digestion"</note> in alcohol, it still remains significantly purgative. When the rhubarb has yielded to the alcohol all that this solvent <note>original: "menstruum"</note> can extract, it still imparts a deep color, as well as a laxative quality, to water. 

A dram of the extract, formed by thickening the watery infusion through evaporation <note>original: "inspissating"</note>, is no more effective than a scruple of the raw root; however, half a dram of the extract made from the alcohol-based tincture proves to be a moderate laxative, though it is hardly more effective than an equal quantity of the powder. The alcohol-based extract dissolves almost completely in water; therefore, the tincture (like the alcohol-based infusions of most other vegetables) does not turn milky when mixed with water-based liquids. Of the water-based extract, scarcely more than one-fourth is dissolved by pure alcohol, and the part that does not dissolve proves more laxative than the part that does. From this, it appears that rhubarb contains much more gummy or mucilaginous material than resinous matter, and its laxative quality seems to reside chiefly in a combination of gummy and salty components.

Tinctures of this root are prepared in pharmacies <note>original: "shops"</note> using proof spirit <note>a mixture of equal parts alcohol and water</note> and mountain wine, in the proportion of one ounce of rhubarb to one pint of the solvent. These preparations are used primarily as mild laxatives and strengthening tonics for stomach weakness, indigestion, diarrhea, colic, and similar complaints. They are commonly flavored with a little cardamom seed and saffron—specifically, two drams of the former and one of the latter to the amount of root mentioned above—and thus are formed the wine-based and spirit-based <note>original: "vinosa & spirituosa"</note> tinctures of rhubarb. 

For some purposes, a tincture called the *sweet tincture of rhubarb* <note>original: "tinctura rhei dulcis"</note> is made from rhubarb and cardamom seeds using proof spirit, with two ounces of white sugar-candy dissolved in the strained liquid. For other purposes, instead of sweets and aromatics, gentian and snake-root are added (in the proportion of a dram and a half of the former and a dram of the latter), with the addition of a scruple of cochineal <note>a dried insect used to create a deep red dye</note> as a coloring ingredient. This last tincture is called the *tincture of rhubarb...* <note>original: "tinctura rhei"</note>

### APPENDIX TO

Bitter rhubarb <note>original: *rhei amara*</note> is, in many cases, a useful assistant to Peruvian bark <note>A common term for cinchona bark, used to treat malaria.</note> in the cure of intermittent fevers <note>original: "intermittents"</note>.

The Turkey rhubarb is generally preferred to the East India sort, though the latter is more astringent <note>A substance that causes body tissues to contract or tighten.</note>, but has slightly less of an aromatic flavor. Tinctures made from both, with equal quantities of distilled alcohol <note>original: "rectified spirit"</note>, have nearly the same taste: on drawing off the solvents <note>original: "menstrua"</note>, the extract left by the tincture of the East India rhubarb proves to be considerably stronger in taste than the other. They seem both, says Dr. Lewis <note>William Lewis (1708–1781) was a famous English chemist and physician known for his works on pharmacy.</note>, to be the product of the same climate and roots of the same species of plant, likely harvested at different seasons or cured in a different manner.

The yellow color of rhubarb, it is said, is much more stable <note>original: "less destructible"</note> than many other vegetable yellows. Nitric acid <note>original: *Aqua fortis*</note> and other acids which destroy the color of saffron, turmeric, etc., make no change in that of rhubarb, or at most render it only cloudy <note>original: "turpid"</note>. Ammonia <note>original: "Volatile spirits"</note> heightens the color and inclines it toward red. Fixed alkaline salts <note>Such as potash or soda.</note> have this effect to a greater degree. Mr. Model <note>Johann Georg Model (1711–1775) was a pharmacist who identified calcium sulfate in rhubarb.</note> affirms that a considerable quantity of selenite crystals <note>original: "selenites"; these are crystals of calcium sulfate.</note> is contained in rhubarb. In one experiment, he obtained six ounces of selenite from four pounds of rhubarb; and, in the other, no less than an ounce of selenite from two ounces and five drams of old rhubarb.

The Indian rhubarb sown in our gardens has this peculiar property: it yields a fine and clear gum. This is perfectly white and transparent <note>original: "pellucid"</note>; and in the months of June and July, it is so plentiful that an ounce may sometimes be gathered at a time from a single plant. It exudes <note>original: "exsudates"</note> by itself from all parts of the stalks and ribs of the leaves, and sometimes from the underside of the leaves themselves. It stands in some places in large drops, and in others the stalks and parts of the plant seem only to be covered with a thin layer of it; and the underside of some leaves have it in the form of twisted wires or long icicles. The plant may always be seen "wounded" by a sort of corrosive juice <note>original: "caustic"</note> in the places where the bud <note>original: "germen"</note> makes its way out, and these paths may be followed with any pointed instrument through the skin; in some parts of the plant, this juice is found to have turned into gum within it and looks like clear ice. As this is the only known soft-stemmed <note>original: "herbaceous"</note> plant that yields a true gum like that of trees, it would be worthy of observation whether some of our own native plants may not have some natural tendency to form a juice of the same kind. It would be most proper to look for this in plants of the same genus that are as nearly related to rhubarb as possible. The docks, so common in our fields, are of the same genus; and sorrel shows by its taste that it is particularly allied to the plant; for both are alike of the dock kind, and both alike sour. It would be proper to look carefully around the leaves of sorrel a little before it flowers to see whether anything like the same gum appears on it.

# CULPEPER'S BRITISH HERBAL.

...there still exists a further similarity <note>original: "analogy"</note> between true rhubarb and monk's rhubarb; specifically, that the roots of our common sorrel, when boiled in water with a little alum <note>A mineral salt used as a mordant to fix dyes to fabric.</note>, dye the water a vibrant red. This demonstrates that the plant possesses a dyeing property <note>original: "tinctority"</note> as well as a certain degree of astringency <note>The ability to shrink or contract body tissues.</note>, though we will not detail the decrease of that quality here.

There is a yellow oil prepared by crushing <note>original: "bruising"</note> and distilling the flowers with common water. This is an extremely concentrated and aromatic essence on the palate, and the taste remains on the tongue for a long time. The gum from the bark is well known by the name **gum-arabic**. However, although the plant yields it naturally, it is found that the bark will not produce it as abundantly through human intervention <note>original: "by art"</note> as it does naturally. It is said that the bark is first cut to allow the gum to flow, and the following year the tree is felled. This gum is categorized among the various gums derived from the **acacia**; indeed, what is usually found in apothecary shops is the gum of that name. It is also found along the Nile, from Alexandria to Grand Cairo. In the botanical system, this plant is classified with the *Mimosa*, or **Sensitive Plant** <note>Plants that fold their leaves inward when touched or shaken.</note>. It is also found in the Levant <note>The region of the eastern Mediterranean.</note>, from where it is brought to us in large quantities. In the Nile region, it grows to the size of a tree. It is a prickly plant and is the *Acacia* described by **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work was the primary botanical text for 1,500 years.</note> and the Greeks. It is also known as the **Egyptian Thorn**. The flower is pale, and the fruit is a pod containing many seeds. It is found in Abyssinia and also in the East Indies.

All the parts of this water-lily <note>Likely referring to the Egyptian Lotus (*Nymphaea nelumbo*).</note> are diuretic <note>Promoting the production of urine.</note> in nature. The root, when boiled in water, is good for treating "the stone" <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note>. When the flowers fall, they are replaced by a large, roundish, prickly fruit similar to a chestnut. This fruit is about the size of a small melon, reddish-brown on the outside, and contains many seeds which are eaten after boiling. It is said that the flower of this plant has the property of turning to face the sun; however, it is more certain that it opens as the sun rises and shuts again at night. The fruit has a sweetish and aromatic flavor and is eaten at dinner, having, as they say, a cooling and refreshing quality. It is also found in the desert of the Red Sea, having been brought there from Egypt. It has a pleasant acidity, and its substance is like that of an apple, but it is larger and thicker; its shape is round and about the size of a walnut. In the *New British Herbal*, the Acacia is mentioned as a tree growing in the West Indies.

<header>CULPEPER’S BRITISH HERBAL.</header>

There is yet this further analogy between this rhubarb and our common sorrel: the husks of our sorrel, boiled in water with a little alum <note>a mineral salt used as a mordant to fix dyes to fabrics</note>, turn the liquid to a fine red color; the husks of rhubarb do the same, and both plants often turn red as they decay.

The juice of the rhubarb roots—extracted by crushing and steeping them in common water—becomes a clear, non-flammable gum once the liquid is strained and evaporated; this gum melts in the flame of a candle. This gum, as well as the sap found in the stalks and leaves, has a flavorless taste. It is notable that although the plant naturally produces this gum in such large quantities, it will not flow from intentional cuts <note>original: "wounds made by art"</note> made in any part of the plant. By considering the flavorless taste of this gum and the fact that it dissolves in water, we may find a probable explanation for the plant’s different <term>purging and binding</term> <note>purging refers to a laxative effect, while binding refers to an astringent effect used to treat diarrhea</note> virtues.

The woody fibers have a strong taste and, in all probability, are the only part endowed with the <term>astringent</term> <note>a substance that causes the contraction of body tissues, typically used to stop bleeding or secretions</note> quality. An infusion of rhubarb is known to purge (act as a laxative), while rhubarb powder is known to bind (stop diarrhea); the reason is easily seen when considering these properties. When steeped in water, the infusion takes up all of this gummy juice and the other saps but leaves the fibrous parts behind; consequently, it purges without binding. However, when the powder is administered, the juices have mostly evaporated during the drying process, leaving the woody parts almost entirely on their own. Therefore, the powder purges very little and proves to be powerfully astringent.

### INDIAN ROCU (MITELLA)

The rocu <note>now commonly known as the Annatto tree or *Bixa orellana*</note> is a tree of considerable height, bearing pale red flowers similar to European apple blossoms. When the flowers fall off, a seed head follows which is oblong and round in shape, and prickly like a chestnut. This contains those beautiful red seeds which the Indians crush or soak; when placed in water, the seeds sink to the bottom, turning the fluid into a most elegant, transparent red tincture. They pour off this tincture at their leisure, and the sediment formed by the seeds at the bottom is allowed to dry into little cakes. They use these to paint various figures on their naked bodies, which they consider a very great ornament.

This tree is the *urucu* described by Willem Piso <note>a Dutch naturalist and physician (1611–1678) known for his work on Brazilian botany</note>. Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, having grouped it with two species of American *Cortusa*, calls it *Mitella*; this is because the fruit of this tree, as well as that of the American *Cortusa*, bursts open to reveal the shape of a bishop's mitre <note>a traditional, pointed ceremonial cap worn by bishops</note>. Therefore, in his *Institutes of Botanical Matters* <note>original: "Institut. Rei Herb."</note>, he entitles it the *largest American Mitella, used for dyeing* <note>original: "Mitella Americana, maxima, tinctoria"</note>.

### SPEEDWELL. VERONICA.

The flower of speedwell has a permanent calyx <note>original: "empalement"; the outer protective layer of a flower</note>, divided into five sharp segments, and one tubular petal the length of the calyx. The edge is divided into four oval, flat segments that spread open, and two stamens <note>original: "stamina"</note> which end in oblong anthers <note>original: "summits"</note>. It has a flattened ovary <note>original: "germen"</note> supporting a slender, downward-leaning style, topped by a single stigma. The ovary becomes a flattened heart-shaped capsule with two cells filled with rounded seeds.

The common male speedwell is also called Paul’s betony; brooklime is also a species of the speedwell. Some authors identify thirty-five different species.

This herb is held in great esteem among the Germans for disorders of the chest, both those involving excess mucus <note>original: "catarrhous"</note> and those involving ulcers, and it is used for purifying the blood and bodily fluids. Infusions of the leaves, which are not unpleasant to the taste, are drunk as tea and are found to act noticeably as a diuretic <note>original: "operate sensibly by urine"</note>. It is frequently used as an ingredient in medicines intended to treat scurvy <note>original: "antiscorbutic"</note> and to remove internal blockages <note>original: "deobstruent"</note>.

### STARRY ANISEED. ILLICIUM.

We find an account of the starry aniseed, together with an illustration of it taken from the botanist Clusius, in Parkinson’s *Theatre of Plants*, page 1569. There, he observes that some branches of it—containing only the husks and seeds, without leaves or blossoms—were brought into England from the Philippine Islands during the reign of Queen Elizabeth by Sir Thomas Cavendish, who encountered it during his voyage around the world. These branches were given to Mr. Morgan, the Queen’s apothecary, and to Mr. James Garrat, from whom Clusius received them.

Monsieur Geoffroy, in his *Materia Medica* <note>original Latin: "Medical Materials," a reference work on the properties of drugs</note>, translated in 1736 by Dr. G. Douglas, page 322, calls it *Anisum Sinense* <note>Chinese Anise</note>, *semen badian* <note>badian seed</note>, and *fructus stellatus* <note>starry fruit</note>. He says it is highly esteemed in China and throughout the East. It is used to cure a bad taste in the mouth, as a preventative against the effects of "bad air" <note>a historical belief that diseases like malaria were caused by foul-smelling air</note>, and also for kidney stones and gravel. The Indians likewise steep this fruit in water and afterwards ferment the liquid to make a wine-like liquor. Both the Dutch in the East Indies and the native people mix this fruit with their tea and sherbet.

Kaempfer, in his *Amoenitates Exoticae* <note>original Latin: "Exotic Pleasures" or "Exotic Delights"</note>, page 880, calls it *somo* or *shimmi* <note>likely "shikimi," the Japanese star anise</note>, and has provided a very good illustration of a branch with its leaves, flowers, and fruit. He found it in Japan and says that the Japanese and Chinese consider it a sacred tree; they offer it to their idols and burn its bark as a perfume on their altars. They also lay branches upon the graves of the dead as an offering to the ghosts of their pious departed friends. He further notes that public watchmen use the powder of this aromatic bark, strewing it in small winding grooves or little channels on

> "Near here my son found a lovely, fragrant tree with leaves like the sweet bay, which smelled like sassafras and produces a very strange kind of seed-pod; but all the seed was shed. The severe frost had not hurt it; some of them grew nearly twenty feet high—a charming, bright evergreen aromatic."

This observation by Mr. Bartram regarding its ability to withstand a severe frost may afford a useful hint for the cultivation of this tree, especially as I am convinced—from repeated accounts of the weather in West Florida—that the frost is much more intense there (where those plants were brought from) than in East Florida. Therefore, the experiment is well worth making with one of them to see how well it will stand the severity of our British winters. Should it succeed, it would be a very great acquisition for our gardeners and be highly ornamental to our plantations of evergreens.

The medicinal properties of this tree are certainly worth inquiring into. The leaves provide a most agreeable bitter flavor. When a sprig of it was set to rot in a vial of water, the bark soon became full of a clear mucilage <note>a thick, gluey substance produced by plants</note>. The young blossoms, when put into water with a small quantity of salt of tartar in liquid form (<note>original: *tartar per deliquium*; potassium carbonate that has turned to liquid by absorbing moisture from the air</note>), changed from a dark reddish color to a light brown; but from the same proportion of oil of vitriol <note>original: *oil of vitriol*; an old term for sulfuric acid</note> in water, they turned to a fine carmine <note>vivid red</note> color, which stained the paper a beautiful red. This points out its astringent <note>skin-tightening or tissue-contracting</note> quality.

The flower is of a dark red color. Kaempfer <note>Engelbert Kaempfer (1651–1716), a German naturalist and physician who traveled to Japan.</note> calculates the number of petals at sixteen and the rays, or seed vessels, at eight. In our variety, the number of petals ranges from twenty-one to twenty-seven, and there are twelve or thirteen seed vessels that ripen. Regarding the form and growth of the tree, they are much the same; for instance, both grow to the size of a cherry tree. Their leaves are of an oblong oval shape, pointed at both ends, fleshy, with few veins, and grow alternately in tufts at the ends of the small branches.

Linnaeus, who bases his classification of the *Illicium anisatum* <note>Japanese Star Anise</note> (<term>Genera Plantarum</term> <note>original: *Gen. Plant.*; Linnaeus's landmark work "The Genera of Plants"</note> b. 244.) on Kaempfer's findings, places it among the <term>Dodecandria Polygynia</term> <note>original: *dodecandria polygynia*; a class of plants with twelve stamens and many female styles.</note>. However, I am convinced that, based on the following characteristics, this must belong to the <term>Polyandria Polygynia</term> <note>original: *polyandria polygynia*; a class of plants with many stamens (usually more than twenty) and many styles.</note> and should be placed next to the **Magnolia**.

### *Characteristics of the <term>Illicium floridanum</term>, or Florida Starry Aniseed Tree.*

**CALYX.** The perianth <note>original: *perianthium*</note>, or flower-cup, consists commonly of five small, membranous, and colored leaves that soon fall off; they are of a concave, oblong, oval form, and pointed at the ends. Sometimes we find only four little leaves, sometimes six, in the flower-cup. Kaempfer observed four in his specimen.

**COROLLA.** The flower consists of many petals (from twenty-one to twenty-seven) which are spear-shaped <note>original: *lanceolated*</note>. These come in three sizes and in equal numbers in each circle; the outer ones are long (about an inch), concave, blunt <note>original: *obtuse*</note>, and spread open. The next are a little shorter and narrower, and the innermost are still shorter, much narrower, and very sharp-pointed; but these are not nectaries <note>original: *nectaria*</note> as Linnaeus supposes.

**STAMINA.** The filaments are many (about thirty), very short and flat, placed over one another and surrounding the germens <note>original: *germina*; the rudimentary ovaries</note> or embryo seed-vessels. These support an equal number of anthers <note>original: *antheræ*</note>, or summits, which are erect, oblong, and notched <note>original: *emarginated*</note> at the top, with a cell on each side full of pollen <note>original: *farina*</note> that appears globular when magnified.

**PISTILLUM**, or female organ. The germens, or embryo seed-vessels, are twenty or more in number, placed in a circular order above the receptacle of the flower. They are compressed, erect, and end in many sharp-pointed styles that bend outward at the top. The stigmas <note>original: *stigmata*</note>, or openings on the top of the styles, are downy and placed lengthwise along the upper part of each style.

**PERICARPIUM**, or seed-vessel, consists of twelve, or more often thirteen, little pods or capsules that ripen. These are of a compressed oval shape and a hard leather-like substance, with two valves to each, and are arranged edgewise in a circular order, like the rays of a star.

**SEMINA.** The seeds <note>original: *semina*</note> are smooth and shining, of an oval shape, a little compressed, and appear to be cut off diagonally at the base. There is one seed in each capsule.

## SUGAR MAPLE TREE. *ACER.*

*An Account of the Sugar Maple Tree of the United States, and of the Methods of obtaining Sugar from it, together with Observations upon the Advantages, both public and private, of this Sugar: in a Letter to Thomas Jefferson, Esq. Secretary (now President) of the United States, and one of the Vice-Presidents of the American Philosophical Society, by Benjamin Rush, Professor of the Principles <note>original: "Institutes"; referring to the fundamental principles or theory of medicine</note> and of Clinical Medicine in the University of Philadelphia.*

The subject of this excellent paper seems at first sight to relate more particularly to the United States; however, it may—and we hope it will—very essentially affect the general state of the world by increasing the supply of an article whose uses are still imperfectly known because of its high price. If the monopoly of the West India islands—where the wasteful cultivation by slaves, in the absence of the owner, is the only way it can be supported—should be gradually diminished and at last abolished by a plentiful production of sugar from the maple, humanity would no longer suffer, the product would find its true market level, and every nation would be more or less benefited.

The *Acer saccharinum* <note>original: *Acer saccharinum*; the botanical name for the sugar maple</note> of Linnaeus, or sugar maple tree, grows in great quantities in the western parts of all the middle states of the American union. It is as tall as the oak and from two to three feet in diameter; it puts forth a white blossom in the spring before any appearance of leaves. Its small branches provide food for cattle, and its ashes yield a large quantity of excellent potash <note>Potash is a potassium-rich salt historically used for making soap, glass, and fertilizer.</note>. Twenty years are required for it to reach its full growth. Tapping the tree does not injure it; on the contrary, it provides more syrup, and of a better quality, the more often it is tapped. A single tree has not only survived but flourished for forty years after being tapped. Five or six pounds of sugar are usually provided by the sap of one tree—though there are instances of the quantity exceeding twenty pounds. The sugar is separated from the sap either by freezing, by natural <note>original: "spontaneous"</note> evaporation, or by boiling. The latter method is the most used. Dr. Rush describes the process, which is simple and practiced without any difficulty by farmers.

From frequent trials of this sugar, it does not appear to be in any respect inferior to that of the West Indies. It is prepared at a time of the year when neither insects nor the pollen of plants exist to contaminate <note>original: "vitiate"</note> it, as is the case with common sugar. From calculations based on existing facts, it is ascertained that America is now capable of producing one-eighth <note>original: "one eight"</note> more than its own consumption; that is, on the whole, about 135,000,000 pounds, which in that country may be valued at fifteen pounds weight for one dollar. Dr. Rush mentions many other benefits his country may derive from this invaluable tree and concludes his paper with an account of some of the advantages of sugar to mankind—not merely as it is commonly considered a luxury, but as an excellent, wholesome, and nourishing article of food.

## TEA-TREE. *THEA.*

The tea-tree, *Thea*, in botany, is the name of a genus of plants belonging to the class of many stamens and one pistil <note>original: "polyandria monogynia"</note>. Its characteristics are as follows: the cup <note>the calyx</note> is a very small, flat, permanent outer covering <note>original: "perianthium"</note>, divided into five or six roundish, blunt leaves; the flower consists of six or nine large, roundish, concave, and equal petals; the stamens <note>original: "stamina"</note> consist of numerous filaments—about two hundred—which are very slender, hair-like, and shorter than the flower; the anthers <note>original: "antheræ"</note> are simple; the ovary <note>original: "germen"</note> of the pistil is globe-shaped and three-sided; the style is awl-shaped <note>original: "subulated"</note> and the same length as the stamens; the stigma is simple; the fruit is a capsule formed of three globular bodies growing together; it contains three cells and opens into three parts at the top. The seeds are single, globe-shaped, and angled on the inside.

From an original drawing taken of the tree when it was in flower, it appears that the tea-tree—as Mr. Philip Miller <note>a famous 18th-century English botanist</note> first observed—actually belongs to the order of plants with three pistils <note>original: "trigynia"</note>. Carl Linnaeus <note>the father of modern taxonomy</note> was led into the mistake of placing it in the order of plants with one pistil <note>original: "monogynia"</note> because he never had the opportunity to examine anything other than dried specimens of this shrub. Of this genus, Linnaeus lists two species: namely, *Bohea Tea*, which has flowers with six petals, and *Green Tea*, which has flowers with nine petals.

Dr. Lettsom <note>John Coakley Lettsom, a prominent physician and botanist</note>, in his botanical description of the tea plant, thinks it most probable that there is only one species. He believes the difference between green and bohea <note>a type of black tea</note> teas depends on the nature of the soil, cultivation, age, and the manner of drying the leaves. He adds that it has even been observed that a green-tea tree planted in the bohea country will produce bohea tea, and vice versa. Furthermore, upon examining several hundred flowers brought from both the bohea and green-tea regions, their botanical characteristics always appeared identical.

We are principally indebted to Engelbert Kaempfer, Louis Le Comte, and Jean-Baptiste Du Halde for an authentic history of the cultivation of this exotic shrub and the manner of preparing or curing its leaves. The most important details they recorded have been carefully collected, and the subject further explained with additional observations by Dr. Lettsom.

The tea-tree prefers to grow in valleys at the foot of mountains and upon the banks of rivers where it enjoys southern exposure to the sun. However, it endures considerable variations of heat and cold, as it flourishes in the northern climate of Beijing <note>original: "Pekin"</note> as well as around Guangzhou <note>original: "Canton"</note>. It is observed that the winter cold in Beijing is as severe as in some of the northern parts of Europe. Nevertheless, the best tea grows in a mild, temperate climate; the country around Nanjing <note>original: "Nankin"</note>, situated between the other two locations, produces better tea than either Beijing or Guangzhou.

-># MR. MENZIES'S ACCOUNT OF THE BOTANY<-

<unclear>The Northwest coast of America is the site <note>original: "theatre"</note> of a very extensive commerce between the different ports of China and the inhabitants of the various sounds and inlets on that coast. This commerce is carried on using the skins of the Sea Otter (*Enhydra lutris* <note>original: "Mustela lutris," the scientific name used at the time</note>), which are collected from the native people by the ships of different nations and carried to the Chinese markets, where they find a ready sale. It is a trade which was first suggested by the late Captain Cook and has since been carried on with great success.</unclear>

<unclear>From the accounts of the different voyagers who have visited these shores, it appears that the country is very fertile in many places and that it produces a great variety of plants, many of which are unknown to European botanists.</unclear>

<unclear>This voyage was performed in the years 1786, 1787, 1788, and 1789. The collection of plants was made at various times and at different places on the coast, but chiefly at Nootka Sound <note>A complex inlet on the west coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia, which was a major hub for the maritime fur trade</note>, where we remained for some time. For many of the following remarks, I am indebted to the late</unclear> **Dr. Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1735–1788), a prominent English botanist and author of *Flora Scotica*</note>, <unclear>of Uxbridge, whose botanical knowledge and passion <note>original: "zeal"</note> are well known, and who was the companion of my early excursions to the</unclear> **Highlands of Scotland**.

<unclear>It is with much pleasure that I now lay before the Linnean Society <note>A leading society for the study of natural history, founded in London in 1788</note> an account of some of the most interesting plants which I have collected on the Northwest coast of America; I hope that it will be found to contain information which may be of use to the botanical world.</unclear>

# CULPEPER'S BRITISH HERBAL.

The root resembles the peach tree; the leaves are green, longish at the point, and quite narrow—about an inch and a half long—and serrated <note>original: "jagged"</note> all around. The flower is much like that of the wild rose, but smaller. The fruit comes in different forms—sometimes round, sometimes long, or triangular—and is the usual size of a bean. Each fruit contains two or three seeds of a mouse-gray color, and each seed includes a kernel. These are the seeds by which the plant is propagated. A number of seeds, from six to twelve or fifteen, are randomly <note>original: "promiscuously"</note> placed into a single hole about four or five inches deep, with certain distances kept between each hole. The seeds grow without any other care, though more industrious farmers annually remove the weeds and manure the land. The leaves that follow are not fit to be plucked before the third year of growth, at which time they are plentiful and in their prime.

In about seven years, the shrub reaches the height of a man. Because it then bears fewer leaves and grows slowly, it is cut down to the stem. This causes a profusion <note>original: "exuberance"</note> of fresh shoots and leaves the following summer; some, however, delay cutting them until they have reached ten years of growth. In Japan, the tea tree is cultivated around the borders of fields regardless of the soil quality; however, because the Chinese export considerable quantities of tea, they plant entire fields with it.

The best time to gather tea leaves is while they are still small, young, and juicy. The different periods in which they are gathered are described in detail by Kaempfer <note>Engelbert Kaempfer (1651–1716) was a German naturalist and physician whose writings provided Europeans with their first detailed accounts of Japanese tea culture.</note>. The leaves are plucked carefully one by one. Despite the apparent tediousness of this task, laborers are able to gather between four and fifteen pounds each in a single day. The tea trees that often yield the finest leaves grow on the steep slopes of hills where it is dangerous, and sometimes impossible, to collect them. The Chinese are said to overcome this difficulty by an unusual method <note>original: "singular contrivance"</note>. The large monkeys that inhabit these cliffs are provoked, and in retaliation, they break off the branches and throw them down, allowing the leaves to be collected from the ground.

The buildings, or drying houses, that are built for processing <note>original: "curing"</note> tea contain anywhere from five to twenty small furnaces. These are about three feet high, and each has a large, flat iron pan at the top. There is also a long, low table covered with mats where the leaves are laid and rolled by workmen who sit around it. After the iron pan is heated to a certain degree by a small fire in the furnace underneath, a few pounds of the fresh-gathered leaves are placed upon it. The fresh and juicy leaves crackle when they touch the pan. It is the worker's <note>original: "operator's"</note> job to move them as quickly as possible with his bare hands until they become too hot to handle easily. At this moment, he removes the leaves with a fan-like shovel and pours them onto the mats in front of the rollers. These workers take small quantities at a time and roll them in the palms of their hands in one direction, while others fan them so that

This process is repeated two, three, or more times before the tea is placed into storage, in order to ensure that all moisture in the leaves is thoroughly evaporated <note>original: "dissipated"</note> and their curl is more completely preserved. With every repetition, the pan is heated less, and the operation is performed more slowly and cautiously. The tea is then separated into different grades and deposited in storage for domestic use or export.

The Chinese are unfamiliar with names like "imperial tea," "flower of tea," and many other titles which in Europe serve to distinguish the quality and price of this fashionable product <note>original: "commodity"</note>. However, besides common tea, they distinguish two other kinds: namely, *voui* <note>likely Wuyi tea</note> and *soumlo* <note>likely Songlo tea</note>, which are reserved for people of high status and those who are sick. We have two principal kinds of tea in Europe: namely,

**Green tea**, which is the common tea of the Chinese, etc. Father Le Comte <note>original: "F. le Compte"; referring to Louis Le Comte, a French Jesuit missionary who wrote about China in 1696</note> calls it *bing-tea* and says it is gathered from the plant in April. It is considered very good for digestion and slightly astringent; it gives a pale green color <note>original: "tincture"</note> to water, and its leaves are tightly twisted. The second is,

**Bohea tea**, which is the *voui* tea, or *bou-tcha*, of the Chinese. Father Le Comte claims this only differs from green tea because it is gathered a month earlier—in March, while still in the bud. This explains the smallness of the leaves as well as the deep color of the infusion it gives to water. Others consider it to be tea from a specific province, as the soil is found to alter the properties of the tea as much as the season of gathering. It is all purchased at Nanjing <note>original: "Nankin"</note> and then brought to Europe, where it is now very popular.

Regarding the differences in color and flavor peculiar to these two kinds and their varieties, Dr. Lettsom <note>John Coakley Lettsom (1744–1815), an English physician and botanist who wrote a famous treatise on tea</note> believes there is reason to suspect that these qualities are, to some extent, artificial <note>original: "adventitious"</note> or produced by craft. He has been informed by intelligent people who resided for some time at Canton <note>modern Guangzhou</note> that the tea around that city has very little smell while growing. The same is observed of the tea plants now in England, as well as the dried specimens from China. However, as he observes, we should not conclude from this that art alone gives cured teas the smell unique to each kind; for our own grasses, for instance, have little to no smell until they are dried and made into hay.

As for the opinion that green tea owes its vibrant color to a chemical coating <note>original: "efflorescence"</note> acquired from the copper plates on which it is supposed to be cured or dried, he shows that there is no foundation for this suspicion. Infusions of the finest "imperial" and "bloom" teas undergo no change when a volatile alkali <note>such as ammonia</note> is added to them. This test would detect even the smallest amount of copper by turning the liquid blue. With just as little evidence, the fine green color of these teas has been attributed to green copperas <term>an old name for ferrous sulfate (iron sulfate), often used in dyes and inks</term>; if this metallic salt were dissolved in water, it would immedi-

On the whole, Dr. Lettsom <note>John Coakley Lettsom (1744–1815), a prominent physician and author of *The Natural History of the Tea-Tree* (1772)</note> thinks it not improbable that some green dye, prepared from vegetable substances, is employed in the coloring of the leaves of green teas. Additionally, Neumann <note>Caspar Neumann (1683–1737), a German chemist known for his pharmaceutical research</note> suspects that the brown color and the flavor of the Bohea varieties are introduced by art. Both green and Bohea teas have an agreeable smell and a lightly bitter, slightly astringent taste; when mixed with a solution of iron vitriol <note>original: "chalybeate vitriol"; iron sulfate, used here as a chemical reagent</note>, they produce an inky blackness. They release their smell and taste to both watery and alcohol-based solvents <note>original: "spirituous menstrua"</note>; the green varieties give water their own green tint, while the Bohea gives it a brown tint. However, when using pure alcohol <note>original: "rectified spirit"</note>, both impart a fine deep green. The extracts obtained by gently evaporating the solvents from the filtered liquids are considerably astringent and quite unpleasant <note>original: "ungrateful"</note> to the taste, though the alcohol-based extract is the most so.

Savary <note>likely Jacques Savary des Brûlons, author of a famous 18th-century dictionary of commerce</note> also speaks of a sort of red tea, or Tartar tea, called *honan tcha*, which tints the water a pale red and is said to be extremely helpful for digestion. It is said that because of this tea, the Tartars are able to eat raw flesh. Its taste is earthy and by far the least agreeable of them all; however, this variety is scarcely known in England.

Tea should be chosen for having the freshest <note>original: "briskest"</note> smell and for being as whole as possible. The greatest care must be taken to ensure it has not been exposed to the air, which causes it to become stale <note>original: "pall"</note> and lose its flavor through evaporation.

The drink, tea, is made in China and throughout most of the East in the same way as in Europe: by infusing the leaves in boiling water and drinking the liquid hot. Indeed, among us, it is common to temper its bitterness with sugar, but the Orientals use it without the addition of sugar or milk. However, the Japanese are said to prepare their liquor in a somewhat different way: by grinding the leaves into a powder, stirring the powder into hot water, and drinking it as we do coffee. According to the account given by Du Halde <note>Jean-Baptiste Du Halde (1674–1743), a Jesuit historian who wrote extensively about China</note>, this method is not unique to the Japanese but is also used in some provinces of China.

The common people, who have a lower quality <note>original: "coarser"</note> tea, boil it for some time in water and use the liquid as their regular drink. Early in the morning, the kettle is filled with water and regularly hung over the fire for this purpose. The tea is either put into the kettle inside a bag or pressed to the bottom of the vessel using a basket of a suitable size, so that there is no difficulty in pouring off the water. Only *Bantsjaa* tea <note>likely Bancha, a common Japanese green tea</note> is used in this manner, as its medicinal properties <note>original: "virtues"</note> are more firmly set and would not be fully extracted by simple infusion.

The Chinese are always drinking tea, especially at meals; it is the primary treat with which they welcome their friends. The most moderate people drink it at least three times a day;

# APPENDIX TO

With regard to the commercial history of tea, we may observe that it was first introduced into Europe by the *Dutch East-India Company* very early in the last century. A quantity of it was brought over from Holland by *Lord Arlington* and *Lord Ossory* around the year 1666, at which time it was sold for sixty shillings a pound. However, it appears that even before this time, drinking tea was not uncommon, even in public coffee houses in this country; for in 1660, a tax of eight pence per gallon was placed on the liquor made and sold in all coffee houses.

The current consumption of tea is immense. *Dr. Lettsom* <note>John Coakley Lettsom (1744–1815), a physician and botanist</note> tells us that he has been informed that at least three million pounds are allowed for annual home consumption, not including the incredible quantity smuggled into the kingdom. He also notes that the *East-India Company* generally has a three-year supply in their warehouses. By the act of **13 George III, chapter 44** <note>The Tea Act of 1773</note>, no license shall be granted to the *East-India Company* to export tea unless there remains in their warehouses a quantity of no less than ten million pounds in weight.

As to the properties of tea, they are strangely debated. The Eastern nations are at least as convinced of its extraordinary virtues as the Europeans; but this is, perhaps, because imagination has as much influence there as it does here. The reason why gout and **kidney stones** <note>original: "the stone"</note> are unknown in China is credited to the use of this plant.

Tea is praised as the greatest of all medicines. When taken moderately and properly, it acts as a gentle astringent and <term>corroborative</term> (a strengthening tonic). It strengthens the stomach and bowels and is good against nausea, indigestion, and diarrhea. It also acts as a diuretic <note>promotes urination</note> and a diaphoretic <note>promotes sweating</note>. However, the immoderate use of it has been very harmful to many, who have consequently been driven into diabetes. 

In Europe, infusions of tea leaves have been excessively condemned by some and praised by others. From the contradictory opinions of even medical writers on this subject, the natural conclusion seems to be that tea possesses neither harmful nor beneficial powers to any significant degree. When used moderately, it seems for the most part to be harmless; in some cases, it appears to be healthy, and in others, it is clearly harmful. It thins "thick juices" <note>referring to bodily fluids or humors</note> and quenches thirst more effectively than more watery fluids, passing through the natural <term>emunctories</term> (organs of waste elimination) more freely. It refreshes the spirits during times of heaviness and sleepiness and seems to counteract the effects of intoxicating liquors.

Because of its obvious astringency, tea has been supposed to strengthen and brace up the <term>solids</term> (the firm tissues and fibers of the body); but experience does not support this effect, as it is found in disorders...

# CULPEPER’S BRITISH HERBAL.

In constitutions where strengthening medicines <note>original: "corroborants"</note> are more useful, the excessive use of tea is particularly harmful. This applies to people with sluggish temperaments <note>original: "cold indolent habits"</note>, wasting diseases <note>original: "cachexies"</note>, anemia <note>original: "chlorosis," often called "green sickness" in this period</note>, fluid retention <note>original: "dropsies"</note>, and weaknesses of the nervous system.

Dr. Lettsom has specifically investigated the medical qualities and effects of tea. Having observed that infusions of black tea <note>original: "bohea"</note> and green tea help to keep small pieces of beef fresh when soaked in them, he concludes that they have an antiseptic power when applied to dead animal tissue. Furthermore, because the tea turns a purple color when mixed with iron salts, he deduces that they possess an astringent quality <note>Astringents are substances that shrink or constrict body tissues.</note>. From other experiments, he concludes that the potency of tea mainly lies in its fragrant and volatile parts. He believes that whether the use of tea is beneficial or harmful to any particular person depends principally on this fragrant, aromatic principle. He suggests that the safest course is to use infusions of the most common types of this plant, which contain less of this aromatic principle. Alternatively, the tea may be boiled for a few minutes to evaporate this volatile part, which is blamed for causing or worsening those nervous conditions said to be produced by drinking this liquid. This boiling process also more effectively extracts the stable, bitter, and stomach-strengthening <note>original: "stomachic"</note> parts of the plant. Dr. Lettsom, who seems fully convinced of the occasionally harmful effects of this volatile principle—especially in the finer teas—recommends this method of making tea, or substituting an extract for the leaves. By doing so, the relaxing effects on the nerves that follow tea drinking in the usual way would be largely avoided. This extract has been imported here from China in the form of small cakes, each weighing no more than a quarter of an ounce; ten grains of this would be enough for one person's breakfast. However, it could easily be made here through simple boiling and evaporation by those who suffer from the harmful qualities of the plant's volatile parts.

It may further be observed that the effect of drinking large quantities of any warm, water-based <note>original: "aqueous"</note> liquid is that it quickly enters the bloodstream and passes out just as quickly through urine, perspiration, or other bodily secretions. Its effect on the solid parts of the body would be relaxing, and therefore weakening. If this warm liquid were taken in large amounts, its effects would be significant, and even greater if it were used as a substitute for actual nourishment. However, the infusion of tea has two unique traits: it possesses both a sedative quality and a significant astringency. Because of this, the relaxing power attributed to a simple water-based liquid is somewhat corrected. For this reason, it is perhaps less harmful than many other herbal infusions which—aside from a very slight aromatic flavor—have very little, if any, tissue-binding quality <note>original: "stypticity"</note> to prevent their weakening and relaxing effects.

->APPENDIX TO<-

So far, therefore, tea—if it is not too high quality <note>original: "fine"</note>, if it is not drunk too hot, and if it is not consumed in too great a quantity—is perhaps preferable to any other known plant-based infusion. And if we also consider its known stimulating <note>original: "enlivening"</note> energy, our attachment to it appears to be due to its superiority in taste and effects compared to most other plants.

Tea may be considered a very powerful aphrodisiac; accordingly, a physician of considerable eminence in his profession attributes the amazing population of China, among other causes, to its general use.

**Various Acts of Parliament on the Subject of Tea.** — No tea is allowed to be imported except from the place where it is grown, under penalty of forfeiture (Act of 11 George I, chapter 30). By the Act of 24 George III, chapter 38, called the **Commutation Act**, all the taxes <note>original: "duties"</note> on tea imported, sold, or used in this kingdom ceased on September 15, 1784. At that time, the East India Company was released from paying taxes on the tea in their warehouses. Afterward, a tax of £12 10s. per cent <note>A tax of 12.5%</note>, calculated based on the gross prices, shall be paid for all tea delivered by the Company to purchasers. This tax shall be refunded <note>original: "drawn back"</note> upon exportation to any place where such a refund is already allowed. 

The Company is required to hold four sales per year and to sell enough to supply the demand, provided an increase of one penny per pound is bid above the starting prices <note>original: "prices at which the teas shall be put up"</note>. At the first four sales after the act passed, these prices were not to exceed the following rates: 
* For **Bohea** tea: 1s. 7d. per lb. 
* For **Congo** <note>Now usually spelled Congou</note> tea: 2s. 5d. per lb. 
* For **Souchong** tea: 3s. 3d. per lb. 
* For **Singlo** tea: 3s. 3d. per lb. 
* For **Hyson** tea: 4s. 11d. per lb. 

Afterward, the starting price must not exceed the original cost <note>original: "prime cost"</note>, along with the freight and shipping charges, legal interest from the time the tea arrived in Great Britain, and the standard insurance premium. In place of the taxes on tea, this act substitutes an additional tax on windows <note>The "Window Tax" was a property tax based on the number of windows in a house, used to recover lost tea revenue while discouraging smuggling.</note>.

By this same act, the domestic taxes <note>original: "inland duties"</note> on cocoa nuts and coffee ceased on September 15, 1784, and the following additional taxes were applied: 
* For every pound of cocoa nuts produced in British America: 6d. 
* For those produced in any other place: 1s. 6d. 
* For every pound of coffee produced in British America: 6d. 
* For those produced in any other place: 2s. 6d. 

These taxes are subject to an additional tax <note>original: "impost"</note> of five percent, plus another five percent imposed by the acts of 19 George III, chapter 25, and 22 George III, chapter 66.

No tax refund <note>original: "drawback"</note> is allowed on exported tea, except when sent to Ireland, in which case the entire import tax is refunded (18 George II, chapter 26; 17 George III, chapter 27).

Any person having more than six pounds of tea in their possession is considered a dealer; anyone selling without a license (which costs 12 pence <note>One shilling</note>) shall forfeit £5 per month (11 George I, chapter 30; 15 George II, chapter 11). Every person dealing in tea, etc., must have the words “Dealer in Coffee, Tea,” painted or written over the door of his shop.

### VERVAIN (*VERBENA*).

This herb is described, with an illustration, in the *Herbal* on page 379; but, as it has lately come into great repute for curing scrofula <note>original: "scrophula"</note>, or the King’s Evil <note>Scrofula is a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck; it was historically called the "King's Evil" due to the belief that the touch of a monarch could cure it.</note>, I cannot make this appendix complete without giving some account of its use in that dreadful disorder.

Take a piece of fresh common purple vervain root, about three or four inches long, and about the thickness of the patient’s little finger for men or women. For young children and infants, it should be as large as their thumb, and in similar proportion for others, but no smaller; this is because it shrinks significantly and contains very little medicinal power <note>original: "virtue"</note> if too small. All the small root fibers are to be cut off smoothly, and as little of the outer skin <note>original: "rind"</note> as possible should be removed. It is to be worn constantly at the pit of the stomach <note>The epigastrium, the upper part of the abdomen just below the ribs.</note>, tied with a yard of white satin ribbon, half an inch wide, around the neck of men and women of average height. If the person is taller, an ell <note>A historical unit of measurement; an English ell was 45 inches.</note> of ribbon will be needed, and children should have a length in proportion. No other colored ribbon is suitable because the dye in some colors may be harmful. The root must never be wetted—not even when first gathered—but should be wiped clean with a dry cloth. It must not be sewn up or covered with anything, but must always be worn bare against the pit of the stomach. If, after wearing it, the ends of the fibers stick out and prick or hurt the stomach, they must be cut off with a sharp knife as they were at first. When it has been worn for a few days, it will shrink from the heat of the body <note>original: "stomach"</note>; at that point, the ribbon must be tied tighter. Ensure the root is not decayed or rotten, but fresh and green when first applied; it is necessary to replace it with a fresh one every spring and autumn.

The sores should be washed night and morning with a lotion composed of one-third vinegar, one-third red Port wine, and one-third distilled vervain water. If distilled vervain water cannot be easily obtained, an infusion of the leaves may be used instead; that is, boiling water poured over the herb like tea, which is then covered and allowed to cool. After washing, the sores should be dressed with an ointment made of green vervain leaves mixed with a fourth part of houseleek leaves <note>Sempervivum tectorum, a succulent plant frequently used in traditional medicine for skin conditions.</note>. These should be boiled in pork lard until the mixture reaches a good consistency and the watery part has evaporated <note>original: "wasted"</note>.

# WURZEL MANGEL, OR ROOT OF SCARCITY.
<note>original: "Wurzel Mangel." This is the Mangelwurzel or field beet. The name "Root of Scarcity" comes from a historical mistranslation of the German "Mangold Wurzel" (beet root) as "Mangel Wurzel" (scarcity root).</note>

In times of scarcity, this root provides humanity with a healthy and pleasant food; and when animal feed <note>original: "fodder"</note> is expensive, it offers—in both summer and winter—a plentiful and cheap nourishment for cattle. It yields an abundant and certain harvest in all seasons and all types of land, and its cultivation is simple, and its harvest and preservation are easy.

This root should not be classified with either turnips or carrots; and although it resembles beets in its outward appearance and seed, it is much superior to those plants in every respect and seems to be a distinct genus. Its cultivation is so easy and its advantages so numerous—supplying as it does the lack of other food—that I believe it deserves not only to be adopted everywhere, but to be preferred over all other roots used to feed cattle, even in the most plentiful years. It is planted in open and fallow ground and succeeds well in all soils, especially in moist and light lands. In stiff and clayey soil, where it cannot extend its roots <note>original: "fibres"</note> deep into the earth, it spreads horizontally and grows as large on the outside as it would have grown underground if it were not obstructed by the tightness of the soil.

This valuable root is not affected by the changing of the seasons; it has no destructive enemy; the all-spoiling <term>vine-fretter</term> <note>A term historically used for aphids or other small insects that destroy crops.</note> does not bite it; no other insect hurts it; mildew never affects it; and its growth is never hindered by the driest summer. It does not deplete the soil that nourishes it; on the contrary, it prepares the ground for receiving seeds of every other kind afterward.

In the months of March and April, once the land is well-prepared, manured, and made light, the largest and healthiest "scarcity-root" seeds must be chosen, soaked in water for twenty-four hours, and then dried a little so they may be handled.

Lay a marking line across the field as if you were to plant the roots, nineteen inches apart on each side. With your finger, make holes one inch deep, putting only one seed <note>original: "grain"</note> in each, and cover it immediately with earth. After ten or twelve days it will sprout, and every seed will have four, five, or six roots growing together. As soon as these small roots show their fourth leaf, the weakest of them must be carefully pulled out, leaving only the finest and most vigorous root. In a short time, the growth of the roots selected in this way will be astonishing; not one will fail. In this manner—which is equally simple and easy—you avoid the need to transplant the roots and obtain leaves four or five weeks sooner; the roots grow finer and larger and take root better; and in light soil, much labor is saved.

Since the roots naturally grow a little above the ground, you must take note of those that do not appear and uncover them by removing the earth from around their tops. Broadcast <note>original: "Sow... at random"</note> the rest of your seeds so that you may transplant the roots where
you

...as you please. If you choose to leave these in the same place, they must be thinned and dug around early; however, this is very troublesome, and roots planted this way never grow as large as those grown from seeds that were specifically set. Experience has proven this difference.

At the end of June or the beginning of July, when the outer leaves are about one foot long, the first gathering of them should be made by breaking them off close to the root. To do this, lean your thumb on the inside at the very bottom of the leaf. You must take care not to leave a stump and to gather only the leaves that lean toward the ground, always sparing those at the heart of the plant; they will then regrow and grow faster.

Immediately after the first gathering, the ground around the root should be dug again with a <term>mattock</term> <note>A tool similar to a pickaxe with a flat blade, used for loosening soil.</note>. During this process, the surface of the ground must be removed from the top of the roots with a wooden <term>spatula</term> <note>In this historical context, a flat-bladed wooden tool used to clear soil from the crown of the root without bruising the plant.</note> so that every root is uncovered by about two inches. The root then appears to be planted in a kind of basin nine or ten inches in diameter. A child can easily do this. In light soil, it is enough to pull the weeds and use the spatula well. After this second very important operation, there is nothing more to be done but to use the leaves as desired. From this moment, the roots begin to stretch and grow wonderfully. Be careful to destroy all large weeds that steal their nutrition, and give the plants the advantage of the open air, where they may be left to their own incredible growth.

In good soil, the leaves of these roots may be gathered every twelve or fifteen days. I have often noticed that the leaves grow to a length of nearly two and a half inches and a breadth of one and a half inches within twenty-four hours; by the second gathering, they are twenty-eight to thirty inches long and twenty to twenty-two inches wide. This account may appear exaggerated until experience proves the truth of it.

Oxen, other cattle, and sheep are fond of these leaves, which easily feed and fatten them to the greatest advantage. They eat them whole as they are brought from the field, but for poultry, the leaves must be minced and mixed with bran. They are also very good nourishment for horses during the summer; for this purpose, they only need to be minced with the kind of knife I will describe later and mixed with cut straw. Swine also eat them very heartily.

The leaves of the <term>scarcity-root</term> <note>original: "scarcity-root." A common 18th-century name for the Mangelwurzel, resulting from a mistranslation of the German name.</note> also provide a wholesome and pleasant food for humans. The stalks are eaten like those of beets but do not have the same earthy taste. They may be prepared in different ways; when cooked like <term>spinage</term> <note>original: "spinage," modern: spinach.</note>, many people prefer them to it. Because they produce a continual succession of leaves from spring until November, they are very useful to farmers and others who must feed many servants. In winter, the roots are eaten and can also be prepared in various ways. They are wholesome and have an agreeable taste, much superior to the red beet.

at least equal to the turnip. The leaves produced by the roots when preserved in a cellar during the winter are very soft and delicate.

The approach of severe frosts shows the time for harvesting the roots. This precious harvest must be carried out in fine weather, even if it is a few days sooner than otherwise necessary, as the preservation of the roots depends very much on their being housed dry. The roots must be plucked early in the morning and left exposed to the air and the sun. Children should follow the person who plucks them and cut the leaves down to the heart—an operation which may also be performed one or more days before the harvest. In the evening, the roots must be collected together and, if sufficiently dried, stored in a place well secured against severe frosts. If there is no fear of rain, those which have been plucked in the evening may be left in the field and carried home the next day. It is best to leave them exposed to the air for two or three days when the weather permits. As their skin is very thin, they must be handled gently, and great care taken not to bruise them, which would be <term>prejudicial</term> <note>original: "prejudicial"; meaning harmful or damaging to the quality of the plant.</note> to their preservation.

The harvest time is precisely when the roots intended for bearing seed should be chosen. The best roots for this purpose are those that have attained only a middle size, are smooth and even, rosy on the outside, and white or marbled white and red within; such is the description of the roots which ought to be preserved for cultivation. Those which are entirely red or entirely white are either degenerated roots or real red-beets, whose seeds were not carefully separated by the sower. It is necessary to separate and shelter from all moisture and frost the roots designed for seed.

In the beginning of April, those roots set apart for seed must be planted in the open field, three feet distant from each other. As their stems grow five or six feet high, they must be supported with props seven feet high, placed a foot and a half into the ground. Small rods should be placed between them to form a kind of trellis to which the stems are tied as they grow up, to prevent them from being broken by the wind.

The seed usually ripens toward the end of October and must be gathered immediately after the first <term>hoar-frosts</term> <note>A grayish-white frost consisting of tiny ice crystals, usually appearing on grass or leaves.</note>. The stems are then cut and placed against a wall or palisade if the weather permits; if not, they are tied in small bundles and hung up in a sheltered, airy place until they are quite dry. Finally, the seed is collected and preserved in bags, like other kitchen garden seeds.

The seeds of the <term>scarcity-roots</term> <note>original: "scarcity-roots"; referring to the Mangelwurzel (a type of beet), popularized in the 18th century as a "famine food" or "root of scarcity" because of its high yield and reliability.</note> degenerate like all others if the soil is not changed every year or every two years. Care must be taken, therefore, to sow seed grown in a light or sandy soil into a <term>stiff soil</term> <note>Heavy, dense soil, typically with a high clay content.</note>, and to sow seed grown in a strong and compact soil into light soil. ...those who own such or such lands may be of great service to one another by making annual exchanges of seeds. This seed preserves all its qualities for three or four years.

If the quantity of roots you intend to preserve is too great to be stored in the house, you should dig pits in the field—or any other place sheltered from water—a few days before they are pulled from the ground. After the inside of these pits has been left to dry for eight or ten days, the bottom and sides must be covered with a small quantity of straw. The roots should then be placed inside regularly, one by one, taking care not to bruise them and cleaning them well of any soil. Then, cover the top layer of roots with straw, which is then to be covered three feet deep with the earth dug from the pit. This earth must be packed down firmly and sloped so that rainwater may easily flow off.

The dimensions of the pits ought to be proportioned either to the rise of the ground or its slope. They may be from two to three feet deep. Their length depends on the quantity of roots to be stored, but their breadth is commonly three and a half feet.

Because these roots possess the valuable quality of being able to be preserved until the month of June without the least change, it is a good idea to create multiple pits. You might make one for each month, beginning in March, when winter provisions are ordinarily finished. The reason for this advice to use multiple pits is that if the roots—after having been deprived of air—are exposed to it again, they do not stay fresh for long. Using multiple pits will prevent this inconvenience.

Every pit absolutely requires an air-hole through which the <term>fermentation</term> <note>original: "fermentation"; here referring to the natural gases and heat released by stored organic matter which can cause rot if trapped.</note> of the roots may evaporate; without this precaution, all the roots you intend to preserve underground will rot. The air-hole must be made in the following manner: before anything is put into the pit, a pole six or seven feet long and two inches in diameter must be planted in the middle of it. Then, place the roots inside and arrange them in a sloping direction. When the pit is full and the roots are half a foot above the level of the ground in the middle, twist a rope of hay about an inch thick around the pole, taking care not to bind it too tightly. After that is done, throw on the earth and pack it down as mentioned before. When the pit is quite covered, take out the pole; the hay will remain in the hole, through which the vapors arising from the fermentation of the roots will pass. After some days, the hole must be covered with a roof tile, and as severe cold approaches, shut it completely with a flat stone.

To ensure that cattle of every kind may eat the roots, they must be cut or minced after they have been washed and cleaned. This is done with a specific kind of knife: an iron blade one foot long and two inches broad, bent like an S, to the middle of which

Since these roots possess the valuable quality of being capable of preservation until the month of June without the least spoilage <note>original: "alteration"</note>, it will be useful to multiply the number of pits and make one for each month, beginning in March, when the winter provision is ordinarily over. The reason for this advice to multiply the pits is because if the roots, after having been deprived of the action of the air, are exposed to it anew, they do not preserve their freshness for long. The multiplying of the pits will prevent this inconvenience.

Every pit absolutely requires an air-hole through which the gases from the fermentation <note>The author is referring to the natural respiration and heat produced by stored root vegetables, which can cause rot if trapped.</note> of the roots may evaporate; for without this precaution, all the roots you intend to preserve under the earth will rot. The air-hole must be made in the following manner: before anything is put into the pit, a pole six or seven feet long and two inches in diameter must be planted in the middle of it. Then place the roots inside and arrange them in a sloping direction. When the pit is full, and the roots are half a foot above the level of the ground in the middle part, twist a rope of hay about an inch thick around the pole, taking care not to bind it too tightly. After that is done, throw on the earth and arrange and pack it as mentioned before. When the pit is quite covered, take out the pole; the hay will remain in the hole, through which the vapors arising from the fermentation of the roots will pass. <page-num>70</page-num>

...is soldered a socket about six inches long. In this socket is fixed a wooden handle, about three feet six inches long. With this knife, which at first sight seems intended for printing the letter S <note>The author is describing a curved, S-shaped blade used for chopping</note>, the roots are minced as equally as they are easily. This operation is performed in a bucket or trough used for that purpose only. A single man in one hour is able to mince a quantity of roots sufficient to feed twelve oxen a whole day. Before the roots are put into the trough, they must be cut into large pieces. It will be best to mince them to the size of a walnut.

The roots, being prepared as described above, may be given to horned cattle and sheep without being mixed with any other food, especially to those which are to be fattened. However, if it is necessary to be frugal with the roots, they may be mixed with one-fourth part or more of hay and minced straw. It is even advisable to follow this method for the first three or four weeks when feeding lean cattle intended for fattening. Dry <term>trefoil</term> <note>A type of clover</note>, <term>sainfoin</term> <note>A perennial legume used as high-quality forage</note>, and similar plants are best for this use. Those who have a hay-knife for cutting dry fodder—of the same sort used in Germany with so much success and advantage—will save much time and consume less of their supplies.

Horses may be fed during the winter with the <term>scarcity-roots</term> <note>original: "mangel-wurzel"</note> by adding to them one half of hay and straw minced together, which will make them healthy, fat, and vigorous. But during seasons of hard and constant labor, a small quantity of oats must be added from time to time. This is the practice in those provinces of Germany where the <term>scarcity-roots</term> serve almost as a substitute for meadows, and where the horses are well known and highly esteemed.

Swine eat these roots very well when raw, minced, and mixed into their greasy or milky drink. They become as fat as those fed with potatoes, which require the extra step of boiling. By using this root, the expense of wood and coals, as well as the trouble of boiling, is saved.

Besides the advantages already listed, the <term>scarcity-roots</term> provide many others; in particular, they guarantee an abundant harvest regardless of bad weather or unfavorable seasons <note>original: "intemperature of the seasons"</note>.

If the cultivation of this root is adopted, it will no longer be necessary to let cattle eat the grass of natural or artificial meadows during the summer; all of that grass can instead be converted into hay. Consider how much hay could then be sold, since more than two-thirds of it will be saved during the winter! And, as the roots make it easier to feed cattle in stables year-round, the quantity of dung <note>manure</note>—so necessary to agriculture—will be increased. When this root becomes well known to farmers, there is no doubt they will prefer it to all other fodder of a similar kind.
